entry.title: Venice Closes in Minor Keys, Abu Dhabi Opens Under Frieze, and Ayutthaya Lights Its First Krathongs
entry.summary: The culture week of November 21, 2026: Venice and Tallinn close on Sunday, the first Frieze Abu Dhabi closes with them, Tokyo opens a museum of sound, and Thailand floats its first krathongs at Ayutthaya.
entry.content:
Weekend Features — Saturday Culture

Objective

Venice Closes in Minor Keys, Abu Dhabi Opens Under Frieze, and Ayutthaya Lights Its First Krathongs

Three closings stand on one Sunday and four openings stand within four days of them: Venice ends six months in minor keys, Abu Dhabi ends its first four days under a new name, and Tallinn ends its thirtieth festival, while Tokyo opens a museum by sound, Dublin opens a sea borrowed from Sharjah, Sharjah opens an architecture triennial and closes a calligraphy biennial down to its smallest dot, and Thailand floats the first krathongs of its full-moon week at Ayutthaya. The desk files the week in that order.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0410 ET, Saturday, November 21, 2026. The third Saturday Culture Feature of this paper, filed ahead of the day's watches under the Weekend Features ruling of November 4, 2026. International by house rule: no country's framework is applied to another country's culture. The clippings the report was drawn from are filed beneath it, each stamped subjective.

The Week in Brief

Three of the year’s longest cultural runs end on the same Sunday, and the week’s openings are dated to the day on either side of them: the 61st Venice Biennale, open since May 9, closes on November 22; the first Frieze Abu Dhabi, open since November 19, closes on November 22; and Tallinn’s 30th Black Nights festival, open since November 6, closes on November 22. Against those three endings the file carries four beginnings inside four days: Tokyo’s Museum of Narratives opened its first exhibition, Feel the Sound, on Friday, November 20; Dublin’s Irish Museum of Modern Art opened A Sea for Borrowed Time, drawn from the Sharjah Art Foundation collection, on Thursday, November 19; Sharjah’s third Architecture Triennial, open since November 14, closed its six-day opening programme on November 19 and runs to April 14, 2027; and in Thailand three Loi Krathong festivals open today, November 21, at Ayutthaya, Tak and Samut Songkhram, inside a national calendar that ends at the full moon on November 24.

Venice: Six Months End on Sunday, at Five Euros

The 61st International Art Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia, titled In Minor Keys by Koyo Kouoh, runs from May 9 to Sunday, November 22, at the Giardini and the Arsenale, in locations across Venice and at Forte Marghera, and this Saturday stands in its final weekend. The Biennale’s own page, filed below, counts 110 invited participants and 100 National Participations, 29 in the historic Pavilions at the Giardini, 25 at the Arsenale and 46 in the city centre, with seven countries participating for the first time and El Salvador participating for the first time with its own pavilion; 31 Collateral Events stand across the city. The exhibition is the one Koyo Kouoh conceived: the Biennale records that, with the full support of her family, it carried out her exhibition following the project just as she conceived and defined it. The final ten days, from November 13 to November 22, carry a public programme of performances, lectures, discussions and roundtables at the Arsenale, with an Assembly of ten artist-led organisations and collectives. The closing is priced for the city that hosts it: admission today is €5 for residents of the Comune di Venezia, the metropolitan area and the Veneto region, and on Sunday it is €5 for all visitors, in the Biennale’s own listing filed below. Two Visitors’ Lions stand established for this edition in the same listing; the desk files the establishment and does not file a result, because none stands in the record at the stamp.

Inside the Giardini, one installation states the edition’s method in built form. Chimera brings together contributions from approximately 150 artists associated with Denniston Hill, the artist-founded cultural laboratory founded in 2004, presented as part of In Minor Keys, in the university account filed below. Its structure is the Exquisite Corpse: alumni artists made works for parts of a collective body, the head for dreams and invention, the torso for voice and transformation, the legs for movement, migration and journeys into the future, without seeing the whole. The setting, designed by Koray Duman, centres on an arena-like gathering space with the works on totem-like armatures, in a passage between the bookstore and the restrooms that the account’s subjects describe as a social condenser. The team also ran an indigo-dye workshop with artists who work with dyers in rural northeast Thailand, and the account records that the magazine frieze named the contribution among the exhibition’s most compelling realisations of Kouoh’s vision. A six-month exhibition ends, in this corner of it, as a body assembled by 150 people who never saw it whole.

Abu Dhabi: A First Frieze, Sold by the Hour

The inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi runs at Manarat Al Saadiyat from November 19 to Sunday, November 22, and its first public days have produced a record of sales made inside hours. The fair is organised by the Department of Culture and Tourism, Abu Dhabi, in partnership with Frieze, and it replaces Abu Dhabi Art, founded in 2009; it was opened by Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, in the Media Office account filed below, which presents the edition as building on Abu Dhabi Art’s 17 years and as the emirate’s entry into Frieze’s network of fairs in London, New York, Los Angeles, Chicago and Seoul. The ground reports count 89 exhibitors against 142 at Abu Dhabi Art last year, in the Artnet report and in the Ocula report, both filed below; the disagreement in the fair’s counts is filed whole in the Cocked Hat. Around 40 percent of exhibitors are from West Asia, North Africa and South Asia, and the fair’s director, Dyala Nusseibeh, who previously directed Abu Dhabi Art, calls the partnership a step change in how art from the region is understood, in the Artnet account.

The Masters section sold the fair’s oldest objects first. David Aaron, one of nine Masters galleries showing under the theme of the Indian Ocean as a historic avenue for trade, sold a 2,000-year-old funerary stele naming a woman from Qataban, in modern-day Yemen, for seven figures within the first few hours, the work’s first return to the Arabian Peninsula in 70 years, in the Artnet account; the Ocula account describes the same object as a yellow-calcite alabaster stele from ancient Yemen, its sale pre-agreed, and adds a second seven-figure-class sale, Daniel Crouch Rare Books’ first map to name Abu Dhabi, dated 1832, at an asking price understood to exceed $1 million. Around those sales the reports price the contemporary floor: Timothy Taylor sold out its presentation of Hilary Pecis at $65,000 to $205,000; a Sheila Hicks textile went at $350,000; Pace prices Emily Kam Kngwarray up to $750,000; and Efie Gallery anchors its booth with El Anatsui hangings at $525,000 to $1.8 million. The fair’s own commission stands outside the booths: Dala Nasser’s Qubbat Duris, the Artist Award work, encases a recreation of an architectural ruin in southern Lebanon in earthen-hued textile paintings. Both ground reports also file the conditions: flight paths disrupted and some plans cancelled in the Ocula account, attendance better than expected in the same account, and the fair’s chief executive on the record in the Artnet account that the fair is in it for the long haul. The edition closes on Sunday, two days shorter than its predecessor ran.

Tallinn: 489 Titles End on Sunday

The 30th Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival, POFF, runs in Tallinn and Tartu from November 6 to Sunday, November 22, and its arithmetic is exact: 230 feature films and 259 shorts sum to the 489 titles its programme release announces, from 87 countries, with 107 world premieres and 47 international premieres across the festival and its Just Film and POFF Shorts strands, in the programme release filed below. The anniversary edition places the region at its centre: Focus: Baltics brings Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania into sharper view, presenting recent Baltic films and the teams behind them, in the Baltic Review account filed below. The festival began in 1997 and has held the International Federation of Film Producers Associations’ accreditation since 2014, in the same account, which records its standing as one of Northern Europe’s largest festivals and the region’s only accredited competitive feature festival. Its industry arm has already closed: Industry@Tallinn and Baltic Event, in its 25th edition, ran from November 9 to 20 and expected nearly 2,000 guests from more than 50 countries, in the programme release. The anniversary stands in the city as well as in the cinemas: the Estonian animator Priit Pärn made its design, and a commemorative stamp and a tram carrying the festival’s artwork mark the year, in the Baltic Review account. What remains at the stamp is two days of screenings in two cities, and then the festival’s thirtieth year is a record.

Tokyo: A Museum Opens by Sound

MoN Takanawa, the Museum of Narratives in Minato, Tokyo, opened Feel the Sound on Friday, November 20, as its opening commemorative programme, and the exhibition runs to March 22, 2027. The museum stands inside Takanawa Gateway City at 3-16-1 Mita and is operated by the East Japan Railway Foundation for Cultural Innovations, in the MANA account filed below. The exhibition is co-produced with the Barbican Centre in London, where it ran from May 22 to August 31, 2025; this presentation is its first in Japan, and the Tokyo edition carries new adaptations of existing works and three new works made for the occasion, in the MANA account and in the NiEW account filed below. Its premise is stated in its poster’s tagline, rendered in the MANA account as: that sound reaches the body before the ear. The installations combine sound, vibration and light, and the featured list opens with Sensing Streams, invisible, inaudible: focused edition, 2025, by Ryuichi Sakamoto and Daito Manabe, which turns electromagnetic waves beyond human perception into sound and light; Max Cooper, Miyu Hosoi, Ei Wada and Yuri Suzuki stand among the featured artists. The museum keeps late hours for the opening weekend’s second day: 10:00 to 19:00 ordinarily, and until 21:00 on Fridays and Saturdays, with regular tickets at 2,500 yen, 1,100 yen for visitors aged 25 and under, and 550 yen for elementary to high-school students, in the MANA account. Where Venice closes a six-month exhibition this weekend, Tokyo opens a four-month one, on the same Saturday, at the opposite end of the same trade in attention.

Sharjah: A Triennial in Its First Week, a Biennial in Its Last Room

Sharjah holds two positions in the week at once: a beginning and an ending, in two different art forms. The third Sharjah Architecture Triennial, Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures, curated by Vyjayanthi Rao with associate curator Tau Tavengwa, opened on November 14 and runs to April 14, 2027, across the Emirate; its opening programme ran from November 14 to 19, bringing 35 international participants together in installations, participatory projects, performances, film screenings, lectures and panel discussions, and closed with a two-day international conference on November 18 and 19, in the ArchDaily listing filed below. The Triennial’s proposition, as the listing states it, is that architecture fosters collective life through social relationships, shared knowledge and civic engagement, and the exhibition now stands open for five months on that proposition. The ending is calligraphic. The 12th Sharjah Calligraphy Biennial, organised under the theme Balance, closed its main run on November 15; its final stop, the exhibition In Due Measure: From Dot to Meaning at the House of Wisdom, opened on November 11 and runs to January 24, 2027, in the UAE News account filed below. The exhibition builds its subject from its smallest unit: five sections carry the visitor from the dot that measures every letter, through the letter, the word and the sentence, to contemporary practices beyond measure, with the pioneers of the proportional system, Ibn Muqla, Ibn al-Bawwab and Yaqut al-Musta’simi, introduced beside the contemporary hands, and tables where visitors draw the dots and practise the letters themselves. One emirate therefore files both ends of the season in the same week: an architecture exhibition with five months to run, and a calligraphy exhibition reduced, deliberately, to the dot it began from.

Dublin: A Sea Borrowed From Sharjah

The Irish Museum of Modern Art opened A Sea for Borrowed Time in its House Galleries on Thursday, November 19, and the exhibition runs to July 4, 2027, with free admission. It is a major exhibition of contemporary Palestinian art made in partnership with Sharjah Art Foundation and drawn from that foundation’s collection, curated by Hoor Al Qasimi, in the museum’s announcement filed below. Eight artists stand in the show, Tarek Al-Ghoussein, Basma Al Sharif, Simone Fattal, Shadi Habib Allah, Rula Halawani, Hazem Harb, Khalil Rabah and Abdul Hay Mosallam Zarara, spanning three generations and working in photography, sculpture, installation, film and painting; the exhibition moves between testimony, memory, lived experience and imagination rather than following a chronology. Its objects carry their histories in plain terms in the announcement: Fattal’s lava stone inscribed with locations in Palestine and Lebanon associated with massacres; Harb’s work centred on the suitcase he carried when he left Gaza in 2006; Halawani’s photographs of everyday movement through military checkpoints, commissioned by the Sharjah Art Foundation in 2017. At the centre of the Zarara focus stands a relief connected to Ireland, discovered in the artist’s studio shortly before his death in 2020 and shown publicly for the first time in this exhibition. A collection assembled in Sharjah thus opens in Dublin in the same week Sharjah itself opens an architecture triennial and closes a calligraphy biennial: the week’s map has Sharjah at three of its points.

Thailand: Three Festivals Open Today

Thailand’s Loi Krathong calendar reaches its full moon on Tuesday, November 24, and three of its festivals open today, Saturday, November 21. The festival centres on floating decorated krathongs as an expression of gratitude and respect for water, observed on the full moon of the twelfth Thai lunar month, in the nationwide calendar filed below. The principal venue this year is Ayutthaya, the former royal capital and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, where the festival runs from November 21 to 24 at the Ancient Palace grounds near Wat Phra Si Sanphet, in the Tourism Authority’s announcement filed below. Ayutthaya revives Chong Priang, an ancient royal tradition of ceremonial lantern-lighting, and centres its nights on Saeng Nathi Si Sanphet, a 45-minute production of light, sound and theatre animating 417 years of the city’s history, performed nightly at 7:30 p.m. before 1,000 complimentary seats; admission is free from 4:30 to 10:00 p.m., a period-style market carries more than 70 local vendors, and today’s opening ceremony recreates an Ayutthaya-era lantern procession. At Tak, the Loi Krathong Sai festival opens today on the Ping River and runs to November 24, its signature a competition of 1,000 illuminated krathongs floating in continuous streams. At Samut Songkhram, the Mae Klong festival opens today on the Tourism Authority’s dates and will float more than 100,000 krathongs made from banana stalks on the Mae Klong River; the nationwide calendar’s dating of the same festival is filed in the Cocked Hat. Around the three openings the calendar is already running: Sukhothai’s candlelight festival has run at the Historical Park since November 15 and ends on the full-moon night; Bangkok’s Rattanakosin Waterways programme runs from November 17 to 29; Chiang Mai’s Yi Peng follows from November 23 to 25, with authorised sky lantern releases on November 24 and 25; and the Authority states its expectation for the period at approximately 6 billion baht of domestic tourism revenue, up 8 percent, on an estimated 1.83 million domestic trips, up 6 percent, in the announcement. The expectation is the Authority’s; the openings are today’s.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, the size of the first Frieze Abu Dhabi: 84 galleries from 64 cities across 37 countries in the Experience Abu Dhabi listing; more than 85 galleries from 67 cities and more than 35 countries and regions in the fair’s own line-up release of October 22; and 89 exhibitors counted in each of the two opening reports from the ground, Artnet and Ocula. The desk prints each count as its source’s and merges none of them; the comparison both ground reports agree on, 142 galleries at Abu Dhabi Art last year, stands uncontradicted. Second, the fair’s opening day: the fair is dated November 19 to 22 in every source, the Media Office records the Crown Prince opening the fair, and the Artnet report records the fair as opened to the public at the stamp of its filing; the dated run and the public admission are both in the file, and the desk does not collapse them into one day. Third, Venice’s counts: 110 invited participants and 100 National Participations stand on the Biennale’s own page, and those are the figures the desk prints; a foundation release in the week’s wider coverage counts 111 invited participants, and the difference of one stands unresolved in the file. Fourth, Samut Songkhram: the Tourism Authority’s announcement of November 18 dates the Mae Klong festival from November 21 to 24, and the Authority’s nationwide calendar lists its banana-stem festival on November 24; the desk prints the announcement’s run for the festival’s opening today and the calendar’s date beside it, unreconciled. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts are single-valued: the Venice Biennale runs May 9 to November 22 in its 61st edition under the title In Minor Keys; Frieze Abu Dhabi runs November 19 to 22 at Manarat Al Saadiyat in its inaugural edition; Tallinn’s 30th festival runs November 6 to 22 with 230 features and 259 shorts; Feel the Sound opened in Tokyo on November 20 and runs to March 22, 2027; the Sharjah Architecture Triennial runs November 14, 2026, to April 14, 2027, and In Due Measure runs at the House of Wisdom to January 24, 2027; A Sea for Borrowed Time opened in Dublin on November 19 and runs to July 4, 2027; and Loi Krathong’s full moon is November 24, with its Ayutthaya, Tak and Samut Songkhram festivals opening on November 21. The log proceeds to Saturday’s watches.

The Clippings Filed With This Feature

Everything the desk read for the feature above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective — a source with a position, printed because it is useful — and described by what it says. The desk's feature is the only item in this file stamped objective. Sixteen items.

Subjective
La Biennale di Venezia — Biennale Arte 2026, In Minor Keys, May 9 to November 22

Venice: the 61st International Art Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia, titled In Minor Keys by Koyo Kouoh, runs from Saturday, May 9, to Sunday, November 22, 2026, at the Giardini and Arsenale venues, in various locations across Venice and at Forte Marghera; La Biennale records that, with the full support of Koyo Kouoh's family, it decided to carry out her exhibition following the project just as she conceived and defined it; the invited participants number 110, among them individual artists, collaborative duos, collectives and artist-led organisations; the exhibition also includes 100 National Participations, 29 in the historic Pavilions at the Giardini, 25 at the Arsenale and 46 in the city centre of Venice, with seven countries participating for the first time, the Republic of Guinea, the Republic of Equatorial Guinea, the Republic of Nauru, Qatar, the Republic of Sierra Leone, the Federal Republic of Somalia and the Socialist Republic of Viet Nam, and El Salvador participating for the first time with its own pavilion; 31 Collateral Events take place across the city; a public programme of performances, lectures, discussions and roundtables runs at the Arsenale from Friday, November 13, to Sunday, November 22, the final ten days of the exhibition, with an Assembly bringing together ten artist-led organisations and collectives; on Saturday, November 21, admission is 5 euros for residents of the Comune di Venezia, the Venice metropolitan area and the Veneto region, and on Sunday, November 22, admission is 5 euros for all visitors; and the Biennale's news list records that two Visitors' Lions have been established for the Biennale Arte 2026.

Subjective
Syracuse University Today — Chimera, a collective body of 150 artists, in the Giardini

Venice, November 16: as the 61st International Art Exhibition approaches its November 22 conclusion, the collaborative installation Chimera, by Lawrence Chua, associate professor in the School of Architecture, and his colleagues, is drawing international attention; the installation brings together contributions from approximately 150 artists associated with Denniston Hill, the artist-founded cultural laboratory Chua co-founded in 2004 with artists Julie Mehretu and Paul Pfeiffer, and is presented as part of this year's exhibition, In Minor Keys, in Venice's historic Giardini; it is inspired by the Surrealist parlour game the Exquisite Corpse, in which participants contribute fragments to a collective composition without seeing the whole, with the head representing dreams and invention, the torso voice and transformation, and the legs movement, migration and journeys into the future; the physical setting, designed by architect Koray Duman, founder of B-KD, centres on an arena-like gathering space, with individual artworks displayed on totem-like armatures; the Biennale assigned Denniston Hill an interstitial space between the bookstore and restrooms in the Giardini pavilion, along the passage connecting the national pavilions and cafe; the team also organised an indigo-dye workshop with artists Philip Huang and Chomwan Weeraworawit, who work with local dyers in rural northeast Thailand; and the account records that the magazine frieze, in its review of In Minor Keys, highlighted Denniston Hill's contribution as one of the exhibition's most compelling realisations of the vision of the late artistic director Koyo Kouoh.

Subjective
Artnet News — Frieze Abu Dhabi opens with fewer booths and a seven-figure sale

Abu Dhabi, November 19: the first edition of Frieze Abu Dhabi has opened to the public at Manarat Al Saadiyat; Frieze teamed up with Abu Dhabi's Department of Culture and Tourism to replace Abu Dhabi Art, the event founded in 2009; there are fewer galleries, 89 against 142 at Abu Dhabi Art last year; around 40 percent of exhibitors are from West Asia, North Africa and South Asia, in the account's abbreviation WANASA, and most are platforming regional artists, in the words of the fair's director, Dyala Nusseibeh, who called the partnership a really important step change in how art from the region is understood; Gagosian, which last participated in Abu Dhabi Art in 2014, has returned with a booth dedicated to Roy Lichtenstein, with editioned works from $20,000 to $300,000; Pace presents paintings and batiks by Emily Kam Kngwarray priced up to $750,000; at David Aaron, one of nine galleries in the Masters section, whose theme is the Indian Ocean as a historic avenue for trade, a rare 2,000-year-old funerary stele naming a woman from Qataban, in modern-day Yemen, sold for seven figures within the first few hours of the fair, the first time the work has returned to the Arabian Peninsula in 70 years; Efie Gallery anchors its booth with wall hangings by El Anatsui priced from $525,000 to $1.8 million; Frieze chief executive Simon Fox said the geopolitics have been difficult and that the fair is in it for the long haul; and the fair runs through Sunday, November 22, at Manarat Al Saadiyat.

Subjective
Ocula — Frieze Abu Dhabi opens with optimism

Abu Dhabi, November 20: Frieze made its Middle Eastern debut yesterday at Manarat Al Saadiyat, running through Sunday, amid a busy month for culture in the United Arab Emirates that also carries the art and design showcase NOMAD and the ongoing Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial; the account records that the war in Iran has escalated military tensions across the Gulf and disrupted some regional flight paths, that some plans were cancelled, and that first-day attendance was better than expected regionally and internationally; director Dyala Nusseibeh, who previously directed Abu Dhabi Art, now overseen by Frieze in partnership with the Department of Culture and Tourism, said it is very much business as usual and that Abu Dhabi is a very safe and secure place; in Frieze Masters, David Aaron announced the pre-agreed, seven-figure sale of a yellow-calcite alabaster stele from ancient Yemen, and Daniel Crouch Rare Books sold the first map to name Abu Dhabi, dated to 1832, for an undisclosed asking price understood to be in excess of $1 million; Timothy Taylor sold out its solo presentation of Hilary Pecis, priced between $65,000 and $205,000; the Paris-based galerie frank elbaz sold a $350,000 textile work by Sheila Hicks to a private collection in the region; Thaddaeus Ropac placed three sculptures by Imran Qureshi, priced at $60,000 each, with collections in the Emirates; the fair's Artist Award commission, Dala Nasser's Qubbat Duris, 2026, encases a recreation of an architectural ruin in southern Lebanon in earthen-hued textile paintings; the account counts 89 exhibitors, records that the fair runs two days shorter than its predecessor, Abu Dhabi Art, and reports Sotheby's figure of a 70 percent increase in bidding from the Middle East over the past five years, Christie's first fine art auction in Abu Dhabi earlier this month at $8.9 million, and Sotheby's own Abu Dhabi auction to follow next month.

Subjective
Abu Dhabi Media Office — the Crown Prince opens the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi

Abu Dhabi, November 19: Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council, has opened the inaugural edition of Frieze Abu Dhabi, organised by the Department of Culture and Tourism, Abu Dhabi, in partnership with Frieze, taking place at Manarat Al Saadiyat until November 22; during a tour of the fair, he viewed a selection of artworks and projects presented by participating galleries, featuring artists and cultural organisations from the Emirates and around the world, with a particular focus on artistic practices from West Asia, North Africa and South Asia; bringing Frieze to Abu Dhabi for the first time builds on the achievements of Abu Dhabi Art over the past 17 years in supporting artists and galleries and advancing the local and regional art scene; the inaugural edition marks the emirate's entry into Frieze's international network of art fairs in London, New York, Los Angeles, Chicago and Seoul; and the opening is presented as advancing the Abu Dhabi Cultural and Creative Industries Strategy, to build a sustainable cultural and creative sector and increase its contribution to economic diversification.

Subjective
Frieze Abu Dhabi — the inaugural edition's global line-up, November 19 to 22

Abu Dhabi, October 22: the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi will take place from November 19 to 22, 2026, at Manarat Al Saadiyat, in the Saadiyat Cultural District; it features more than 85 galleries from 67 cities and more than 35 countries and regions, presenting works from antiquity through the 20th century to the present day, and it joins Frieze's network of fairs in London, Los Angeles, New York, Chicago and Seoul; the fair is established in partnership with the Department of Culture and Tourism, Abu Dhabi, builds on Abu Dhabi Art's seventeen years in the region, and is led by Director Dyala Nusseibeh; its main Galleries section brings together more than 60 galleries from 56 cities and 32 countries; its curated sections are Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi, selected by Marika Sardar around the theme of the Indian Ocean, and Global Futures, selected by Tarini Malik; and its regional line-up is anchored by galleries from the United Arab Emirates, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Tehran and Istanbul, with 20 European galleries taking part.

Subjective
Experience Abu Dhabi — Frieze Abu Dhabi, 84 galleries, November 19 to 22

Abu Dhabi: for its inaugural edition, Frieze heads to Abu Dhabi bringing 84 galleries from 64 cities across 37 countries; Frieze Abu Dhabi runs from 19 to 22 November 2026 at Manarat Al Saadiyat in the Saadiyat Cultural District, marking the first Frieze fair in the region, in proximity to Louvre Abu Dhabi and the wider cultural district; the schedule is 19 to 22 November, 2:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m.; general admission tickets are 36.75 dirhams and multi-day passes are priced at 173.25 dirhams, available through abudhabiculture.ae; and the inaugural edition combines leading international galleries with artists and institutions from the Emirates and the wider WANASA region.

Subjective
POFF programme release — the full 30th edition, 489 titles from 87 countries

Tallinn, October 30: the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival, POFF, has announced the full programme for its 30th edition, featuring 230 feature films and 259 shorts from 87 countries, taking place in Tallinn and Tartu from November 6 to 22, 2026; POFF and its youth and children's film festival Just Film and POFF Shorts, dedicated to short films, together present 107 world premieres and 47 international premieres; the Doc@POFF International and Baltic competitions ran from November 7 to 13, followed by the Official Selection, First Feature, Rebels with a Cause, Critics' Picks and Baltic Film competitions from November 13 to 19; Industry@Tallinn and Baltic Event, in its 25th edition, runs from November 9 to 20 and expects to welcome nearly 2,000 guests from more than 50 countries; and the release records the festival's standing as one of Northern Europe's largest film festivals and the region's only FIAPF-accredited competitive feature film festival.

Subjective
Baltic Review — POFF30 puts Baltic cinema at the centre of Estonia's film season

Tallinn, November 17: the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival, known by its Estonian acronym POFF, is giving Baltic cinema a particularly prominent place in Estonia's cultural calendar this November, running from November 6 to 22, 2026, in Tallinn and Tartu; this year's central regional initiative is Focus: Baltics, bringing Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania into sharper view and presenting recent Baltic films, intended not only to showcase finished films but also to support the region's next generation of filmmakers; POFF began in 1997 and has grown into one of Northern Europe's largest film festivals, holding accreditation from the International Federation of Film Producers Associations since 2014; its industry event, Industry@Tallinn and Baltic Event, is holding its 25th edition during the same period; alongside the main competition the festival includes Just Film, its youth and children's programme, and POFF Shorts, dedicated to short and animated films; the festival has connected its visual identity with Estonian animation by inviting filmmaker and artist Priit Parn to create the anniversary design, and the organisers have highlighted the festival's history through a commemorative stamp and a Tallinn tram carrying POFF-related artwork; and the anniversary programme continues through November 22, with screenings in Tallinn and a parallel programme in Tartu.

Subjective
NiEW — Feel the Sound opens at MoN Takanawa, Tokyo, November 20

Tokyo: Feel the Sound, an immersive exhibition exploring the experience of sound beyond hearing, opens at MoN Takanawa, the Museum of Narratives in Tokyo, on November 20, 2026, and runs through March 22, 2027; co-produced with London's Barbican Centre, the exhibition comes to Japan for the first time following its London debut in 2025, and, combining sound, vibration and light, its installations offer visitors new ways to experience sound through their entire bodies; the Tokyo edition brings together works from the original Barbican exhibition, reimagined versions of existing installations and three new works created for the occasion; featured artists include Ryuichi Sakamoto, Daito Manabe, Max Cooper, Miyu Hosoi, Ei Wada and Yuri Suzuki; one highlight is Sensing Streams, invisible, inaudible: focused edition, 2025, a collaboration between Sakamoto and Manabe that turns electromagnetic waves beyond human perception into sound and light; the venue is MoN Takanawa, Box1500, on the fifth floor, at 3-16-1 Mita, Minato-ku, Tokyo, inside Takanawa Gateway City; and tickets are available through the museum's website and ArtSticker, with advance booking required.

Subjective
MANA — Feel the Sound opens at MoN Takanawa, with the Tokyo edition's particulars

Tokyo, November 19: tomorrow, November 20, 2026, MoN Takanawa, the Museum of Narratives, presents the Japan premiere of Feel the Sound, an immersive sound exhibition co-produced with London's Barbican Centre, on view through March 22, 2027, in Box1500; the museum, at 3-16-1 Mita, Minato-ku, Tokyo, inside Takanawa Gateway City, is operated by the East Japan Railway Foundation for Cultural Innovations; the official press release of November 4, 2026, issued with the Barbican Centre, announces the Japan first presentation of Feel the Sound, the immersive exhibition that ran at the Barbican from May 22 to August 31, 2025, with MoN Takanawa as organiser and co-producer and the original concept and production the Barbican's; the Tokyo edition includes new adaptations of existing works and three new works added specially for this presentation; the poster's Japanese tagline is rendered in the account as: that sound reaches the body before the ear; opening hours are 10:00 to 19:00, and until 21:00 on Fridays and Saturdays, with last entry 30 minutes before closing; advance tickets, on sale from October 30 to November 19, were 2,300 yen general, 900 yen for ages 25 and under, and 350 yen for elementary to high-school students, and regular prices from November 20 are 2,500 yen, 1,100 yen and 550 yen; and the official featured list opens with Sensing Streams, invisible, inaudible: focused edition, 2025, by Ryuichi Sakamoto and Daito Manabe.

Subjective
ArchDaily — Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026, November 14 to April 14

Sharjah, November 10: the third edition of the Sharjah Architecture Triennial, Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures, curated by Vyjayanthi Rao with associate curator Tau Tavengwa, takes place across the Emirate of Sharjah from November 14, 2026, to April 14, 2027; the opening programme, November 14 to 19, brings together 35 international participants to explore how architecture can foster collective life through social relationships, shared knowledge and civic engagement; the six-day programme features installations, participatory projects, performances, film screenings, lectures and panel discussions, culminating in a two-day international conference on November 18 and 19, 2026; and the Triennial's listed venue address is 7 Sheikh Saqr Bin Khalid Al Qasimi Street, Al Manakh, Sharjah.

Subjective
UAE News 24/7 — In Due Measure, the Calligraphy Biennial's closing exhibition, at the House of Wisdom

Sharjah, November 11: the House of Wisdom in Sharjah has opened In Due Measure: From Dot to Meaning, an exhibition exploring the geometric and aesthetic foundations of Arabic calligraphy and the precise principles of measurement and proportion that shape Arabic letters, from the dot, the alif and the circle to the formation of words and sentences; running until January 24, 2027, the exhibition marks the final stop of the 12th Sharjah Calligraphy Biennial, organised by the Sharjah Department of Culture under the theme Balance; it presents calligraphic artworks, reproductions of historic Qur'an manuscripts and traditional writing tools across five sections, The Dot: Unit of Measurement, The Letter: Geometry of Beauty, The Word: Rhythm and Composition, The Sentence: From Composition to Meaning, and Beyond Measure: Contemporary Practices; it introduces the pioneers of Arabic calligraphy, Ibn Muqla, associated with establishing the foundations of proportional calligraphy, and Ibn al-Bawwab and Yaqut al-Musta'simi; its works are by Sheikha Khawla Bint Ahmed Bin Khalifa Al Suwaidi, calligraphers Khalid Al Jallaf, Khalifa Al Shimi and Humaid Al Saadi, and Ali Al Hammadi, alongside a sculpture by Nasser Al Salem from the Barjeel Art Foundation collection; and at its Dot and Pen Table and Letter-Writing Table, visitors can draw dots of different sizes to explore letter proportions and follow video demonstrations into guided writing exercises.

Subjective
IMMA — A Sea for Borrowed Time opens in Dublin, November 19 to July 4

Dublin, November 9: the Irish Museum of Modern Art presents A Sea for Borrowed Time, a major exhibition of contemporary Palestinian art in partnership with Sharjah Art Foundation, in the House Galleries from November 19, 2026, to July 4, 2027, with free admission; bringing together works by Tarek Al-Ghoussein, Basma Al Sharif, Simone Fattal, Shadi Habib Allah, Rula Halawani, Hazem Harb, Khalil Rabah and Abdul Hay Mosallam Zarara, drawn from the Sharjah Art Foundation collection, the exhibition examines how contemporary artists have responded to histories of political resistance, displacement, occupation, memory and solidarity through photography, sculpture, installation, film and painting; it moves between testimony, memory, lived experience and imagination rather than following a chronological approach, spanning three generations; Simone Fattal's In Our Lands of Drought the Rain Forever is Made of Bullets, 2006, inscribes lava stone with locations in Palestine and Lebanon associated with massacres; Hazem Harb's Sustainable Waiting, 2012, centres on the suitcase he carried when he left Gaza in 2006; Rula Halawani's photographic series The Bride is Beautiful but she is married to another man, 2017, commissioned by the Sharjah Art Foundation, documents everyday movement through military checkpoints; the exhibition includes a major focus on Abdul Hay Mosallam Zarara, 1933 to 2020, whose relief connected to Ireland was discovered in the artist's studio shortly before his death and is shown publicly for the first time; and the exhibition is organised by IMMA and Sharjah Art Foundation and curated by Hoor Al Qasimi.

Subjective
TAT Newsroom — Loi Krathong 2026, led by Ayutthaya, November 21 to 24

Bangkok, November 18: the Tourism Authority of Thailand has announced its Loi Krathong 2026 celebrations, led by the Ayutthaya Loi Krathong Festival 2026 from November 21 to 24, with support for five other provincial celebrations in Chiang Mai, Sukhothai, Tak, Samut Songkhram and Roi Et, complementing celebrations across Thailand during the full moon of the twelfth Thai lunar month; Ayutthaya, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and former royal capital, is the principal venue, and the festival is staged at the Ancient Palace grounds near Wat Phra Si Sanphet in Ayutthaya Historical Park under the theme Chong Priang Loi Khom Chom Wang Si Ayutthaya; it centres on Saeng Nathi Si Sanphet, a 45-minute light, sound and theatrical production animating 417 years of Ayutthaya's history, performed nightly at 7:30 p.m. with 1,000 complimentary seats, 500 reservable online and 500 available at the venue from 5:00 p.m.; admission is free from 4:30 to 10:00 p.m. daily; the festival revives Chong Priang, an ancient royal tradition of ceremonial lantern-lighting, alongside the floating of krathongs, with a period-style market of more than 70 local vendors, and its opening ceremony on November 21 features a recreation of an Ayutthaya-era lantern procession led by Anna Sueangam-iam, Miss Universe Thailand 2022; the Tak Loi Krathong Sai Festival, from November 21 to 24 along the Ping River, features a signature competition of 1,000 illuminated krathongs floating in continuous streams; Samut Songkhram's festival, from November 21 to 24, will illuminate the Mae Klong River with over 100,000 krathongs made from banana stalks; Sukhothai's festival runs from November 15 to 24; Chiang Mai's Yi Peng Festival runs from November 23 to 25, with authorised sky lantern releases on November 24 and 25; Roi Et's festival runs November 23 and 24 with a mass traditional dance of 11,101 participants on November 23; and the Authority expects approximately 6 billion baht in domestic tourism revenue during the Loi Krathong period, an 8 percent year-on-year increase, on an estimated 1.83 million domestic visitor trips, up 6 percent.

Subjective
Thailand.go.th — the nationwide Loi Krathong 2026 calendar

Bangkok: the Tourism Authority of Thailand presents a nationwide calendar of Loi Krathong 2026 celebrations, featuring riverside ceremonies, illuminated historical landmarks and regional traditions; observed on the full moon of the twelfth Thai lunar month, the festival centres on floating decorated krathongs as an expression of gratitude and respect for water, and this year the full moon falls on November 24, with celebrations on different dates across the country; in Bangkok, the Rattanakosin Waterways festival runs from November 17 to 29, with Rama VIII Bridge from November 16 to 25, Phra Sumen Fort and Maha Kan Fort from November 23 to 25, and a historical route linking Wat Saket, Wat Ratchanatdaram, Wat Thepthidaram and Maha Kan Fort from November 17 to 29; Sukhothai's candlelight and fireworks festival runs from November 15 to 24 at Sukhothai Historical Park; Tak's Loi Krathong Sai, 1,000 floating krathongs, runs from November 21 to 24 at the foot of the Rattanakosin 200th Anniversary Bridge in Mueang Tak District; Chiang Saen's Yi Peng, Light of Faith on the Mekong, runs from November 20 to 24; Kamphaeng Phet's festival runs from November 16 to 24; Phuket's Loi Krathong by the Sea at Saphan Hin runs from November 16 to 25; Phang-nga's festival runs from November 19 to 28; and the calendar lists the Mae Klong banana-stem festival at Wat Phumarin Kudi Thong in Amphawa, Samut Songkhram, on November 24.

entry.title: Kyiv's Bridges Stand Closed in the BBC's Account and Partly Open in Kyiv's Own as Mr. Rutte Comes to Warsaw, California Subpoenas Nvidia in the Market's Quiet Hours, and the Strait Counts Eleven Crossings for Friday
entry.summary: The overnight file for Saturday, November 21, 2026: Kyiv’s three bridges closed in the BBC’s account and carrying restricted traffic in Kyiv’s own, with the alliance’s Secretary General due in Warsaw today; California’s attorney general subpoenas Nvidia and the accounting inquiry stands unanswered; the strait’s count for Friday rises to eleven crossings; a bulker lies aground on the Landes coast; France’s police law stands unpromulgated with its referral promised; and Valencia’s bullring fills at noon. Collected at 0400.
entry.content:
The Night File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Kyiv’s Bridges Stand Closed in the BBC’s Account and Partly Open in Kyiv’s Own as Mr. Rutte Comes to Warsaw, California Subpoenas Nvidia in the Market’s Quiet Hours, and the Strait Counts Eleven Crossings for Friday

The night file: a capital’s crossings closed in one account and carrying restricted traffic in another, with the Secretary General due in Warsaw today; a subpoena from California and an accounting inquiry over the chipmaker in the market’s quiet hours; eleven crossings counted in the strait for Friday against eight at Friday’s evening stamp, and a tanker still without a name; a grounded bulker on the Landes coast with 19 of its crew airlifted off; the text of Paris’s police law, still unpromulgated; and 300 buses rolling toward a bullring in Valencia. Saturday carries the Culture Feature.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Saturday, November 21, 2026. This edition continues the file from Edition No. 70, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, from Edition No. 69, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Friday, from Edition No. 68, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Friday, and from Edition No. 67, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Friday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the overnight figures differ from the earlier figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Night in Brief: A Bridge Count That Will Not Agree With Itself, a Subpoena in the Quiet Hours, and Eleven Crossings

The night’s file is a capital whose bridges are closed in one account and carrying traffic in another, an alliance Secretary General on his way to Warsaw, a second legal front opened against the chipmaker while the market slept, and a strait count for Friday that rose after the evening stamp had fixed it at eight. The BBC’s updated file, carried in the BBC account filed below, reports Kyiv’s three struck bridges closed to traffic, against restricted traffic resumed in the assessment filed below and a crossing restored at 3 p.m. in the latest account filed below—the desk prints the disagreement in the Cocked Hat and resolves none of it. Secretary General Rutte is due in Warsaw today, in the assessment and in the Council account filed below. California’s attorney general served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia on Thursday, in the crash account filed below, a fact that reached the overnight file after Friday’s close had already priced the accounting inquiry. The strait’s counter now puts Friday at eleven crossings, in the strait count filed below, against eight as of the evening stamp. The desk takes the files in that order.

What the night settled is the week’s close, which no overnight account reopens; the subpoena, which is a document and not a report; the strait’s revised Friday count; and the grounded bulker’s position on the Landes coast. What it left open is the rest: the bridges’ true state this morning, the alliance’s answer beyond a visit, Beijing’s word on the guardrails, the tanker’s name, the police law’s referral, and the router’s verdict, now eight days outstanding.

Kyiv and Warsaw at 0400: Nine Dead Confirmed in the Updated File, Three Bridges in Two States, and a Visitor Due Today

The updated British file fixes the night’s toll where the evening file left it rising. At least nine people were killed nationwide, seven in Kyiv and two in Lviv, with at least 28 injured, in the BBC account above, and Mayor Klitschko puts the capital’s toll at at least seven dead and 17 injured, in the same account; the Interior Minister’s figure of 30 injured across Ukraine stands beside it, in the latest account. The two killed outside the capital died in strikes on the Sknyliv railway station in Lviv, in the BBC account, and in Kharkiv a drone damaged a hospital, wounding four people and blowing out more than 50 windows, in the same account’s reporting of the mayor there. The package stands as the file has carried it: 27 ballistic missiles, 84 cruise missiles and 404 drones, in the assessment, with strikes recorded at 23 locations, in the latest account, and the Western Ukrainian 750-kilovolt substation struck and the nuclear plants forced to reduce generation, in the same account.

On the bridges the night’s accounts divide, and the division is the fact. All three struck crossings—the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, the Darnytskyi and the Southern—have been closed to traffic, in the BBC account. Restricted traffic has resumed across the damaged bridges, in the assessment, and traffic across the Podilskyi crossing was restored at about 3 p.m. local time on Friday, in the latest account, with the Darnytskyi assessment continuing and the Pivdennyi partly restricted, in the same account. A third wire reading has the Podilskyi closed from the right bank to the left, the Darnytskyi damaged, and the Southern open only toward the right bank under the weight limits the file has carried all day, in the wire account filed below. The desk prints the three states in the Cocked Hat. No account in the overnight file describes the Darnytskyi’s structural damage, and none gives a repair timetable for any of the three.

In Poland the night added the alliance’s itinerary to the week’s words. Investigations stand open at the three fall sites—Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik nad Sanem and Molodycz—in the Council account, and Poland has formally requested additional allied assets, airborne early warning aircraft and F-35s among them, under Operation Eastern Sentry, in the Warsaw account filed below. That account’s headline has Poland invoking the alliance’s Article 4; its text describes urgent consultations with allies and the asset request, and no alliance statement in the file uses the article’s name—the desk prints the gap in the Cocked Hat. On the non-interception, the commander’s reason stands as the midnight file printed it: the conditions did not meet the rules of engagement, in the assessment. A second account puts the pilots’ window at about three minutes to identify and assess the objects before they came down in farmland, in the Warsaw account, and a third records that the command’s first warning signals came at 01:40 and that two early warning aircraft patrolled in the morning without an interception, in the drills account filed below. France’s foreign minister’s call for a meeting of the Security Council stands as Friday made it, in the Council account, and Poland’s foreign minister has signalled that Warsaw intends to raise the incident before the Council as well, in the Warsaw account. Mr. Rutte, who called the violations grave and clearly dangerous, is due in Warsaw today, in the barrage account filed below. Settled: the toll, the sites, the request, and the visit. Open: the bridges’ state, the Council’s meeting, and what the visit brings beyond solidarity.

New York at 0400: The Week Sleeps Where It Closed, and the Chipmaker’s File Gains a Subpoena

The market’s overnight is a quiet one, and the desk records the quiet as a quiet. No account in the file reopens Friday’s close: the Dow down 8.0 percent on the week, the S&P 500 down 8.6 percent, the Nasdaq Composite down 10.0 percent, and the chip index down 17.1 percent, its worst week since 2001, as the midnight file printed them. The week’s weight gained one figure overnight: the Nasdaq’s members lost more than $4 trillion in market value this week, in the wipeout account filed below, which records that by Friday afternoon most of the debut’s initial gain had washed away along with the index’s gains for the year. Friday night’s only forward readings are small and upward: the funds tracking the Dow, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100 climbed 0.9, 1.0 and 1.5 percent in Friday-night trading, in the futures account filed below, and the futures themselves reopen Sunday at 1800 Eastern, in the same account. One position was closed in the fall: the investor Michael Burry locked in profits on half of his bearish bets against Nvidia and against a fund tracking the semiconductor sector on Friday, in the wrap account filed below, which also puts Strategy, the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, down 30.3 percent on the week, the worst performance on the Nasdaq 100. The Friday detail stands in the wrap’s companion account filed below: AMD down another 13 percent after Thursday’s 8 percent on a short-seller report, CoreWeave down 12 percent, Nebius down 16 percent, and Micron, SanDisk and Western Digital down between 12 and 16 percent.

The chipmaker’s file, which Friday closed on a reported inquiry, gained a second legal front in the overnight reading—one dated Thursday, before the inquiry’s focus was reported. California’s attorney general, Mr. Bonta, served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia on Thursday in connection with Mr. Huang’s reported relationship, in the crash account above: “My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information—and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” Mr. Bonta said, in the same account. The federal inquiry stands where Reuters left it: enforcement staff scrutinising potential accounting issues, on the word of two people briefed on the matter, in the inquiry account filed below, with the Commission declining to comment and the company not immediately responding, in the same account. The reporting around both fronts centres on the same ground: the change last year in geographic revenue reporting, from billing addresses to customer headquarters, which removed Singapore from the breakdown as sales booked there rose toward half of global revenue, in the inquiry account, with $19.7 billion recorded in fiscal 2026 from customers headquartered in China, in the overnight account filed below, published at 1:10 a.m. Eastern today. The company’s only words in the file remain its interim chief’s from Tuesday’s earnings call—proud of the company’s role in supporting the industry, and more selective henceforward about industry financing deals, in the focus account filed below. No charges stand in the file on either front, and both accounts print the standing caution: an investigation is not evidence of wrongdoing, and many close without enforcement action. Settled: the subpoena’s service and its stated scope, and the week’s close. Open: the company’s answer to either front, the inquiry’s scope, and the succession, on which the board’s position—no reinstatement intended, a search under way—stands unaltered.

Washington and Beijing at 0400: One Term, No Text, and No Word From Beijing in the File

The guardrails’ file did not move overnight, and the desk records what the file does and does not hold. The one concrete term stands as Secretary Bessent stated it on Friday: humans always involved in military decisions the technology touches, and no major military operation launched without a human being involved, in the Secretary’s account filed below, in the same words in the wire account filed below. No text, no timetable and no negotiating agency stands in the file, and no confirmation in Beijing’s own words stands in the overnight file either; the nearest parallel remains the embassy statement the week’s file carried, that the two sides should strengthen communication and keep the technology under human control. The chip half of the Secretary’s interview gained its machinery overnight: the Commerce Department’s steps on Monday extend the export restrictions to remote access, so that Chinese entities cannot rent computing power on overseas data centres to run advanced workloads, in the curbs account filed below. The H200 remains the most advanced chip China may purchase under licence, Chinese orders for it have been few, and Mr. Bessent put the Chinese stack “probably many years behind,” in the Secretary’s account; he also downplayed the differences between the Treasury and Commerce views, saying the administration’s officials are all committed to following the President’s instructions, in the same account. On the Huang question the two tellings stand unreconciled, as the midnight file printed them: discussed with President Xi, in the President’s telling; not raised in the bilateral, in the Secretary’s. Settled: the term as stated, and the curbs as described. Open: the text, Beijing’s confirmation, and how the human-involvement safeguard is to be applied in practice, which the curbs account names as its own watch line.

The Gulf at 0400: Eleven Crossings for Friday in the Revised Count, Four So Far on Saturday, and a Ship Still Without a Name

The strait’s counter revised Friday upward after the evening stamp had closed the day. Eleven commercial ships crossed on Friday, eight inbound and three outbound, three of them tankers, in the strait count above, against the eight the evening file carried as of 1802 UTC; four have crossed so far on Saturday, three inbound and one outbound, none of them tankers, as of 0759 UTC, with the container ship Tarlan the most recent, outbound at 0501 UTC, in the same count. The seven-day figure stands at 52 crossings, an average of 7.4 a day, about 9 percent of the pre-crisis 84.8, and the status stands severely restricted with the threat level severe, in the same count, which counts ships visible on the identification system and states plainly that ships sailing dark are missed. The week’s other instrument stands unreconciled beside it, as the midnight file printed it: 263 transits in the Maritime Trade Operations agency’s weekly overview, against the counter’s 47 for the same span it then covered. The desk prints the disagreement in the Cocked Hat.

The tanker struck off Khasab on Friday afternoon ends the night as it ended the day: unnamed in every account in the file. The warning stands as Warning 214-26, a projectile on the port bow at about 1500 UTC, eight nautical miles north of Khasab, a fire reported by the company security officer, no casualties and no environmental impact, in the tanker account filed below and in the wire account filed below. The Guards’ account gained a sentence overnight: the vessel was operating with support from the United States military, its navy said, blaming the incident on the ship’s use of an unauthorized passage and saying images of the explosion would be released later, in the Guards’ account filed below. No images stand in the file at the stamp, and the mine explanation remains unverified in every account that carries it. A separate encounter stands in the night’s maritime file: at 1102 UTC on Friday a skiff carrying six armed persons approached an eastbound bulk carrier in the recommended transit corridor, about 95 nautical miles southwest of Al Mukalla, under Warning 213-26, in the situation account filed below. Oil’s week stands as the midnight file closed it—Brent settled Friday at $92.57, the December contract at $83.98, both down on the week for a third straight week—and the OPEC+ ministers meet on November 29. Settled: the revised count and the week’s settlement. Open: the tanker’s name, flag, cargo and state; the weapon; the missing men of the week’s earlier ships; and the true count of the strait.

The night’s second ship is on the other side of the world and has a name. The bulk carrier Miro G, Malta-flagged, 169 metres and about 28,200 tonnes deadweight, built in 2011, lies aground on sand near Lit-et-Mixe on France’s Landes coast, where she came ashore at 00:55 local time on Friday after dragging both anchors in gusts of 48 knots from an emergency anchorage 1.8 nautical miles offshore, in the situation account and in the grounding account filed below. She was sailing in ballast from Bayonne toward Rouen, where tracking data put her to load 30,000 tonnes of wheat for Libya, in the capsize account filed below. Nineteen of her 22 crew were airlifted off by an Air and Space Force helicopter from Cazaux and taken to shelter at Saint-Julien-en-Born; three remain aboard to secure the ship, in the grounding account and in the rescue account filed below. The hull rests on the seabed, in the capsize account; the aim is a plan to refloat her by pulling her back out to sea and to prevent her capsizing as the tide changes, in the same account; she carries a little over a hundred tonnes of diesel, no pollution has been detected, the maritime response stands at its third level, the beach at Cap de l’Homy is closed, and a formal notice has gone to the shipowner, in the same accounts. No refloating stands in the file at the stamp. Settled: the position, the crew, and the plan. Open: the refloating, and the hull’s state when the tide turns.

Paris and Madrid at 0400: A Law’s Text, Still Unpromulgated, and a Bullring Filling at Noon

France’s file gained its text overnight and no new act. The law the Senate adopted on Friday by 205 votes to 110, with 27 abstentions and six senators not voting, creates a rebuttable presumption that national police officers and gendarmes used their firearms lawfully, in the text account filed below; it creates no new Penal Code defence and amends Article L.435-1 of the Internal Security Code, in the same account. Firearms use remains permitted in the five situations the article names, every use must remain absolutely necessary and strictly proportionate, the presumption does not cover municipal police, and any contrary evidence may rebut it at any time, in the same account. The Interior Minister’s position stands in both tellings: protection for officers in dangerous conditions, in the Paris account filed below, and, in the text account, that the measure does not authorise unrestricted shooting and prosecutors can still open investigations. Against it stand the United Nations rapporteur’s letter, as the file has carried it, and an opinion of November 5 from the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe’s democracy office recommending that the measure be reconsidered, in the text account. The law has not been promulgated and has not entered into force, in the same account; the Socialist group says it will refer the bill to the Constitutional Council before promulgation, and promulgation should follow within 15 days unless the Council is seized, in the same account. No filing of the referral stands in the overnight file: the referral is promised, not yet made, as the midnight file left it. Settled: the vote and the text. Open: the referral, and the Council’s word.

Spain’s Saturday is a rally, and the night’s file carries its arrangements rather than its result. The People’s Party will mobilise about 300 buses to fill the Valencia bullring today, in the rally account filed below; the party’s Valencian organisation expects between 12,000 and 14,000 people, doors open at 10:30, the rally begins at noon, and Mr. Feijóo closes it, with the mayor of Valencia, Ms. Catalá, and the president of the Generalitat, Mr. Pérez Llorca, among the speakers, in the same account, whose speakers recall the party filling the same bullring in 1995 and in 2011. Mr. Feijóo’s Friday went to El Hierro in the Canary Islands, the campaign having replaced the Las Palmas rally with a visit to the island facing the arrival of thousands of people in small boats, in the campaign account filed below; Sunday takes him to Murcia and Monday to Cádiz, in the same account. The debate’s verdict stands where Friday’s two polls put it—Mr. Feijóo the perceived winner, 51 to 29 and 43 to 33, before 10.2 million viewers, in the Madrid account filed below—and no post-debate voting-intention poll stands in the file. Spain votes on November 29, with the second debate agreed for about November 26. Settled: the arrangements and the verdict. Open: the bullring’s count, and whether any of it moves the vote.

The Air at 0400: No Root Cause in the Night’s File, and the Holiday Week at the Door

The promised announcement did not arrive in the night’s file either, and the desk records the standing at eight days. The agency’s question-and-answer briefing, updated on November 20, names the equipment for the first time in the file: it believes it addressed the initial cause by disabling the functionality of “the originating Juniper routers,” has disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers as a precaution, and has paused installing them, in the costs account filed below. The maker’s answer stands beside it in the same account: Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper Networks, said the equipment had operated according to its installed configuration. The briefing still says the agency and the contractor L3Harris are investigating the root cause, in the same account, and the overnight summaries hold the same line—preliminary findings pointing to overloaded legacy switches and router hardware generating the traffic, conclusions stressed as preliminary while the technical analysis completes, and no evidence of a malicious intrusion, in the holiday account filed below. The day’s count stands in the costs account at approximately 12,462 cancellations, of which the major airlines accounted for 9,082 and not all directly caused by the stop; the wider counts the week has carried stand in the Cocked Hat. The money stands estimated, not disclosed: about $345 million before tax for the four largest airlines, in one analyst’s estimate, against more than $1 billion for the industry in another’s, both carried in the costs account, and no airline has disclosed a figure, in the same account. Ahead of the file stands the holiday: the Port Authority projects 3.1 million passengers across its four New York and New Jersey airports between November 23 and 30, in the stop account filed below, and the Senate Commerce Committee is owed its technical answers on November 23, the first day of that window. Settled: the equipment, the precaution, and the two sites. Open: the root cause itself, and whether the system that failed on November 13 carries the year’s heaviest week without a second failure.

Saturday Ahead: A Culture Feature, a Secretary General in Warsaw, and a Bullring at Noon

Saturday carries the paper’s Culture Feature, in the FT Weekend manner, filed ahead of the day’s watches. It also carries Mr. Rutte in Warsaw, the Valencia rally at noon, and the French left’s promised referral, whenever it is filed. The futures reopen Sunday at 1800 Eastern. The week ahead carries the Senate Commerce Committee’s technical answers on the ground stop, due November 23; Alaska’s certification on November 25; Spain’s second debate, about November 26, and its vote on November 29; the OPEC+ ministers on November 29; the Federal Reserve’s decision on December 8 and 9; the end of government funding after December 11; and the Bank of Japan’s decision on December 18. The Midday Watch collects at 1200.

The Cocked Hat

Where the night’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Kyiv’s bridges: all three closed to traffic, in the BBC’s updated file; restricted traffic resumed across the damaged bridges, in the assessment; the Podilskyi restored at about 3 p.m. and the Pivdennyi partly restricted, in the latest account; and the Podilskyi closed right bank to left bank with the Southern open only toward the right bank under weight limits, in the wire account. On Kyiv’s injured: 28 in the BBC’s file, 30 across Ukraine in the Interior Minister’s count, and 17 in Kyiv in the mayor’s. On the non-interception in Poland: the conditions did not meet the rules of engagement, in the operational commander’s account; a window of about three minutes to identify and assess, in the Warsaw account; and first warning signals at 01:40 with patrols flown and no interception, in the drills account. On the alliance’s procedure: Article 4 invoked, in the Warsaw account’s headline; urgent consultations and a formal request for additional assets, in its text; and no alliance statement in the file using the article’s name. On Anthropic’s Friday: down 8.5 percent to $88.91 in the wrap’s companion account and the Journal’s weekly account, against down 9.1 percent to $88.30 in the close account the midnight file carried. On the strait’s Friday: eleven crossings in the counter’s revised count, against eight as of 1802 UTC in the evening file’s reading of the same counter; and on its week, 52 crossings in the counter against 263 in the Maritime Trade Operations agency’s weekly overview. On the ground stop’s cancellations: approximately 12,462 on the day in the agency’s count, against about 18,000 cancelled after the stop in the week account the midnight file carried and more than 18,500 within, into or out of the United States by the morning of November 16 in the costs account’s reading. On its cost: about $345 million before tax for the four largest airlines in one estimate, against more than $1 billion for the industry in another. Inside the triangle is where the night honestly stands, and the log turns on it.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 39 items.

Subjective
Vocemundi, carrying the BBC file — Kyiv: 3 bridges shut, at least 9 killed in Ukraine, BBC says

In its November 21 update the BBC reports at least nine people killed nationwide, seven in Kyiv and two in Lviv, with at least 28 injured, and Mayor Klitschko puts the toll in the capital at at least seven dead and 17 injured. Three bridges over the Dnipro were hit—the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge—and all three have been closed to traffic, the BBC reports. In Lviv two people were killed in strikes on the Sknyliv railway station, and in Kharkiv a drone damaged a hospital, wounding four people. The Austrian and Dutch embassies in Kyiv were reportedly damaged; the BBC presents this as unconfirmed.

Subjective
Institute for the Study of War — Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 20, 2026

Russian forces launched the largest missile and drone strike of November 2026 against Ukraine on the night of November 19 to 20: 27 ballistic missiles, 84 cruise missiles and 404 strike drones, targeting critical infrastructure and bridges in Kyiv City. Ukrainian officials reported damage to the Podilsko-Voskresensky, Darnytskyi and Southern bridges, and the Kyiv authorities resumed restricted traffic across the damaged bridges. A Kh-101 missile crashed near Nowy Lipowiec, a second missile, possibly a Kh-101, near Rudnik nad Sanem, and a jet-powered drone, possibly a Geran-5, near Molodycz. The Polish operational commander said Poland and the alliance did not try to down the missiles and the drone because the conditions did not meet the rules of engagement. Prime Minister Tusk called the violation an intentional provocation, and Secretary General Rutte will visit Poland on November 21.

Subjective
Europe Says, carrying the Kyiv Independent file — Russia strikes 3 Kyiv bridges in massive aerial assault, at least 9 dead

A huge, hours-long Russian missile and drone attack overnight on November 20 killed at least nine people, disrupted electricity, heating and water, and damaged three bridges in Kyiv. Seven people were killed in Kyiv and 17 injured, in Mayor Klitschko’s updated toll, and two more were killed in other regions, in the Prime Minister’s account; the Interior Minister put the injured across Ukraine at 30. Traffic across the Podilskyi crossing was restored at about 3 p.m. local time; the Darnytskyi assessment continues and the Pivdennyi remains partly restricted. The attack struck the Western Ukrainian 750-kilovolt substation and forced the nuclear plants to reduce generation. Estonia will close all its road border crossings with Russia on December 1.

Subjective
Europe Says — France calls for UN Security Council meeting after Russian strikes

France has called for a meeting of the United Nations Security Council after the latest Russian strikes in Kyiv, the foreign minister said on Friday. Russia violated Poland’s airspace overnight with three objects that were probably two missiles and a drone, the Polish defence minister said, denouncing what he called a provocation by Moscow. Prime Minister Tusk said Secretary General Rutte would visit Warsaw on Saturday, and Rutte said in a post that the incident was “clearly dangerous” and that the alliance stood in solidarity with Poland. The British Prime Minister said the violation of Polish airspace was “utterly unacceptable.” Investigations were under way at three locations: Nowy Lipowiec, Molodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem.

Subjective
Global 1 News — Russian Missiles Fall in Poland as NATO Drills Run Nearby

Three objects crossed into Polish airspace early Friday: a Kh-101 cruise missile came down among farm buildings about 50 kilometres from the Ukrainian border at Nowy Lipowiec at about 6:30 in the morning, a second object, also believed to be a missile, landed at Rudnik nad Sanem, and a third, most likely a jet-powered drone, came down at Molodycz. There were no injuries and no damage to critical infrastructure. The Polish command received its first warning signals at 01:40. Two alliance airborne early warning aircraft began patrolling over Poland in the morning, and still no object was intercepted. Prime Minister Tusk said: “It seems we are dealing with an intentional provocation.” The two-week exercise Koalicja 26.2 opened at the Nowa Dęba training range on November 9, with eleven countries taking part.

Subjective
Europe Says — Poland Invokes Article 4 After Russian Missiles Crash on Its Soil — and Demands NATO Act

Two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone came down inside Polish territory on Friday morning, near Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik nad Sanem and Mołodycz, all within 30 to 50 kilometres of the Ukrainian border, with no reported casualties or infrastructure damage. Poland held urgent consultations with allies and formally requested additional alliance assets—including airborne early warning aircraft and F-35s—under Operation Eastern Sentry. Poland’s air defences had been on heightened alert, with interceptor jets scrambled and Patriot batteries activated around 3:30 a.m., and all three weapons crossed the border unimpeded; pilots reportedly had a window of only about three minutes to identify and assess the objects. Poland’s foreign minister signalled that Warsaw intends to raise the incident before the United Nations Security Council.

Subjective
SOFX — Russian Missiles and Drone Crash in Poland During Overnight Barrage on Ukraine

Polish officials tied the timing of the falls to a nearby exercise where troops from eleven European nations are rehearsing a possible postwar mission in Ukraine, and Warsaw will ask the alliance for more Eastern Sentry forces. The barrage followed President Putin’s warning of a “far more painful” response to Ukraine’s strikes on the Kerch Bridge. Secretary General Rutte is due in Warsaw on November 21, and said he had discussed the “grave violations of Polish airspace” with Prime Minister Tusk and declared the alliance “in solidarity with Poland.”

Subjective
Particle News — Russian Missile and Drone Barrage Damages Kyiv Bridges and Lands in Poland

A large Russian attack overnight between Thursday and Friday used cruise missiles and hundreds of drones to hit Kyiv and other regions, killing at least eight people across Ukraine and wounding dozens. Mayor Klitschko and the city authorities said three Dnipro bridges—Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi—were damaged, disrupting east-west commutes. Buildings housing the Austrian and Dutch embassies suffered light damage and embassy staff were reported uninjured. Polish officials reported two missiles and a drone fell on southeastern Poland, one identified as a Kh-101 cruise missile, which prompted alliance jets to scramble and led Poland to open formal radar and ground investigations.

Subjective
Bury Times, carrying the wire file — Deadly attacks on Kyiv damage bridges and cut power

Russia launched missiles and drones overnight across Kyiv that killed at least eight people, injured two dozen more and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure, local authorities said. The Kyiv City Military Administration said the attack struck four districts of the capital and caused widespread electricity disruptions. Mayor Klitschko said a ballistic missile attack damaged the Podilskyi Bridge, forcing authorities to close traffic from the right bank to the left bank of the Dnipro; the Darnytskyi Bridge was also damaged, and a further strike hit the Southern Bridge, where traffic remains restricted to vehicles up to 10 tonnes travelling toward the right bank and public transport up to 18 tonnes.

Subjective
The Wall Street Journal — Anthropic’s IPO Turmoil Caps $4 Trillion AI Wipeout on Wall Street

Nothing this week could persuade investors that the selloff was merely a speed bump. Not even the biggest initial public offering in history, from Anthropic, could stop the bleeding: by Friday afternoon most of the initial pop from the offering had washed away, along with the Nasdaq Composite’s entire gains for the year, and this week alone the tech-heavy benchmark’s members lost more than $4 trillion in market value. Friday’s selling hit almost all of the major artificial intelligence players, dragging every member of the Magnificent Seven lower. The Nasdaq fell 5.3 percent, Anthropic tumbled 8.5 percent, and Nvidia dropped 14 percent on the day. For the week the S&P 500 dropped 8.6 percent, closing in correction territory, the Nasdaq plunged 10 percent, capping its worst week since March 2020, and the Dow industrials lost 8 percent.

Subjective
MarketWatch — Dow, S&P 500 enter correction as Nasdaq suffers worst week since 2020

When the closing bell rang Friday, the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average joined the Nasdaq Composite and the Russell 2000 in correction territory. For the S&P 500 it was the first fall of 10 percent or more from a recent closing high since the April 2025 tariff episode. The Nasdaq erased its year-to-date gains and finished in the red for the year for the first time since April. Anthropic shares plunged nearly 10 percent on Friday, finishing below $90, not far from the offering price of $83. Nvidia shares have fallen by nearly 50 percent from their October 6 record high and on Friday tallied their worst one-day loss since the DeepSeek selloff. All eleven S&P 500 sectors fell by more than 1 percent this week for the first time since April 4, 2025.

Subjective
Investor’s Business Daily — Dow Jones Futures: Market Has Worst Week Since Covid Amid Nvidia, Anthropic. Does Fear Gauge Offer Hope?

Dow Jones futures will open Sunday evening, along with S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq futures. The stock market had a terrible week, with the Dow Jones and the Nasdaq suffering their worst losses since March 2020. Exchange-traded funds tracking the Dow Jones, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100 index climbed 0.9 percent, 1 percent and 1.5 percent respectively on Friday night. Nvidia’s earnings were strong, but the post-Huang hangover continues, with the Securities and Exchange Commission reportedly expanding a probe to include accounting issues. Anthropic fell back toward its offering price on Friday. United States crude oil futures fell 5.2 percent to $83.98 a barrel last week, down 19.2 percent so far in November. The semiconductor exchange-traded fund fell 17.8 percent on the week.

Subjective
TradingView, carried from Stocktwits — Nasdaq 100 Ends Worst Week Since 2020, S&P 500 In Correction Territory As AI Rout Sours Sentiment

The S&P 500 eased about 8.6 percent on the week, the Nasdaq 100 lost 10.4 percent, and the Dow Jones index fell 8 percent in the week ending November 20. On Friday the Dow fell 2 percent to 48,147.33, the S&P 500 fell 3.7 percent to 6,910.39, and the Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6 percent to 25,028.98.
