Strategy, the world’s largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, dropped 30.3 percent this week and was the worst-performing stock for the week on the Nasdaq 100. The investor Michael Burry locked in profits on half of his bearish bets against Nvidia and an exchange-traded fund that tracks the semiconductor sector on Friday. Anthropic eclipsed SpaceX in investor demand during its initial public offering, the largest public market debut on record.

Subjective
TradingView, carried from CNBC TV18 — US markets wrap, November 21

United States markets had a brutal day on Friday amid intense selling pressure as the artificial intelligence trade continued to unwind. The Dow Jones fell another 950 points, taking the drop for the week to 4,100 points. The S&P 500 fell 3.7 percent on Friday, while the Nasdaq Composite and the Nasdaq 100 fell over 5.5 percent each; the Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6 percent on Friday, capping its worst week since March 2020. Chipmaker and software stocks remained the worst hit: Nvidia fell 14 percent on Friday; AMD, which fell 8 percent on Thursday after a short-seller report, fell another 13 percent; CoreWeave fell 12 percent and Nebius Group 16 percent; and Micron, SanDisk and Western Digital fell between 12 and 16 percent on Friday. Anthropic listed at a 34 percent premium to its issue price of $83, trimmed those gains to 17 percent on listing day, and fell another 8.5 percent on Friday, closing at $88.91.

Subjective
Reuters — Nvidia’s accounting is a focus of US SEC investigation, sources say

The Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia’s accounting practices, said two people briefed on the matter. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that the Commission was probing Nvidia but could not ascertain the focus; the people said enforcement staff are scrutinising potential accounting issues. A spokesperson for the Commission declined to comment, and spokespeople for Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not determine when the inquiry opened or exactly what it examines. Last year Nvidia changed how it reports geographic revenue, using customer headquarters rather than billing addresses, which removed Singapore from its geographic breakdown; the Financial Times reported that Singapore sales had soared to almost half of global revenue. The Commission’s enforcement chief said last month that the agency was examining artificial intelligence companies’ disclosures.

Subjective
The Motley Fool — Here’s Why Nvidia Stock Crashed on Friday

Shares of Nvidia plunged 14 percent on Friday following reports that the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating the company’s accounting practices. On Thursday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia related to Mr. Huang’s reported affair. “My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information—and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” Mr. Bonta said. Reuters noted that investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close without enforcement action. Nvidia’s quarterly results released on November 17 were impressive: revenue rose 103 percent year over year to $115.8 billion and net income rose 105 percent to $65.3 billion.

Subjective
The Motley Fool — After Its Worst Week in 18 Years, Nvidia Now Faces an SEC Investigation. What It Means for Investors

Published at 1:10 a.m. Eastern on November 21: on Friday Nvidia stock plunged 14 percent as Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission had opened an accounting probe into the company, three days after the Journal said the Commission was investigating without saying what for. The probe could focus on how Nvidia reports geographic revenue, which potentially obscures where its chips end up; in fiscal 2026 Nvidia recorded $19.7 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China. An investigation does not mean the company committed fraud or will face enforcement action; a probe is not evidence of wrongdoing, and many are closed without going further. The investigations are likely to hang over the company for at least several months. Executives at Super Micro Computer, a server maker and close partner of Nvidia, were charged by the Department of Justice with conspiring to divert artificial intelligence servers to China, though Super Micro’s internal investigation found no one on its senior management team was aware of the scheme.

Subjective
BigGo Finance — SEC Zeroes In on Nvidia Accounting

Enforcement staff at the Securities and Exchange Commission are examining Nvidia’s accounting treatment, with the direction of the investigation revealed for the first time and focused on potential accounting problems, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter. Following the news, Nvidia’s Friday decline widened from an initial drop of more than 6 percent to roughly 13 percent, ending the session down 14.01 percent at $125.53—a seventh consecutive losing session and a seventh straight weekly decline, the longest losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis. An opening of an investigation does not mean regulators have concluded the company violated any rules. The interim chief executive, Ms. Kress, said at Tuesday’s earnings call that the company is proud of its role in supporting the industry’s development but will apply stricter screening standards when participating in industry financing deals in the future.

Subjective
Reuters — Trump, Xi agreed that military AI decisions should involve humans, Bessent says

President Trump and President Xi agreed that humans should always be involved in military decisions that use artificial intelligence technologies, Treasury Secretary Bessent told CNBC on Friday after returning from the Shenzhen meeting, calling the agreement among the major achievements of the trip. No major military operation should be launched without a human being involved. Mr. Bessent said the allegations involving the former Nvidia chief executive, Mr. Huang, did not come up in the bilateral meeting, and that Nvidia’s second-tier H200 chip remained the most advanced chip China could purchase with licences, with few orders from Chinese buyers. The Commerce Department took steps on Monday to further restrict China’s access to advanced chips, including those used by overseas data centres where Chinese entities can rent computing power.

Subjective
The Frontier — US-China Curb Remote Access to Advanced AI Chips

President Trump and President Xi agreed humans must stay involved in military artificial intelligence decisions, while new Commerce rules cut Chinese access to overseas artificial intelligence computing. The agreement is a diplomatic commitment rather than a technical product, addressing how the technology may be used in military decision-making as both governments compete over advanced chips and models. The Commerce Department’s new rules extend export restrictions on advanced chips to remote access, meaning Chinese entities cannot rent computing power on overseas data centres to run advanced workloads. Mr. Bessent said the proper chip restrictions are in place and remote access has been curtailed, and that American laboratories must maintain their technological lead. The account’s watch line: whether Washington and Beijing publish detail on how the human-involvement safeguards will be applied in practice.

Subjective
Bloomberg Tax — Trump, Xi Agreed on AI Curb in Military Action, Bessent Says

President Trump and China’s Xi Jinping agreed that artificial intelligence should never be allowed to make autonomous major military actions, Treasury Secretary Bessent said Friday. “President Trump, and President Xi agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions,” Mr. Bessent told CNBC, using the President’s preferred abbreviation for the technology.

Subjective
Reuters — Fire reported on tanker after projectile strike off Oman, UKMTO says

A tanker sailing outbound through the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an unknown projectile eight nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Friday, and the vessel’s company security officer reported a fire on board. No casualties or environmental impact were reported, and authorities are investigating. The Guards said shortly afterwards that an oil tanker had caught fire after hitting a mine while attempting to transit near Khasab.

Subjective
MarineLink, carrying Reuters — Tanker On Fire After Struck By Projectile Near Strait

A tanker caught fire after being struck by an unknown projectile while sailing outbound through the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Friday. The incident occurred eight nautical miles north of the Omani town of Khasab, and no casualties or environmental impact were reported. The Guards said shortly afterwards that an oil tanker had caught fire after hitting a mine while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz near Khasab.

Subjective
Kayhan — IRGC: Tanker Explodes After Striking Naval Mine Near Khasab

The Islamic Revolution Guards Corps said Friday that a tanker attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorized route exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines near the entrance to Oman’s Khasab port. The Guards’ navy said the vessel was operating with support from the United States military and blamed its use of an unauthorized passage for the incident. It said images of the explosion would be released later.

Subjective
ShipUniverse — Another Tanker Catches Fire in Hormuz as Shipping Traffic Falls 15%

A tanker sailing outbound was struck on its port bow by an unidentified projectile at approximately 1500 UTC on November 20, about eight nautical miles north of Khasab, under United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Warning 214-26. No casualties or environmental impact were reported in the initial warning. The tanker was not identified, and its damage and operational status remained unconfirmed. The Guards claimed an oil tanker near Khasab had struck a naval mine, an explanation not independently verified. The incident follows multiple attacks on tankers in the same area earlier in the week.

Subjective
Hormuz.now — Strait of Hormuz News Today: Latest Status Update, 21 Nov 2026

Four commercial ships have crossed the strait so far on November 21, three inbound and one outbound, none of them tankers, as of 0759 UTC. Eleven crossed on November 20, eight inbound and three outbound, three of them tankers. Fifty-two crossed in the last seven days, an average of 7.4 a day, about 9 percent of the pre-crisis 84.8. The most recent crossing detected was the container ship Tarlan, outbound, at 0501 UTC on November 21. The status stands restricted, severely restricted, and the threat level severe. The count is of ships visible on the automatic identification system; ships sailing dark are missed, so trackers that also detect them report higher numbers.

Subjective
The DeepDraft — SITREP: Hormuz Tanker Struck and Set Ablaze, MIRO G Grounds Off France (November 21, 2026)

An outbound tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz, causing a fire eight nautical miles north of Khasab; the ship remains officially unidentified, and conflicting accounts of the weapon have not been resolved. Warning 214-26 records the attack at 1500 UTC on November 20. Warning 213-26 records a separate encounter at 1102 UTC on November 20, about 95 nautical miles southwest of Al Mukalla, where an eastbound bulk carrier in the recommended transit corridor was approached on its port side by a skiff carrying six armed persons. The Malta-flagged bulk carrier Miro G grounded near Lit-et-Mixe on the French Atlantic coast shortly after midnight on November 20, after 48-knot gusts caused its anchors to drag from an emergency anchorage about 1.8 nautical miles offshore; 19 of the 22 people on board were evacuated by helicopter, and France activated maritime ORSEC Level 3.

Subjective
gCaptain — Crew Airlifted After Bulk Carrier Grounds on French Coast

The 169-metre Miro G grounded near Lit-et-Mixe in southwestern France’s Landes region shortly after midnight on November 20, after its crew reported difficulty manoeuvring in deteriorating weather. The vessel had alerted the CROSS-A Étel rescue coordination centre on Thursday evening after encountering heavy swell and strong crosswinds. Following the grounding, a French Air and Space Force search-and-rescue helicopter operating from Cazaux evacuated 19 of the vessel’s 22 crew members. The Miro G, a bulk carrier built in 2011 with a deadweight capacity of approximately 28,200 tonnes, was sailing without cargo when the grounding occurred.

Subjective
Baird Maritime — French rescuers airlift 19 crew from bulker aground on Landes coast

A French Air and Space Force helicopter airlifted 19 of the 22 crew members from the bulk carrier Miro G after the vessel ran aground near Lit-et-Mixe on France’s Atlantic coast early on Friday, November 20. The vessel grounded on sand at 00:55 local time after dragging both anchors. “The ship is not moving at present, but as the tide changes it could become unstable, and that is when the risk of capsizing arises,” a spokesman said. The vessel was built in 2011, is 169 metres long and has a deadweight of 28,200 tonnes.

Subjective
Europe Says — Capsize fear as Malta-flagged cargo vessel runs aground off southwest France

The vessel Miro G grounded overnight off the southwest department of Les Landes, with emergency services evacuating 19 crew safely by helicopter. It was not carrying any cargo. “The hull is resting on the seabed,” Commander Laurent Falhun, spokesman for the maritime prefecture, said. “The current aim is to draw up a plan to refloat the vessel by pulling it back out to sea and prevent it from capsizing.” No pollution has been detected so far, but there would be a risk if the vessel capsized, given it is carrying a little over a hundred tonnes of diesel fuel in its tanks. The ship was en route to the port of Rouen. Tracking data put the vessel on course to load 30,000 tonnes of wheat for Libya at Rouen.

Subjective
Reuters — French Senate approves police shootings law dubbed ‘licence to kill’ by critics

Senators gave final approval on Friday to a law presuming that police officers who use their weapons are acting lawfully, backing it by 205 votes to 110. The law gives an officer who has shot someone the benefit of the doubt unless there is proof to the contrary. The Interior Minister supports it as an important measure to protect officers who work in dangerous conditions. The left-wing groups plan to refer the law to the Constitutional Council in a last effort to halt it. The United Nations special rapporteur on extrajudicial executions wrote ahead of the vote that the burden of disproving lawfulness should not fall on victims and their families, especially where the authorities control the key evidence.

Subjective
Bars Across — France Approves Rebuttable Presumption for Police Firearms Use

France has approved a bill creating a rebuttable presumption that National Police officers and gendarmes used firearms lawfully. The Senate adopted it on November 20 by 205 votes to 110, with 27 abstentions and six senators not voting; the National Assembly approved the text in July. It has not yet been promulgated or entered into force. The measure creates no new Penal Code defence; it amends Article L.435-1 of the Internal Security Code. Firearms use remains permitted in five situations, and every use must remain absolutely necessary and strictly proportionate. The presumption covers national police and gendarmes, not municipal police, and any contrary evidence may rebut it at any time. The Interior Minister said the measure does not authorise unrestricted shooting and prosecutors can still open investigations. An opinion issued on November 5 by the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe’s Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights recommended reconsidering the measure. The Socialist group says it will refer the bill to the Constitutional Council before promulgation; promulgation should follow within 15 days unless the Council is seized.

Subjective
Statement — France shields police who use weapons

On November 20 the French Senate gave final approval to a law under which a police officer’s use of a weapon is presumed lawful unless proven otherwise. The presumption also applies when an officer shoots and kills someone. Senators backed the law by 205 votes to 110. Left-wing parliamentary groups plan to challenge it before the Constitutional Council.

Subjective
Reuters — Spanish PM Sanchez’s conservative rival wins TV face-off, polls show

Mr. Feijóo emerged as the perceived winner of Thursday night’s face-off: 51 percent to 29 percent in the Sigma Dos poll and 43 percent to 33 percent in the 40dB poll, the remainder naming neither man or a tie. The audience was 10.2 million, nearly double the 2023 debate’s. Housing stood at the centre of the debate, with rival plans on rents and affordable supply; the two men also sparred over migration and traded accusations over corruption scandals attached to their parties. An overwhelming majority of polls show an advantage for a bloc of the People’s Party and Vox. Spain votes November 29, with a second debate agreed for about November 26.

Subjective
El Constitucional — The PP mobilizes 300 buses to fill the València Bullring in a rally with Feijóo, Catalá, and Pérez Llorca

The People’s Party will mobilize around 300 buses to fill the València Bullring this Saturday, in a rally the party considers one of the central events of the campaign for the November 29 general election. The venue will gather between 12,000 and 14,000 people, the party’s Valencian organisation says. The rally will begin at 12:00, with doors scheduled to open at 10:30, and will feature the candidate for prime minister, Mr. Feijóo, the head of the list for Valencia and mayor of the city, Ms. Catalá, and the president of the Generalitat, Mr. Pérez Llorca, among other party leaders. Campaign speakers recall that the party filled the bullring in 1995 and again in 2011.

Subjective
Europe Says, carrying Demócrata — Feijóo strengthens campaign in Murcia, Cádiz and Valencia

Mr. Feijóo is scheduled to campaign on Sunday, November 22, in Murcia and on Monday in Cádiz. Before that he travels on Friday to the Canary Islands: the campaign replaced the rally scheduled in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria on Friday, November 20, with a visit to El Hierro, in light of the migration emergency the island is facing, with the arrival of thousands of people in small boats. On Saturday he will lead the central event of the campaign in the Valencian Community at the bullring in Valencia, accompanied by Ms. Catalá and Mr. Pérez Llorca. The party expects to fill the bullring, a venue it considers emblematic of its stages of absolute majorities.

Subjective
Nomad Lawyer — FAA Ground Stop: 12,462 Flights Cancelled Before Thanksgiving

The nationwide ground stop of November 13 resulted in 12,462 flight cancellations. The disruption began at about 3:30 p.m. Eastern on November 13, manifesting as instability in the telecommunications infrastructure; instability was reported across 17 of the 22 en route centres. The network was overwhelmed by roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. The agency identified two primary points of origin: a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas. The ground stop was lifted by 8:15 p.m. that evening, and about 3,500 airborne aircraft landed safely. The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey projects a throughput of 3.1 million passengers across its four major airports between November 23 and 30.

Subjective
Travel Market News — FAA Ground Stop Cause: Router Probe and Airline Costs

The investigation into the November 13 ground stop centres on a newly installed router at a remote radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas. In its November 20 update the agency’s question-and-answer briefing names the equipment: it believes it addressed the initial cause by disabling the functionality of “the originating Juniper routers,” has disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers in the system as a precaution, and has paused installing them. Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper Networks, said the equipment had operated according to its installed configuration. The briefing still says the agency and the contractor are investigating the root cause. The agency’s count puts cancellations on the day at approximately 12,462 flights, of which major airlines accounted for 9,082, and not all were directly caused by the stop. Bernstein puts the cost to the four largest airlines at about $345 million before tax; Bloomberg says airlines could lose more than $1 billion.

Subjective
The Traveler — How the Nov. 13 FAA Ground Stop Shapes 2026 Holiday Travel

A rare nationwide ground stop on November 13 has intensified scrutiny of the air traffic control network just as tens of millions of travellers head into the Thanksgiving and Christmas rush, with operations largely back to normal but political fallout and lingering disruption risks shaping how airlines and passengers plan the holidays. Federal statements attribute the disruption to problems within ageing network infrastructure interacting with ongoing modernisation work, not to a cyberattack. Early findings point to overloaded legacy switches and router hardware at several sites generating unusually high volumes of network traffic. Officials stress that these conclusions remain preliminary while contractors and federal investigators complete a technical root-cause analysis. Secretary Duffy and Administrator Bedford have both emphasised that there is currently no evidence of a malicious intrusion.

entry.title: Friday Closes With Wall Street in Correction After the Worst Week Since 2020, the Guardrails Given One Term in Washington, Nine Dead in Kyiv With the Alliance's Answer Still to Come, and a Tanker Still Unnamed in the Strait
entry.summary: The midnight file for Saturday, November 21, 2026: what Friday settled and what it left open. Wall Street closed its worst week since March 2020 with the Dow and the S&P 500 in correction and the chip index down 17.1 percent, its worst week since 2001; Secretary Bessent gave the joint guardrails their one concrete term, a human in every military decision; Kyiv's count stands at nine dead with Poland's falls answered by condemnation and no interception; the strait's tanker is still unnamed; and the root cause of the November 13 ground stop ends the week unannounced. Collected at 0000.
entry.content:
The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Friday Closes With Wall Street in Correction After the Worst Week Since 2020, the Guardrails Given One Term in Washington, Nine Dead in Kyiv With the Alliance’s Answer Still to Come, and a Tanker Still Unnamed in the Strait

The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: a week closed in correction, with the chips down 17.1 percent; a guardrail that gained one term and no text; nine dead in Kyiv and three weapons down in Poland, unanswered by fire; a tanker burning off Khasab with no name in the file; a law passed in Paris and a verdict confirmed in Madrid; and a promised root cause that the week ends without.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Saturday, November 21, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 69, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Friday, in Edition No. 68, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Friday, in Edition No. 67, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Friday, and in Edition No. 66, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 on Friday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Friday Settled, What It Left Open

Friday settled the week’s measure, the guardrails’ one term, the French Senate’s vote, and Madrid’s verdict—and left the inquiry, the alliance’s answer, the tanker’s name, and the router’s verdict open at the turn of the log. Wall Street closed down 3.70 percent on the S&P 500 and 5.28 percent on the Nasdaq Composite, in the close account filed below, completing the worst week since March 2020 for two of the three indexes and a fall of 17.1 percent for the chip index, its worst week since 2001, in the weekly account filed below. Secretary Bessent said the guardrails agreed with President Xi carry one concrete term: a human being involved in every military decision the technology touches, in the Secretary’s account filed below. Kyiv’s count stands at nine dead, in the latest account filed below, and the weapons that fell in Poland were not fired on, in the assessment filed below. The tanker struck off Khasab stands unnamed in every account in the file. The desk takes the files in that order.

What Friday settled is the close and the week, the vote in Paris at 205 to 110, the debate’s verdict on two instruments, and the shape of the Securities and Exchange Commission’s inquiry as far as its reporting goes. What it left open is the rest: the guardrails’ text, the inquiry’s scope and the company’s answer, the Darnytskyi Bridge’s damage, the Security Council’s meeting, the strait’s weapon, and the root cause of the November 13 ground stop, promised for this week and not announced in it.

New York at Midnight: The Week’s Measure, Taken Whole

The evening file carried the close; the midnight file carries the week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points on Friday, or 1.93 percent, to 48,147.33, and 8.0 percent on the week, a drop of some 4,100 points and its worst week since March 2020; the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points, or 3.70 percent, to 6,910.39, and 8.6 percent on the week, its worst week since April 2025; and the Nasdaq Composite fell 1,261.47 points, or 5.28 percent, to 22,617.73, and 10.0 percent on the week, in the close account and the weekly account above. The Nasdaq 100 fell 10.4 percent on the week, its worst since March 2020, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 17.1 percent, its worst week since the week ending September 21, 2001, in the weekly account; the Russell 2000 fell 7.5 percent. The Dow and the S&P 500 closed in correction, down more than 10 percent from their peaks; the Nasdaq stands 18 percent below its October 6 record and negative for the year, its gain of 18.7 percent erased, in the year account filed below. The volatility index closed at 35.89, up 26.20 percent on the day and 86 percent on the week, in the pulse account filed below, having reached 38.50 in the week, its highest in 19 months, in the year account. The ten-year Treasury yield stood at 4.91 percent, down 14 basis points; Bitcoin at $58,955, down 4.76 percent, in the pulse account. Gold fell for a fifth straight day and 9 percent on the week, below $4,000 an ounce, and silver 15 percent, in the weekly wrap filed with the futures account below. Friday night’s only forward reading is a small one: the funds tracking the Dow, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100 climbed 0.9, 1.0 and 1.5 percent in Friday-night trading, and the futures themselves reopen Sunday at 1800 Eastern, in the futures account filed below.

The debut’s second day ends five dollars above its price and no further. Anthropic closed at $88.30, down 9.1 percent, in the close account, and at $88.91, down 8.50 percent, in the quote account filed below—the desk prints the two closes in the Cocked Hat—after a low of $83.05, five cents above the $83 offering price, and an after-hours reading of $88.48 at 4:50 p.m. in the quote account. Thursday’s arc stands as the file printed it: priced at $83, first trade $111.50, high $115.10, close $97.17. The week’s question about the offering is now a question about Monday: whether the shares hold the price they were sold at when the market reopens after its worst week in six years.

The chipmaker’s file gained its cause on Friday and ends the week without the company’s answer. Nvidia closed at $125.53, down $20.45, or 14.01 percent, in the chip quote account filed below, a seventh straight lower close; on the week the shares fell 22.7 percent in the year account and 22.9 percent in the futures account, their worst week since October 2008, and the company’s market value stood at about $3.03 trillion, below Alphabet at about $3.25 trillion, in the value account filed below. The fall steepened after 2:15 p.m., when Reuters reported that Securities and Exchange Commission enforcement staff are scrutinising potential accounting issues at the company, on the word of two people briefed on the matter, in the inquiry account filed below. The Journal had reported the probe’s existence on Tuesday without its focus. The reporting around the inquiry centres on the company’s change last year in geographic revenue reporting—from billing addresses to customer headquarters—which removed Singapore from the breakdown as sales booked there rose toward half of global revenue, some $104 billion for 2025 in the probe account filed below; whether that change is inside the inquiry’s scope is not established in any account in the file. The Commission declined to comment; the company did not immediately respond; no charges stand in the file, and an inquiry is not a finding. The board’s position, stated Tuesday by its chairman, stands unaltered at midnight: the board does not intend to reinstate Mr. Huang, and the search firm Heidrick & Struggles is engaged to find a permanent chief executive, with Ms. Kress as interim. Against it stands the President’s word on Friday, in the Washington file below. Settled: the week, the correction, and the inquiry’s reported focus. Open: the inquiry’s scope, the company’s answer, and the succession.

Washington at Midnight: One Term for the Guardrails, and Two Tellings of the Huang Question

The noon conference’s one announcement gained its content on Friday from the Treasury Secretary, speaking after the return from Shenzhen. President Trump and President Xi agreed that humans should always be involved in military decisions that use artificial intelligence, and that no major military operation should be launched without a human being involved, Mr. Bessent told CNBC, in the Secretary’s account above, calling the agreement among the trip’s major achievements and saying it would stand apart from the two countries’ competition in the technology. That is the whole of the guardrails’ stated content at midnight: no text, no timetable, and no negotiating agency stands in the file, and no confirmation in Beijing’s own words stands in the file either; an earlier embassy statement carried in the week’s file, that the two sides should strengthen communication and keep the technology under human control, is the nearest parallel. Mr. Bessent added the chip position in the same interview: the H200 remains the most advanced chip China may purchase under licence, and Chinese orders for it have been few. The President’s own conference stands as the evening printed it—the trip a resounding success, data centres to be built at home and penalised abroad, only older chips for China—in the conference account filed below.

On the chipmaker’s former chief, Friday produced two tellings that do not meet, and the desk prints both. The President said he had discussed Mr. Huang with President Xi, that President Xi agreed Mr. Huang was a brilliant man, and that Mr. Huang had made some bad decisions: “I would like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back…we’re a country of second chances,” in the conference report filed below. Mr. Bessent said the allegations involving Mr. Huang did not come up in the bilateral meeting, in the Secretary’s account. The board’s stated position, against both tellings, is the one in the New York file: no reinstatement intended, a search under way. Settled: the guardrails’ one term, stated by the Secretary. Open: their text, Beijing’s confirmation, and which telling of the Huang conversation is the record.

Kyiv at Midnight: Nine Dead, Restricted Traffic, and an Answer Made of Words

The night’s count finished where the evening left it, and the midnight file records the finished figures and the day’s military reading together. At least nine people were killed: seven in Kyiv and two in other regions, in the latest account above, with the injured at 30 across Ukraine in the Interior Minister’s count and 17 in Kyiv in the mayor’s; a second full account puts the dead at at least eight, six in Kyiv and two in Lviv—the desk prints the spread in the Cocked Hat. The package stands at 27 ballistic missiles, 84 cruise missiles and 404 drones, the largest of November, in the assessment above, with air defences downing or suppressing three ballistic missiles, 79 cruise missiles and 380 drones and strikes recorded at 23 locations, in the latest account. The strike hit the Western Ukrainian 750-kilovolt substation, the largest in Europe, and forced the nuclear plants to reduce generation, with parts of Kyiv and ten regions without electricity, in the same account. Ukraine’s own strikes in the same hours hit three Russian ballistic missile launchers, destroying one, in the strike account filed below, and the Druzhba pumping station in Tatarstan on Thursday, damaging three storage tanks, in the latest account.

In Kyiv the repair advanced a step past the evening file. Traffic across the Podilskyi crossing was restored at about 3 p.m. local time, in the latest account, and the assessment records restricted traffic resumed across the damaged bridges generally; the Darnytskyi assessment continues and the Pivdennyi remains partly restricted, in the same account. In Poland the day produced the alliance’s fullest statement of what it did and did not do. Two Kh-101 missiles came down at Nowy Lipowiec and Rudnik nad Sanem and a jet-powered drone, possibly a Geran-5, at Molodycz, with no damage at any of the three, in the assessment; as many as 11 missiles and drones in Ukrainian airspace were tracked as potential threats to Poland’s, Polish, Swedish and Dutch aircraft were scrambled, and Poland and the alliance did not try to down the missiles and the drone because the conditions did not meet the rules of engagement, the operational commander said, in the same account. Prime Minister Tusk called the falls an intentional provocation; the Secretary General condemned the attack and the violation; France’s foreign minister called for a meeting of the Security Council; and Estonia will close its road border crossings with Russia on December 1, in the provocation account filed below and the latest account. President Zelensky’s reading stands against the week’s diplomacy, as the evening printed it: the attempt in Shenzhen to redraw the world had failed. UNICEF’s figures for the year stand beside the night’s: 1,144 children killed or injured between January and October. Settled: the count, the reopening in restricted form, and the non-interception, stated plainly by the commander who ordered it. Open: the Darnytskyi damage, the Council’s meeting, and the alliance’s answer beyond words.

The Gulf at Midnight: A Tanker Unnamed, a Weapon in Dispute, and Two Counts That Do Not Meet

Friday’s strike in the strait ends the day as it began it in the file: a ship with no name. A tanker on an outbound transit was struck on its port bow by an unknown projectile at about 1500 UTC, eight nautical miles north of Khasab, and its company security officer reported a fire on board, under Warning 214-26, in the fire account filed below; no casualties and no environmental impact were reported, and no later account in the file names the vessel, gives its flag or cargo, or reports the fire’s end. The Guards said the tanker caught fire after hitting a mine on an unauthorised transit; the mine explanation has not been independently verified, in the tanker account filed below. The week’s run now has a count of its own: seven strikes involving six vessels in the Gulf in the period, four of them tankers hit within 13 nautical miles of Khasab over three days, including the Tara Gas, attacked twice, in the surge account filed below, which puts maritime security incidents at their highest weekly level since mid-October.

The strait’s traffic ends the week with two counts that cannot both be the traffic. Eight commercial ships crossed on Friday as of 1802 UTC, five inbound and three outbound, two of them tankers, and 47 in the last seven days, an average of 6.7 a day against 84.8 before the crisis, in the strait count filed below. The Maritime Trade Operations agency’s weekly overview reports 115 outbound and 148 inbound transits over the preceding seven days, down from 139 and 169 the week before, in the surge account—263 crossings against the strait count’s 47. The desk prints the disagreement in the Cocked Hat without resolving it: the two instruments are not counting the same strait in the same way, and the file does not say how either counts. Oil’s week closed against its day: Brent settled Friday at $92.57 a barrel, up 0.64 percent, and December West Texas Intermediate at $83.98, up 0.93 percent, in the settlement account filed below, while the week’s readings put Brent down near 5 percent and the December contract down 6.5 percent, a third straight weekly decline, in the weekly account filed below, and United States crude futures down 19.2 percent for November, in the futures account. The OPEC+ ministers meet November 29. Settled: the strike, the settlement, and the week’s direction in oil. Open: the tanker’s name and state, the weapon, the true count of the strait, and the missing men of the week’s earlier ships.

France and Spain at Midnight: A Law Passed, a Referral Promised, and a Verdict Confirmed

France’s file closed in the Senate and reopens at the Council. Senators gave final approval to the law presuming that police officers who use their weapons are acting lawfully, by 205 votes to 110, in the Paris account filed below; the law gives an officer who has shot someone the benefit of the doubt unless there is proof to the contrary. The Interior Minister, Mr. Nuñez, supports it as protection for officers in dangerous conditions; the United Nations special rapporteur on extrajudicial executions wrote ahead of the vote that the burden of disproving lawfulness should not fall on victims and their families; and the left-wing groups plan to refer the law to the Constitutional Council in a last effort to halt it, in the same account. No filing of that referral stands in the file at midnight: the referral is promised, not yet made. Settled: the vote and the text. Open: the referral, and the Council’s word.

Spain’s verdict, split on Thursday night, stands confirmed on two instruments at midnight, as the evening printed it: Mr. Feijóo the perceived winner of the debate, 51 percent to 29 percent in the Sigma Dos poll and 43 percent to 33 percent in the 40dB poll, before an audience of 10.2 million, in the Madrid account filed below. The standing instruments show an advantage for a bloc of the People’s Party and Vox; no post-debate voting-intention poll stands in the file. The second debate stands agreed for about November 26, and Spain votes November 29. Settled: the verdict. Open: whether it moves the vote.

The Air at Midnight: The Week Ends Without Its Root Cause

The week’s Washington promise stands unkept at the midnight stamp, as it stood at the evening’s. The Federal Aviation Administration said on Thursday that the government expected to announce this week the root cause of the November 13 ground stop; Friday’s file contains no announcement, and the week that contained the promise has now closed. The narrowed field stands as the evening printed it: a radar site at Amarillo, Texas, and a radio site at El Dorado, Arkansas, where the contractor L3Harris had been installing a new router in a copper-to-fibre upgrade; data flooding the network at 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilising 17 of the 22 en route centres, in the funding account filed below; the two routers at a laboratory in Florida for examination, and no evidence of a cyberattack, in the week account filed below. Secretary Duffy’s formulation remains the file’s firmest: the installation or the router was the bad actor. The installations stand paused and the new routers’ broadcasting function disabled. Congress is questioning the Secretary’s $50 billion modernisation request while the inquiry proceeds, in the funding account, and the Senate Commerce Committee is owed its technical answers by November 23—the first date of the Thanksgiving travel week, which now stands directly ahead of the unanswered question. Settled: the equipment, the two sites, and the precaution. Open: the root cause itself, a week and a day outstanding.

The Week Ahead: A Short Market Week, a Certification, and Two Votes

Saturday carries the paper’s Culture Feature, in the FT Weekend manner, and the Overnight Watch collects at 0400. The futures reopen Sunday at 1800 Eastern. The week ahead is short in New York—Dell’s earnings, the second estimate of the product, and the PCE reading, with the markets closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and closing at 1300 on Friday—and full elsewhere: the Senate Commerce Committee’s technical answers on the ground stop, due November 23; Alaska’s certification on November 25; Spain’s second debate, about November 26, and its vote on November 29; the OPEC+ ministers on November 29; the French left’s referral of the police law to the Constitutional Council; the Federal Reserve’s decision on December 8 and 9; the end of government funding after December 11; and the Bank of Japan’s decision on December 18. The Midnight Watch collects at 0000.

Institute for the Study of War — Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 20, 2026

Russian forces launched the largest missile and drone strike of November 2026 against Ukraine on the night of November 19 to 20, targeting critical infrastructure and bridges in Kyiv: 27 ballistic missiles, 84 cruise missiles and 404 strike drones, the largest package of the month. Ukrainian officials reported strikes on energy production and transmission lines, logistics infrastructure and defence-industrial facilities across at least 15 oblasts and Kyiv City, and damage to the Podilsko-Voskresensky, Darnytskyi and Southern bridges; the Kyiv authorities resumed restricted traffic across the damaged bridges. Russian forces fired missiles and drones into Polish airspace during the strikes: a Kh-101 missile crashed near Nowy Lipowiec, a second missile, possibly a Kh-101, near Rudnik nad Sanem, and a jet-powered drone, possibly a Geran-5, near Molodycz. Polish and allied aircraft were scrambled and ground-based radar activated; as many as 11 missiles and drones in Ukrainian airspace were identified as potential threats to Polish airspace. The Polish operational commander said Poland and the alliance did not try to down the missiles and the drone because the conditions did not meet the rules of engagement. The assessment holds that the violations were timed to a Coalition of the Willing exercise in Poland.
