The Claude chatbot maker's shares were down about 5 percent in post-market trading, while crypto perpetual futures on the Hyperliquid blockchain indicated a similar decline. That followed a debut in which the shares closed with a 17 percent gain from the initial public offering price, after rising as much as 39 percent shortly after the open. The offering raised a record $107.3 billion.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — Anthropic shares fall 5% in after-hours after record $107.3 billion IPO

Anthropic PBC shares were down about 5 per cent in post-market trading as the artificial intelligence developer wrapped up its first day as a public company after a record-setting $107.3 billion offering. The late moves pared a debut pop of 17 per cent on Thursday, which provided a rare bright spot as the Nasdaq fell 2.2 per cent. Anthropic closed at $97.17 Thursday in New York, paring an opening surge that took it as much as 39 per cent above the IPO price of $83.

Subjective
Kotak Neo — Anthropic's Blockbuster Nasdaq Debut Loses Shine as Apple's Rival AI Plans Send Shares Lower After Hours

Anthropic shares fell more than 3 percent in after-hours trading on Thursday, November 19, 2026, following reports that Apple is developing a rival artificial intelligence agent. The decline came shortly after the Claude maker completed its record Nasdaq debut, closing at $97.17 per share with a fully diluted valuation of approximately $1.77 trillion. The stock, which trades under the ticker ANT, had opened at $111.50, up 34.34 percent from its initial public offering price of $83. Anthropic shares climbed to an intraday high of $115.10 before losing much of their early gains and ending the regular session 17.07 percent above the issue price. The stock came under further pressure in extended trading after Bloomberg reported that Apple was recruiting engineers to develop an autonomous AI assistant capable of performing tasks across applications and websites. Anthropic shares were trading at $95.38, down 1.84 percent from Thursday's closing price, at around 5:13 pm Eastern Time, according to Benzinga. Subsequent market reports indicated that the decline had widened to more than 3 percent, with Investing.com reporting a fall of nearly 4 percent later in the evening.

Subjective
The Wall Street Journal — Anthropic Shares Drop in After-Hours Trading

Anthropic shares are off about 2 percent in the after-hours session, trading around $95.30.

Subjective
KuCoin — Anthropic IPO Surpasses Expectations with 17% Surge on Nasdaq Debut

Anthropic shares finished the session at $97.17, a gain of 17.07 percent. Anthropic shares traded between $92.72 and $115.10 during the session. Benzinga Pro data showed Anthropic shares declining 4.70 percent to $92.60 in after-hours trading.

Subjective
TipRanks — Anthropic IPO Fails to Lift Market Sentiment

Futures on the Nasdaq-100, the S&P 500 Index, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were down 1.10 percent, 0.51 percent, and 0.23 percent, respectively, as of 1:37 a.m. EST on November 20. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq each fell by more than 2 percent on Thursday, and 460 S&P 500 stocks ended in the red. On Friday, traders will be watching for November's final reading of the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment report.

Subjective
Stocktwits — Why Are Nasdaq, Dow, S&P 500 Futures Trading Lower After Anthropic's Debut?

U.S. stock futures slipped overnight late Thursday as broader markets faced pressure following Anthropic's record debut on Nasdaq. As of 9:21 p.m. EST, Dow futures fell 0.24 percent, while the S&P 500 futures declined 0.21 percent and Nasdaq-100 futures slumped 0.59 percent. On Thursday, the three U.S. benchmark indexes closed lower. The Nasdaq Composite led the decline, shedding 550 points to end the session down 2.25 percent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed 2.19 percent lower and the S&P 500 fell 2.02 percent. On Friday, traders will be watching for November's final reading of the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment report.

Subjective
TradingView, carried from CNBC TV18 — US futures offered no relief as S&P 500 contracts dipped

US futures offered no relief as S&P 500 contracts dipped 0.1 percent after the index suffered its longest slide since 2024, while Nasdaq 100 contracts lost 0.3 percent after the gauge closed at its lowest level since April. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq each fell by more than 2 percent, and 460 S&P 500 stocks ended in the red.

Subjective
Reuters — Oil prices edge higher as Houthi attacks on Riyadh raise supply concerns

Oil prices edged higher on Friday, though set for a weekly decline, as concerns over supply disruptions grew following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures rose 24 cents, or 0.3 percent, to $92.22 a barrel by 0118 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate futures for December climbed 19 cents, or 0.2 percent, to $83.40 a barrel, while the more-active January contract gained 20 cents, or 0.2 percent, to $82.64. Both benchmarks settled little changed on Thursday but Brent is set for a 3.5 percent decline for the week while the December WTI contract is set for a 6 percent weekly drop as expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels. Brent and WTI are set to fall for the third week in a row. Two oil tankers also hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and “exploded” and “are burning”, Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement carried by state media on Thursday. OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29.

Subjective
FXStreet — WTI steadies above $82.50 as Middle East tensions offset surplus supply outlook

West Texas Intermediate, the US crude oil benchmark, is trading around $82.75 during the early Asian trading hours on Friday. WTI holds steady as reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz offset pressure from rising US crude inventories and forecasts for a global oil surplus. Iran's navy said in a statement that two oil tankers hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday and “exploded.” Meanwhile, the Iran-aligned Houthi movement also fired missiles at the Saudi Arabian capital Riyadh. Overnight, Deutsche Bank points out that “oil prices have stabilised after the New York Times reported that President Trump was considering plans for further strikes on Iran, although he was yet to make a decision.”

Subjective
Hormuz.now — Strait of Hormuz News Today: Latest Status Update (20 Nov 2026)

On 20 November 2026, 1 AIS-visible commercial ship has crossed the Strait of Hormuz so far, 1 inbound into the Gulf, 0 outbound, 0 tankers, as of 05:48 UTC. The 7-day average is 5.9 a day, about 7 percent of normal. Yesterday, on 19 November 2026, 6 commercial ships crossed, 5 inbound, 1 outbound, 3 tankers. In the last 7 days, 41 crossings, 18 inbound, 23 outbound, including 11 tankers and 0 LNG or LPG carriers. The most recent crossing detected was GUAN YUAN FU XING, a bulk carrier, inbound into the Gulf, at 20 Nov 2026, 00:30 UTC. Status: Restricted, severely restricted. AIS-visible commercial traffic is about 7 percent of normal: 5.9 a day over the past week, against 84.8 before the crisis.

Subjective
Skardu Times — Iran's Guards say oil supertanker sinks in Strait of Hormuz

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Sunday that a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil sank in the Strait of Hormuz after striking a naval mine, an announcement with no independent confirmation that, if true, would be one of the largest vessel losses in the waterway since Tehran began restricting traffic there. The Guards said two oil tankers travelling on what it called an unauthorised route in the southern part of the strait hit mines and caught fire. One of these vessels, a super tanker carrying over two million barrels of crude oil, sank in the southern waters of the Persian Gulf. It gave neither the names nor the flags of the ships. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said on Sunday it was aware of a report by Indian shipping authorities of an attack on a tanker in the Gulf, but it was unclear whether that was the same incident the Guards had announced. UKMTO said the crew were safe and that the damage and environmental impact were unknown.

Subjective
Splash247 — Fresh tanker strike adds to bloody week in Hormuz

Another tanker has been struck in the Strait of Hormuz, the latest in an escalating series of attacks on merchant shipping that has left two seafarers missing and more than a dozen injured this week. UK Maritime Trade Operations issued a fresh warning overnight after receiving reports that an unidentified tanker was hit by a projectile in its engine room while sailing out of the strait on Wednesday evening. The incident occurred approximately six nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, at 16.45 GMT. All crew were reported safe and accounted for, although the extent of the damage and any environmental impact remain unknown. The latest attack follows confirmation from Abu Dhabi's ADNOC Logistics & Services that one of its tankers was struck on Tuesday evening, leaving one seafarer missing and 11 injured. This is the second time the Navig8 Messi has been attacked in four months, with some 18 confirmed attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz this month alone.

Subjective
Daily Baku — World

The overnight wire carries the day's items in brief: Saudi air defences destroyed two Houthi drones; the Houthis claimed drone and missile strikes on four Saudi Arabian targets; a tanker caught fire after hitting a mine east of the Strait of Hormuz; Genoa airport suspended flights after unidentified drones were detected, the airport completely suspending its operations for four hours during the night from November 19 to 20; an Israeli airstrike hit a Hezbollah missile facility in eastern Lebanon; the boat that capsized off Senegal killed four; and a 5.6-magnitude earthquake struck near New Caledonia.

Subjective
Pollar — Sánchez and Feijóo spar in TV debate before 29N vote

Pedro Sánchez and Alberto Núñez Feijóo met in a face-to-face televised debate on the evening of 19 November, lasting a little over an hour and a half. Feijóo pressed the prime minister over corruption cases, while Sánchez defended his record and the reinforcement of public services. Both camps claim victory. Feijóo reached the People's Party headquarters on Génova after midnight, where supporters, many of them young members of Nuevas Generaciones, chanted ‘Feijóo a la Moncloa’. He said he was ‘very satisfied’ with the exchange. The People's Party spokesman Borja Sémper said the debate had shown that Sánchez ‘does not have the desire’ to govern. The PSOE and the PP both presume they won, while their coalition partners criticised the exchange and Vox stayed silent. RTVE's expert panel mostly favoured Feijóo, citing his more aggressive approach and his demands for explanations about the government's record over the past eight years. Journalist Esther Palomera said Feijóo lost the debate on manners, describing him as rude, aggressive and constantly interrupting. Political scientist Ramón Espinar said Sánchez had in effect not appeared in the debate, while communication expert Iván Redondo said it was anything but inspiring and gave no winner, calling it totally bland. Feijóo is scheduled to be in the Canary Islands on 20 November and at the Valencia bullring on 21 November. The general election takes place on 29 November.

Subjective
Outono — Sánchez's downfall: the faces at Ferraz and as many as four socialist media outlets confirm it

The account says the debate was a disaster for the Socialist leader, and that even left-leaning media outlets sympathetic to his government acknowledge it. According to a poll by Eldiario.es, Feijóo emerged as the winner, polling at 53 percent. Feijóo also won the poll conducted by Elplural.com, by an even wider margin than in the Eldiario.es survey. Feijóo also comes out on top in the Cadena SER poll. In the socialist-aligned newspaper El País, seven analysts declare Feijóo the winner over Sánchez; not one names Sánchez. The account says no remotely credible election poll has predicted a victory for the left in this election, and that every poll points to an absolute majority for the combined forces of the People's Party and Vox.

Subjective
Dainik Jagran — Spain Election 2026: Sanchez Faces Feijoo in Heated Debate

The high-profile confrontation came just 10 days before Spain's November 29 general election, with both leaders seeking to strengthen their political positions. According to a PF Global poll conducted for POLITICO, the People's Party was projected to receive 29.5 per cent of the vote, compared with 27.2 per cent for Sanchez's Socialist Workers' Party. Spain's Congress of Deputies has 350 seats, and a party or coalition requires at least 176 seats to secure an outright parliamentary majority. The projections indicated approximately 130 seats for the PP, 110 for the PSOE and 63 for the far-right Vox party, potentially making coalition negotiations essential.

Subjective
Demócrata — 29N Survey: PP and Vox add up to 192 seats, according to 40dB

PP and Vox maintain a clear absolute majority ten days ahead of the general elections on 29 November, according to the daily tracking by 40dB for El País and the Cadena SER published this Thursday. The poll, released hours before the face-to-face between Pedro Sánchez and Alberto Núñez Feijóo, gives the conservatives 32.2 percent of the votes and 134 seats if their coalition with UPN is included, while Vox would obtain 17.6 percent and 58 deputies. Between the two parties they would add up to 192 seats, 16 more than the 176 needed for an absolute majority. The PSOE stands at 30.2 percent and 120 seats. The parties that have supported Sánchez's government would total 155. Sánchez surpasses Feijóo as preferred president: 31.8 percent of those surveyed prefer the socialist candidate, compared with 23.1 percent who choose the popular leader. The turnout estimated by 40dB is around 69 percent, below the 75 percent target that Sánchez has defended during his campaign events.

Subjective
Reuters — Trump pardons late baseball legend Pete Rose for tax crimes

President Donald Trump said on Thursday he had pardoned late baseball legend Pete Rose for tax crimes, the latest part of an effort to rehabilitate the reputation of Major League Baseball's all-time leader in hits. Trump announced the pardon in a social media post. Rose died in 2024 at age 83. The next year, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred posthumously lifted his ban from the sport after prodding from Trump, who has repeatedly called for him to be enshrined in the Hall of Fame. Earlier in November, Trump said he would consider a pardon for Rose. In his Thursday social media post announcing the pardon, Trump called Rose “a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND.”

Subjective
USA Today — Trump gives a posthumous pardon to baseball hit leader Pete Rose

President Donald Trump gave a posthumous pardon to baseball icon Pete Rose, the sport's hit leader who was convicted of cheating on his taxes and kept out of the National Baseball Hall of Fame. “I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND, whose record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken,” Trump said in a social media post. Rose, baseball's career hits leader at 4,256, entered guilty pleas on April 20, 1990, to two counts of filing false tax returns, admitting he failed to report $354,968 during a four-year period. MLB commissioner Rob Manfred posthumously removed Rose from the ineligible list in May 2025 and later acknowledged that Trump urging him to do so in an April meeting at the White House influenced his decision. Rose is now eligible for Hall of Fame consideration. As a player whose contributions largely came before 1980, he will be under consideration by the 12-person Classic Baseball Committee. The group will next vote in December 2027 for induction in July 2028.

entry.title: Thursday Closes With Wall Street Down Two Percent After Anthropic's Debut Reverses, the Senate Rejecting the Iran War-Powers Resolution, and the Spanish Debate Ending Without a Clear Winner While the Strait's Fire Comes Under Control
entry.summary: The midnight file for Friday, November 20, 2026: what Thursday settled and what it left open. Wall Street closed down about two percent after Anthropic's debut reversed from a $111.50 first trade to a $97.17 close; the Senate rejected the Iran war-powers resolution 51 to 48; the Justice Department moved to drop its Alaska suit as Ms. Peltola's count stood at 144,486; the Spanish debate ended without a clear winner; and the fire aboard the Tara Gas came under control with one seafarer still missing. Collected at 0000.
entry.content:
The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Thursday Closes With Wall Street Down Two Percent After Anthropic’s Debut Reverses, the Senate Rejecting the Iran War-Powers Resolution, and the Spanish Debate Ending Without a Clear Winner While the Strait’s Fire Comes Under Control

The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: a debut that opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17 on a day the indexes fell two percent; a war-powers vote that failed 51 to 48; a lawsuit the government moved to drop the day after the race was decided; a debate in Madrid that ended without a winner; and a fire in the strait brought under control, with one man still missing.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Friday, November 20, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 65, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Thursday, in Edition No. 64, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Thursday, in Edition No. 63, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Thursday, and in Edition No. 62, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 on Thursday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Thursday Settled, What It Left Open

Thursday settled the market’s direction, the Senate’s answer on war powers, the Alaska lawsuit’s end, and the Spanish debate’s lack of a winner — and left the rest of the file where the evening left it. Wall Street closed down about two percent after Anthropic’s debut reversed from a $111.50 first trade to a $97.17 close, in the close account filed below. The Senate rejected the Iran war-powers resolution, 51 to 48, in the vote account filed below. The Justice Department moved to drop its suit to bar certification of Ms. Peltola’s Senate victory in Alaska, in the filing account filed below. The debate in Madrid ended without a clear winner, in the verdict account filed below. The fire aboard the Tara Gas came under control, in the tanker account filed below, with one seafarer still missing. What the day left open is the rest of the file: the French Senate’s bill, the trade truce’s length, the strait’s missing men, the Kerch Bridge’s repairs, and the Federal Aviation Administration’s promised root cause. The desk takes the files in that order.

The Markets at Midnight: A Morning Bought, an Afternoon Sold, and a Debut That Closed Seventeen Percent Up

The evening file carried the reversal; the midnight file carries its measure. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,101.11 points, or 2.19 percent, to 49,097.06; the S&P 500 lost 147.80 points, or 2.02 percent, to 7,175.83; and the Nasdaq Composite sank 550.69 points, or 2.25 percent, to 23,879.20, in the close account above, after the Nasdaq had been up 2.1 percent at its high shortly after the opening bell and traded in a range of more than four percentage points. The S&P 500’s fall is its sixth straight loss. The volatility index rose 15.8 percent to 28.44. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 5.051 percent, the two-year to 4.777 percent and the 30-year to 5.400 percent, and gold futures fell $54.70 to $3,682.10 an ounce. The Russell 2000 retreated 2.2 percent, and the indexes hit fresh multimonth lows, in the futures account filed below.

The debut is the day’s event, and its arc is the market’s in miniature. Anthropic priced 980 million shares at $83 on Wednesday, raising about $81 billion. The first trade crossed at $111.50, about 34 percent above the offering price, just before midday; the shares reached a high of $115.10 and closed at $97.17, up $14.17, or 17.07 percent, on the offering price, in the close account and the futures account. Volume passed 813 million shares. At the open the company was valued at about $2.01 trillion on a fully diluted basis; at the close one reading puts the value at about $1.3 trillion, in the close account, against about $1.7 trillion fully diluted in the evening file — the desk prints the disagreement in the Cocked Hat, on different share counts. After hours the shares fell about 5 percent in extended trade, in the futures account, with the level unsettled between readings. The rest of the board fell with the indexes. Nvidia closed at $145.98, down $4.98, or 3.30 percent, in the company account filed below, despite record fiscal third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103 percent year over year, and a forecast of about $130 billion for the fourth quarter; Morgan Stanley trimmed its price target to $260 while keeping an Overweight rating, and the November 12 resignation of Mr. Huang continued to weigh on the shares. AMD closed at $489.19, down 7.72 percent, after Hunterbrook announced it was short the company over potential China export-control violations, and Broadcom closed at $346.65, down 2.09 percent. Walmart closed at $126.04, down 1.04 percent, after its earnings beat, in the earnings account filed below: adjusted earnings of $0.65 a share against $0.64 expected, revenue of $188.84 billion, and full-year guidance raised to $2.84 to $2.89 a share. Williams-Sonoma was the worst performer in the S&P 500, in the retailer account filed below, closing at $220.66, down 15.16 percent, after Pottery Barn’s comparable revenue grew 1.8 percent against 5.1 percent in the second quarter; United States pending home sales fell 4.7 percent in October from September, the lowest level on record.

For the Federal Reserve, the day’s new statement is a bank’s forecast, not the bank’s. J.P. Morgan said on Thursday it expects quarter-point hikes in December, January and March, taking the rate to 4.50 to 4.75 percent by March, in the forecast account filed below, joining Bank of America and Deutsche Bank in expecting three consecutive hikes; the market prices a December hike at near-certain, a quarter point, with an 8 percent chance of a half point. Overnight, Dow futures were little changed, S&P 500 futures fell 0.15 percent and Nasdaq-100 futures lost 0.35 percent, in the futures account. Settled: the close, the debut’s arc, and the beat that sold. Open: whether the reversal is the week’s turn or its pause, and what the shares do after hours.

Washington at Midnight: The War-Powers Vote, the Suit Dropped, and a Cause Still Promised

The Senate rejected the Iran war-powers resolution on Thursday, the first Iran vote in either chamber since the November 3 midterms. The resolution, which had passed the House, failed 51 to 48 in the vote account above; three Republicans voted for it — Senators Collins of Maine, Murkowski of Alaska and Paul of Kentucky — and Senator Fetterman of Pennsylvania was the only Democrat to vote against it. Senator Murphy of Connecticut did not vote. The resolution was H.Con.Res.93, passed by the House on September 15 by 220 to 204. Senator Kaine of Virginia said the midterm result reflected Americans’ unhappiness about the war and higher prices for food, fuel and other goods linked to the conflict. The war began February 28, in the vote account.

In Alaska, the government moved on Thursday to end its own case. Justice Department attorneys urged the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to declare the suit to block certification of Ms. Peltola’s victory moot, and to vacate the lower court’s dismissal and remand for dismissal on that ground, two days after the race was decided, in the filing account above. The challenge centred on a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican Senator Dan Sullivan; the Alaska Supreme Court had already ruled the second Sullivan’s candidacy is legal. The updated count in the filing account stands at Ms. Peltola 144,486 votes, 50.13 percent, against 131,965, 45.79 percent, for Senator Sullivan, with Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. at 4,765, 1.65 percent, on 401 of 401 precincts reporting and 290,323 voters cast of 605,433 registered, 47.95 percent — against about 144,302 and 50.12 percent in the evening file, a difference the desk prints in the Cocked Hat. Ms. Peltola is the Democrats’ 56th senator and their ninth Senate pickup of the midterms. Certification is scheduled for November 25. The court had not ruled on the mootness request by midnight, and Mr. Sullivan has not conceded. In the House race, Mr. Begich won the ranked-choice tabulation on Wednesday evening, 51.35 percent to 48.65 percent over the independent Mr. Hill, in the House account filed below: the final round stood at 140,346 to 132,961, with Mr. Hafner taking 22,715 first-choice votes, 7.92 percent, and 11,465 of his voters’ ballots exhausted when he was eliminated. Mr. Hill conceded on Wednesday night.

In the House, Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky spent an hour on the floor on Thursday under a rarely used rule that lets a member respond to attacks on his integrity, reading Speaker Mike Johnson’s denials aloud and accusing him of blocking the push to release the Epstein files, in the floor account filed below. A week earlier Mr. Johnson accused Mr. Massie of a “political stunt,” a day after Mr. Massie’s petition to force a vote on a second Epstein files bill reached 218 signatures. Mr. Massie said Mr. Johnson refused to schedule the Epstein Files Transparency Act and refuses to schedule the second bill, and that the House session was cut a day short, delaying the vote. Mr. Johnson called the first bill “reckless” in July 2025, then voted for it when it passed 427 to 1. Mr. Massie said his bill requires redactions to protect victims, their families and survivors, and that the Justice Department has committed to withholding 3 million files; he said $32 million was spent against him, that he lost his primary after President Donald Trump campaigned against him, and that he leaves Congress January 3. The account attributes its primary reporting to another outlet, and the desk files it as a secondary account.

In the air, the week’s root cause is promised, not yet delivered. The Federal Aviation Administration’s administrator said on Thursday that the government expects to announce this week the root cause of the router outage that led to the nationwide ground stop on Friday, November 13, which disrupted more than 18,000 flights and a million passengers, in the aviation account filed below. The Transportation Secretary has said a Juniper router installed by L3Harris in a remote Arkansas facility triggered the nearly five-hour stop, the longest since September 11, 2001, and the FAA has paused Juniper router installations while testing continues. The administrator said the FTI network that L3Harris has operated since 2002 was in desperate need of replacement, calling it a patchwork, archaic federal telephone network, and that 68 prior Juniper router installations had not led to any problems. The Secretary has asked Congress for another $50 billion for air traffic control and airport upgrades, against $12.5 billion approved last year. The Senate Commerce Committee is owed its technical answers by November 23. Settled: the vote, the suit’s end, and the House race. Open: the certification, the court’s ruling on the mootness request, and the router’s verdict.

Shenzhen and Berlin at Midnight: A Declaration With Four Points, a Call Told Four Ways, and a Bridge Struck a Third Time

The day’s first room has now been read in full, and its text is shorter than its occasion. The three presidents met in Shenzhen on Thursday in the first trilateral talks among the three countries, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, in the summit account filed below. The talks lasted 90 minutes in that account, against about an hour in a second and 80 minutes including 10 minutes of opening remarks in a third — the desk prints the disagreement in the Cocked Hat. The joint statement, the declaration text filed below, pledges a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation, reform of the United Nations, increased production and supply of refined petroleum products, and the principle of state consent and the immunities of state officials, with the International Criminal Court and similar bodies not to abuse their jurisdiction. It names neither Ukraine nor Iran, sets no arsenal cuts and no timetable, and announces no lifting of sanctions. The three leaders reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. President Xi, according to Chinese state media, described nuclear weapons as “the sword of Damocles hanging over humanity.” Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported the Korean Peninsula situation was discussed, along with Ukraine and the Middle East, in the Seoul account filed below, though the declaration itself makes no reference to North Korea’s nuclear programme. The President, speaking to NBC after the meeting, rated the summit a 12 on a scale of zero to 10, and said on his way back to Washington that it was a great and highly consequential trip, with a news conference to come at noon on Friday, in the return account filed below. He told NBC that he and President Xi discussed artificial intelligence and agreed on guardrails “at least on a minimal basis,” and, asked about President Zelensky’s exclusion, said he would not make decisions about Ukraine’s future without Kyiv’s input. The APEC leaders adopted by consensus the 2026 Leaders’ Declaration, issued as the Shenzhen Outlook, with three outcome documents on trade, connectivity and innovation, in the APEC account filed below; China announced $20 million for APEC practical cooperation, and Vietnam will host APEC in 2027. On the trade truce, no new extension was reported on Thursday: the file stands at the November 9 extension, with the truce as agreed running to January 10, 2027.

Berlin’s reply stands as the evening printed it, and the call to Berlin has now been told a fourth way. The joint statement by Germany, France, Britain and Ukraine called on Russia to agree to an energy ceasefire throughout the winter and to a ceasefire allowing food exports from the Black Sea region, in the Berlin account filed below, and reaffirmed 70 billion euros in military assistance in 2026 and at least the equivalent in 2027, with legally binding security guarantees, defensive in nature and closely coordinated with the United States. The President telephoned the meeting from Air Force One, and the late account, published at 20:57 Eastern and filed in the call account below, adds a fourth telling: three officials said he voiced strong doubts about the coalition committing billions more to Ukraine; another participant described his remarks as general in nature, stressing the death toll and urging governments to stop pouring money into the conflict; two participants in a separate account described an angry outburst, and a third a savings argument. Against all of them stands Prime Minister Burnham’s denial, carried in the evening file, that the call ran that way at all. Chancellor Merz said at the joint press conference that funding for Ukraine’s defence was intended “to enable peace negotiations in the first place and to conduct them from a position of strength,” and said: “We are not providing this strong support to prolong the war. We want to end this war.” Mr. Kushner said Mr. Trump came away believing that peace is achievable. President Macron said the allies should reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to NATO. Settled: the declaration’s text, Berlin’s text, and the disagreement about the call. Open: the truce’s length, the talks’ date, and the guarantees’ shape.

The war did not wait for either room, and the bridge is the day’s third front. A third Ukrainian aerial attack in four days on the Kerch Bridge halted rail traffic on Thursday, in the bridge account filed below, after strikes on November 16 and 17 shut down the road section. Some rail traffic resumed on Thursday afternoon, according to Russia’s transport ministry, and Russian officials said it will take about a week to determine how long repairs will last. Ukraine’s General Staff said it used Neptune coastal missiles and damaged the railway section, and Ukraine’s Defence Ministry said hits were confirmed near the arch and the railway tracks. President Putin, at his press conference in Shenzhen, said that after the strike on the bridge there would be no agreement on a ceasefire or on not hitting energy infrastructure, and that Russia’s response would be “much more painful” than what Kyiv had done. He said the crossing is used only for civilian purposes and not to transport military equipment or petroleum products, and said he had ordered the bridge closed to the transport of military hardware — against the accounts that describe it as a key military supply route. Russia’s Investigative Committee opened a criminal terrorism probe into the damage.

The day’s strikes ran wider than the bridge. Russia launched anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine, with hits recorded at 18 locations, and a daytime drone attack on Kyiv killed one person, a 26-year-old man in the Podilskyi district, and injured five, in the Kyiv account filed below; the Dutch and Austrian embassies were damaged, St. Volodymyr’s Cathedral had its cornices damaged, and cars and a security post were damaged. A second death is reported in the Kyiv region, outside the city, in the bridge account. Russia said it hit two power substations in Odesa, a fuel storage facility in Chornomorsk and a cargo ship bound for Odesa, and a substation in Sumy. Settled: the third strike, the vow, and the day’s dead. Open: the repairs’ length, and what the promised response strikes.

The Gulf at Midnight: A Fire Under Control, Fourteen Attacks in Nineteen Days, and a Decision Deferred to January

Thursday added no new strike to the Gulf file, and the desk records the quiet as a quiet — with one tower struck in Riyadh. The fire aboard the Tara Gas is under control, two days after the Panama-flagged LPG tanker was hit in the engine room by a drone on November 16, in the tanker account above. The ship has been brought into a sheltered bay west of Shishah, on the basis of a heat signature detectable on thermal imaging yesterday but now dampened down, attended by the anchor handling tug Valiant Vortex. Twenty-four of 25 crew have been rescued, two injured sailors taken to Khasab Hospital, and one crew member remains missing. No new statement on Thursday from Oman, India, Iran or the operator was found in the file. The Guards’ claim of two supertankers struck by mines stands uncorroborated and unnamed, as the evening printed it, and a shipping monitor’s note that the figures match a claim from November 12 stands beside it. The crew count on the attacked ADNOC tanker stands unresolved: the company said one missing and 11 injured; India’s shipping minister said all crew are safe and accounted for; Jordan’s foreign ministry says its sailor, Mr. Al-Otaibi, is still missing.

The month’s count now has a number. Iran has mounted about 14 attacks on vessels in and near the Strait of Hormuz in the first 19 days of November, according to a United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations count cited by Bloomberg, in the Hormuz account filed below, including limpet mines, naval mines and anti-ship cruise missiles, which an unnamed American official described as “far more lethal than drones,” following the collapse of Muscat-hosted diplomacy between Iran and Oman on November 17. Brent crude futures have fallen approximately one-fifth in November, and total Middle East oil flows have largely recovered to near pre-war levels through alternative routes and ship-to-ship transfers. IMF PortWatch recorded just 11 tanker transits through Hormuz between November 1 and 15 — an average of 0.7 per day, compared with 665 in the same period of 2025, a 98 percent fall. Hormuz-specific flows fell from about 13.4 million to about 10 million barrels per day in the first 10 days of November. About 80 mines remain in the strait’s historic shipping lanes. Oil settled on Thursday at Brent $91.98 a barrel, up $0.03, and West Texas Intermediate $83.21, down $0.05, its lowest since August 26, in the oil account filed below, after moving through a roughly $2 range; nationwide crude inventories rose by 3.4 million barrels last week. The International Energy Agency said on Thursday that the war could reshape global energy markets for years.

On the question of strikes, the President said on Thursday that he is not rushing. He told Axios aboard Air Force One: “I am not rushing into any decision [on Iran]. We will see what happens after the beginning of the year,” in the decision account filed below, and he has not authorised another major operation. The New York Times reported that Prime Minister Netanyahu is pushing for a joint operation lasting four to seven days, citing concerns that Iran is rebuilding missile and drone capabilities and advancing chemical and biological weapons programs, and Mr. Netanyahu reportedly told Israeli security officials on Wednesday evening that an operation against Iran was “unavoidable.” The White House has requested Pentagon and intelligence assessments of how Iran might retaliate against American strike scenarios, particularly against Gulf oil and natural gas infrastructure, and potential targets under consideration include Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear complex. Iran said it will not engage on the nuclear weapons issue until the question of the Strait of Hormuz is settled. Inflation in Iran exceeds 90 percent and the rial is plunging, in the decision account.

In Riyadh, the tallest skyscraper in the capital was struck on Thursday. A Houthi attack on a tower in the King Abdullah Financial District caused material damage to several floors and nearby buildings, with no injuries reported, in the Riyadh account filed below; the statement did not identify the tower, but a photograph published by the state news agency showed the PIF Tower, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, its windows blown out across seven to eight floors. The Houthis said they had targeted the financial centre twice on Thursday, first at dawn and again in the evening, and also said they had attacked King Khalid International Airport, Khamis Mushait airbase and a petrochemical company in Jubail; there was no immediate Saudi confirmation of those other attacks. This was the second time in less than two weeks that a Houthi attack damaged a landmark in Riyadh’s financial district, with Aramco’s building hit in a November 8 attack. Saudi aircraft carried out airstrikes on Sanaa early on Thursday. Saudi officials now foresee the campaign stretching on for up to six months. In Gaza, the Israeli military said on Thursday it had completed its ground operation north of the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza and reopened Salah al-Din Street, in the Gaza account filed below; about 6,000 people had fled their homes on Wednesday. Four Palestinians were killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza City on Thursday. More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to an AFP tally, and the Israeli military says seven of its soldiers and one civilian contractor have been killed in the same period. The Board of Peace, in its first annual assessment delivered to the Security Council on Tuesday, warned that the agreement risks collapse if its terms are not fully implemented, in the Board account filed below: “A ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely.” At the centre of the stall is the technocratic civil administration the board created to run Gaza on an interim basis, which Israel has still not allowed to take up its job. Settled: the fire under control, the oil settlement, and the decision deferred. Open: the missing men, the mines, and the January question.

The World at Midnight: A Debate Without a Winner, a Vote Delayed, a Court’s Word Answered, and Two Counts Unresolved

Spain’s Thursday is one room, and at the midnight stamp the room has finished talking without choosing a winner. Mr. Sánchez and Mr. Feijóo faced each other at 10 p.m. Madrid time in the only head-to-head debate before the general election on November 29, in the verdict account above. El Plural said it ended “without a clear winner” amid accusations of disinformation and dirty tactics. A Sociómetro quick poll of 1,019 people, non-representative, put Mr. Sánchez ahead 58 percent to 42 percent; pre-debate polling averages had Mr. Sánchez about five points behind. Housing dominated, mentioned more than 20 times by each man, in the debate account filed below; Mr. Sánchez mentioned Vox or Mr. Abascal at least 16 times, and Mr. Feijóo interrupted Mr. Sánchez on more than 29 occasions, 10 in the social-policy block. In the defence block Mr. Sánchez put the cost of Mr. Feijóo’s 5 percent of GDP defence commitment at €80 billion a year. Mr. Sánchez in his golden minute: “Spain does not bow to powerful forces” and “Vote with all your soul and all your strength.” Mr. Feijóo: the country “knows how to manage” and “needs a change.” Mr. Sánchez afterwards told Socialist Party members at Ferraz that the debate was “good politics and poor education.” A second debate has been agreed for around November 26.

France’s Thursday ends with its bill still unvoted. The Senate delayed a final vote on the police firearms bill until Friday after left-wing senators used procedural tactics to extend debate past a Thursday night deadline, in the Senate account filed below; the government secured an emergency slot on Friday’s agenda, with 76 amendments still on the table. Senators from the Socialist, Ecologist, and La France Insoumise groups said they would jointly refer the bill to the Constitutional Council if adopted. The Interior Minister, Mr. Nuñez, accused the left of “obstruction” and said the presumption “will simply lift the automatic custody of the police officer or gendarme who used their weapon.” A senator of the left said that tomorrow it will no longer be for the officer to justify his shot, but for the courts and the families to prove he should not have fired. Outside the Senate, several hundred opponents gathered, and a mock cemetery of 35 tombs was installed before the Luxembourg Gardens gates, representing as many victims of fatal police shootings since 2017, according to the organisers. A petition against the bill has gathered more than 700,000 signatures in this account, against 732,086 in the evening file. The retirees marched in Paris from the Montparnasse station forecourt to Place Vauban near Les Invalides, in the march account filed below; the organisers had aimed for about 30,000 in Paris, and no final turnout figure was found in the sources read — the only figure in the file is “more than a thousand people.” The Senate adopted its version of the Social Security budget on Wednesday, November 18, by 201 votes to 124, with 15 abstentions.

The Hague’s word on Myanmar drew its first answers on Thursday. The International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar’s security forces’ killings and widespread sexual violence against the Rohingya in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide — the first time the court has held a state responsible for genocide. The reactions stand in the reactions account filed below: the UN human rights chief, Mr. Türk, said “This judgment clearly concludes the State of Myanmar stands responsible for one of the most egregious crimes known to humankind”; Ms. Ullah, a Rohingya activist in Gambia’s delegation, said “Today is a day of justice. I am a survivor of genocide… Today the world’s highest court has looked at what was done to the Rohingya and named it for what it was. Genocide”; Sheikh Hasina said “Bangladesh played a central role in the investigations… This is a proud moment for Bangladesh.” By a majority of its 14 judges, the court found six violations of the 1948 Genocide Convention, in the ruling account filed below; the ruling runs 191 pages, the session lasted more than three hours, and the court’s estimate, supported by the evidence, is that 10,000 Rohingya were violently killed in clearance operations, 1.2 percent of the targeted population in northern Rakhine, with 392 villages destroyed and 700,000 fled in 2017. The United Kingdom’s Foreign Secretary, Mr. Miliband, announced the expulsion of Myanmar’s defence attaché and called urgently for a UN Security Council session. Gambia welcomed the ruling with “profound satisfaction”; Bangladesh urged implementation without delay; the United States said it was studying the ruling. Myanmar had not responded as of Thursday evening. Myanmar has two years to submit a report on restitution and compensation; the Court will decide the amount. The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, but the court has very limited means of enforcement.

Off Senegal, the boat’s count stands unresolved at midnight. A pirogue capsized off Yenne, south of Dakar, at about 2 a.m. local time on Wednesday, and dozens are missing, in the boat account filed below. One survivor told police about 100 people were aboard, another told Reuters about 50; bodies recovered stand at one, two and four in different accounts. Nearly 600 people have died this year trying to reach the Canary Islands from West Africa, according to the United Nations refugee agency, and nearly 8,200 migrants using the route had reached the Canary Islands in the first 12 days of November. In Bangladesh, the banned Awami League’s nationwide dawn-to-dusk lockdown brought fresh violence on Thursday, in the lockdown account filed below, with mixed success: the attempted shutdown worked mostly in the southern districts where the League is strongest, and garment workers demanding higher wages also blocked a highway into Dhaka. Police said two members of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party were killed on Wednesday night; houses of two BNP lawmakers in Gopalganj were vandalised and set alight; at least six buses and pickup vans were set on fire along with a section of railway line; crude bomb blasts were reported across six districts overnight. Ninety-seven platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh fanned out across seven districts. In Dhaka, police arrested 107 people suspected of links to the Awami League in 24 hours, including former education minister Nurul Islam Nahid — against 565 arrested in the capital in one account and 537 in another, a difference the desk prints in the Cocked Hat. Prime Minister Rahman blamed India for the unrest, without naming it: “the country across the border, where they have fled to, is their master.” At least four people have been killed over the past two days. Ms. Hasina, 79, plans to return in December; Tuesday marked a year since a court sentenced her to death.

In Brussels, the European Commission confirmed on Thursday that it was targeted by an AI-generated cyber campaign, detected on October 22 and confirmed after investigation on October 26, in the cyber account filed below. Several internal applications were taken offline as a precaution and most restored; whether staff data was compromised is not established, and the investigation has not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff. Politico, which reported the incident first, said systems taken offline included Sysper, the human resources platform for payslips and time management, and a system for medical reimbursements; other accounts add a project-management system and translation services, with more than 10 days of disruption. Politico’s sources said attackers used ARTEX, a Chinese AI penetration-testing tool; the FBI noted on November 13 that more than 1,600 ARTEX consoles were exposed to the internet. No perpetrator was named. In Copenhagen, Denmark’s parliament approved a deal with Greenland and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic, 109 to 0, in the Greenland account filed below; Greenland’s parliament approved the deal on November 3, 16 to 0 with 7 abstentions, and it enters into force once Denmark formally notifies the United States by diplomatic note. The United States can modernise and expand Pituffik Space Base in the northwest, and set up defence areas at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east; only NATO members can establish manned or unmanned military installations on Greenland; the text allows the “Golden Dome” missile-defence system. In Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia’s parliament approved the resignation of President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa after accusations by another politician in the ruling party that he had benefited financially from a government railway project seven years ago, in the Mongolia account filed below; he announced his resignation on Tuesday, denying the allegations, the vote passed with 92.3 percent of members present backing the measure, the parliamentary speaker assumes presidential duties, and a presidential election must be organised within four months. In Japan, a magnitude-5.7 earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture at about 02:22 local time, in the quake account filed below, at a depth of about 10 km, with a maximum intensity of lower 5 on Japan’s scale in five municipalities; at least two people were injured, eight Shinkansen services were suspended, affecting about 5,600 passengers, and the weather agency urged vigilance for about a week. Settled: the debate’s verdict, the Court’s word and its answers, the Greenland vote, and the resignation. Open: the boat’s count, the lockdown’s toll, and the breach’s extent.

Friday Ahead: A News Conference at Noon, a Vote in Paris, and the Root Cause’s Week

Friday carries the President’s news conference at noon at the White House, on the China trip and the trade deals with Thailand, the Philippines and others; the French Senate’s police bill, whose vote is set for Friday afternoon with 76 amendments on the table; the Spanish debate’s first polls, with a second debate agreed for around November 26; the Federal Aviation Administration’s promised root-cause announcement, expected this week; and the first full reading of Thursday’s market reversal. Alaska certifies on November 25. The Senate Commerce Committee is owed its technical answers on the ground stop by November 23. Spain votes November 29; the Federal Reserve decides December 8 and 9; government funding runs out after December 11. The Overnight Watch collects at 0400.

The Cocked Hat

Where the midnight’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On the debut’s close: about $1.3 trillion in one reading, against about $1.7 trillion fully diluted in the evening file, and $1.76 trillion and $1.77 trillion in other readings, on different share counts. On its after-hours level: down about 5 percent in extended trade in one account, $92.60, down 4.70 percent, at 20:00 Eastern in a second, and $94.93, down 2.3 percent, in a third. On the trilateral’s length: about an hour in one account, 80 minutes including 10 minutes of opening remarks in a second, about an hour and a half in a third, and 4:16 p.m. to 6:01 p.m. in a fourth. On the President’s call to Berlin: scepticism about the allies’ spending in one account, a report that President Putin wants to end the war in a second, “Enough already” in a third, the Prime Minister’s denial that the call ran that way in a fourth, and in the late account three officials on doubts about billions more against one participant on a general death-toll telling, two on an angry outburst, and one on a savings argument. On the British pledge: more than 1,000 long-range strike drones in the government’s account, 1,000 long-range cruise missiles in a second. On the bridge’s rail: halted until about 4 p.m. local time in one account, services continuing on schedule in a second, trains still able to transit in a third, and some rail traffic resumed on Thursday afternoon in a fourth. On the attacked tanker’s crew: one missing and 11 injured in the company’s account, all safe and accounted for in the Indian minister’s, and a Jordanian sailor still missing in Jordan’s account. On the Senate’s war-powers vote: 51 to 48 in one ordering, 48 to 51 in the other, the same outcome. On Alaska’s count: 144,486 votes and 50.13 percent in the November 18 summary, against about 144,302 and 50.12 percent in the evening file. On Spain: the Popular Party at 32.2 percent and 134 seats in one tracking and 28.9 percent and 118 in another, the Socialists at 30.2 percent and 120 in the first and 31.9 percent and 134 in the second, and a quick poll of 1,019 people, non-representative, at 58 to 42 for Mr. Sánchez. On Mr. Feijóo’s interruptions: more than 29 in the body of one account, 26 in its summary line. On the Senegal boat: about 100 aboard in one survivor’s account and about 50 in another’s, with one, two and four bodies recovered. On the Bangladesh arrests: 107 Awami-linked in Dhaka in 24 hours in one account, 565 in the capital in a second, 537 in a third. On the French petition: 732,086 signatures in the evening file, more than 700,000 in the late account. On the Houthi missiles: four in one account, five in another. On the December rate decision: a near-certain quarter point with an 8 percent chance of a half point in one reading, against 92 percent and 7 percent in the evening file. On Walmart’s day: down 1.04 percent to $126.04 at the close, against 1.7 percent in one account’s text. On Williams-Sonoma: down 14 percent in an intraday reading, 15.16 percent at the close. On the overnight futures: levels differing by timestamp. Inside the triangle is where the day honestly stands, and the log turns on it.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 40 items.

Subjective
The Wall Street Journal — U.S. Stocks Slide as AI Bust Continues Despite Anthropic IPO

The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,101.11 points, or 2.19 percent, to 49,097.06; the S&P 500 lost 147.80 points, or 2.02 percent, to 7,175.83; and the Nasdaq Composite sank 550.69 points, or 2.25 percent, to 23,879.20, after the Nasdaq had been up 2.1 percent at its high shortly after the opening bell and traded in a range of more than four percentage points. Anthropic rose 17 percent to $97.17 in its debut after pricing at $83, raising about $81 billion. Nvidia fell 3.3 percent to $145.98. The volatility index rose 15.8 percent to 28.44. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 5.051 percent. Gold futures fell $54.70 to $3,682.10 an ounce.

Subjective
Investor’s Business Daily — Dow Jones Futures: Techs Slide, Anthropic Retreats After Ugly Market Reversal To New Lows

Dow Jones futures were little changed overnight, while S&P 500 futures fell 0.15 percent and Nasdaq-100 futures lost 0.35 percent, with the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.02 percent in the overnight read. Anthropic began trading at $111.50 just before midday, hit $115.10, then faded to close at $97.17, up 17 percent on the $83 offering price, and fell 5 percent in extended trade. The Dow sank 2.2 percent, the S&P 500 tumbled 2 percent after initially regaining its 200-day line, the Nasdaq closed down 2.25 percent, and the Russell 2000 retreated 2.2 percent, with the indexes hitting fresh multimonth lows. AMD tumbled 7.7 percent after Hunterbrook announced it was short the company over potential China export-control violations.

Subjective
Reuters — J.P. Morgan sees Fed rate hikes at next three meetings as inflation persists

J.P. Morgan said on Thursday it expects the Federal Reserve to deliver quarter-point rate hikes in January and March 2027, on top of a previously forecast December increase, as sticky inflation keeps further tightening in play. Strategists led by Michael Feroli said the hikes are not to deliver a bad labour market but to preserve credibility when there is no compelling narrative for a pause, and that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has left the policy path without an overarching narrative. Minutes from the October 27–28 meeting, released on Wednesday, showed almost all policymakers agreed further hikes would be needed if the economy evolved as expected. Markets see a near-certain 25-basis-point increase in December and an 8 percent chance of a half-point move, according to the CME FedWatch tool. Bank of America and Deutsche Bank also expect hikes at each of the next three meetings.

Subjective
The Motley Fool — Stock Market Today, Nov. 19: Nvidia Slides as Investors Weigh CEO Transition Fallout Despite Strong Q3 Results

Nvidia closed at $145.98, down $4.98, or 3.30 percent, despite strong third-quarter results, a raised outlook and early support from Anthropic’s debut, as traders weighed the leadership change and AI spending. On November 17 Nvidia reported record fiscal third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103 percent year over year, and forecast fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of about $130 billion. Morgan Stanley trimmed its price target to $260 while keeping an Overweight rating. The November 12 resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang continued to weigh on shares, and the government tightened rules on Monday to prevent Chinese businesses from remotely accessing advanced Nvidia AI chips through overseas data centres. AMD closed at $489.19, down 7.72 percent, and Broadcom at $346.65, down 2.09 percent.

Subjective
Crypto Briefing — Walmart delivers Q3 beat, raises FY27 outlook

Walmart reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.65, above the consensus estimate of $0.64, and revenue of $188.8 billion, above estimates of about $187.3 to $187.4 billion, with third-quarter revenue up 5.2 percent. The company raised its fiscal 2027 adjusted earnings-per-share outlook to $2.84 to $2.89, from $2.80 to $2.87. Walmart U.S. net sales rose 3.6 percent to $125 billion, with comparable sales excluding fuel up 2.9 percent; global e-commerce sales grew 17 percent, Walmart U.S. e-commerce grew 23 percent, and the global advertising business grew 25 percent. The shares closed at $126.04, down 1.04 percent on the day, despite the beat and the raised outlook.

Subjective
Barron’s — Williams-Sonoma Stock Is Worst in S&P 500 Today. It’s Another Victim of the Housing Slump.

Williams-Sonoma was the worst performer in the S&P 500 on Thursday after reporting a growth slowdown at its flagship Pottery Barn brand, which makes up about 38 percent of total revenue. Comparable brand revenue for Pottery Barn grew 1.8 percent in the third quarter, up from 1.3 percent a year ago but down from 5.1 percent in the second quarter. Total same-store sales climbed 5.1 percent, missing calls for 5.6 percent growth, while West Elm same-store sales grew 7 percent. Management cited a weak housing market, elevated tariffs and high oil prices as headwinds. Total revenue grew 5.8 percent to $1.99 billion, and adjusted earnings of $2.19 a share aligned with consensus estimates. United States pending home sales fell 4.7 percent in October from September, marking the lowest level on record, according to the National Association of Realtors.

Subjective
Reuters — US Senate rejects resolution curbing Trump’s Iran war powers

Senate Republicans on Thursday rejected legislation directing President Donald Trump to end the war in Iran or obtain Congress’ approval to continue it, backing the president weeks after midterm elections largely tied to frustration with the conflict. The Senate voted 51 to 48 to defeat a war powers resolution that had previously passed the House. Only three Republicans — Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky — voted with Democrats in favour of the resolution. One Democrat, John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, voted with Republicans against it. The vote was the first time the Senate had considered a major Iran war-related measure since Democratic victories in the midterm elections on November 3. Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia said the midterm result reflected Americans’ unhappiness about the war and higher prices for food, fuel and other goods linked to the conflict.

The Associated Press, carried by WVLT — Trump administration moves to have lawsuit dismissed in challenge to Alaska’s US Senate race

The Trump administration on Thursday moved to effectively drop its lawsuit that sought to block certification of Democrat Mary Peltola’s victory in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race. Justice Department attorneys urged the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to declare the case moot, and to vacate the lower court’s dismissal and remand for dismissal on that ground, two days after the race was decided. The challenge centred on a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. The Alaska Supreme Court had already ruled the second Sullivan’s candidacy is legal. Ms. Peltola won an outright majority to become Democrats’ 56th senator, the ninth Senate pickup for the party in the midterms. Ms. Peltola said: “Now that the election is over and the voters sent a very clear message about the direction they want our state to go in, I’m eager to move forward and get to work on behalf of all Alaskans.” The department filed the suit at President Donald Trump’s direction.

Subjective
Democracy Docket — Alaska’s real spoiler wasn’t Dan Sullivan. And he helped the GOP

Alaska’s election for its lone U.S. House seat went to ranked-choice tabulation on Wednesday night after no one reached the 50 percent threshold for first-choice votes. Representative Nick Begich emerged victorious in the final round with 51.35 percent of the vote, defeating independent Bill Hill. Mr. Hill was backed by Democrats over Eric Hafner, who identified as a Democrat on the ballot, is serving a 20-year prison sentence in New York and has reportedly never been to Alaska. Mr. Hafner still received 8 percent of first-choice votes — 22,715 votes, more than the difference between Mr. Begich and Mr. Hill. When Mr. Hafner was eliminated, more than half of his voters’ ballots (11,465) were exhausted, meaning they did not pick either Mr. Hill or Mr. Begich as their second choice. In the Senate race, the second Dan Sullivan received 4,765 votes, less than half the margin of Ms. Peltola’s victory.

Reuters — US plans to announce cause of outage that led to nationwide ground stop, FAA says

The head of the Federal Aviation Administration said Thursday the government expects to announce this week the root cause of the router outage that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday that disrupted more than 18,000 flights and 1 million passengers. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford declined to discuss the findings but said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy would brief the public on the results. Mr. Duffy has said a Juniper router installed by L3Harris Technologies in a remote Arkansas facility triggered a nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop on Friday, the longest in the United States since September 11, 2001. Mr. Bedford said the FTI network that L3Harris has operated since 2002 was in desperate need of replacement, calling it a patchwork, archaic federal telephone network. Mr. Duffy has asked Congress to approve another $50 billion to complete upgrades to the air traffic control system and airports, after lawmakers approved $12.5 billion last year.

Europe Says — Germany, France, UK, Ukraine urge Russia to agree to winter energy ceasefire

The leaders of Germany, France, the UK and Ukraine called on Russia on Thursday, November 19, to agree to an “energy ceasefire” throughout the winter as a first step toward ending hostilities, in a joint statement following the Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin. They also stressed the need for a ceasefire to allow food exports from the Black Sea region, citing safe passage and freedom of navigation for global food security. The four leaders reaffirmed long-term political, diplomatic, military, financial and civilian support for Ukraine, identified strengthening air defence, particularly against ballistic missiles, as a priority, and said they would make extra efforts ahead of winter, with third countries, to provide additional missile defence. Any future ceasefire must include robust, legally binding security guarantees for Ukraine, defensive in nature and closely coordinated with the United States. They backed direct dialogue between Ukraine and Russia with American and European participation, and said international borders must not be changed by force.

Some rail traffic resumed on Thursday afternoon, according to Russia’s transport ministry, which said earlier there were no casualties. Ukraine’s General Staff said it used Neptune coastal missiles and damaged the railway section; Ukraine’s Defence Ministry said hits were confirmed near the arch and the railway tracks. Mr. Zelensky described previous strikes, conducted exclusively with Ukraine-made weapons, as the seventh stage of “an unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure.” Speaking in Shenzhen after the trilateral, Mr. Putin threatened retaliation, said the bridge serves “purely peaceful purposes,” said the road side had been “seriously damaged” and vowed to rebuild it, and said there would be no agreements on a Black Sea or energy moratorium after the bridge strikes. Kyiv came under renewed drone attack on Thursday afternoon.

The Maritime Executive — LPG Tanker Fire Brought Under Control in the Strait of Hormuz

Two days after it was hit in the engine room by an IRGC drone on November 16, the fire on the Panama-flagged LPG tanker Tara Gas seems to be under control. The ship appears to have been brought into a sheltered bay west of Shishah, on the basis of a heat signature detectable on NASA FIRMS thermal imaging yesterday but now dampened down. The fire was attended to by the Liberian-flagged anchor handling tug supply vessel Valiant Vortex. All the crew have been rescued, with two injured sailors taken to Khasab Hospital, save for one crew member who remains missing. Moving the tanker into a sheltered bay, under steep cliffs and without nearby coastal settlements, has reduced the risk of collateral damage and of fire spreading to the pressurised LPG tanks.

Europe Says — Iran Mounts 14 Hormuz Attacks in November as Brent Falls

Iran has mounted about 14 attacks on vessels in and near the Strait of Hormuz in the first 19 days of November, according to a United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations count cited by Bloomberg. The attacks have included limpet mines, naval mines and anti-ship cruise missiles, which an unnamed American official described as “far more lethal than drones,” and followed the collapse of Muscat-hosted diplomacy between Iran and Oman on November 17. Brent crude futures have fallen approximately one-fifth in November, and total Middle East oil flows have largely recovered to near pre-war levels through alternative routes and ship-to-ship transfers. The International Energy Agency projected in its November Oil Market Report that global oil supply will exceed demand in the fourth quarter of 2026 for the first time since the Iran conflict began. IMF PortWatch recorded just 11 tanker transits through Hormuz between November 1 and 15 — an average of 0.7 per day, compared with 665 in the same period of 2025, a 98 percent fall. Kuwait wrote to the International Maritime Organization about attacks on eight of its tankers in recent weeks.

Brent futures settled just below $92 a barrel after moving through a roughly $2 range. Prices pared earlier gains after Mr. Trump told Axios he was not “rushing into a decision” on Iran. The International Energy Agency said on Thursday that the war could reshape global energy markets for years, and that if a resolution were reached soon, both oil and natural gas could turn into buyers’ markets. United States data showed nationwide crude inventories rose by 3.4 million barrels last week.

Devdiscourse, carried from Reuters — Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper hit in Houthi strike on Saudi wealth fund HQ

Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, was struck on Thursday in a Houthi attack. Saudi Arabia’s civil defence said a Houthi attack on a tower in Riyadh’s financial centre caused material damage to several floors of the building and nearby buildings, but no injuries were reported, state news agency SPA said. The statement did not identify the tower, but an accompanying photograph published by SPA showed the PIF Tower. Saudi aircraft carried out airstrikes on Sanaa early on Thursday, according to the Houthi-run Saba news agency. Vozia, reporting the Associated Press account — Board of Peace report to the UN Security Council warns Gaza ceasefire risks collapse

The Board of Peace, the body overseeing the United States-brokered ceasefire in Gaza, delivered its first annual assessment to the UN Security Council on Tuesday, November 17, warning that the agreement risks collapse if its terms are not fully implemented. A copy was obtained by the Associated Press. The report says the distance between what was agreed and what is happening on the ground is the principal risk to the process, and that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely.” It points to continued Israeli strikes and Hamas military activity, and to the blocking of humanitarian aid, with Gaza’s civilian population facing another winter in tents and rubble. At the centre of the stall is the technocratic civil administration the board created to run Gaza on an interim basis: Israel has still not allowed it to take up its job in the territory, and that delay has held up the international stabilisation force, an Israeli troop withdrawal, the disarmament of Hamas and the start of reconstruction. The board appealed to the Security Council to back the agreement, saying neither party may treat the other’s delay as a licence for its own inaction, and that the outcome must lead to a credible pathway to Palestinian self-determination and statehood. The story adds that the Israeli military announced on Thursday that it had completed its operation north of the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza and reopened Salah al-Din Street, the main north-south road.

The International Court of Justice in The Hague ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed state-sponsored genocide against the Rohingya in 2017, the first time it held a state responsible for genocide. The case was filed by Gambia. The story collects initial reactions from the UN human rights chief, Amnesty International, Rohingya activists, Sheikh Hasina, Human Rights Watch, and others. Subjective
Le Monde — Rohingya: Historic International Court of Justice ruling finds Myanmar guilty of genocide

By a majority of its 14 judges, the court found six violations of the 1948 Genocide Convention; the ruling runs 191 pages, and the session lasted more than three hours. The court’s estimate, supported by the evidence, is that 10,000 Rohingya were violently killed in clearance operations, 1.2 percent of the targeted population in northern Rakhine; 392 villages were destroyed, and 700,000 fled in 2017. Myanmar had not yet responded as of Thursday evening. The United Kingdom’s Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the expulsion of Myanmar’s defence attaché and called urgently for a UN Security Council session. Gambia welcomed the ruling with “profound satisfaction” and called on Myanmar to comply “fully and without delay.” Bangladesh urged implementation without delay. The United States said it was studying the ruling. Myanmar has two years to submit a report on restitution and compensation; the Court will decide the amount.

SRN News, carried from Reuters — Violence rises in Bangladesh as Hasina supporters escalate protests, PM Rahman blames India

Fresh violence broke out in Bangladesh on Thursday as former prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s supporters tried to bring businesses and public transport to a halt, with mixed success, and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman blamed India for the unrest. The Awami League called Thursday’s nationwide lockdown at the end of a week-long campaign against the government’s rejection of Ms. Hasina’s request for a new passport that would allow her to return.
