World of Now — Xi, Putin and Trump’s Shenzhen Summit: What Is at Stake?

The account carries the three leaders due to meet on Thursday, November 19, Presidents Xi and Putin having criticised protectionism and sanctions in Shenzhen, the President arriving after meetings in Manila, possible subjects including Ukraine, Iran, trade, artificial intelligence and nuclear weapons, and the statement that as of November 18 the encounter is planned and its outcome has not yet been reported.

Subjective
Daily Caller — Trump, Xi and Putin Summit Officially On the Books

The account carries China’s confirmation of the November 19 meeting, Beijing describing it as a historic development focused on international security and strategic stability, the President intending to make nuclear reductions a central topic in a spokeswoman’s account, officials cautioning against expecting an immediate breakthrough, and a report that the President is not expected to raise Ukraine during the three-way meeting.

Subjective
France 24, carried by DAMM News — French Police Hold Paris Rally After Weeks of Protests

The account carries French police staging a demonstration in front of the Interior Ministry in Paris on Wednesday, including members of the CRS riot unit, after weeks of protest marches around the country, published November 18 at 13:15 UK time in the source’s reading.

Subjective
Demócrata — General Election Poll: Vox Loses Four Seats and PP and PSOE Advance, According to 40dB Tracking

The account carries the 40dB tracking published November 18, on fieldwork of November 13 to 17: the Popular Party at 131 seats, the Socialists at 122, Vox at 55, down three on the day, the right bloc at 188 seats including the Navarre coalition, and Mr. Sánchez continuing as the preferred candidate to lead the government.

Subjective
El Constitucional — How the General Election Polls for 29-N Are Going

The account carries the SW Demoscopia poll released by La Séptima, on 9,500 telephone interviews from October 26 to November 16: the Socialists first at 31.9 percent and 134 seats, the Popular Party at 28.9 percent and 118, Vox at 16.5 percent and 54, and the right’s two parties together not reaching an absolute majority on that instrument.

Subjective
Pollar News — Sánchez and Feijóo Prepare for Thursday’s Only Televised Debate

The account carries the only head-to-head debate on Thursday, November 19, at 22:00 at the Academia de Televisión, moderated by María Casado; Sigma Dos tracking on 3,759 interviews from November 11 to 16 putting the Popular Party at 30.7 percent and 123 to 129 seats, the Socialists at 26.4 percent and 108 to 114, and Vox at 19.8 percent and 62 to 67.

Subjective
The Immortal Times — FAA Nationwide Ground Stop: Latest Updates and Investigation

The account carries the November 18 update: the Secretary saying the agency and its contractors are addressing the failures that contributed to Friday’s stop, testing continuing at a laboratory in Florida with the agency, Cisco and the FBI involved, the installation pause remaining in place, investigators having recreated the sequence without establishing a root cause, and Senate Commerce Committee Democrats having formally requested technical answers by November 23.

Subjective
Aerospace Global News — FAA Pauses Router Upgrades After Nationwide US Ground Stop

The account carries the pause on new Juniper router installations, the same function disabled on more than 60 other routers as a precaution, bursts of about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds disrupting communications and radar, the sites at El Dorado, Arkansas, and Amarillo, Texas, the stop from about 3:30 p.m. to 8:15 p.m. Eastern on November 13, and the Senate letter citing 400 of 3,648 planned routers installed and 69 operational.

Subjective
IANS — Rubio Says Zero Evidence Links US Flight, Banking and Microsoft Outages

The account carries the Secretary of State’s Wednesday statement in Manila that Washington had found no evidence connecting the disruptions to Microsoft services, air traffic control and banking, or indicating malicious actors; the agency’s preliminary finding of no indication of a cyberattack in Friday’s stop; and a senator’s preliminary assessment on Tuesday in the same direction.

Subjective
BytesEU — Local, National Health Officials Respond as U.S. Loses Measles Elimination Status

The account carries the loss of elimination status announced Tuesday after twelve months of continuous circulation, 5,412 confirmed cases nationwide as of November 12 and six deaths in the CDC’s 2026 count in that account, a Minnesota outbreak centred in Todd County at 136 cases as of November 12, and officials identifying declining vaccination coverage as the primary reason for the resurgence.

Subjective
Virginia Times — US Measles Elimination Status Lost, CDC Confirms

The account carries the withdrawal also covering Mexico and Bolivia, the CDC Director’s statement that vaccination, not the designation, protects Americans, $100 million provided since August for state and local responses, federal teams deployed in six states, and kindergarten MMR coverage at 92.7 percent, down from 95.2 percent before the pandemic.

Subjective
National Medical Association — NMA Responds to Loss of U.S. Measles Elimination Status

The association’s November 17 statement carries deep concern at the loss after 26 years, more than 5,400 reported cases and eight deaths in 2026 in its figures, a call to maintain coverage of approximately 95 percent in communities, and an estimate that between nine and fifteen million children nationwide may be vulnerable because of insufficient coverage.

Subjective
TradingView / Dow Jones — Asian Equities Decline as Caution Prevails

The account carries Thursday morning in Asia, published at 02:46 UTC on November 19: Asian equities broadly lower, the Kospi down 0.9 percent after giving up early gains, the Taiex off 2.7 percent, Chinese benchmarks in the red, the Nikkei swinging between gains and losses and last 0.1 percent higher, WTI futures down 0.1 percent at $83.15 and Brent up 0.3 percent at $92.21 in its reading, and continuing attacks against ships in the Strait of Hormuz named in its oil account.

Subjective
Walmart — Walmart to Host Third Quarter Earnings Conference Call November 19, 2026

The company’s notice carries its third-quarter results to be released at 6 a.m. Central on Thursday, November 19, with a conference call at 7 a.m. Central hosted by its president and chief executive and its chief financial officer, and fiscal 2026 revenue of $713 billion with approximately 2.1 million associates worldwide.

entry.title: ICE Deportation Flights: The Restraints, the Third Countries, and the Offer to Leave Voluntarily
entry.summary: Who flies on ICE’s removal flights, in what restraints, to which countries—from flight trackers, court files, the agency’s handbook, and DHS’s own statements.
entry.content:
Special Report

Immigration · Removal Flights · Third Countries · Self-Departure · The United States

Objective

ICE Deportation Flights: The Restraints, the Third Countries, and the Offer to Leave Voluntarily

ICE publishes no flight data. What is known about the removal flights comes from flight trackers watching public transponder data, from court files, from the agency’s own operations handbook, and from the department’s own statements. The record assembled here covers who flies, in what restraints, to which countries, under what court orders—and the second door the same department holds open: a paid ticket home, a stipend, and no chains, for the man who agrees to leave on his own.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 2000 ET, Wednesday, November 18, 2026.

The Record in Brief

Three ways out. A person under a removal order leaves the United States in one of three ways in the present record. He is flown out by ICE Air Operations on a chartered aircraft, restrained under the standard written in the agency’s 2024 operations handbook: handcuffs, waist chains, and leg irons for the duration. Or he is flown to a third country—not his own—under agreements the Department of Homeland Security has made since February 2025, a practice the Supreme Court has allowed to proceed without yet ruling on whether it is lawful; argument is set for December 2026. Or he leaves voluntarily under the department’s CBP Home program: a government-paid ticket, a stipend of $1,000 on confirmed arrival home, forgiveness of failure-to-depart fines, and no restraints reported on the voluntary flights in any account in this record.

The scale. ICE publishes no flight data of its own. Human Rights First’s ICE Flight Monitor, which tracks public flight data, counted at least 7,454 enforcement flights between January 20 and August 31, 2025—to at least 66 countries, 34 percent more than the same period in 2024 and the highest count since the tracking began in 2020—and 2,253 deportation flights to 79 countries in the year ending January 20, 2026. Gillian Brockell, a journalist and former flight attendant who built a tracker of the wide-body carrier Omni Air International, counts an average of roughly 70 ICE flights a day across all carriers in 2026 and about 25,000 people sent to nearly three dozen third countries. The two instruments count different things over different periods; both are printed here, unmerged.

The disputed numbers. Two numbers dominate the public argument, and the record carries both with their instruments attached. The department states that 70 percent of ICE arrests are of persons charged with or convicted of a crime in the United States—arrests, with charges counted alongside convictions. The independent instruments that count convictions only, among persons booked into custody or held in detention, find about 27 to 35 percent with a conviction and 5 to 7 percent with a violent conviction. On self-deportation, the department’s headline figure of 1.6 million voluntary departures rests on a survey estimate by the Center for Immigration Studies whose own authors flag it as preliminary; the department’s own releases put users of the CBP Home program itself at “tens of thousands,” and independent estimates of voluntary departures beyond the normal baseline, attributed to the enforcement climate, run from about 200,000 to 405,000 for 2025. Section 5 and Section 6 print each figure beside its method.

Related record. This report covers the flights themselves. The paper’s November 8 report, Deportation in America, set out the removal law, and its November 12 report, Deportation, Counted, counted removals and returns across eight administrations.

1. The Flights Themselves

The structure. ICE Air Operations, a division of ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations, owns no aircraft in the record through 2025. It charters them. All ICE flights are brokered through CSI Aviation under a contract worth up to $1.5 billion, according to Brockell’s reporting in The American Prospect of October 2, 2026. The carriers include GlobalX, which has flown more than half of ICE’s deportation flights in 2024 and 2025 and 74 percent of the 1,564 deportation flights counted in 2024, and Omni Air International, a charter airline based in Tulsa, Oklahoma, whose wide-body jets fly the long routes—Africa, Asia, the Middle East. ICE’s own website, in a passage a group of senators noted in 2026 had not been updated since August 8, 2023, says ICE Air stages 12 aircraft. Because ICE publishes no flight data, every count in this section comes from outside trackers reading public transponder and flight records.

The Omni record. Brockell, who worked as a flight attendant and later covered the charter industry, built her tracker from flight data after Omni crews recognized ICE passengers on their aircraft. Her count for Omni alone, from February to mid-June 2026: a minimum of 76 removal stops, 10 of them confirmed third-country removals, and 11 trips lasting 32 to 68 hours, with passengers shackled at the ankles, wrists, and waist for the duration. Flight data backed one man’s account of 73 hours or more in shackles on a routing to Laos and Vietnam; a second group’s trip ran 82 hours, the longest she recorded. Attendants who recently quit Omni described to her suicidal passengers held in full-body straitjackets and guards refusing the attendants’ safety instructions. Omni’s stated price in an earlier era of the work was $34,000 per flight hour, a figure Brockell drew from court documents in a 2019 suit over a single Asia trip priced at $1.8 million.

The Chicago end of Omni. Omni’s parent, Air Transport Services Group, was acquired by the investment firm Stonepeak in April 2025 for about $3.1 billion. Stonepeak also sought to buy Chicago’s parking-meter concession, a 75-year lease dating to 2008, and Chicago aldermen made the two deals one question: the council would not approve the meter purchase unless Stonepeak divested Omni. Committee hearings in June and July 2026 heard the flight record, including the hours passengers spend shackled. Brockell states in her article that she spoke at one of the organizing meetings and at a committee hearing in early July; the paper prints that disclosure with her findings. A negotiated settlement announced in September added reduced true-up fees, a $75 million payment earmarked for city pensions, and a 5 percent profit share estimated at $375 million over the remaining 57 years of the lease. The sale of Omni to a newly created company, OAI Holdings LLC, was announced September 28, 2026; the City Council approved the meter deal 46 to 3 on September 29, at a $2.53 billion bid; ATSG’s account dates the closing of the Omni sale to November 9, 2026. Brockell calls the Chicago outcome a blueprint that can be replicated in other cities; that is her characterization, filed below as a clipping. Three ICE charter carriers in total stopped flying ICE work in the past year, by her count, including Avelo Airlines, which ended its ICE flying amid boycott pressure and internal backlash.

2. The Restraints

The standard, in the agency’s own book. The 2024 ICE Air Operations Handbook, quoted in a May 11, 2026 letter from members of Congress to the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, states that detainees transported on ICE Air aircraft “will be fully restrained by the use of Authorized Restraint Devices; i.e., handcuffs, waist chains, leg irons.” The handbook also authorizes spit masks, mittens, leg braces, cargo straps, and the WRAP, a full-body restraint suit that immobilizes the legs and torso and holds the wearer upright and seated. The manufacturer, Safe Restraints Inc., describes the device as a de-escalation tool; the department has bought $268,523 worth of the devices since late 2015, and the maker produced a modified version for ICE with a ring at the front to which cuffed hands can be attached during flights and long bus trips.

The government’s account. Asked about restraints by the Associated Press and by The Guardian, DHS spokeswoman Tricia McLaughlin gave the same answer: “The use of restraints on detainees during deportation flights has been long standing, standard ICE protocol and an essential measure to ensure the safety and well-being of both detainees and the officers/agents accompanying them,” and the practices are “fully in line with established legal standards.” The department also defended the WRAP specifically as legal and standard. ICE would not provide the AP with records documenting the WRAP’s use, would not answer detailed questions about it, and refused the AP’s request for the policy governing when and how it is used; the agency did not specify the authorities its practices align with.

The other accounts. The AP’s investigation, published in October 2025, identified multiple uses of the WRAP on deportation flights: five people described being restrained in it, sometimes for hours, on flights dating to 2020, and witnesses and family members in four countries described its use on at least seven other people in 2025. One man, a Nigerian national who is a plaintiff in a federal lawsuit, told the AP that officers woke his group at night in September 2025, shackled them, refused their requests to call a lawyer, and put them in the WRAP for a 16-hour flight to Ghana, a country none of them was from; the lawsuit alleges he was kept in the device for 16 hours, with the lower part undone once so he could use the bathroom. The AP reported that deportees said the device was used as punishment or intimidation, including for asking for attorneys or expressing fear. The AP also found that a 2023 report by the civil rights division of DHS itself had raised internal concerns about the WRAP, in part because of deaths involving its use by local law enforcement; the AP identified a dozen cases in a decade in which local police or jailers used the device and autopsies found restraint played a role in the death. Those deaths were in local custody, not on ICE flights; the paper prints the distinction because the record carries it.

The crews. ProPublica reported on April 1, 2025, from interviews with current and former flight attendants on GlobalX deportation flights, that attendants were trained to evacuate an aircraft but were never told how to evacuate passengers whose hands and legs were shackled. A typical flight carried more than 100 detainees, a dozen or more guards employed by Akima, one ICE officer, and two nurses. Attendants said they were told not to talk to the detainees, not to feed them, and not to make eye contact; some said they spoke to passengers anyway. The attendants’ stated concern was evacuation: a cabin of passengers bound at the wrists and ankles cannot move at the speed an emergency exit requires. The congressional letter of May 11, 2026, carried the same point to the FAA: former attendants, it said, revealed there was no plan or training for evacuating restrained passengers, and the members asked the agency for written answers by June 1, 2026.

3. The Third Countries

The practice. A third-country removal sends a person under a final removal order to a country that is not his own and was not named in his removal proceedings—used, the department says, where the home country will not take him or where his order names a country that cannot receive him. The expansion dates to February 18, 2025, when DHS directed its officers to review the cases of persons granted withholding of removal or protection under the Convention Against Torture for removal to third countries instead. A March 30, 2025 memorandum from Secretary Kristi Noem set the department’s procedures, resting on diplomatic assurances: a receiving government’s commitment that the person will not be persecuted or tortured. By Brockell’s tracker count, roughly 25,000 people have been sent to nearly three dozen—about 35—third countries. The receiving countries in the record include South Sudan, Eswatini, Ghana, Laos, and Vietnam.

The Djibouti episode. In May 2025 the government put a group of men—from Cuba, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, and Mexico, several with violent-crime convictions in the United States—on a military flight toward South Sudan, a country none of them was from, then held them at Camp Lemonnier, the U.S. base in Djibouti, for about six weeks, in a converted shipping container, while the courts decided whether the flight could proceed. A federal judge found the removal violated his injunction. The Supreme Court then cleared the way, and on July 4, 2025, a military plane flew the men to South Sudan, where, by Brockell’s reporting, they were imprisoned on arrival. Their lawyers reported no contact with them after the transfer. The court fight that produced that outcome is Section 4.

The operating rule since July 2025. On July 9, 2025, after the Supreme Court’s stay, acting ICE Director Todd Lyons issued the memorandum that now governs, summarized here from the Congressional Research Service’s account of it. Where the State Department finds a receiving country’s diplomatic assurances credible, the person “may be removed without the need for further procedures”—no individual notice process at all. Where assurances are absent or not found credible, ICE serves a Notice of Removal naming the country, read in a language the person understands; ICE does not ask whether he fears removal to that country—he must state a fear on his own; ICE then waits at least 24 hours before the removal, or as little as six hours in “exigent circumstances,” provided he has a reasonable means and opportunity to speak with an attorney and a senior DHS attorney approves. Whether assurances are credible is, under the memorandum, the State Department’s call.

4. The Case: Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D.

What the lower court ordered. Four men with final removal orders sued in the District of Massachusetts in March 2025. On April 18, 2025, Judge Brian E. Murphy certified a class and enjoined the government from removing any person to a third country not named in his removal order without written notice in a language he understands, a meaningful opportunity to raise a fear of persecution or torture, and, if he shows a reasonable fear, a reopening of his proceedings. On May 21, 2025, Judge Murphy found the government had violated that injunction in the Djibouti case: the men had not been given the meaningful opportunity the order required. The First Circuit declined to pause the injunction on May 26.

What the Supreme Court did. On June 23, 2025, the Supreme Court stayed the injunction. The order was brief and gave no reasons. It did not hold that third-country removals are lawful; it paused the lower court’s order while the case proceeds, which had the effect of letting the removals resume. Justice Sotomayor dissented, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson. On July 3, 2025, the Court clarified that the stay also covered Judge Murphy’s May remedial order in full; the Djibouti group was flown to South Sudan the next day. The district court reached a final judgment against the government on February 25, 2026, holding that persons facing third-country removal are entitled to meaningful notice. On September 29, 2026, the Supreme Court stayed that judgment as well and took the case itself, before judgment in the court of appeals, as No. 26-426. The questions it will decide include whether the district court had jurisdiction, whether it could enter class-wide relief under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1), and whether the government’s third-country guidance is unlawful under the removal statute, the Due Process Clause, or the Convention Against Torture and its implementing law. Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson would have denied the application. Argument is set for the December 2026 session. As of this report, no court has ruled on the merits; the government has won every stay, and the removals proceed under a stay, not under a holding.

5. The Other Door: Self-Departure

The offer, as the department states it. On March 10, 2025, the department renamed the CBP One application—which until January 2025 had scheduled appointments for migrants seeking protection—as CBP Home, with an “Intent to Depart” feature for notifying the government of a voluntary departure. On May 5, 2025, DHS announced travel assistance and a stipend: any person who uses CBP Home to self-deport receives $1,000, “paid after their return to their home country has been confirmed through the app.” The department books and pays for the travel, helps obtain travel documents for those without a valid passport, and deprioritizes participants for detention and removal while they prepare to leave. Secretary Noem: “If you are here illegally, self-deportation is the best, safest and most cost-effective way to leave the United States to avoid arrest.” The department’s arithmetic: an average arrest, detention, and removal costs $17,121; the CBP Home route, stipend included, was projected to cut the cost of a departure by about 70 percent. On June 9, 2025, the department added forgiveness of failure-to-depart fines for those who self-deport through the app; it said it had issued more than 9,000 fine notices totaling almost $3 billion, at rates approaching $1,000 a day. On May 9, 2025, Presidential Proclamation 10935 established Project Homecoming, directing a concierge service at airports and an exit bonus, funded in part, per the Migration Policy Institute, by $250 million in repurposed refugee-assistance funds and promoted in a $200 million international advertising campaign. On December 22, 2025, the department raised the stipend to $3,000 for those who signed up by the end of the year.

The first flight. On May 19, 2025, the department ran its first Project Homecoming charter: 64 people from Houston to Honduras and Colombia—38 to Honduras, 26 to Colombia, in the department’s own breakdown. DHS stated: “This was a voluntary charter flight, not an ICE enforcement operation,” and that all participants received travel assistance, the $1,000 stipend, and preserved the possibility of returning legally one day. The contrast with Section 2 is in the record and needs no emphasis from the desk: the removal passenger boards in handcuffs, waist chains, and leg irons under a written standard; the Homecoming passenger boards as a volunteer on a government-paid charter, with money waiting on confirmed arrival. No account in this record reports restraints on a voluntary flight.

The promise about coming back. The department says participation “may help preserve the option for an illegal alien to re-enter the United States legally in the future.” The Migration Policy Institute’s account of the same program states the statutory difficulty plainly: a person unlawfully present more than 180 days but less than a year faces a three-year bar on re-entry; more than a year, a ten-year bar; the bars apply even to those who leave voluntarily, and leaving without a judge’s grant of voluntary departure can result in a removal order. How the department’s promise and the statute fit together is not explained in the department’s releases; the paper prints both.

The uptake, by instrument. The counts divide into two kinds, and the record keeps them apart. The first kind is documented use of the program itself. More than 5,000 people had logged a return through CBP Home as of April 9, 2025, per Fox News as cited by MPI. About 35,000 had used the program’s incentives by October 2025, per The Atlantic as cited by the Center for Migration Studies. DHS-reported data summarized in trade reporting put app use at nearly 38,000 from March through November 25, 2025. And the department itself, on December 22, 2025, described CBP Home users as “tens of thousands.” The second kind is a population estimate. On September 23, 2025, the department announced that 2 million people had been removed or had self-deported since January 20, “including an estimated 1.6 million who have voluntarily self-deported”; on October 27 it raised the deportation component to more than 527,000 while leaving the 1.6 million unchanged; on December 22 it raised the self-deported component to 1.9 million. The releases publish no methodology for the figure.

Where the 1.6 million comes from, and what is said against it. The traceable basis is an August 12, 2025 analysis by Steven Camarota and Karen Zeigler of the Center for Immigration Studies, working from the Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey, a monthly survey of about 60,000 households. CIS found the total foreign-born population down 2.2 million between January and July 2025 and preliminarily estimated the unauthorized population down 1.6 million, to 14.2 million. CIS’s own caveats: the decline could in part reflect immigrants’ reluctance to answer a government survey during stepped-up enforcement, and administrative data needed for the estimate was not yet available, making it preliminary. The Pew Research Center, reading the same survey, found a smaller total decline—1.4 million, from 53.3 million in January to 51.9 million in June—published no unauthorized-only figure, and cautioned that falling participation could explain part of the drop. Jed Kolko of the Peterson Institute for International Economics called the 2.2 million decline “implausibly large and uncorroborated”: the survey’s response rate fell from 68.8 percent in January 2025 to 67.1 percent in July, and under reasonable assumptions about foreign-born nonresponse, that fall “could therefore explain the entire reported decline.” Economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis reached the same mechanical point on December 29, 2025: because the survey is weighted to fixed population totals, a fall in counted immigrants appears as an equal rise in the native-born, and the implied native-born rise far exceeds the Congressional Budget Office’s projected growth. Edward Kissam of the Center for Migration Studies, triangulating from the documented figures—the app users, the government’s arrival-departure records, and Mexican survey data on returning migrants—estimated about 200,000 self-deportations by the end of 2025, about one-tenth of the department’s year-end claim. The Brookings Institution, modeling flows separately, estimated 210,000 to 405,000 voluntary departures beyond the normal baseline attributable to the enforcement climate in 2025, alongside 310,000 to 315,000 removals, and stated that “there is little data to assess the degree to which immigrants have increased their voluntary exit rates in 2025.” MPI’s summary of the whole question: because voluntary departure is self-directed, “data on the number of people who have self-deported so far are thin or anecdotal.” The historical baseline in its account: the 2008 Scheduled Departure pilot drew 8 volunteers out of 457,000 eligible. The disagreement stands as printed: documented program use in the tens of thousands; independent estimates of extra voluntary departures in the low hundreds of thousands; a survey-based population estimate of 1.6 million, carried by the department as a count of self-deportations. The instruments measure three different things.

6. Who Is on the Planes

The government’s figure, with its denominator. The department’s standing claim, repeated by Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin on October 27, 2025, and since, is that “70% of ICE arrests are of criminal illegal aliens charged with or convicted of a crime in the U.S.” Three features of the claim are in its own wording: the denominator is arrests, not removals and not the detention population; the numerator counts a pending charge the same as a conviction; and it reaches any crime, with no severity threshold stated. The department adds that the figure is “just in the U.S.” and does not account for persons wanted in their home countries, INTERPOL notices, gang members, or terrorists; FactCheck.org notes the department has provided no data for the home-country claim.

The baseline in ICE’s own book. The last full annual report with a criminal-history breakdown is ICE’s FY2024 report. Of 113,431 administrative arrests that year, 81,312—71.7 percent—had a conviction or pending charges, the same combined definition as the 70 percent claim. But of the year’s 271,484 removals, only 88,763—32.7 percent—involved persons with convictions or pending charges; most removals that year began as border apprehensions by CBP, not ICE arrests. The same agency, the same definition, the same year: 71.7 percent of arrests, 32.7 percent of removals. Of the convictions held by arrested persons in FY2024, the largest category was traffic offenses, 24.7 percent; immigration offenses were 15.5 percent; assault 9.7 percent; dangerous drugs 14.1 percent. No FY2025 annual report with a criminal-history breakdown appears in the record assembled; secondary reporting of ICE’s FY2025 data puts removals at 442,637, with about 38 percent of deportees having criminal histories on the combined definition.

The independent instruments. FactCheck.org, analyzing individual-level ICE arrest data obtained by the Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley and UCLA through FOIA litigation, for January 20 to October 15, 2025, found 36.5 percent of arrestees with prior convictions, 29.8 percent with pending charges, and about a third with neither—66 percent combined, which FactCheck describes as the figure the administration has rounded to 70. A New York Times analysis of the same project’s data over the same period found 37 percent with any conviction and 7 percent with a violent conviction. CBS News, from an internal DHS document covering 392,619 arrests from January 21, 2025, to January 31, 2026, found nearly 60 percent with charges or convictions of any kind, 13.9 percent with charges or convictions for violent offenses, and nearly 40 percent with no criminal record. The Cato Institute, analyzing nonpublic ICE book-in data leaked to it for October 1 to November 15, 2025, found 73 percent of persons booked into custody with no conviction, 47 percent with neither a conviction nor pending charges, and 5 percent with a violent conviction; the department called the analysis “made up,” and Cato answered that it had checked the data against three sources, including the department’s own public data, and that the department’s claim counts arrests while its own counts book-ins. TRAC at Syracuse University, reading ICE detention data obtained by FOIA, counted 65,735 persons in detention on November 30, 2025, of whom 48,377—73.6 percent—had no criminal conviction; TRAC’s series counts convictions only, so a person with a pending charge and no conviction stands in the 73.6 percent. The Migration Policy Institute, in an October 2026 analysis of FOIA and Deportation Data Project records covering January 20, 2025, to July 31, 2026, counted about 980,000 deportations—its term covers formal removals and returns together—of which 190,000, or 20 percent, involved a person with a criminal conviction; among formal removals only, 31 percent. Its most common conviction categories among criminal removals were illegal entry and re-entry, 23 percent, and traffic offenses including DUI, 21 percent. The department rejected the MPI analysis.

The disagreement, printed. The instruments do not contradict each other so much as they count different populations at different doors of the same building. Count arrests, and count a charge as a conviction, and the criminal share is 60 to 70 percent. Count the people actually held or booked, convictions only, and the convicted share is 27 to 35 percent, with violent convictions at 5 percent of book-ins (Cato) and violent charges or convictions at 13.9 percent of arrests (the department’s own internal document, via CBS). Count removals, and ICE’s own FY2024 figure is 32.7 percent charged or convicted; MPI’s conviction figure for 2025–26 is 20 percent of all deportations and 31 percent of formal removals. Two adjustments move every number in the set: pending charges add roughly 30 points wherever they are counted, and immigration and traffic offenses—the two largest conviction categories in both ICE’s and MPI’s tables—are counted as criminal convictions in every instrument here. The claim that most of the people on the planes are dangerous criminals is not carried by any instrument in this record: on the only measures that separate violence out, violent convictions stand at 5 to 7 percent. The claim that the planes carry mostly people with no business being counted as criminals is equally beyond the record: on the arrests measure the department uses, a majority of arrestees have been charged with or convicted of something in the United States. Both statements are printed because the record carries both, each with its instrument named.

7. The Government’s Own Fleet

The purchase. The charter system described in Section 1 is the system the department also tried to replace. In early 2026, under Secretary Noem, DHS bought ten aircraft from Daedalus Aviation Corporation for $464 million under a no-bid contract, according to New York Times reporting summarized in an October 21, 2026 letter from Rep. Bennie G. Thompson to Secretary Markwayne Mullin: seven Boeing 737-700s, formerly flown by Avelo Airlines, for deportation operations, and three executive jets. Five of the aircraft were acquired in March 2026, on Secretary Noem’s final day in the job, at markups over recent purchase prices, per the same account. The department said a government-owned fleet would ease reliance on contract airlines and expand deportation operations; in May 2026 it said the jets would be ready for use within weeks.

The idle months, and the first flights. Flight-tracking data from ADS-B Exchange, reported by Bloomberg, showed the seven 737s parked at Lake Charles Regional Airport in Louisiana, each with fewer than five flights since April 2026. Brockell’s October 2 account had it the same way from the other side: as of her writing, the purchased Boeings had flown no removal flights at all, and could not in any case replace the charter fleets. In September 2026 the department proposed repurposing four of the jets for congressional delegations and other official travel. In late October 2026, a DHS-owned 737-700 made the fleet’s first removal flights—two trips from Texas to Mexico on consecutive days, confirmed by flight-tracking data and by Human Rights First. As of this report, the charter system still carries the removal program; the owned fleet has flown two removal trips.

8. What the Record Does Not Show

The gaps, stated. ICE publishes no flight data; every flight count in this report is an outside count, and none can be checked against an official ledger because there is none public. ICE has published no FY2025 annual report with a criminal-history breakdown in the record assembled, and the department has published no methodology for its 1.6 and 1.9 million self-deportation figures; the traceable basis for the first is a preliminary survey estimate whose authors printed their caveats with it. No court has ruled on the merits of third-country removals; the practice proceeds under a Supreme Court stay, with argument set for December 2026. No court finding on the WRAP or on the restraint standard appears in the record assembled here; the restraint record consists of the agency’s handbook, the department’s statements, an internal 2023 civil-rights report described by the AP, detainee and attendant accounts, and pending lawsuits. And no instrument in the record counts the passengers flight by flight—who was on any given plane, with what record, in what restraints, to what destination. The planes are counted. The people, in the public record, are estimated.

Errata — Filed November 19, 2026

This report as first filed carried two statements the record does not support as printed. The desk corrects them here, in the open, the day after publication; the text above stands as filed, and these errata are the correction of record.

Section 4, the case. Section 4 stated that the Supreme Court took Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D. before judgment in the court of appeals, and that “argument is set for the December 2026 session.” The record is otherwise. The First Circuit ruled on September 18, 2026, in No. 26-1212, and oral argument is set for December 9, 2026. The cert-before-judgment framing and the session date as printed are corrected accordingly.

The Human Rights First clipping. The description of the ICE Flight Monitor’s December 2025 report in the filed clippings below tied the figure of 2,253 deportation flights in the year ending January 20, 2026 to the Monitor’s reporting “as carried in the congressional letter below.” The carrier phrase is wrong. The Monitor’s own December 2025 report counts 2,201 removal flights for calendar 2025 and 2,138 for January 20 to December 31, 2025. The figure of 2,253 deportation flights for the year ending January 20, 2026, printed in the report above, stands as filed; the correction is to the attribution, not to the count.

The Filed Clippings

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective, a source with a position, printed because it is useful, and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Sixteen items.

Subjective
Human Rights First—ICE Flight Monitor: U.S. Immigration Enforcement Flights Report (December 2025)

The outside count of the flights, built from public flight data because ICE publishes none: at least 7,454 enforcement flights from January 20 to August 31, 2025, to at least 66 countries, 34 percent above the same period in 2024; and 2,253 deportation flights to 79 countries in the year ending January 20, 2026, per the Monitor’s reporting as carried in the congressional letter below.

Subjective
The American Prospect—Gillian Brockell, “The City That Brought Down an ICE Airline” (October 2, 2026)

The Omni file from flight data: 76 removal stops from February to mid-June 2026, 10 confirmed third-country removals, trips of 32 to 68 hours, the 73- and 82-hour accounts, the Stonepeak purchase and the Chicago divestiture fight, the $1.5 billion CSI Aviation contract, and the author’s disclosure that she spoke at an organizing meeting and a committee hearing, and her conclusion that the Chicago outcome is a blueprint for grounding the flights until they can be abolished.

Subjective
WNYC Studios, On the Media—“The ICE Flight Tracker” (November 18, 2026)

Brockell interviewed on the tracker itself: roughly 70 ICE flights a day across carriers, about 25,000 people sent to some 35 third countries, the Djibouti group’s six weeks in a shipping container and their July 4, 2025 flight to South Sudan, and attendants’ accounts of suicidal passengers in full-body straitjackets.

Subjective
Associated Press—“ICE’s Use of Full-Body Restraints During Deportations Raises Concerns Over Inhumane Treatment” (October 2025)

The WRAP investigation: five people restrained on flights dating to 2020, witnesses in four countries, the Nigerian plaintiff’s 16-hour flight to Ghana, the punishment allegations, the 2023 internal civil-rights concerns, the dozen local-custody deaths in which autopsies found restraint played a role, the $268,523 in purchases from Safe Restraints Inc., and DHS spokeswoman McLaughlin’s answer that restraints are long-standing, standard, and legal.

Subjective
ProPublica—McKenzie Funk, “Inside ICE Air: Flight Attendants on Deportation Planes Say Disaster Is ‘Only a Matter of Time’” (April 1, 2025)

The crews’ account: attendants on GlobalX flights trained to evacuate but never told how to evacuate shackled passengers; a typical flight of more than 100 detainees, a dozen or more Akima guards, one ICE officer, two nurses; instructions not to talk to, feed, or make eye contact with detainees; and the attendants who spoke to passengers anyway.

Subjective
Members of Congress—Letter to the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (May 11, 2026)

The oversight letter: the 2024 ICE Air Operations Handbook’s restraint standard quoted in full, the AP’s WRAP findings, the attendants’ evacuation accounts, the 84 percent rise in deportation flights across 2025 on the Human Rights First count, and a request for written answers by June 1, 2026.

Subjective
Congressional Research Service—“Immigration Removals to Third Countries” (updated August 24, 2026)

The research service’s account of the policy and the case: the February 2025 directive, the March 30, 2025 Noem memorandum, the July 9, 2025 Lyons memorandum’s procedures—credible assurances and no further process; otherwise notice, a self-stated fear, 24 hours, six in exigent circumstances—and the D.V.D. litigation through the Supreme Court’s stays.

Subjective
Department of Homeland Security—“DHS Announces Historic Travel Assistance and Stipend for Voluntary Self-Deportation” (May 5, 2025)

The offer in the department’s words: travel assistance and a $1,000 stipend paid after return is confirmed through the CBP Home app, deprioritization for detention while departure is prepared, the preserved possibility of legal return, the $17,121 average cost of an arrest, detention, and removal, and the projected 70 percent saving.

Subjective
Department of Homeland Security—“New Milestone: Over 2 Million Illegal Aliens Out of the United States in Less Than 250 Days” (September 23, 2025)

The headline claim: 2 million removed or self-deported since January 20, including an estimated 1.6 million voluntary self-deportations and more than 400,000 deportations, with a projection of nearly 600,000 deportations by the end of the first year. No methodology is published in the release.

Subjective
Migration Policy Institute—“Can the Trump Administration’s Self-Deportation Campaign Succeed?” (2025)

The program examined: the $200 million advertising campaign, the $250 million in repurposed refugee funds, the nearly $2 billion in failure-to-depart fines imposed by late May 2025, the three- and ten-year re-entry bars that apply even to voluntary departures, the 2008 pilot’s 8 volunteers out of 457,000 eligible, and the judgment that data on self-deportation are thin or anecdotal.

Subjective
Center for Immigration Studies—Andrew Arthur, “The Curious Debate Over ‘Self-Deportation’” (October 8, 2025)

The defense of the estimate the department adopted: Camarota and Zeigler’s Current Population Survey analysis of August 12, 2025—the foreign-born population down 2.2 million from January to July, the unauthorized population preliminarily down 1.6 million—with the authors’ caveats about survey reluctance and preliminary data, and the institute’s later restatement that the point estimates have fluctuated since July.

Subjective
Peterson Institute for International Economics—Jed Kolko, “Seeing Economic Data Through the Fog of Immigration Estimates” (September 4, 2025)

The survey critique: the 2.2 million decline is implausibly large and uncorroborated; the Current Population Survey’s response rate fell from 68.8 percent in January 2025 to 67.1 percent in July; under reasonable assumptions about foreign-born nonresponse, the fall could explain the entire reported decline—without proving the population has not declined.

Subjective
Cato Institute—David J. Bier, “5% of People Detained by ICE Have Violent Convictions, 73% No Convictions” (November 24, 2025)

The book-in count from nonpublic ICE data: 73 percent of persons booked into custody from October 1 to November 15, 2025 with no conviction, 47 percent with neither a conviction nor pending charges, 5 percent with a violent conviction; the department’s answer that the chart was made up, and Bier’s reply that the department’s claim counts arrests, not book-ins.

Subjective
FactCheck.org—Robert Farley, “As ICE Arrests Increased, a Higher Portion Had No U.S. Criminal Record” (January 28, 2026; reprinted at Northern Plains News)

The arrests analysis from Deportation Data Project records: 36.5 percent convicted, 29.8 percent with pending charges, about a third with neither, for January 20 to October 15, 2025; the no-record share rising from 21.9 percent in the first three months to 40.5 percent in the three months ending in mid-October; and the note that the department has provided no data for its home-country-records claim.

Subjective
Bloomberg (via Aviation Pros)—“Trump’s DHS-Owned Deportation Fleet Makes First Removal Flights” (November 3, 2026)

The owned fleet’s first work: a DHS 737-700’s two removal trips from Texas to Mexico in late October 2026, confirmed by flight tracking and Human Rights First, after months in which each of the seven jets flew fewer than five times since April, and the department’s September proposal to repurpose four of them for official travel.

Subjective
Rep. Bennie G. Thompson—Letter to Secretary Markwayne Mullin on DHS Aircraft Purchases (October 21, 2026)

The purchase questioned: $464 million in a no-bid contract to Daedalus Aviation for ten aircraft—seven Boeing 737s and three executive jets—five of them acquired on Secretary Noem’s final day in office at steep markups, per New York Times reporting; a year of delayed briefings; and a demand for the contracts, justifications, and a status report on the seven 737s by November 4, 2026.

entry.title: Wall Street Closes Mixed With the Dow Down 566 Points and Nvidia Down 2.89 Percent at $150.96, the October Minutes Put Almost All Behind Further Hikes, Anthropic Prices at $83 Above Its Range, and Pending Home Sales Fall to a Record Low
entry.summary: Wall Street closes mixed with the Dow down 566 points and Nvidia down 2.89 percent at $150.96, the October minutes put almost all officials behind further hikes, Anthropic prices at $83, and pending home sales fall to a record low.
entry.content:
The Evening File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Wall Street Closes Mixed With the Dow Down 566 Points and Nvidia Down 2.89 Percent at $150.96, the October Minutes Put Almost All Behind Further Hikes, Anthropic Prices at $83 Above Its Range, and Pending Home Sales Fall to a Record Low

The evening file: the day’s developments whole, and the first considered responses from every side. A quarter that was bought before the bell and sold by the close; a central bank whose minutes widened the December argument from whether to how much; a listing priced above its range after the close; a housing print at the lowest reading in its series’ history; a second earnings report, after the bell, that the market bought; three presidents photographed together in Shenzhen on the eve of their meeting; a fire still burning and a seafarer still missing in the strait; and a count in Alaska that does not run until three hours after this edition collects.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Wednesday, November 18, 2026. This edition continues the file from Edition No. 60, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 today, from Edition No. 59, the Morning Watch, collected at 1006 today, from Edition No. 58, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Tuesday, and from Edition No. 56, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Monday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the evening figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Evening in Brief: A Beat Sold at the Close, a Size Argued for December, and a Price Set Above the Range

The day’s three market facts closed in three different directions, and the evening file prints them in that order. The Dow fell 566.39 points to 50,193.03 and the S&P 500 fell for a fifth straight day while the Nasdaq Composite rose, in the closing account and the wire’s closing account filed below. Nvidia, whose $115.8 billion quarter the morning file carried, closed at $150.96, down 2.89 percent, in the quote account filed below, after standing down 0.48 percent at 1000 and down 1.71 percent at 1054 in the midday file. The minutes of the October meeting, released at 1400, recorded that “almost all” participants judged further rate increases would likely be appropriate, in the wire’s minutes account filed below. Anthropic priced at $83 a share, above its $70 to $78 range, in the pricing account filed below. Pending home sales fell to the lowest reading since the series began in 2001, in the wire’s housing account filed below. The desk takes the files in that order.

What the evening settled is the session, the minutes’ wording, and the listing’s price. What it left open is the rest of the file: the tabulation in Juneau at 2100 Eastern, the trilateral in Shenzhen on Thursday, the seafarer still missing in the strait, and December 8 and 9 themselves.

The Markets at the Close: The Dow Down 566, the S&P Down a Fifth Day, the Nasdaq Up, and Nvidia at $150.96

New York’s verdict on the quarter arrived in stages and the close completed it. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 566.39 points, or 1.12 percent, to 50,193.03; the S&P 500 lost 18.00 points, or 0.24 percent, to 7,322.53, its fifth consecutive decline; and the Nasdaq Composite gained 101.50 points, or 0.39 percent, to 24,429.89, in the preliminary closing data carried in both closing accounts filed below. A companion account of the same close puts the Dow down 561.25 points, or 1.11 percent, to 50,198.17, the S&P down 16.90, or 0.23 percent, to 7,323.63, and the Nasdaq up 0.42 percent to 24,429.88; both printings stand in the Cocked Hat. The S&P reversed its modest gains after the minutes were released at 1400, in the wire’s account, and rate-sensitive shares moved lower on the hawkish reading, in the closing account.

Nvidia’s session is the day in one stock. The shares opened at $159.19, traded as high as $159.70 and as low as $150.40, and closed at $150.96, down $4.50, or 2.89 percent, from Tuesday’s close of $155.46, in the quote account filed below; after hours the share stood at $150.11 at 1654 Eastern, down a further 0.56 percent, in the same account. The figures the trade was judging did not move: revenue of $115.84 billion against $109.10 billion expected, adjusted earnings of $2.68 a share against $2.48, and guidance of about $130 billion stand where the morning and midday files left them. One afternoon account, updated at 1455 Eastern, had the shares down roughly 2.2 percent near $153 and the fall from the post-earnings peak at more than $230 billion of market value; the close carried the fall further. The accounts’ explanations are printed as theirs: uncertainty over the company’s course after its chief’s departure, in one; the leadership question and the market’s wait-and-see posture, in another. The board’s sentence stands where the morning file left it: it will not reinstate Mr. Huang and is searching for a permanent successor.

The morning’s retailers closed against their midday marks and are printed at the close. TJX closed at $140.30, up $10.45, or 8.05 percent, from $129.85, in its quote account filed below, below its midday readings of up 10.01 and 10.20 percent. Target closed at $165.93, up $6.40, or 4.01 percent, from $159.53, in its quote account. Lowe’s closed at $222.78, up $2.32, or 1.05 percent, from $220.46, in its quote account, recovering the midday account’s down 5.7 percent mark. The three beats and the tariff refunds inside them stand as the midday file printed them. Gold’s morning fall, to futures of $3,764.60, stands in the midday file; no closing gold figure stands in the evening accounts the desk read. Settled: the beat was sold, the Dow bore the day, and the retailers kept part of their morning. Open: Thursday, which carries the listing’s first trade and Walmart’s report.

The Fed at the Close: “Almost All” for Further Hikes, Some for October Itself, a Couple Open to More Than a Quarter-Point, and Two Governors Speaking the Same Day

The instrument the midday file waited for published at 1400, and its wording is the evening’s central document. The minutes of the October 27 and 28 meeting record that “almost all” participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labour market, further increases in the target range would likely be appropriate in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective, in the wire’s minutes account and in the minutes account filed below. Some participants had favoured an increase of 25 basis points at the October meeting itself, in the same accounts; the meeting held the range at 3.75 to 4.00 percent by 10 to 2, with Governor Cook and President Hammack dissenting for a quarter-point hike. A few participants said inflation could prove more persistent and require a shift to a more restrictive stance than currently expected, in the wire’s account, and a couple said a hike larger than 25 basis points could warrant consideration at the December 8 and 9 meeting if incoming inflation data were unfavourable, in the buildout account filed below. Many participants treated the buildout of artificial intelligence capacity as a material source of inflation risk, in the same account. The minutes’ own caution stands in that account: their descriptions rest only on what the committee knew at the meeting, and they predate the October jobs, prices and retail reports published in November.

The day’s two governors spoke on either side of the release and in the same direction. Governor Waller told CNBC in the morning that he is “very, very concerned” about inflation, that about 70 percent of core services items are rising at a rate above 3 percent, and that a half-point hike in December is probably needed unless the committee signals a faster pace to come, in the broker’s minutes account filed below. Governor Barr, speaking at an event in New York on Wednesday, also said he saw the need for further rate hikes, in the minutes account above. Against them stands the week’s other voice, unchanged: New York President Williams said on Tuesday that another hike is likely and dismissed the suggestion that a large hike needs consideration, in the wire’s account. The market’s pricing after the release stands in the broker’s account: a quarter-point hike in December fully priced, with more than 80 basis points of tightening priced through September 2027, and minimal odds on more than a quarter-point in December. The administration’s position stands in the wire’s account: that elevated inflation is temporary and the Federal Reserve should ignore it. Settled: the direction, in the committee’s own record, is up, and the argument is now over size. Open: December 8 and 9.

Anthropic at the Close: Priced at $83, Above the Range, the Offering Enlarged, and Trading Thursday as ANT

The listing the week waited for priced after the close, and it priced above the range. Anthropic priced its offering at $83 a share, above the targeted $70 to $78, in the pricing account above, a Reuters account sourced to a person familiar with the matter who said the size of the offering had also increased; the company had initially planned to sell 825 million shares, and the company declined to comment, in the same account. Bloomberg News first reported the pricing, in the same account. At $83, the original 825 million shares raise about $68.5 billion in gross proceeds, and the value stands at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, in the pricing account and the calculation account filed below; excluding options and restricted shares, the $78 figure in the earlier accounts falls closer to $1 trillion, and at $83 on the shares outstanding in the amended filing the value stands nearer $1.04 trillion in the upsize account filed below. Both bases are printed in the Cocked Hat, unblended. The demand figures stand as reports: institutional indications of about $400 billion and retail indications approaching $100 billion, neither binding, in the upsize account; retail requests close to $100 billion in the calculation account, with underwriters setting aside up to 20 percent of the shares for individual investors in the Reuters reporting it carries. The separate $26 billion placement of non-voting shares to seven suppliers—AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC—stands in the pricing accounts as filed. The offering is the second large artificial-intelligence listing of the year, after June’s SpaceX sale, in the pricing account; whether it tops that record depends on the enlarged size, which no evening account states as a final number. Trading begins Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Settled: the price, $83. Open: the final size, and Thursday’s first trade.

The Housing File at the Close: Pending Sales at 63.0, the Lowest Since 2001, Against a Forecast Fall of 2.0 Percent

The afternoon’s other official print completed the morning’s two-way housing file in one direction. Contracts to purchase previously owned homes fell 4.7 percent in October, and the Pending Home Sales Index fell to 63.0, the lowest level since the series began in 2001, in the wire’s housing account above and in the association’s release filed below. Economists polled had forecast a fall of 2.0 percent, in the wire’s account. Pending sales fell 16.7 percent from a year earlier, and fell in the month in all four regions and in the year in all four regions, in both accounts; the regional falls in the month run from 0.8 percent in the Northeast to 6.9 percent in the West, in the analysis account the wire’s figures accompany. October was the second straight month of large decreases, in the wire’s account, and the association reported last week a drop in home resales to the lowest level in more than 16 years in October, in the same account. The association’s chief economist, Dr. Yun, said October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out, in the release. The rate stands where the midday file left it: the 30-year fixed mortgage at 7.18 percent last week, after reaching near 7.40 percent in mid-October, in the wire’s account. Read with the morning’s print—starts up 9.9 percent, permits down 7.4 percent—the housing file at the close is a building trade still starting houses and a contract market at its recorded floor. Settled: the index, at 63.0. Open: whether Dr. Yun’s low point is October’s or a later month’s.

After the Close: Palo Alto Networks Reports $3.44 Billion, Raises the Year, and Buys an Artificial Intelligence Company for $4.5 Billion in Stock

The day’s second report came after the bell and ran the other way from the first. Palo Alto Networks reported revenue for its fiscal first quarter, ended October 31, of $3.44 billion, up 39 percent on the year, against its own previous forecast of $3.30 to $3.31 billion, in the after-close account filed below. Net income on the reported basis rose to $482 million, or 57 cents a diluted share, from $334 million, or 47 cents; on the adjusted basis it rose to $881 million, or $1.05 a share, from $662 million, or 93 cents, in the same account. Annual recurring revenue from its next-generation security business rose 66 percent to $9.73 billion, against guidance of $9.54 to $9.56 billion. The company raised its full-year outlook: revenue of $14.52 to $14.57 billion, from $14.1 to $14.2 billion, and adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 a share, from $4.16 to $4.19; for the current quarter it forecast revenue of $3.53 to $3.55 billion. With the results it announced the acquisition of Applied Compute, an artificial intelligence company, for $4.5 billion in stock, the transaction expected to close in its fiscal third quarter subject to regulatory clearance, in the same account. The shares had gained nearly 10 percent in the regular session ahead of the release and climbed another 8 percent after hours, in the same account. One guidance account filed below prints the quarter’s earnings at $0.46 a share against a consensus of $0.97 and a miss of $0.51; that printing stands against the after-close account’s figures and is carried in the Cocked Hat, unreconciled. Settled: the report, the raise, and the purchase, in the after-close account. Open: the two earnings figures, which the desk does not blend.

Shenzhen at the Close: A Hug on the Tarmac, a Handshake at the Banquet, the Place of Honour at the Table, and Thursday’s Two Meetings

The summit’s Wednesday closed as it opened, in ceremony, and the evening accounts add the banquet’s furniture to the midday file. The President was met at the aircraft by President Xi—the first time Mr. Xi has greeted any visiting leader at an airport in his time in power, in the wire account filed below, reciprocating the President’s greeting at Joint Base Andrews in September—and the two men shook hands and embraced, in the arrival account and the greeting account filed below. At the welcome banquet, Mr. Putin walked over and shook the President’s hand as Mr. Xi stood beside them, before the group photograph, in the greeting account and in the summit account filed below. Classical musicians performed “America the Beautiful” as the President arrived for the banquet; Mr. Xi gave him the spot of honour next to him in the group photograph and seated him by his side at the head table, in the greeting account. Mr. Xi’s banquet address pointed to Shenzhen’s four decades from a fishing village to a city filing 20,000 international patents a year as proof of China’s opening, in the banquet account the midday file carried.

The day’s speeches stand where the midday file left them: Mr. Xi pledged to stand against trade protectionism and for free and open trade; Mr. Putin criticised Western sanctions; and the two men met for the fifth time this year, Mr. Putin’s first in-person appearance at an APEC leaders’ gathering since 2017, in the summit account. Thursday’s order stands confirmed in every evening account: the President and Mr. Xi hold a working lunch first, its subject the economic side and the implementation of the trade agreement in a senior administration official’s preview in the greeting account, and the first trilateral of the three presidents follows—the first meeting of the leaders of the United States, Russia and China—with nuclear arms, the war in Ukraine and the war with Iran named by the President on his departure from Washington, Ukraine named by Moscow, and trade and artificial intelligence in the summit’s own papers. Settled: the welcome, in full, and the order of Thursday. Open: everything Thursday will say.

The Gulf and Oil at the Close: A Build of 3.4 Million Barrels Against 5.28 in the Industry Count, Brent Down More Than 2 Percent, and a Fire Still Being Fought

The official inventory figure landed at midday and the market took it down. Crude stocks rose by 3.4 million barrels in the week ended November 13, to 417.8 million barrels, about 3 percent below the five-year average, against expectations in the wire’s poll of a rise of 58,000 barrels, in the inventories account filed below; gasoline stocks rose 5.2 million barrels to 215.9 million, against 1.6 million expected, and distillate stocks rose 1.6 million to 104.9 million, in the same account. The industry institute’s count for the same week, published Tuesday, put the crude build at 5.28 million barrels; the two instruments stand 1.88 million apart and are printed apart in the Cocked Hat. Oil fell on the official figure: Brent futures shed $2.03, or 2.18 percent, to $91.11 a barrel by 1316 Eastern, in the oil account filed below, against the morning’s readings of $92.98 and $92.53 to $92.60 in the accounts the midday file carried; the companion account puts West Texas Intermediate down 1.98 percent to $84.31 on the same release. Bahrain’s defence force said on Wednesday it had intercepted Iranian aerial attacks on the country, a day after the two sides traded the strikes the morning file carried, in the same accounts.

In the strait, the evening file gains no ending. Oman’s authorities said efforts to put out the fire aboard the Tara Gas were still under way, and the search continued for the one missing crew member, in the wire account filed below; the operator’s sentence stands as it stood: one crew member remains unaccounted for, with search and rescue operations ongoing. The midday file joined the operator’s unnamed vessel and the Tara Gas as one ship; the evening accounts carry the two statements in one story without naming the operator’s vessel, and the join stands as the midday file made it, no stronger. The injury counts stand apart, eleven in the operator’s statement and two in hospital in the authorities’, as they have stood all day. On the Bahrain radar, no assessment from any capital stands in the evening file, for a fifth day. Settled: the inventories, and the price’s answer to them. Open: the fire, the missing man, and the radar.

Alaska at the Close: The Senate Settled and Unconceded, and a Tabulation at 2100 Eastern That This Edition Does Not Wait For

The Senate file stands closed as a count and open as a case, where the midday file left it. Ms. Peltola’s count stands at 144,302 votes, 50.12 percent, to Senator Sullivan’s 131,844; the Senator’s campaign has said he will not concede at least until certification, targeted for November 25; the Justice Department’s appeal and the federal and state investigations stand open. The evening file adds the considered responses in brief: Ms. Peltola declared victory on Tuesday night, and the arithmetic that answers the ballot dispute—hand the Senator every other vote in the race and he finishes 708 behind—stands unrevised.

The House seat is tonight’s fact, and the evening desk prints the hour and the models and files before the count, as the log requires. The Division of Elections runs its official ranked-choice tabulation at 1700 Alaska time, 2100 Eastern, and will livestream it, in the accounts the midday file carried. The unofficial tally from the cast vote record, updated at 0530 Alaska time on Wednesday on 290,003 ballots, puts Mr. Begich ahead in the final round at 51.4 to 48.6 percent, by 7,405 votes in the updated tally account filed below, by 7,478 in the midday file’s reading of the same model, and by 7,967 to 7,998 in the November 16 record; first choices stand at 136,215 for Mr. Begich and 119,689 for Mr. Hill in the Alaska account filed below, with Mr. Hafner at 22,669, and Mr. Begich needing about a quarter of the redistributed preferences to reach a majority, in the analysis account filed below. The tally account’s conclusion is printed as its conclusion: on the ballots remaining, Mr. Begich will win. The official word comes at 2100 Eastern, three hours after this edition collects; the Midnight Watch will carry it. Settled: the Senate. Open, until tonight: the House.

Measles at the Close: The First Considered Responses—Grief From the Checkers, Resignation Calls From the Hill, and a Recommendation From the Secretary

The Evening Watch’s remit is the first considered responses, and the measles decision of Tuesday drew them on Wednesday from every side of the question. The chairman of the verification body’s advisory committee, Dr. Andrus, told the Guardian there was no question the decision was emotional, because the work had run for decades, in the responses account filed below; public health leaders in the same account called the loss significant damage and renewed calls for the Secretary’s removal, with Senator Cassidy’s Sunday sentence—that the Secretary’s tenure has been “a series of failures”—carried in it, and Senator Warnock’s criticism beside it. Representative Crockett blamed the administration and the Secretary by description, in the blame account filed below, which also carries the Secretary’s own timing point: the chain that cost the status began on January 20, 2025, before his confirmation on February 13, a point he made to a Senate committee in April in his own words—“the measles epidemic began before I came into office.”

The administration’s answer stands as the morning file carried it, with one addition. The Secretary posted on Tuesday that the United States “will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status,” and added: “I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” with his department working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust, in the responses account and in the decision account filed below. The CDC’s Director said the designation is not what protects Americans and vaccination does. Nearly 150 health care organisations wrote to the Secretary and the Director on Tuesday urging stronger action, in the status account filed below. An investigation published Tuesday, carried in the decision account, found in data from 13 states and New York City a larger pullback in vaccination among younger children in 2025 than in any year since records of that kind, including the pandemic years; the department declined the investigators’ request to interview the Secretary, and a White House spokesman said the Secretary and the President had encouraged vaccination and worked with states on outbreak response, in the same account. The counts stand where the morning file left them: 5,412 confirmed cases in 2026 through November 12, the highest since 1991; the deaths stand apart at six in the CDC’s 2026 count and at ten and thirteen in other accounts, in the Cocked Hat. The corrective action plans are due in the coming weeks. Settled: the status, and every side’s first answer to it. Open: the plans, and the twelve months without transmission that winning the status back requires.

France and Spain at the Close: The Police March on Paris for Their Own Allowance, and a Second Instrument Puts Spain’s Right 16 Seats Apart From the First

France’s Wednesday produced the week’s reversal: the police marched. Several hundred officers, called out by the Alliance Police Nationale union, marched in Paris on Wednesday toward the Élysée and the Ministry of the Interior at Place Beauvau, demanding an immediate increase in the special police allowance, in the march account filed below. The allowance, the ISSP, stands at 28.5 percent of base salary and has not been increased since 2019; the unions demand 35 percent in stages, and the Minister’s offer of November 13—five points in three stages to 33.5 percent by 2029—was rejected by the unions, in the same account. The day before, more than 1,200 riot police requested medical checkups, a course the account describes as a way around the ban on police strikes, and the figures presented put 1,600 officers and gendarmes injured in the recent weeks of protests and urban violence, in the same account. No major demonstration was confirmed in central Paris on Wednesday, in the schedule account filed below. Thursday carries two gatherings in the capital—a pensioners’ march from Montparnasse toward Les Invalides and a protest outside the Senate against the police firearms bill, which the Senate debates Thursday afternoon—and the roundabout occupations from Friday, in the same account. The strike file behind the day stands where the morning file left it: 146,000 demonstrators counted by the Interior Ministry on Tuesday against more than 500,000 by the CGT, and a strike rate of 2.59 percent in the state civil service, in the tracker accounts the morning file carried.

Spain’s evening gain is a second instrument, and the desk prints the two side by side. The 40dB tracking’s sixth instalment stands as the midday file printed it: the Popular Party at 32.2 percent and 131 seats, the Socialists at 30.7 and 122, Vox at 17.0 and 55, its lowest of the campaign. Sondaxe, published the same Wednesday, puts the Popular Party at 29.0 percent and 121 seats, the Socialists at 27.0 percent and 111, and Vox at 19.4 percent and 71 seats, in the useful-vote account and the average account the midday file carried. The two instruments agree on the order and on the right’s majority, and disagree on Vox by sixteen seats; both stand in the Cocked Hat. Thursday carries the campaign’s single head-to-head debate; polls may publish until November 23; Spain votes November 29.

The Air File at the Close: Steps Promised Against a Repetition, Responsibility Accepted, and Answers Owed to the Senate by November 23

The ground-stop file gained its oversight chapter on Wednesday. The Secretary said the agency and its contractors are addressing the failures that contributed to Friday’s stop, and the Administrator accepted responsibility for the disruption, while officials review contractor performance and the steps to prevent a recurrence, in the investigation account filed below, which carries the day’s addition under the wire’s reporting of the Secretary’s statements. Testing continues at the contractor’s laboratory in Florida, with the agency, Cisco and the FBI involved, in the same account; the installation pause remains in place, and 68 earlier installations had operated without the same reported problem, in the same account. The vendor’s position entered the file: the routers functioned as configured by the installer and did not fail, in the rollout account filed below, which shifts the account’s scrutiny to installation and configuration; the contractor has said it is cooperating with the investigation. The Senate Commerce Committee’s Democrats have formally requested technical answers by November 23, in the investigation account. The agency has published no final technical report establishing whether the initiating failure involved the device, its configuration, its installation, the monitoring, the network architecture, or a combination, in the same account, and the desk prints Wednesday’s statements as reported developments, not as a root cause. No second nationwide stop stands in any account the desk read; Wednesday’s only stop remains the morning’s weather stop at Fort Lauderdale. Settled: the pause, the testing, and the date the Senate is owed its answers. Open: the cause, which the recreation still has not supplied.

Thursday Ahead: A Lunch, a Trilateral, a First Trade, a Debate, and a Senate Bill

Thursday carries the President’s working lunch with Mr. Xi and the first trilateral of the three presidents in Shenzhen; the first trade of Anthropic’s shares as ANT; Walmart’s report before the open; Spain’s single head-to-head debate; the police firearms bill in the French Senate, with the pensioners’ march and the Senate protest in Paris; and, tonight before any of it, Alaska’s tabulation at 2100 Eastern. Alaska certifies on November 25, the day the Treasury Secretary’s ten days also run to. The Senate Commerce Committee is owed its technical answers on November 23. Spain votes November 29; the Federal Reserve decides December 8 and 9; government funding runs out after December 11. The Midnight Watch collects at 0000.
