The President flies into the Philippines on Tuesday at the tail end of the ASEAN summit, where he could face protests, ahead of the first meeting in two years of the Quad leaders—the United States, Japan, Australia and India—in the wire account above. It will be his first Quad meeting; the last gathering of the group was two years ago, in the same account. His Tuesday, as published in the schedule account filed below, runs: arrival at Ninoy Aquino International Airport; at 6:20 p.m. he greets the Quad leaders for a photo opportunity; at 6:30, the multilateral meeting; at 7:45, an ASEAN-United States Summit Special and reception; at 8:25, a United States-ASEAN dinner. He skips the East Asia Summit, joins the special summit, signs a joint statement with Thailand’s Prime Minister on an agreement on reciprocal trade on Tuesday, and meets the Philippine President on Wednesday, in the wire account.

The room’s other case was made on Monday, before he lands. Premier Li Qiang told the ASEAN leaders on Monday that economic achievements between China and ASEAN were ‘truly extraordinary’ in the face of global trade restrictions, expressed Beijing’s commitment to free trade, and called on the region to ‘stand united, ward off interference, and work together,’ in the wire account. ASEAN’s leaders spent Tuesday in meetings with counterparts from Japan, South Korea, China and India ahead of the East Asia Summit, in the same account. The wire’s framing of the trip stands in its lede and is printed as its framing: the visit comes after the midterm defeat, with spy allegations and new American curbs on China’s access to advanced chips complicating a fragile trade truce. Settled: the arrival, the schedule, and the order of the week—Manila on Tuesday, a state visit welcome on Wednesday, Shenzhen on Thursday. Open: what the Quad says, and whether the protests the wire expects materialize.

Shenzhen at 0400: ‘Groundbreaking’ in Beijing, Four Agendas in Four Capitals, and a Fourth Chair Still Empty

Thursday’s session gained a Korean bearing in the night, and it is the bearing of the country that hosts the forum’s other business and sits closest to the fourth chair. A Seoul paper’s account, in the APEC account filed below, records that none of the parties most exposed to the agenda will be at the table—Ukraine, South Korea, or the Middle Eastern states if Iran comes up—that APEC decides by consensus and its decisions are voluntary and non-binding, and that the leaders’ meeting of November 18 and 19 puts bargaining alongside an agenda of trade, artificial intelligence and connectivity. Mr. Kim’s attendance remains uncertain in the same account: the President looks to the host to bring Mr. Kim into the lineup, and President Putin keeps a seat ready for his treaty ally, in its telling.

The agendas stand in their four versions, and the desk prints them as four. Beijing’s, from Monday’s confirmation: ‘in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations,’ in the APEC account, and ‘groundbreaking significance’ from the Foreign Ministry spokeswoman, Ms. Mao Ning, in the Hong Kong account filed below. The President’s, from his departure: denuclearization, ‘tough subject because it’s very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes’; Iran, ‘in very good shape’; Ukraine, ‘my favourite subject’; and economics and trade, in the departure account filed below, which also carries his unattributed figure of 25,000 soldiers a month lost by Russia and Ukraine together. His officials’: nuclear stockpiles and Iran, a conversation to begin, no agreements expected, and Ukraine not on the trilateral agenda, in the Hong Kong account. The Kremlin’s: the meeting confirmed, no agenda stated, and a one-on-one between the President and President Putin being arranged, in the Kremlin aide’s account in the departure file—against no such meeting agreed, in the agency account carried in the Hong Kong file, and no separate meeting planned, in the White House’s earlier telling. On the fourth chair, the President’s words stand alone in the file: Mr. Kim ‘may come,’ any meeting would be in China, and ‘that’s up to President Xi’; no confirmation from Pyongyang or Beijing had accompanied the remarks, and he did not say whether an invitation had been extended, in the departure account. Before Shenzhen, the President is in Shenzhen’s host country from Wednesday for the APEC leaders’ meeting President Xi chairs.

The Gulf at 0400: A Tanker Named Off Oman, Six Sunk in a Claim and None Confirmed, and No Word on the Radar for a Third Day

The Hormuz file gained a name in the night, and the name is the night’s hardest fact in the Gulf. A British maritime agency reported a tanker attacked about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, while leaving the strait, and a security monitor identified the ship as the Panama-flagged ON PHOENIX, hit three nautical miles off Oman, in the Hormuz account filed below, which compiles a Pakistani paper, a broadcaster, a Gulf paper, the maritime agency and a strait-tracking site. It is the first vessel named in a week of claims. Against it stands Tehran’s arithmetic, grown again: six tankers caught fire and sunk since Sunday in the Guards’ claim as carried in the same account, two of them said to have struck mines on an unauthorised route, and a third tanker left immobilised after striking a mine east of the strait on Monday in the regular navy’s claim. The claims could not be independently verified, and Iranian authorities did not identify the vessels involved, in the same account. Tracking data showed no commercial ship had crossed the strait at all by early Tuesday morning, in the same account.

Two files in the Gulf did not move. On the radar at Al-Riffa, the overnight file adds no assessment from any capital for a third day: the Guards’ six drones and a struck radar, Manama’s intercepts, the Ambassador’s all-intercepted sentence, Friday’s two drones down in the American denial, and no impacts to American forces in the spokesman’s sentence, which did not address the machine. One aggregator’s timeline, updated Tuesday morning, carries a further claim dated Tuesday, attributed to the Guards and naming radar equipment at Sheikh Isa, in the timeline account filed below; no capital has confirmed it, and the desk prints it as a claim in a timeline and nothing more. On the inspectors, Tehran’s deputy foreign minister said on Sunday that Iran will not let United Nations inspectors visit its damaged nuclear facilities until the war ends and the United States meets its conditions, in the Hormuz account. The rest of the file stands where the week left it: three American carriers in the region, the blockade in force, the President’s words that new strikes are highly unlikely while negotiations progress, Tehran’s words that it remains in a state of war, and the Khor Mor strike unclaimed.

The Airlines at 0400: Tuesday Opens After a 344-Cancellation Monday, the Secretary Takes His Case to the Senate Republicans’ Lunch, and the Money Argument Meets at $4 Billion

Tuesday opens on the recovery’s second ordinary day, with Monday’s last reading standing at 344 cancellations and 4,800 delays by 1800 and Tuesday’s own cancellations counted at 68 in the morning’s earlier accounts, in the midnight file. Monday’s one stumble has been given its official size: the United outage was a company matter of about an hour, and ‘this is not an FAA system-wide problem,’ the Secretary said, in the AAP account filed below. No second nationwide stop stands in any account the desk read.

The money argument moved on Monday, and its two sides now cite the same small number for different purposes. The Majority Leader, Mr. Thune, said only $4 billion of the $12.5 billion approved last year had been spent, and that explanations are owed, in the accounts filed below; the Democrats’ Monday account puts the figure as spent or committed at just $4 billion, in the wire account filed with the midnight edition, against the $11 billion unspent in their earlier reading of the same appropriation. The Democratic Leader, Mr. Schumer, answered that the Administration has money, does not use it, and asks for more, and his party wants hearings into Friday’s failure, in the same accounts; Senator Schmitt answered that the funding was long overdue. The Secretary takes the case in person on Tuesday, sitting in on the Senate Republicans’ weekly lunch, in the funding account filed below, which records that as of Monday he had not released comprehensive details of how the $50 billion would be spent, that department staff will brief congressional staffers this week, and that the request now sits inside the negotiations to avoid a shutdown after December 11, when government funding runs out. The President’s sentence stands in the equipment account filed below: what the country saw on Friday was ‘very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,’ and the system should be blown up and put in new. The cause file itself gained nothing in the night: a router installed during a contractor’s copper-to-fibre work at El Dorado, a second site at Amarillo, no cyberattack in the officials’ ruling, and the root cause still unnamed. Settled: the recovery, and that both parties now argue from the unspent balance. Open: the root cause, and whether Congress pays before December 11.

France and Spain at 0400: A Strike Day Opens on the Eighth Anniversary, and a Fifth Tracking Moves the Seats Without Moving the Gap

France’s next fact is a weekday fact, and it opens today. Six union federations—the CGT, Solidaires, FSU, UNSA, CGC and FAFP—have called a nationwide strike and demonstrations for Tuesday, November 17, after the Prime Minister’s social conference, saying the government had announced only crumbs, in the week’s file; November 17 is the date the Yellow Vest movement launched in 2018, and organisers plan to mark the eighth anniversary on roundabouts and at toll booths, in the accounts filed below. The government’s wage answer stands at a 1.6 percent minimum-wage increase effective December 1, taking net monthly pay to about €1,502—a €24 increase the unions call too small—in the wage account filed below; earlier accounts in the file carried a 0.6 percent figure as the promise the unions rejected, and both figures are printed in the cocked hat. Saturday’s fifth day stands at 106,000 nationwide in the Interior Ministry’s count, 24,000 of them in Paris, and 200,000 in the student unions’, in the Saturday account filed below. The movement whole—from the September school blockades through the largest day, November 5, at 575,000 in the Ministry’s count and 1.6 million in the union’s—stands in the protests account filed below, which records the pan-European protests called for November 20 to 22. The police bill goes to the Senate on Thursday; a sixth Saturday is called for November 21. Settled: the strike is called, by six federations, for the anniversary. Open: its size, which Tuesday will supply.

Spain’s campaign gained a fifth daily reading in the night, and it moved the seats without moving the gap. The fifth instalment of the daily tracking puts the Popular Party at 31.8 percent, up three-tenths; the Socialists at 30.6, up three-tenths and 1.2 points past their figure at the tracking’s start; and Vox at 17.5, down half a point—with the seat projection moving against Vox alone: the Popular Party gains three seats to 133, the Socialists one to 120, and Vox loses four to 58, taking the two right parties’ combined total from 192 to 191, fifteen above the 176 needed, in the tracking account filed below. The gap between the two large parties holds at 1.2 points, and in the preference to lead the government the Socialist leader stands first at 32.8 percent, in the same account. Monday’s other polls stand apart from the tracking and from each other, in the Reuters account filed below: one projects 201 to 205 seats for the right pair and 102 to 104 for the Socialists at 26.1 percent; another puts the Socialists at 26.9 and the right bloc at 194 seats; and the state pollster stands as a major outlier, projecting 134 to 143 Socialist seats against 155 to 171 for the right. The head-to-head debate between Mr. Sánchez and Mr. Feijóo stands on Thursday, November 19; polls may publish until November 23; Spain votes on November 29.

Tuesday Opens: Sales at 0830, a Lunch, a Landing, a Count, and a Report After the Close

Tuesday carries October retail sales at 0830, the Secretary’s lunch with Senate Republicans, France’s strike day, the President’s arrival in Manila and the Quad at 1830 there, Alaska’s next count, and Nvidia’s earnings after the close. Wednesday carries the pricing of the Anthropic listing—$70 to $78 a share on 825 million shares, about $61 billion at the middle of the range in the listing account filed below, about $1.2 trillion of value at the midpoint in the same account and $1.3 to $1.45 trillion fully diluted in the test account filed below, six times oversubscribed in one report and trading in pre-listing contracts at $101.72, some 30 percent above the range’s top—the October meeting minutes, the first day of APEC in Shenzhen, Alaska’s tabulation, and Japan’s trade figures. Thursday carries the first trading day under the ticker ANT and the three presidents in Shenzhen, the police bill in the French Senate, and Spain’s debate. The Treasury Secretary’s 10 days run to about November 25, when Alaska’s certification is also targeted. Spain votes November 29; the Federal Reserve decides December 8 and 9; government funding runs out after December 11. The Midday Watch collects at 1200.

The Cocked Hat

Where the night’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Alaska: 49.98 percent on the full denominator, 50.0 rounded in the Press’s Tuesday count, 50.1 on the dashboard’s calculation in the week’s file, and 51.83 in a newspaper’s model of the scanned ballots’ final round; 52 votes short of a majority on the current total, about 6,500 ballots estimated still to count, a victory declared by one candidate, the process left to run by the other, and no call by the Press. On the petition: 180,200 in the wire’s accounts, 181,025 at 0813 Pacific on Monday, 185,600 in one evening account, and 188,548 at 1713 Pacific, the affiliations self-reported in every reading. On the board: a return discussed with confidants in Sunday’s report, a return not weighed in Monday’s three voices and not in talks in Monday’s familiar person, a president who would not mind it and who holds the stock, an investor who made no demands, a Treasury Secretary set against it, and no word from the board. On Nvidia’s Monday session: down 4.12 percent at $156.14 in the closing accounts, down 4.1 in the wire’s, and down 3.7 in the wire’s return account. On Asia’s Tuesday: the Kospi down 2.6 percent at the close in two accounts, with Samsung down 3.1 and SK Hynix down 1.8 in one and Samsung down 3.3 and SK Hynix down 2.0 in the other; the Nikkei down 1.2 in the session and 1.3 at the close; SoftBank down 3.9 in one account and 4.0 in the other. On oil: Brent at $95.40 on Monday morning in the week’s file, $92.44 at Monday’s settlement, $91.80 in the day-ahead account and $91.66 at 0430 GMT, with a surplus forecast against a strait where no commercial ship crossed by early Tuesday. On Shenzhen: Ukraine on the agenda in the President’s words and off it in his officials’, the spying matter maybe raised in the President’s and not to be raised in the officials’, a one-on-one being arranged in the Kremlin aide’s account and not agreed in the agency’s, and a fourth chair that is the host’s to fill in the President’s telling and unconfirmed in every other. On the radar: six drones on target, several attacks destroyed, all drones intercepted, two drones down on Friday, no impacts to forces, a further claim dated Tuesday in one timeline, and no word on the machine, for a third day. On Hormuz: six tankers sunk in the Guards’ claim, a third immobilised in the navy’s, one tanker named and attacked off Oman in the maritime agency’s report, and no sinking confirmed by any party not making the claim. On France’s wage: 0.6 percent as the rejected promise in the earlier accounts and 1.6 percent effective December 1 in Monday’s, called crumbs in both. On the air money: $4 billion spent in the Majority Leader’s figure, $4 billion spent or committed in the Democrats’ Monday account, $11 billion unspent in their earlier one, $50 billion asked, and no comprehensive details yet in the funding account. On Spain: the Socialists at 30.6 percent in the fifth daily tracking, 26.9 and 26.1 in Monday’s other polls, and first in the state pollster’s seats, with the right’s majority standing in all but the outlier. Inside the triangle is where the week honestly stands, and the log turns on it.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 34 items.

Subjective
Juneau Independent — Ms. Peltola at 49.98 percent, about 6,500 ballots estimated still to count, and Senator Sullivan’s spokesman letting the process run its course

Subjective
USA Today — ground stop chaos spurs a fight in Congress over funding: the Secretary at the Senate Republicans’ lunch on November 17, and no comprehensive details yet

Congress is under pressure to act after air traffic control issues grounded flights nationwide last week, setting up a new funding fight on Capitol Hill and further complicating lawmakers’ efforts to avoid another government shutdown before Christmas. Administration officials are pleading for billions of additional dollars to modernize what they acknowledge is an aging system. The Transportation Secretary said he is asking lawmakers to fast-track a $50 billion package to prevent further communications malfunctions like the one that derailed air travel before the weekend. The new funding request could quickly become another variable in the ongoing negotiations to avoid another shutdown after December 11, when government funding is set to run out. The meltdown was caused by a breakdown in the communications network, prompted by the replacement of a router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, as part of an ongoing effort to switch out old copper wires with fiber-optic cable. The President weighed in on the situation for the first time on November 16. The Secretary is expected to sit in on Senate Republicans’ weekly lunch on November 17, where he will continue to make the case for his funding request. As of November 16, he had not released comprehensive details on how the $50 billion request would be spent. Transportation Department and Administration staff will brief congressional staffers about the latest funding request this week.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — the President blames ageing equipment: ‘very, very old equipment that had a heart attack’

The President has urged Congress to approve billions of dollars to replace the country’s ageing air traffic control network. He blamed Friday’s rare nationwide ground stop on ageing aviation infrastructure, saying ‘very, very old equipment had a heart attack,’ as he renewed pressure on Congress to approve billions of dollars to completely replace the network. Addressing the hours-long flight freeze that cancelled more than 9,100 flights and stranded travellers nationwide, he argued that decades of underinvestment had left the United States relying on obsolete hardware that needs to be torn out rather than patched. ‘We have old equipment, broken equipment. We’ve been telling that to Congress,’ he said. ‘We essentially want to blow it up and put new in. We need the funding to get it done.’ Friday’s incident, only the second nationwide ground stop since 2001, stemmed from a telecommunications and router overload triggered while a contractor was replacing legacy copper wiring with fibre-optic lines at remote sites in Arkansas and Texas. Transportation officials ruled out any cyberattack or artificial intelligence involvement.

Subjective
Nutshell Today — more than 100,000 rally nationwide on Saturday, and another nationwide strike planned for November 17

More than 100,000 people took to the streets across France on November 14, as students, workers and trade unions continued protests over education standards, living costs, low wages and police violence. With another nationwide strike planned for November 17, the demonstrations are adding to pressure on the government. The Interior Ministry estimated that 106,000 people joined Saturday’s protests, including 24,000 in Paris; student unions put the nationwide turnout at 200,000. Trade unions have called another nationwide strike for November 17, rejecting the government’s proposed minimum wage increase as ‘crumbs.’ The November 17 strike will coincide with the eighth anniversary of the Yellow Vest movement, which began in 2018 over rising fuel prices and grew into a wider challenge to the government’s economic policies and the cost of living.

Subjective
Newzino — France brings forward a minimum wage increase of 1.6 percent to December 1, at about €1,502 net a month, and the unions call €24 too small

France will raise its minimum wage by 1.6 percent on December 1, taking net monthly pay to about €1,502, after more than two months of protests over the cost of living. Unions called the €24 increase too small and are staging a day of action on November 17. In the account’s timeline: on November 9 the unions rejected the increase as too small—one federation’s leader calls it crumbs in the wider file—and the federation called a new protest for November 17. A prediction market’s question is printed with the account: if other major unions join and schools or transport close for a full day, the protest wave would move beyond student-led demonstrations and become a broader challenge to the government before the election.

Subjective
political.org — France’s protests whole: the movement from the school blockades to the November 17 strike call, and the counts of the largest days

A protest movement that began in late September with students angry about underfunded schools has grown into a nationwide challenge to the government, producing some of the worst street violence in years. The movement began among high school and university students in Paris protesting poor school conditions, teacher shortages and infrastructure problems. The largest single day of protest, Thursday, November 5, drew 575,000 people by the Interior Ministry’s count and 1.6 million by the union’s. On Monday, November 9, the Prime Minister announced a 1.6 percent minimum-wage increase effective December 1; the unions rejected it. Public-sector unions have called a strike and demonstrations for Tuesday, November 17, and some groups have called for pan-European protests from November 20 to 22. The unrest first began in late September. The turning point came on Saturday, October 17. That day’s demonstrations were organized by the coalition of France’s main unions, with students and the Yellow Vest movement joining. France has a long record of street movements that start over a single grievance and widen; the 2018 protests began on November 17 in opposition to rising fuel taxes and swelled into a movement against the President and the biggest challenge of his presidency. The current wave combines union-led strikes, student mobilization and Yellow Vest participation, and is part of a broader wave of discontent across Europe, with young people in several countries staging similar protests in recent weeks.

Subjective
Demócrata — the fifth daily tracking: the Popular Party at 31.8 percent and 133 seats, the Socialists at 30.6 and 120, Vox down four seats to 58, and the combined right at 191

The general election poll by the tracking firm for a national newspaper and a radio network on November 17 places the Popular Party at 31.8 percent of the vote and the Socialists at 30.6 percent. Both parties advance three-tenths compared to Monday, while Vox retreats half a point, to 17.5 percent. The gap between the conservatives and the socialists remains 1.2 points. The most pronounced change appears in the seats: Vox loses four deputies and stands at 58; the Popular Party gains three and reaches 133, including the two from its Navarre partner, while the Socialists add one and reach 120. The combined projection for the two right parties goes from 192 to 191 deputies, 15 above the 176 needed for an absolute majority. Since the first installment, published on November 13, the Socialists have moved from 29.4 percent to 30.6 percent, an increase of 1.2 points; in the same period the Popular Party goes from 31.5 to 31.8. The Socialists have cut nine-tenths off the distance compared to the start of daily tracking. In the preference to lead the government, the Socialist leader stands at 32.8 percent of those surveyed, the Popular leader at 22.2 and the Vox leader at 17.3; those figures measure presidential preference and do not equate to the vote estimate.

Subjective
Reuters — Spain’s right retains a firm poll lead despite Socialist gains: three polls on Monday, and the state pollster a major outlier

MADRID, November 16 (Reuters) — Spain’s conservative People’s Party and Vox would together win a parliamentary majority in the November 29 election, three opinion polls published on Monday showed, though the Prime Minister’s Socialists gained ground. The surveys are the first since last week’s campaign launch, which has focused on housing affordability, immigration, corruption and last month’s deadly train crash. A daily poll showed the Socialists rising to 30.3 percent from 29.9, exceeding the 30 percent mark for the first time in that poll since the 2023 election, with the Popular Party on 31.5 and Vox on 18, together winning more than 190 seats in the 350-seat lower house. A second poll projected 201 to 205 seats for the two right parties combined and 102 to 104 for the Socialists, whose support rose half a point to 26.1 percent. A third showed Socialist support up one point from a week earlier to 26.9 percent, with the right bloc winning 194 seats to the Socialists’ 109. The state pollster remained a major outlier: last week it projected 134 to 143 seats for the Socialists against 155 to 171 for the two right parties combined, suggesting the Prime Minister could retain power through a broad left-wing coalition.

Subjective
Euronews, carried by Ekkow — five things to know before Anthropic goes public: pricing on Wednesday, trading on Thursday under ANT, at $70 to $78 a share

The company will launch an initial public offering on November 19. It is expected to set the final price of its shares on Wednesday, November 18, and begin trading on an exchange in New York the following day under the symbol ANT. The company has proposed a price of $70 to $78 a share, which would value it at about $1.2 trillion in the middle of that range. The listing will be the biggest test yet of whether investors believe artificial intelligence can make money over the long term. Not everyone is convinced: at a briefing organised by an investor-responsibility centre, governance and legal experts warned of ‘red flags’ in the company’s filings, and a New York City financial officer said the company is rushing toward a listing without answering fundamental questions about its readiness to operate as a publicly traded company. The filing shows a large technology company and a search company’s parent among its largest backers. In May, the company raised $65 billion from investors who valued it at $965 billion, the first time a funding round had valued it above its rival. It is offering 825 million shares to the public at $70 to $78 each; at the middle of the price range, that would raise roughly $61 billion, making it one of the largest listings ever. The company is a public benefit corporation, legally required to pursue a stated purpose as well as profit. It has committed to spend at least $518 billion with six suppliers over roughly a decade, to secure the chips, data centres and electricity its models need. Its direct competitor has pushed its own listing back to 2027 at the earliest and was recently valued at about $1.25 trillion in a private round, according to reports.

Subjective
OANDA — the listing as a make-or-break test: six times oversubscribed in one report, $900.9 billion in commitments, and a pre-listing contract at $101.72

The listing has reportedly attracted demand equivalent to approximately six times the shares available, according to a financial wire’s report published on Thursday, November 12. At the upper end of its indicative $70 to $78 price range, the company is seeking to raise approximately $64.4 billion by selling 825 million shares, potentially valuing the company at around $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The offering is expected to be priced on Wednesday, November 18, ahead of its anticipated trading debut under the ticker ANT on Thursday, November 19. These dates remain subject to the final offering timetable. According to its amended registration statement dated November 10, the company disclosed approximately $900.9 billion in aggregate computing and infrastructure commitments over multiple years, including $451.6 billion expected through 2030, and approximately $146.6 billion in available liquidity as of September 30. Its third-quarter revenue reached approximately $17 billion, an increase of 47 percent quarter on quarter, compared with growth of 144 percent recorded in the second quarter. Based on the current price of $101.72 of its pre-listing perpetual futures on a per-share basis, at the time of writing, it is trading at around a 30 percent premium to the upper end of the expected $78.00 price.

entry.title: Monday Closes With Alaska at 52 Votes From a Majority and Its Governorship Conceded, the Airlines at 344 Cancelled With a United Outage Inside the Recovery, the Board Reported by Three Voices Not Weighing Mr. Huang's Return on the Night Before Earnings, and Futures Little Changed With the President Airborne for Manila
entry.summary: Monday closes with Alaska 52 votes from a majority and its governorship conceded, and airlines at 344 cancelled with a United outage inside.
entry.content:
The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Monday Closes With Alaska at 52 Votes From a Majority and Its Governorship Conceded, the Airlines at 344 Cancelled With a United Outage Inside the Recovery, the Board Reported by Three Voices Not Weighing Mr. Huang’s Return on the Night Before Earnings, and Futures Little Changed With the President Airborne for Manila

The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: a count that moved after three days standing still and stopped 52 votes short of the line that ends it; a governorship conceded in the same report; a recovery that held at 344 cancelled and stumbled once, inside one airline, for about an hour; a board whose position is now carried by three voices and still not by the board; a market that fell into a correction by day and stood still by night; and a president in the air between Washington and Manila, with Thursday’s room in Shenzhen still described four ways.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Tuesday, November 17, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 56, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Monday, in Edition No. 55, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Monday, in Edition No. 54, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Monday, and in Edition No. 53, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 on Monday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Monday Settled, What It Left Open

Monday settled the recovery, the shape of the funding fight, and the distance left in Alaska—52 votes—and it left open the root cause of Friday’s stop, the condition of the radar at Al-Riffa, the board’s own word from Nvidia, and the call in Alaska, which is now a matter of arithmetic and one more day of mail. Alaska’s count moved in the state’s report timed 1713 on Monday, in the Alaska account filed below: Ms. Peltola at 141,637 votes and Senator Sullivan at 130,162, and Ms. Wilson’s concession in the governor’s race in the same account. The airlines’ last reading stands at 344 cancellations and 4,800 delays by 1800, with a United outage of about an hour resolved by 1800, in the updated wire account filed below. Nvidia’s board is not weighing a return, three people told the wire, in the return account filed below, and the company reports on Tuesday. Futures stood little changed on Monday night, in the night account filed below. The desk takes the files in that order.

Alaska at Midnight: A Count That Moved 1,821 Ballots, a Lead of 11,475, and 52 Votes to the Line

The count that spent Sunday and Monday morning where Saturday left it moved on Monday afternoon, and it moved toward the line without reaching it. The Division of Elections’ latest unofficial report, timestamped 5:13 p.m. Monday, shows 285,439 ballots counted, an increase of 1,821 from Saturday’s report, with turnout at 47.15 percent of registered voters, in the Alaska account above. In the Senate race Ms. Peltola has 141,637 votes, or 49.98 percent, against Senator Sullivan’s 130,162, or 45.93 percent; she added 1,000 votes in the update and he added 738, and her lead grew from 11,213 to 11,475, in the same account. On the report’s total of 283,377 votes in the contest, a majority is 141,689, and Ms. Peltola stands 52 votes short of it—against 157 short on Saturday’s figures, in the majority account filed below. The threshold rises as more ballots are counted, in the Alaska account; more ballots arriving by mail will be counted on Tuesday, and overseas ballots may arrive through Wednesday, when the ranked-choice tabulation is run for the races that need it, in the same account. The Press has not called the race, in the markets account filed below, whose last reading before the update stood at Saturday’s numbers. Mr. Heikes stands at 6,020 votes and Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. at 4,684, with 874 write-ins, in the Alaska account.

The same report settled the state’s other large race. Ms. Wilson said she called Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins to congratulate him on his win in the governor’s race, in the Alaska account; the Kreiss-Tomkins and Johnson ticket stands at 142,591 votes, or 50.93 percent, above the first-round threshold if the majority holds, against 78,305 for the Wilson and Shower ticket, in the same account. In the House race Mr. Begich leads Mr. Hill 134,456 to 117,607 and remains below a first-round majority at 47.67 percent, in the same account. Ballot Measure 2, which would repeal ranked-choice voting, is losing, 145,133 no votes to 125,303 yes, and Ballot Measure 3, on voter citizenship qualifications, is passing, in the same account. Settled: the governorship, by concession, and the Senate arithmetic at 52. Open: the call, Tuesday’s mail, and Wednesday’s tabulation if the 52 are not found first.

The Airlines at Midnight: 344 Cancelled by 1800, a United Outage of About an Hour, and New Figures in the Funding Fight

Monday’s recovery held to the end of the day, and its last count in the file is the evening count. By 6 p.m. Eastern there were 344 flight cancellations and 4,800 delays, down from more than 2,300 cancelled and 11,000 delayed on Sunday, in the updated wire account above; the day’s series stands at 55 cancelled as of Sunday evening, about 250 by 0400, 533 by 0700, 300 by 0900, 330 by 1330 and 344 by 1800—readings at different hours on different bases, agreeing that the day ran in the hundreds against the thousands of each of the three days before it, which together stand at more than 18,000 cancellations. Inside the recovery, one airline stumbled on its own: United experienced a technology outage affecting its departing flights for about an hour on Monday, resolved by 6 p.m. Eastern and affecting no other airline, and by 6:50 p.m. United had delayed 645 flights, or 20 percent of its schedule, and cancelled 25, in the same account; how many of those were caused by the outage and how many by the recovery from Friday’s stop was unclear, in the same account. No second nationwide stop was ordered on Monday in any account the desk read. Tuesday’s cancellations stood at 68 due to be cancelled, in the morning’s accounts.

The funding fight gained figures from both parties on Monday, and the figures do not meet. Senate Majority Leader Thune said on Monday that only $4 billion of the $12.5 billion approved by Congress to improve air traffic control systems had been spent, and that explanations are owed for why the number is where it is, in the updated wire account; he said that just $12 billion of the larger sum sought was for air traffic modernisation, with the remainder for airport-related projects, in the same account. Senate Democratic Leader Schumer said on Monday that the Administration has money, does not use it, and then comes back and asks for more, in the same account; the Democrats’ figure in the day’s earlier accounts was $11 billion of the $12.5 billion unspent, in the funding account in the evening file, and Representative DeLauro’s sentence stands there: a $50 billion ransom without a real plan. Senator Schmitt answered for the other side that the funding was long overdue and the can has been kicked for a long time, in the updated wire account. The Secretary’s words stand in the same account: “This rickety system is telegraphing to the American people, ‘Hey, we need investment.’ Now is the time to do a big dollar amount to modernize the system.” The President’s sentence stands there too: what the country saw on Friday was very old equipment that had a heart attack. The brokerage estimate of the weekend’s cost to the four largest airlines stands at $345 million, and the Secretary’s estimate of the broader impact in the billions, in the same accounts. The Secretary sits in on the Senate Republicans’ weekly lunch on Tuesday to make the case, and the Democrats want hearings into what led to Friday’s disruption, in the updated wire account. Settled: the recovery, and that both parties now argue from the unspent balance. Open: the root cause, which no account on Monday supplied, and whether Congress pays.

Nvidia at Midnight: Three Voices Against a Return, a Tower Lit in Taipei, and Earnings on Tuesday

The board’s position gained a third voice on Monday and kept its form: it is reported, and it is not stated. Nvidia’s board is not weighing a return for Mr. Huang as chief executive, three people told the wire, in the return account above; one of them said, “The Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen back.” No statement from the board itself, from the company, or from the interim chief, Ms. Kress, stands in the midnight file. The campaign’s counter in the same account stands at more than 180,200 signatures, with more than 8,800 signatories identifying themselves as current employees and more than 94,000 as shareholders, the affiliations self-reported and unverified, in the same account and in the agenda account filed below. Taipei 101, Taiwan’s tallest building, was illuminated on Monday with messages including “Taiwan Loves Jensen,” in the return account. The President said on Monday that he would not mind seeing Mr. Huang reinstated and that “I think he learned a big lesson,” in the same account, which also carries a newspaper’s review of his financial disclosures putting his holdings in the company at between $13 million and $62 million as of the end of August. Mr. Bessent’s position stands where Sunday put it: an outside successor and a dramatic shake-up, in the same account. Mr. Altman, asked on Monday at a public event in San Francisco whether Mr. Huang should return, said he did not have enough information to answer, and said the demand for artificial intelligence would hold up, in the Altman account filed below. The intelligence question inside the file stands in the return account at its reported width: agencies are still trying to determine the extent of the relationship in question, and evidence gathered so far indicates an intelligence asset rather than a fully trained spy, two sources said; no finding by the board, by any committee, or by any court on any allegation in this file has been made, and the desk prints the allegations as allegations.

What the board will not say, the calendar will partly answer on Tuesday. The company reports its third-quarter results on Tuesday at about 4:20 p.m. Eastern, with a call at 5 p.m. led by Ms. Kress, in the accounts filed below; consensus revenue stands at about $109 billion in the week’s readings, against the company’s outlook of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2 percent, and earnings per share at $2.47, in the preview account filed below, which puts the options market’s expected move at 8.6 percent in either direction. The shares fell 4.12 percent to $156.14 in the closing accounts, in the evening file, and 3.7 percent on Monday in the return account—two readings of the same session, printed apart in the cocked hat below. The stock has lost $735 billion in market value since the scandal broke, in the follow account filed below. The Commerce Department’s rule, the Administration’s first policy answer, stands where the evening file printed it: licences for advanced chips going to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, licences for data centres above 12 million in total processing performance that serve companies headquartered in China and other listed countries, 90 days for centres already serving them, and the January 2025 diffusion rule rescinded, in the rule account and the loophole account filed below. Settled: the board is not weighing a return, on three voices. Open: the board’s own word, and Tuesday’s numbers.

The Markets at Midnight: A Correction by Day, Little Changed by Night, and Asia Lower on Tuesday

Monday’s closes stand where the evening file printed them, and the night added stillness, not a turn. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.49 percent to 24,509.76 and stands in a correction, more than 10 percent below its October 6 high; the S&P 500 fell 1.92 percent to 7,416.59; the Dow fell 739.38 points, or 1.41 percent, to 51,608.17; the semiconductor index fell 5.28 percent, in the evening file. Stock futures were little changed on Monday night after the losing session: Dow futures inched up 8 points, or 0.02 percent, S&P 500 futures were up 0.06 percent, and Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 0.1 percent, in the night account above. Asia-Pacific markets opened lower on Tuesday: Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 0.76 percent and the Topix declined 1.06 percent at the open, in the same account. Asian equities fell on Tuesday morning as the Commerce Department’s rule added to the concerns over the artificial intelligence trade, in the Asia account filed below, which reckons the rule’s first day erased an estimated $960 billion in American technology market capitalisation. Chairman Warsh’s Monday speech stands settled as the day’s set piece: three staff scenarios for the technology he calls super intelligence—shared gains, displacement, and disappointed returns—illustrative scenarios, not forecasts, no rate proposed and no guidance given, in the wire account filed below; the external task forces’ recommendations are due around the end of the year, in the accounts filed below. The October meeting minutes are published on Wednesday, and the December decision stands on December 8 and 9. Settled: the correction, and a quiet night. Open: Tuesday’s retail sales at 0830 and Nvidia after the close, which every account in the file names as the week’s deciding facts.

The President’s Road at Midnight: Airborne for Manila, a Premier Already in the Room, and a Word Changed on the Spying Matter

The President is in the air, and the room he lands in has been sitting since the weekend. He departed Washington on Monday for Manila, where the ASEAN summit opened over the weekend and sits through Tuesday, and continues to Shenzhen for the APEC meeting and Thursday’s session of the three presidents, in the accounts in the evening file. In Manila on Monday, Premier Li Qiang opened China’s case to the regional leaders: at a time of growing unilateralism and protectionism, he said, economic relations between China and ASEAN had only strengthened, and he called the ties extraordinary, in the Manila account filed below, which records that the President is due to arrive on Tuesday at the tail end of the summit, that protests are expected in Manila, and that his first meeting of the Quad—the United States, Japan, Australia and India—is the first such gathering in two years. One word of his Monday remarks changed a file the desk has carried since Friday. The President said on Monday that he “might” bring up the spying matter with President Xi, in the trip account filed below; American officials had previously said they did not expect him to start those conversations, and the midday file carried officials saying the President does not intend to raise it, in the same contrast. The rest of the agenda file stands in its four versions, printed in the evening edition and unamended at midnight: Ukraine on the table in the President’s own words and off it in his officials’; nuclear arms and Iran in Washington’s telling; world peace and strategic stability in Beijing’s; a separate meeting with President Putin beyond doubt in the Kremlin aide’s account and not planned in the White House’s; and a fourth leader, Mr. Kim, who may come, at the host’s invitation, in the departure account and the road account filed below. Europe’s seat stands where the evening file left it: no agreement reached on Europeans joining the talks, in Mr. Ushakov’s Monday words, and a clear signal from the Europeans required first, in the condition account in the evening file. Settled: the departure, and the host’s confirmation of Thursday. Open: the agenda, the fourth chair, and whether the spying matter is raised.

The Gulf and France at Midnight: No New Word on the Radar, and a Strike Day Opening in France

The radar file gained no new word on Monday, and at midnight the desk records a second day of silence as a fact of the file. The file stands whole in the explainer account filed below: six drones targeted the radar at Al-Riffa in the Guards’ claim; several attacks intercepted and destroyed in Manama’s account; all drones intercepted in the Ambassador’s Sunday sentence; two drones shot down in Friday’s denial, which concerned Friday’s claim; no impacts to American forces in the Central Command spokesman’s sentence, which did not address the radar; and no assessment of the radar’s condition from any capital, in any account the desk read on Monday. The rest of the Gulf file stands where the week left it: three American carriers in the region in a force of more than 20 ships, the President’s words that new strikes are highly unlikely while negotiations progress, Tehran’s words that Iran remains in a state of war, and the Khor Mor strike unclaimed.

France’s next fact is a weekday fact, and it opens on Tuesday. The unions have called a new day of strikes and demonstrations for Tuesday, November 17, in the strike account filed below: the CGT, Solidaires, FSU, UNSA, CGC and FAFP federations called the day after the Prime Minister’s social conference, saying the government had announced only crumbs, and November 17 is the date the Yellow Vest movement launched in 2018, in the same account. The wider European week stands in the protests account filed below: a European youth strike called for November 20 across six countries, an Italian strike day the same day, and protests called in Lisbon and Brussels. Saturday’s French counts stand at 106,000 nationwide in the Interior Ministry’s and about 200,000 in the organisers’, with 219 detained, in the week’s file; the police bill is examined by the Senate on Thursday, and a sixth Saturday is called for November 21. Spain’s calendar stands: a head-to-head debate reported for Thursday, polls publishable until November 23, and the vote on November 29. Settled: the strike is called, by six federations, for the anniversary. Open: its size, which Tuesday will supply.

Tuesday at Midnight: The Week’s Calendar Is Now the File’s Largest Settled Fact

Tuesday carries October retail sales at 0830, the Secretary’s lunch with Senate Republicans, France’s strike day, the President’s arrival in Manila, Alaska’s next count, and Nvidia’s earnings after the close. Wednesday carries the October meeting minutes, the first day of APEC in Shenzhen, Alaska’s tabulation, and Anthropic’s pricing. Thursday carries the three presidents in Shenzhen, the police bill in the French Senate, Spain’s debate, and Anthropic’s first trading day in New York. The Treasury Secretary’s 10 days for answers on export compliance run to about November 25, when Alaska’s certification is also targeted. Spain votes on November 29; the Federal Reserve decides on December 8 and 9; government funding runs out after December 11. The Overnight Watch collects at 0400.

The Cocked Hat

Where the midnight’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Alaska: 49.98 percent on the state’s full denominator in Monday’s report and 50.1 percent on the dashboard’s calculation in the week’s file, 52 votes short of a majority on the current total and a winner listed on one tracker, a victory declared by Ms. Peltola and no call by the Press. On the money for the air system: $4 billion of the $12.5 billion spent in the Majority Leader’s Monday figure, $11 billion unspent in the Democrats’, $1 billion spent in an earlier Democratic reading, $50 billion asked, $12 billion of the larger ask for modernisation in the Majority Leader’s account, and a ransom without a plan in Representative DeLauro’s. On the day’s flights: 55 cancelled as of Sunday evening, about 250 by 0400, 533 by 0700, 300 by 0900, 330 by 1330 and 344 by 1800, and on United’s own day, 645 delayed and 25 cancelled at 1850 with the outage’s share of them unclear. On Nvidia’s session: down 4.12 percent at $156.14 in the closing accounts and down 3.7 percent in the wire’s return account. On the board: a return discussed with confidants in the Sunday report, a return not weighed in Monday’s three voices, a president who would not mind it and who holds the stock, an investor who never heard of it from the man himself, a Treasury Secretary set against it, and a petition counted at 168,000, 180,000, 180,200 and 185,600 at four hours across two days. On Shenzhen: Ukraine on the agenda in the President’s words and off it in his officials’, the spying matter not to be raised in the officials’ telling and maybe raised in the President’s, no separate meeting in the White House’s account and a meeting beyond doubt in the Kremlin aide’s. On the radar: six drones on target, several attacks destroyed, all drones intercepted, two drones down on Friday, no impacts to forces, and no word on the machine, for a second day. On France: 106,000 in the Ministry’s Saturday count and about 200,000 in the organisers’. Inside the triangle is where the day honestly stands, and the log turns on it.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 24 items.

Subjective
The Alaska Story — Ms. Wilson concedes the governor’s race to Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins, Ms. Peltola inches toward 50 percent, as the last ballots trickle in

The Division of Elections’ latest unofficial report, timestamped 5:13 p.m. Monday, shows 285,439 ballots counted, an increase of 1,821 from Saturday, with turnout at 47.15 percent. In the Senate race Ms. Peltola has 141,637 votes, or 49.98 percent, to Senator Sullivan’s 130,162, or 45.93 percent; her lead grew from 11,213 to 11,475, and on the report’s total of 283,377 votes in the contest a majority is 141,689, leaving her 52 votes short, with the threshold rising as more ballots are counted. Ms. Wilson said she called Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins to congratulate him; their ticket stands at 142,591 votes, or 50.93 percent. Mr. Begich leads the House race at 47.67 percent. Ballot Measure 2 is losing and Ballot Measure 3 is passing. More ballots arriving by mail will be counted Tuesday, and the ranked-choice tabulation is set for Wednesday.

Subjective
Action Network — the Alaska Senate race on November 16: the Press’s count at 0840, the markets, and the trackers apart

As of November 16 at 8:40 a.m. Eastern, the Press’s count shows Ms. Peltola with 140,637 votes (49.9 percent) and Senator Sullivan with 129,424 (46.0 percent), with an estimated 97 percent of votes counted. The Press has still not called the race. One market has the Democrat at 99.8 cents. The trackers stand at different points in the count. If no candidate finishes above 50 percent of first-choice votes, the ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for November 18, and certification is targeted for November 25. More updates from the Division of Elections are due this week.

Subjective
The majority account — Ms. Peltola is 157 votes from a majority

Ms. Peltola is 157 votes short of an outright majority in the Alaska Senate race. As of 5:40 a.m. Pacific time on Monday, the Press count showed Ms. Peltola with 140,637 votes, or 49.9 percent, and Senator Sullivan with 129,424, or 46 percent. The Press estimates 97 percent of the vote has been counted, and has not called the race. Her lead stands at 11,213 votes. If she does not clear 50 percent, the race goes to the ranked-choice count on November 18; the state is set to certify the results on November 25. The gap is not fixed: every newly counted ballot raises the number of votes needed for a majority.

Subjective
Reuters via BusinessWorld — the recovery stumbles on a United pause as the funding fight brews: 344 cancelled by 1800, $4 billion spent in the Majority Leader’s figure

United States air travel largely returned to normal on Monday after more than 18,000 flight cancellations over three days, though the resumption was briefly marred by a United Airlines technology outage affecting its departing flights for about an hour, resolved by 6 p.m. Eastern. As of 6:50 p.m., United had delayed 645 flights, or 20 percent of its schedule, and cancelled 25; how many were caused by the outage was unclear. By 6 p.m. there were 344 flight cancellations and 4,800 delays, down from more than 2,300 cancelled and 11,000 delayed on Sunday. Senate Majority Leader Thune said only $4 billion of the $12.5 billion approved had been spent and explanations are owed; Senate Democratic Leader Schumer answered that the Administration has money, does not use it, and asks for more. The Secretary said the rickety system is telegraphing that it needs investment. The four largest airlines could face a $345 million earnings hit, a brokerage estimates.

Subjective
Reuters via WNCY — air travel largely returns to normal as the funding fight brews: 330 cancelled and 3,000 delayed by 1330

United States air travel largely returned to normal Monday after more than 18,000 flight cancellations over three days stemming from Friday’s longest ground stop in 25 years, suspected to have been caused by a single router installed during routine maintenance. Speaking on CNBC, the Transportation Secretary estimated the economic impact of the disruptions, which also delayed nearly 28,000 flights, would be in the billions of dollars. By 1:30 p.m. Eastern on Monday there were only 330 flight cancellations and 3,000 delays, down from more than 2,300 canceled and 11,000 delayed on Sunday, according to FlightAware. The President said on Monday that funding is needed to upgrade the system. The account lists the aging equipment in use, including Compaq computers, floppy disks, 25-year-old obsolete routers and paper strips to track aircraft.

Subjective
The Sun — airlines confirm when schedules return to normal and what refunds are available after the ground stop

Travellers still looking to get home after the ground stop are seeing signs of relief as airlines confirm operations are returning to normal. Over a million passengers were left stranded or sleeping in airports after all planes in the United States were grounded on Friday. A computer router in El Dorado, Arkansas, installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fiber-optic cable, began sending out faulty signals that flooded data into the system, and officials shut down United States airspace for over four hours. There were 312 United States flights cancelled on Monday morning as of 11 a.m., while another 2,238 flights were delayed, according to FlightAware. Major airlines have confirmed they are close to returning to full operations and are offering refunds or rebooking options, with the conditions of each carrier’s waiver set out.

Subjective
Reuters via 93-5 The Lloyd — Nvidia rules out a Huang comeback as the campaign for his return grows

Nvidia’s board is not weighing a return for Mr. Huang as chief executive, three people told the wire, despite a growing campaign days after affairs involving employees and suspected Chinese intelligence ties forced his resignation. More than 180,200 people have signed a petition demanding his return; the campaign website showed more than 8,800 signatories identifying themselves as current employees and more than 94,000 as shareholders, with affiliations self-reported and unverified. Taipei 101 was illuminated on Monday with messages including “Taiwan Loves Jensen.” The President said he would not mind seeing Mr. Huang reinstated and that he thinks he learned a big lesson; a newspaper’s review of his disclosures put his holdings in the company at between $13 million and $62 million. Intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of the relationship in question, two sources said. Nvidia shares fell 3.7 percent on Monday, a day before the company reports earnings.

Subjective
The agenda account — Nvidia’s board is not weighing Mr. Huang’s return as chief executive

CNBC reports that Nvidia’s board is focused on an investigation into Mr. Huang and is not discussing his return, despite public calls for him to come back. A person familiar with the matter told CNBC on Monday that the board is not considering bringing him back and is focused on the investigation; the company has hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate his conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets. The Financial Times reported over the weekend that Mr. Huang had discussed returning with allies; Mr. Gerstner told CNBC on Monday that Mr. Huang had not discussed a comeback with him. Calls for a return have come from prominent figures in technology and from an online petition that has gathered 180,000 signatures. The President said Monday that he was open to a return. The board said Friday that it was selecting a search firm for the chief executive role.

Subjective
The Altman account — Mr. Huang’s resignation shakes Silicon Valley, and Mr. Altman says strong demand for artificial intelligence will hold up

Mr. Huang’s sudden resignation last week as chief executive, president and board director sent shockwaves through the global artificial intelligence supply chain. Mr. Altman addressed the matter for the first time on Monday at a public event in San Francisco, and when asked whether he believed Mr. Huang should return to Nvidia, he chose to hold back, saying he did not have enough information to answer the question. After the resignation, calls in Silicon Valley for the board to reinstate him have continued to grow; the online petition had gathered more than 170,000 signatures as of the afternoon of November 16, including more than 8,000 self-identified current employees. The President on Monday also voiced support for calls to reinstate him. The account carries a timeline of the resignation, the petition and the coming results.

Subjective
The vacuum account — Nvidia’s leadership vacuum sparks political and market turmoil

Days after Mr. Huang stepped down, the struggle over Nvidia’s top leadership has escalated into a political and capital-driven contest spanning Silicon Valley and Washington. The chief financial officer, Ms. Kress, has been appointed interim chief executive, and the company’s third-quarter results for fiscal 2027 will still be released on schedule on November 17. Mr. Huang has discussed the possibility of returning with close allies, who are assembling a war room to lobby the board. As of 6 p.m. Beijing time on the 16th, the public petition had collected 174,654 signatures, its affiliations self-reported. The Treasury Secretary said on November 15 that the board should look outside the company and that the company needs a major overhaul. One analyst is quoted that any suggestion of Mr. Huang returning is absurd given legal, board and regulatory factors, and that there is no possibility of his returning as chief executive.

Subjective
The preview account — the Nasdaq falls 2.5 percent as the Nvidia turmoil deepens, and all eyes are on Tuesday’s earnings

Wall Street fell sharply on Monday, November 16, in its third straight losing session, as the fallout from Mr. Huang’s resignation soured enthusiasm for artificial intelligence stocks one day before the company’s earnings report. Nvidia fell 4.12 percent to $156.14. All eyes are now on its earnings today, Tuesday, after the close, at around 4:20 p.m. Eastern, with a call at 5 p.m.; Wall Street expects revenue of about $108.7 billion and earnings of $2.47 a share. The interim chief, Ms. Kress, will give the first outlook since the handover, and options traders are pricing an 8.6 percent move in either direction. Futures were little changed overnight after Monday’s sell-off. Tuesday also brings October retail sales at 8:30 a.m. Eastern, plus Home Depot and Disney results before the open.

Subjective
The night account — stock futures are little changed after Nvidia pressures technology to start the week

Stock futures were little changed on Monday night, following a losing session as Nvidia once again dragged down the technology sector. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures inched up 8 points, or 0.02 percent; S&P 500 futures were up 0.06 percent, while Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 0.1 percent. Asia-Pacific markets opened lower on Tuesday: Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 0.76 percent, while the Topix declined 1.06 percent. In regular trading, Nvidia shares pulled back 4.1 percent as traders dumped the chipmaker ahead of its fiscal third-quarter report, due Tuesday after the bell. The stock has dropped almost 24 percent this month. The Dow on Monday slid more than 700 points, or 1.4 percent, while the S&P 500 lost 1.9 percent and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.5 percent, its biggest one-day decline since November 5.

Subjective
The follow account — Nvidia’s 4.1 percent drop hits Wall Street and Asia as Brent falls on Iran war uncertainty

A 4.1 percent fall in Nvidia on Monday dragged the S&P 500 down 1.9 percent to 7,416.59, its third straight loss, and Asian shares followed lower on Tuesday. The Nasdaq 100 slid 2.7 percent and a gauge of United States chip stocks sank 5.3 percent. Nvidia has lost $735 billion in market value since the scandal over Mr. Huang’s alleged affairs and his reported ties to an alleged Chinese spy. Futures on the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 were little changed. The account links Monday’s losses to the leadership crisis, concern that artificial intelligence stocks are overpriced, worries that Democratic midterm wins could restrict new data centre construction, and new administration rules on remote access to advanced chips and servers. The next test comes after the close on Tuesday, when Nvidia reports its first quarterly results under its interim chief.

Subjective
The Asia account — Asian equities fall as the Commerce Department cracks down on chip shipments

Asian equities fell on Tuesday morning as the Commerce Department issued a rule to crack down on chip shipments, exacerbating investor concerns over the artificial intelligence boom and spurring risk-off sentiment. Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil will be added to a list of countries subject to export restrictions, and companies will need licences to ship to those countries; the move is aimed at preventing Chinese clients from accessing data-center capacity in those countries remotely. The bureau said the rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries. One team’s estimate in the account puts the market capitalisation erased in the United States technology sector at about $960 billion.

Subjective
The rule account — the United States tightens chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely

The administration on Monday rolled out new export controls on chips and data centers outside the United States, seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past export controls by remotely accessing infrastructure located in other countries. The Commerce Department will require companies to get licences to export, reexport or transfer chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries. The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance, estimated at roughly the output of about 750 H100 or H200 chips. Existing operators providing covered services have 90 days from the rule’s effective date to get a licence. The rule does not apply to commercial recommendation systems, and it rescinds the January 2025 diffusion rule.

Subjective
The loophole account — the Commerce Department moves to close the chip loophole

The Commerce Department on Monday moved to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to access advanced chips remotely through data centers located in other countries. The interim final rule marks the administration’s first policy response to the scandal involving the former Nvidia chief. The rule would require licences for advanced chip exports to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, and would require data centers to obtain a licence before providing remote access to companies headquartered in China or other restricted destinations; data centers already serving those companies will have 90 days from the rule’s effective date to get a licence. The rule also formally rescinds the regulations implementing the January 2025 diffusion rule. Comments on the interim final rule are due in 60 days.

Subjective
Reuters via 965 WTU — Chairman Warsh says emerging technologies will have a significant impact, but risks need to be watched

Federal Reserve Chairman Warsh said on Monday that emerging technologies will have a significant impact on the economy, but the possible scenarios range from rising growth with broadly shared gains to higher unemployment and a potential slowdown if anticipated investment returns prove disappointing. He refers to artificial intelligence as super intelligence, the language preferred by the President, and said it could prove distinct from earlier technologies as a force to supercharge idea generation. In the best scenario, he told a conference in San Francisco, the technology could lead to an increase in productivity and economic gains shared broadly across labor and the owners of capital, with real growth rising persistently above its long-run average and the country staying close to full employment. He said the risks, including higher unemployment and the use of the technology by bad actors, could also be highly disruptive and economically costly.

Subjective
The trip account — how the President is hoping to use an Asia trip to reassert his authority, and he might bring up the spying matter

The President will attempt this week a long-planned trip through Asia, punctuated Thursday by an unprecedented three-way meeting with his counterparts from China and Russia. Asked Monday morning if he felt the midterm losses could diminish his influence abroad, he replied no, saying he was not the one on the ballot. The scandal involving Mr. Huang’s chips and affair with an alleged Chinese spy will loom over the visit to Shenzhen, even though his aides insist it would not dominate the journey; he said on Monday that he might bring up the spying matter with President Xi, though American officials previously said they did not expect him to start those conversations. At two leaders’ summits, in Manila and in Shenzhen, he will look to counter the narrative of declining power by announcing new commercial deals. The account also records calls from some allies to fire members of his Cabinet, including the secretaries of Commerce and Defense.

Subjective
The departure account — the President opens the door to a meeting with Mr. Kim as he heads to Asia

The President departed for Asia on Monday, turning his focus to economic deals and historic three-way nuclear talks with Russia and China. He said he may meet with Mr. Kim while in China as the United States looks to reengage Pyongyang on its nuclear program. He also said he plans to talk about Russia’s war in Ukraine during the meeting with Presidents Xi and Putin: “We’ll talk about, my favorite subject, Ukraine. Ukraine’s losing Ukraine,” he told reporters at the White House on Monday morning. He suggested he would talk with the leaders about the war even after his officials on Friday told reporters that he would discuss nuclear disarmament and the Iran war but steer clear of the war in Ukraine. He said Mr. Kim may come to Shenzhen but that is up to President Xi. The Kremlin aide Mr. Ushakov also indicated that a one-on-one meeting between the President and President Putin is being arranged.

Subjective
The road account — the President left for Asia, floats a Kim meeting, and adds Ukraine to the Xi-Putin talks

The President departed for Asia on Monday, saying he would discuss Ukraine with Presidents Xi and Putin despite earlier administration statements excluding the war. He also suggested Mr. Kim could join him in China, although no meeting was confirmed. The three-way summit will address the countries’ nuclear stockpiles, with Iran also expected on the agenda. Meetings in Manila precede the APEC summit in Shenzhen. The Kremlin said arrangements for separate talks between the President and President Putin were being discussed. Ukraine’s President Zelenskyy’s concern stands in the account, and the itinerary runs from Manila to Shenzhen.

Subjective
The Manila account — Premier Li lauds extraordinary ties with ASEAN ahead of the President’s visit

China’s Premier Li Qiang on Monday hailed what he called truly extraordinary ties with ASEAN in opening remarks to regional leaders during the ASEAN-China Summit in Manila. At a time of growing unilateralism and protectionism and recurring geopolitical conflict, he said, economic relations between China and ASEAN had only strengthened. The President is due to arrive in Manila on Tuesday at the tail end of the summit ahead of his trip to the APEC forum in Shenzhen, where a trilateral meeting with Presidents Xi and Putin is scheduled. In Manila he will meet ASEAN leaders and attend his first meeting of the Quad group, the first such gathering in two years, and protests are expected. The bloc was due to hold talks on Monday with the leaders of Australia, South Korea, the United Nations and Japan.

Subjective
The explainer account — Iran says it targets a United States radar in Bahrain: what do we know?

The Guards say they launched six drones at an air defence radar system at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base in response to what they describe as hostile United States actions. Sirens sounded in Bahrain as its Interior Ministry urged residents to remain calm and proceed to the nearest safe location; it was the second time in three days that the Guards claimed to have targeted a radar system in Bahrain. Bahrain’s Defence Force said its air defence systems thwarted several aerial attacks targeting the kingdom. The United States military said it intercepted two drones on Friday but has yet to comment on Sunday’s claim. On Friday the Guards said they destroyed an early-warning radar system in retaliation for an attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran; Central Command denied the claim, saying it had shot down two drones and there were no injuries or damage.

Subjective
The strike account — French unions call for a new day of strikes on 17 November

French trade unions have called for another major day of strikes and protests on Tuesday of next week, 17 November. The Prime Minister met with union leaders for a social conference on Monday after a general strike saw 1.6 million take action the week before. By lunchtime, the CGT, Solidaires, FSU, UNSA, CGC and FAFP federations had called strikes for 17 November. The CGT announced a new big day of strikes and demonstrations, saying the government has announced only crumbs. November 17 is the historic date for the launch of the Yellow Vest movement in 2018. The account argues for the strikes to be renewed after the day.

Subjective
The protests account — mass protests shake Europe ahead of a week of nationwide strikes

Over the weekend, protests hit countries across Europe: a mass anti-government protest in Prague, housing protests across Portugal, and youth and Yellow Vest marches in France, before a week of nationwide strikes in several European countries. A coalition of student unions has called a European youth strike on November 20 with actions in Germany, Britain, France, Italy, Spain and Greece. On November 17, French unions have called a one-day nationwide strike, while Italian unions have called such a strike on November 20, the day of a Portuguese public administration strike; protests are called on November 21 in Lisbon and November 23 in Brussels. In France, organisers counted 200,000 participants in the weekend marches, and police reported 219 arrests nationwide.

entry.title: The Jesus Movement and the New Jesus Movement
entry.summary: The Jesus Movement of 1967 to the late 1970s, Calvary Chapel, Chuck Smith, and Lonnie Frisbee, and the claim since 2023 that a new Jesus Movement is under way.
entry.content:
Special Report

The Movement of 1967–1977 and the Claim of a New One, Filed from the Record—California, Chicago, Britain, France, China, Korea, and the Global Counts

Objective

The Jesus Movement and the New Jesus Movement — Special Report

The Jesus Movement is a documented thing with dates: it began in California missions and coffeehouses in 1967, put its name on the cover of Time on June 21, 1971, filled the Cotton Bowl in June 1972, built communes, newspapers, and a music industry, and was absorbed by the late 1970s into church networks—Calvary Chapel and the Vineyard—that stand today. Since February 2023 the name has been carried again, by a film, by ministries, by advocates, and by headline writers, and applied to present events: a sixteen-day prayer meeting at a Kentucky university, rising baptism counts in several denominations, record Bible sales, a French catechumenate that has tripled in ten years, and survey findings that point in both directions at once. This report files the historical record first, in the order it happened, and then the present-tense record country by country, every figure with its instrument named—including the British survey at the center of the “quiet revival” claim, which its own makers withdrew in March 2026. Where the record settles a claim, the report prints the settlement. Where it does not—the size of the crowd at Explo ’72, the number of Christians in China, the role of one preacher two movements wrote out of their histories—the report prints the question as open.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1820 ET, Monday, November 16, 2026.

The Record in Brief

The first Jesus Movement is a closed historical file, and its outlines are not in dispute. Between 1967 and the late 1970s, a population of young converts—many of them drawn from the counterculture the movement’s own preachers had come out of—built an identifiable religious world in the United States: street missions and coffeehouses in San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury, a fast-growing church at Costa Mesa in Orange County, communes across the country, an underground press of some fifty newspapers, a music that became an industry, and a mass gathering in Dallas in June 1972 that drew the honorary chairmanship of Billy Graham. Time put the phenomenon on its cover on June 21, 1971, under the line “The Jesus Revolution,” five years after the same magazine had asked on its cover whether God was dead. The movement’s standard scholarly periodization, in the work of the historian Larry Eskridge, runs from 1966 to 1977. What ended it, on the record, was absorption: its people, its music, and its converts passed into durable institutions—the Calvary Chapel network, the Vineyard churches that split from it, and the contemporary Christian music industry—and the name went out of use as the name of a living thing.

The present-tense use of the name is a separate record, and it begins as a publishing and film event before it begins as anything else. Greg Laurie’s book Jesus Revolution appeared in 2018 with the subtitle “How God Transformed an Unlikely Generation and How He Can Do It Again Today.” The film of the same name, released by Lionsgate on February 24, 2023, took in $54.3 million worldwide on a reported $15 million budget, and its director, Jon Erwin, said in the film’s promotion that a movement was going on in America now and that there could be another Jesus revolution today. In the same month the film opened, a routine chapel service at Asbury University in Wilmore, Kentucky, ran continuously for sixteen days and drew visitors from hundreds of campuses. Since then the name and its synonyms—revival, outpouring, awakening—have been applied to campus ministries, mass baptism events, and survey results. No organization in any country bears the name Jesus Movement as its own. The label is applied by participants, advocates, and media; it is not self-carried, and the desk files its provenance as part of the record in Section 10.

The measured present-tense record is genuinely mixed, and this report prints it mixed. Specific instruments in specific countries register real increases: adult baptisms at Easter in France have tripled in ten years on the French bishops’ annual survey, the hardest institutional series in this file; the Southern Baptist Convention’s own church profile counts five consecutive years of rising baptisms; the Church of England’s Statistics for Mission records adult baptisms at 9,900 in 2025 and a fifth consecutive year of attendance growth; print Bible sales in the United States reached a twenty-one-year high in 2025; the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints reported more convert baptisms in 2025 than in any year in its history.
