The board announced Mr. Huang’s resignation on Thursday and named the chief financial officer, Ms. Kress, interim chief.

Subjective
US News Pulse — the letter at 157,000, a shortlist denied, and no word from the board

Mr. Huang has discussed a possible return to Nvidia with confidants just four days after resigning as chief executive, a British newspaper reported on Sunday, turning the company’s leadership crisis into a public contest between Silicon Valley, Washington and the board. An open letter calling for his reinstatement passed 157,000 signatures by Sunday, including more than 7,500 self-identified employees of the company, about 18 percent of the workforce. The letter asks the board to reinstate him while an independent investigation establishes the facts. Investors Mr. Gerstner and Mr. Baker wrote to the board on Friday urging it to keep a return among the options. The Treasury Secretary said on Sunday that the company’s leadership needs a dramatic overhaul and pressed for an outsider. The board denied reports it had shortlisted the chief of Arm, Mr. Haas. The board has not commented publicly, and the company declined to confirm the newspaper’s report. No return has been announced; Mr. Huang has not said publicly that he wants the job back, and Ms. Kress remains interim chief executive. The company reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, November 17, five days after Mr. Huang resigned.

Subjective
Longbridge, the Dolphin Daily — the Monday-morning wrap from Singapore: a guarantee cut, consensus at $108.7 billion, and the stock down 13 percent on the week

Good morning. It is November 16 in Singapore, and the leadership saga escalated over the weekend: a British newspaper says Mr. Huang is discussing a return, while the Treasury Secretary urges hiring an external chief and demands a response within 10 days on China sales. The stock fell 2.0 percent on Friday, down about 13 percent for the week. Tuesday after the close brings the company’s earnings, the first since Mr. Huang stepped down, and October retail sales. Ahead of the earnings, who runs the company is now harder to price than how much it sells. Reports say the interim chief, Ms. Kress, cut the data centre guarantee to OpenAI from $250 billion to about $105 billion. Consensus revenue stands at about $108.7 billion, up about 91 percent on the year; market focus is on the guide, on hyperscaler tone, and on progress in the chief executive search, and on whether the forward growth guide of roughly 70 percent gets trimmed, and whether 2027 demand is borrowing from 2028.

Subjective
XTB — the morning wrap: the Nikkei down 1.94 percent, the Kospi down 2.6, Japan’s economy contracted, and China’s figures missed

Asian technology stocks slid amid reports of tightening American export restrictions on AI chips. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 1.94 percent to around 59,780 points, a reaction to Japan’s contracting gross domestic product, hawkish statements from a Bank of Japan member, and a global sell-off in semiconductor stocks; Japan’s economy unexpectedly contracted by 0.1 percent annualized in the third quarter, against a consensus expectation of 0.2 percent growth, and the Bank of Japan member called for continued interest rate hikes. In South Korea the Kospi index fell by about 2.6 percent, dragged down by chip giants: SK Hynix down over 6 percent and Samsung Electronics down 4 percent amid concerns over tightening trade barriers and uncertainty around Nvidia. A China index declined 0.87 percent, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng managed modest gains of 0.25 percent, trading around 23,750 points. Brent crude traded around $96.00 a barrel and West Texas crude around $88.86, both little changed; the commodity showed little reaction to unconfirmed Iranian reports of tankers hitting mines in the strait, balanced by oversupply forecasts. The day’s calendar carries the central bank chairman’s keynote address opening a conference on artificial intelligence and productivity at 18:00 Central European Time, noon Eastern.

Subjective
The morning briefing — Taiwan closes down 6.0 percent, the Kospi down 3.6, Bitcoin at $64,641, and gold down 1.0 percent

Monday, November 16: Taiwan’s Taiex closed 6.0 percent lower, and South Korea’s Kospi fell 3.6 percent, as Friday’s sell-off in American chipmakers spread to Asia at the start of a week that brings the company’s results. The Treasury Secretary said the company needs a ‘dramatic shakeup’ in its leadership, while the ousted chief executive is discussing a possible comeback, a British newspaper reported. The American ten-year yield held at 5.14 percent, after rising 25.7 basis points last week, as Federal Reserve officials lined up behind further rate hikes ahead of the chairman’s remarks today. Bitcoin fell 0.6 percent to $64,641, after sliding to a four-month low over the weekend; it dropped 13.0 percent last week. Gold fell 1.0 percent to $3,846 an ounce, and silver fell 2.7 percent. Asian chipmakers slumped at the start of the results week, with Taiwan and South Korea leading the losses. The day’s roadmap also carries Canada’s October consumer prices and speeches by a New York Fed president at 9:05 a.m. Eastern and the chairman at noon Eastern.

Subjective
TradingView News — futures turn lower before the earnings, Bitcoin near $64,400 early Monday, and gold at $3,830

Nasdaq futures turned lower before the company’s earnings and a listing that will test demand for artificial intelligence shares. Bitcoin trades near $65,000 after a bruising weekend; it traded near $64,400 early Monday after touching roughly $62,000 on Sunday. Spot gold slipped to around $3,830 after losing more than 4 percent last week. Brent fell 0.7 percent to $95.10 as traders weighed the prospect of excess supply. The American ten-year Treasury yield held near 5.14 percent. The central bank chairman speaks at noon Eastern on Monday; retail sales follow Tuesday before the company’s results, with the meeting minutes due Wednesday. Analysts expect about $109 billion in quarterly revenue from the company.

Subjective
Particle — the fifth day whole: about 400 stopped, 70,000 police deployed, and a further day called for November 17

Multiple groups including Yellow Vest activists, youth organisations, unions and child-protection activists converged in cities across France on Saturday, November 14, for a fifth day of protest over living costs and related grievances. The Interior Ministry put national attendance at about 106,000, 24,000 in Paris, while organisers claimed roughly 200,000 nationwide, reflecting a recurring dispute over turnout figures. Authorities deployed roughly 70,000 police and gendarmes, and security forces recorded about 400 stops nationwide, with 126 in Paris and 108 people held in custody in the capital, including 38 minors. Police unions warned of fatigue and possible internal unrest after repeated weekend deployments, and unions have already called a further day of action and strike for November 17, raising the risk of sustained political pressure. The nationwide demonstrations show sustained pressure on the government as heavy policing strains officers and unions plan further strike action.

Subjective
HuffPost Spain — the fourth daily tracking: the Socialists past 30 percent, their best since 2023, and the right’s majority standing

The campaign for the November 29 election keeps producing new readings every day. In the fourth daily tracking by the polling firm for a national newspaper and a radio network, the Socialist Party has broken the 30 percent barrier in voting intention, marking its best register since the 2023 election: the Popular Party would be the most voted force at 31.5 percent, followed by the Socialists at 30.3, Vox at 18.0, a broad front at 3.7 and Podemos at 1.1. The main novelty of the latest tracking is that the Socialist recovery is not fed from its natural allies; the broad front also grows slightly, the first time since the campaign began, which shows the advance is not weakening the options to its left. On the conservative side the Popular Party registers a slight uptick while Vox seems to have stalled in recent days. The scenario remains conditioned by a notable pool of undecided voters, especially among those who did not vote in the past election, where 18 percent say they do not yet know to whom they will give their ballot. Internal figures handled by the Socialists, the EFE agency adds, point to the Socialists being the first force on November 29, with the Popular Party falling and Vox beginning to stall.

Subjective
TipRanks — the comeback campaign’s names, a petition at 106,000 in its count, and earnings tomorrow at $108.93 billion expected

Mr. Huang is reportedly receiving support from Mr. Musk and other tech leaders for a possible comeback. According to a British newspaper, a group of Silicon Valley executives is forming a ‘war room’ to urge the board to bring Mr. Huang back. An online petition asking the board to bring him back has received 106,000 signatures in this account, and includes names such as a co-founder of Uber, a tech investor, the chief of Shopify and the chief of Epic Games. Mr. Musk has also publicly backed the campaign, writing on Friday: ‘A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen, and I’m signing it too.’ According to the same newspaper, the board had approached the chief of Arm as a potential successor. The company is set to report its third-quarter results tomorrow, November 17, after the market closes; Wall Street expects revenue to jump nearly 91 percent to $108.93 billion from $57.01 billion a year earlier, and earnings of about $2.47 per share.

Subjective
NordFX — the second morning account: the Kospi down 3.4 percent, the Hang Seng up 0.7, and Bitcoin near $64,900

The morning update for November 16 records Nasdaq 100 futures down about 0.8 percent in the morning. In Asia on Monday: the Nikkei down about 1.9 percent, near 59,960, after Japan’s third-quarter product shrank 0.1 percent annualized, the first contraction in four quarters, against a forecast of growth; the Kospi down about 3.4 percent, near 5,110, with chipmakers leading the losses; Shanghai down 0.4 percent after October data missed, retail sales up 0.4 percent on the year against 0.8 forecast and industrial output up 4.8 against 5.3; and the Hang Seng up about 0.7 percent, near 23,800, bucking the trend. Gold stood near $3,870 after a 4.7 percent weekly drop, with silver near $47.5, down about 2.6 percent. Brent stood near $95.3 and West Texas crude near $87. Bitcoin stood near $64,900 after dipping below $62,000 over the weekend. The week’s key events are listed: the chairman speaks today, retail sales and the company’s earnings on Tuesday, the meeting minutes on Wednesday, and the three presidents’ meeting and a listing on Thursday.

Subjective
investingLive — the Asia-Pacific file: futures give up their gains, Brent near $95.40, and gold toward $3,873

Asian markets slipped on Monday as soft data from Japan and China met hawkish messages from central banks; chipmakers led the losses as worries mounted over AI demand and American export curbs ahead of the company’s results. American stock futures gave up early gains, with S&P 500 futures down about 0.2 percent and Nasdaq 100 futures off roughly 0.5 percent. Recent remarks from three Federal Reserve officials all put inflation at the centre of policy, keeping a December rate hike firmly priced; the chairman opens a conference on AI and productivity at noon Eastern. Brent was steady near $95.40 and West Texas crude around $87.10; expectations of a supply surplus offset unconfirmed Iranian claims that a supertanker sank after hitting a mine in the strait, and a bank forecast Brent easing to $78 by the end of 2027 while flagging near-term upside risks from attacks on shipping. Gold eased to around $3,873 and silver fell more than 3 percent. Bitcoin hovered near $65,100 after hitting a four-month low around $62,000 over the weekend. China confirmed that President Xi will host the first trilateral summit with the President and President Putin in Shenzhen on November 19, alongside the APEC gathering.

entry.title: Sunday Closes at More Than 2,300 Flights Cancelled With the Root Cause Still Unknown, Washington Files Its First Word on the Bahrain Radar — No Impacts to American Forces, With the Radar Itself Unaddressed — and Nvidia's Contest Turns Open, a War Room for Mr. Huang Against a Treasury Call for an Outside Successor
entry.summary: Sunday closes at more than 2,300 cancellations with the ground stop's root cause unknown, and Washington files its first word on the Bahrain radar.
entry.content:
The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Sunday Closes at More Than 2,300 Flights Cancelled With the Root Cause Still Unknown, Washington Files Its First Word on the Bahrain Radar—No Impacts to American Forces, With the Radar Itself Unaddressed—and Nvidia’s Contest Turns Open, a War Room for Mr. Huang Against a Treasury Call for an Outside Successor

The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: a third day of disruption that closed larger than its early count and smaller than Saturday, with its cause narrowed to two routers and its root cause still unnamed; a radar claim that gained one narrow American sentence and no assessment of the radar; a count that spent Sunday unmoved; and a company whose succession stopped being a board matter and became an open contest, six days of it now dated by other men’s deadlines.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Monday, November 16, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 52, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Sunday, in Edition No. 50, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Sunday, in Edition No. 49, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Sunday, and in Edition No. 48, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 on Sunday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Sunday Settled, What It Left Open

Sunday settled the size of its own disruption at more than 2,300 flights cancelled and some 7,700 delayed, settled that Washington will speak about Bahrain in one narrow sentence and no wider, and settled that Nvidia’s succession is now contested in public from two directions at once; it left open the root cause of Friday’s stop, the condition of the radar at Al-Riffa, the call in Alaska, and the board’s answer to everyone. The final flight count stands in the final wire account filed below, against more than 1,600 cancelled in the day’s early count in the early wire account filed below; the same final account carries the second router, at Amarillo, Texas, the disabling of some 60 similar routers, and the Secretary’s sentence that the root cause is not known. The American sentence on Bahrain stands in the radar account filed below: a Central Command spokesman told a newspaper there were no impacts to American forces, and the statement did not say whether radar equipment was damaged. Alaska’s count stands where Saturday left it, at 140,637 to 129,424 in the state’s report filed below, uncalled, with the next count due Monday. Nvidia’s two directions stand in the contest account filed below and in the petition account filed below. Monday carries the first tests of the new week: the airlines read against the Secretary’s fully-normal promise, the President’s departure for Asia, Alaska’s next count, and a central bank chairman’s noon remarks. The desk takes the files in that order.

The Airlines at Midnight: More Than 2,300 Cancelled at the Close, a Second Router at Amarillo, and No Root Cause

The day’s last count is larger than the day’s early count, and the desk prints both, at their hours. More than 2,300 flights were cancelled and some 7,700 delayed on Sunday, with more than 10,000 flights affected, in the final wire account above; the early wire account counted more than 1,600 cancelled and almost 3,600 delayed, and the tracker account counted nearly 1,700 cancelled by 1350, in the accounts filed below. The final shares are heavier than the early ones: 28 percent of JetBlue’s Sunday flights cancelled, against 27 percent earlier, and 17 percent of American’s, against 13 percent earlier, with United, Southwest and Delta at 3 to 5 percent in both counts, in the final account. Saturday stands at more than 6,400 cancelled and more than 8,000 delayed in the same account, and Friday’s stop, which halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours, stands as the longest nationwide halt since September 11, 2001, in the same account. No second stop was ordered on Sunday. Monday’s cancellations stood at 33 on Sunday afternoon in the tracker account, and no later Monday figure stands in the midnight file; Monday will be read, as the evening edition put it, against the Secretary’s promise of a system probably fully normal on Monday, and against the Administrator’s earlier promise of full schedule integrity by Sunday’s close, which Sunday’s final count did not meet.

The cause file gained a second town, a disabled fleet of routers, and an admission. The replacement of a router at El Dorado, Arkansas, triggered problems with a recently replaced router in Amarillo, Texas, which started broadcasting and overloading routers at other centers, the Secretary said on a Sunday programme, in the final wire account above; the functionality of the originating routers has been disabled, and the Administration did the same for about 60 similar routers in the system, in the same account. The routers that experienced issues were purchased in 2001 and were obsolete by 2006, in the same account. On the man who installed the first router, the Secretary said he was a good American patriot and a veteran, that sabotage is not believed, and that there is no evidence of a cyberattack or other malicious intent—and then the admission that closes the file for the night: the Administration still does not know what ultimately caused a problem in maintenance work done thousands of times before without issue, and does not actually have the root cause, in the same account. The money file moved on Sunday in three voices: the President made his first public comments on the weekend’s disruption, calling for the $50 billion upgrade to be approved and done all at once, not in drips and drabs, in the same account; the Secretary’s request stands at $50 billion, up from $30 billion, after Congress approved $12.5 billion last year, in the same account; and two House members answered on Saturday that about $11 billion of that $12.5 billion remains unspent and asked why more is needed, in the same account, against the Secretary’s Sunday answer that last year’s money was earmarked for certain spending and did not include new software. Settled: Sunday’s cost, the two routers, and the absence of any sign of attack. Open: the root cause, in the Secretary’s own words.

Bahrain at Midnight: One Narrow American Sentence, No Word on the Radar, and Article 51 Claimed Both Ways

Washington’s silence, which the evening edition recorded as a fact of the file, ended before midnight—narrowly. A Central Command spokesman, Mr. Hawkins, told a newspaper that there were no impacts to American forces, in the radar account above; the statement did not say whether radar equipment or other property was damaged, and Manama had not answered the newspaper’s question about damage at the site, in the same account. That is the whole of the American word on Sunday’s claim at 0000: it answers for the men and not for the machine, and the desk prints it at exactly that width. The two claims it stands between are unchanged. The Guards say six drones of their Aerospace Force targeted the American air-defence radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base, in a second phase of retaliation, in the Bahrain account filed below; the Defence Force says its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets, in the same account; and no damage and no casualties have been reported in any account in the file.

The written file around the claim is complete, and it is aligned on one side and answered on the other. Manama’s Foreign Ministry statement stands whole in the ministry account filed below: the strongest condemnation, Iran held fully responsible, the transformation of Bahraini territory into an arena for settling scores rejected, Security Council Resolution 2817 cited, and Bahrain’s right of self-defence under Article 51 affirmed, with a call on the Security Council, where Bahrain sits, to condemn the attacks and take decisive measures. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemned the attacks and stood with Manama, in the condemnations account filed below, which carries their four sentences severally: a violation of international law and good neighbourliness from Riyadh, a flagrant violation of sovereignty from Doha, a threat to security and territorial integrity from Amman, and a dangerous escalation from Cairo. Tehran’s spokesman, Mr. Baghaei, defended the strikes as justified in self-defence and said Iran would keep responding to military aggression, in the evening file, and rejected a Cooperation Council demand that Iran pay compensation for its attacks, in the condemnations account above. Article 51 therefore stands claimed in the same file by Manama for its defence and by Tehran for its strikes. The President’s Saturday condition, that he might hold off on attacking Iran if there were no new provocations, stands unapplied to Sunday’s claim in any statement in the midnight file. Settled: the responses, all of them, in writing. Open: what, if anything, was hit at Al-Riffa.

The Count at Midnight: No Sunday Count, 157 Short of a Majority, and Monday as the Next Fact

Alaska’s Senate count spent Sunday exactly where Saturday afternoon left it, and midnight adds nothing to it but the calendar. The state’s unofficial summary, timed 1515 on Saturday, gives Ms. Peltola 140,637 votes, 49.94 percent; Senator Sullivan 129,424, 45.96 percent; Mr. Heikes 6,002; Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. 4,652; and write-ins 872, on 281,587 votes in the race, with all 401 precincts reported, in the state’s report above. The lead is 11,213 votes. A majority of the reported vote is 140,794, and Ms. Peltola stands 157 votes short of it by the desk’s arithmetic; the state’s dashboard, which excludes unresolved write-ins from its display calculation, rounds her share to 50.1 percent, in the lead account filed below, which also records that the latest batch added 2,397 votes for Ms. Peltola and 1,596 for Senator Sullivan. The Press estimates 97 percent counted and has not called the race; one tracker lists a winner; Ms. Peltola declared victory on Saturday; the President declared Senator Sullivan the winner on November 7; and Senator Sullivan has not conceded, in the lead account and in the majority account filed below, which records her campaign’s position that Senator Sullivan has no mathematical path. The next count is due Monday. Overseas ballots may arrive through Wednesday, November 18, when the ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled if no candidate holds a majority; certification is targeted for November 25. Settled at midnight: nothing new, and the desk says so plainly—a day without a count is a fact of a count that has run twelve days. Open: the call, the tabulation, and 157 votes.

Shenzhen and Europe at Midnight: A Departure on Monday, Two Confirmations and a Silence, and Two Sentences From Moscow

The President departs Monday for Manila and the ASEAN meetings and continues to Shenzhen, due there November 17 through 19, and that departure is the next fact in the week’s largest file. The meeting of the three presidents on Thursday, November 19, stands confirmed by the White House on Friday and by the Kremlin on Saturday, and unconfirmed by its host, in the agenda account filed below and in the meeting account filed below; China’s Friday sentence, that it is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state, stands unamended at midnight. The agenda split stands whole: nuclear arms and Iran in the American telling, with no agreement expected in the same telling, and Ukraine off the trilateral agenda in the American telling and on it in the Kremlin aide’s. No third confirmation came on Sunday, and no agenda was agreed in any account in the midnight file.

Europe’s file closed Sunday as it opened, with one spokesman’s two answers carried by the wires and no European answer to either. Asked by the TASS agency whether Europe’s negotiators have attempted to contact Russia, spokesman Peskov answered, “No, not yet,” in the contact account filed below; in an interview with a Vesti correspondent he said that in the absence of a negotiated solution Russia will have to achieve its objectives by force, and that if the Union does not want peace there is no point in discussing a settlement or a European security framework, in the force account filed below. The standing American sentence, that the delegation at Abu Dhabi ensured Europe will be included in future talks, stands where the week left it. No date for a first contact stands in the file, and no next round of the trilateral talks carries a date or a place at midnight.

Nvidia at Midnight: A War Room on One Side, a Treasury Deadline on the Other, and No Answer From the Board

Sunday turned a board matter into an open contest, and both sides of it are now on the record. Mr. Huang has discussed a return with confidants, and allies are assembling a war room of Silicon Valley executives to lobby the board and to seek support from the White House, in the contest account above and in the comeback account filed below. The petition’s counter stood at 154,678 names at 1001 Pacific on Sunday, with 7,459 self-described current employees, 1,406 former employees, 81,896 shareholders and 63,917 other supporters, its affiliations self-reported and its fake entries named in its own accounts, in the petition account above; a later account put the counter at 156,850. The petition’s asks stand in the campaign account filed below: reinstatement while an independent investigation establishes the facts, the investigation’s scope and timetable made public, a substantive opportunity to respond, and, if the board insists he leave, a specific, evidence-backed explanation. The Gerstner and Baker letter asks for a slow and deliberate search that keeps Mr. Huang’s return among the options, in the contest account.

The other side of the contest spoke on a Sunday programme, and it spoke in deadlines. The Treasury Secretary, Mr. Bessent, said on a Sunday programme that the board needs to look outside the company and that Nvidia needs sweeping change in its leadership, in the contest account above; he questioned whether the company knowingly violated export controls on high-end chips, pointed to sales billed through Singapore and to the company’s having stopped disclosing Singapore revenue separately, and said answers are needed from the board and from external counsel within 10 days, in the same account. A House committee chairman said on Sunday that Mr. Huang has agreed to appear for closed-door testimony before three House committees, in the same account. On succession, the board has contacted the chief of Arm as a potential successor and states that no formal process has yet been initiated, in the same account. The board itself had filed no public answer by midnight—not to the petition, not to the Gerstner and Baker letter, and not to the Treasury Secretary—in any account the desk read. No finding has been made by the board, by any committee or by any court on any allegation in this file. Earnings stand on Tuesday, November 17, after the close, with consensus revenue at $108.9 billion against the company’s outlook of $108.0 billion in the week’s file, and the interim chief, Ms. Kress, leads the call. Settled: the contest, its two directions, and its 10-day clock. Open: the board’s first word.

The Markets at Midnight: Futures Open Higher at 1800, Stand Lower by 2036, and Bitcoin Holds Above $65,000

The week’s first market fact is a rise that did not hold. Futures opened higher on Sunday evening: at 1810 Eastern the S&P 500 futures were up 0.2 percent at about 7,600 and the Nasdaq 100 futures up 0.6 percent, with Dow futures little changed and crude slightly lower, in the futures account filed below. By 2036 Eastern the same three contracts stood lower: Dow futures down 0.11 percent, S&P 500 futures down 0.22 percent and Nasdaq-100 futures down 0.58 percent, in the late futures account filed below, which puts Brent at $95.33, down about 0.53 percent, and West Texas crude at $88.26, down 0.34 percent. Friday’s closes stand beneath both readings: the S&P 500 at 7,561.67, down 0.40 percent; the Nasdaq Composite at 25,136.27, down 0.91; the Dow at 52,347.60, up 0.10; and the ten-year yield at 5.15 percent. Bitcoin stood near $65,200 on Sunday evening, down about 5 percent since Friday’s close, after touching about $62,000 on Saturday, its lowest since July, in the futures account above; the day’s other readings, from $61,946 to $65,714, stand in the evening file. The week’s market calendar is dated in every account: the central bank chairman speaks Monday at noon, retail sales and Nvidia come Tuesday, the October meeting minutes come Wednesday, and Thursday carries a retailer’s earnings, a listing, and Shenzhen.

France and Spain at Midnight: A Senate Date on Thursday in Paris, and a New Tracking in Spain

France’s fifth Saturday stands closed at the numbers the evening edition printed, and its next facts are weekday facts. The Interior Ministry’s count stands at 106,000 nationwide, 24,000 in Paris, down from 146,000 the Saturday before, with 219 detained in the week’s file; the organisers’ count stands at about 200,000, in the demonstrations account filed below, which records demands from protecting children and increasing wages to more resources for education and protest against the police bill. That bill, giving officers a presumption of legitimate self-defence when they use firearms and called a licence to kill by its critics in the accounts, is scheduled to be examined by the Senate on Thursday, November 19, in the Senate account filed below. The unions’ Tuesday strike stands, called after the government’s 0.6 percent minimum-wage promise was rejected; Tuesday is also the eighth anniversary of the Yellow Vest movement, and a sixth Saturday is called for November 21.

Spain’s campaign stands where Sunday’s new tracking left it. The first instalment of a new tracking puts the Popular Party at 30.8 percent and 130 seats, the Socialists at 26.4 percent and 106 seats, and Vox at 18.2 percent and 65 seats, a combined 195 seats for the first and third parties against 176 needed for a majority, in the tracking account filed below. The mean of sixteen institutes stands at Popular Party 31.4, Socialists 26.9 and Vox 19.1, in the evening file; the state survey’s Socialist lead stands against both figures where the week left it. A head-to-head television debate is reported set for November 19, and polls may publish until November 23. Spain votes on November 29.

Monday at Midnight: Every File in This Edition Is Dated, and Monday Holds Four of the Dates

Monday carries the recovery’s verdict, the President’s departure, Alaska’s next count, and the central bank chairman’s remarks at noon. The airlines will be read against the Secretary’s fully-normal promise and against Sunday’s final count of more than 2,300 cancelled. Alaska’s count resumes ahead of Wednesday’s tabulation. Tuesday carries retail sales, France’s strike, and Nvidia’s earnings after the close. Wednesday carries the October meeting minutes, the APEC leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, and Alaska’s tabulation. Thursday carries the three presidents in Shenzhen, the Senate’s examination of the police bill in Paris, and a listing in New York. The Treasury Secretary’s 10 days run from Sunday. Spain votes November 29; Mr. Huang’s interview stands dated December 1; the Federal Reserve decides December 8 and 9. The Overnight Watch collects at 0400.

The Cocked Hat

Where the midnight’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Sunday’s cost: more than 2,300 cancelled and some 7,700 delayed in the final wire count, more than 1,600 cancelled and almost 3,600 delayed in the early wire count, nearly 1,700 cancelled by 1350 in the tracker account, and 1,606 cancelled at 1100 in the El Dorado account—readings taken at different hours, agreeing on the day’s order and on nothing finer; and on its shares, American at 17 percent in the final count against 13 percent in the early one, JetBlue at 28 against 27. On the promise: full schedule integrity by Sunday’s close in the Administrator’s Saturday words, probably fully normal on Monday in the Secretary’s Sunday words, and a final Sunday count that met neither in full. On the failed thing: a router at El Dorado triggering a second router at Amarillo and a flood across the centers, some 60 similar routers disabled, equipment purchased in 2001 and obsolete by 2006, and the root cause unknown in the Secretary’s own admission. On Bahrain: intercepts and destruction in the Defence Force’s account, six drones on target in the Guards’, condemnations from four neighbouring capitals, Article 51 claimed by both sides, no impacts to American forces in the Central Command spokesman’s sentence, and no word from any capital on the condition of the radar itself. On Alaska’s share: 49.94 percent on the state’s full denominator, 50.1 on the dashboard that excludes unresolved write-ins, a winner listed on one tracker, no call from the Press, a victory declared by one candidate and a winner declared by the President for the other, and no count at all on Sunday. On Europe: not yet contacted in the spokesman’s answer, included in future talks in the White House’s November 13 sentence, and objectives by force absent a negotiated solution in the spokesman’s interview, with no European answer in the file. On Shenzhen: confirmed by Washington and Moscow, unconfirmed by its host, with Ukraine on the agenda in one capital’s telling and off it in another’s. On Nvidia: a war room and a counter at 154,678 and 156,850 in two Sunday readings on one side, a call for an outside successor and answers within 10 days from the Treasury on the other, and no answer from the board to either. On futures: up 0.2 and 0.6 percent at the 1800 open, down 0.22 and 0.58 percent by 2036. On France: 106,000 in the Ministry’s count and about 200,000 in the organisers’. On Spain: 30.8 percent for the Popular Party in the new tracking, 31.4 in the sixteen-institute mean, and a Socialist lead in the state survey. Inside the triangle is where the day honestly stands, and the log turns on it.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 26 items.

Subjective
Reuters via BusinessWorld — more than 2,300 cancelled and some 7,700 delayed on Sunday at the final count, a second router at Amarillo, and no root cause

United States air travel disruptions continued for a third day with more than 10,000 flights affected on Sunday, but the Transportation Secretary predicted a return to normalcy by Monday as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule following a systemwide ground stop. More than 2,300 flights nationwide were canceled and some 7,700 were delayed on Sunday, according to FlightAware; airlines on Saturday had canceled more than 6,400 flights and delayed more than 8,000. The Secretary said on a Sunday programme that there was no evidence of a cyberattack or other malicious intent, but the cause remained unclear, and that flights would come back to normal on Sunday but probably fully normal on Monday. On Sunday 28 percent of JetBlue flights and 17 percent of American Airlines flights were canceled, with United, Southwest and Delta reporting cancellations of 3 to 5 percent. The replacement of a router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, triggered problems with a recently replaced router in Amarillo, Texas, which started broadcasting and overloading routers at other centers; the functionality of the originating routers has been disabled, as was done for about 60 similar routers. The routers were purchased in 2001 and were obsolete by 2006. The Secretary said the worker who installed the router was a good American patriot and a veteran, that sabotage is not believed, and that the Administration does not actually have the root cause. The President made his first public comments on the weekend’s disruption, calling for additional funding to be approved and done all at once; two House members answered that about $11 billion of the $12.5 billion approved last year remains unspent.

Subjective
Reuters via Virginia Business — more than 1,600 cancelled and almost 3,600 delayed on Sunday in the early count, and a return to normalcy predicted by Monday

United States air travel disruptions continued for a third day on Sunday with more than 5,200 flights already affected, but the Transportation Secretary predicted a return to normalcy by Monday as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule after a systemwide ground stop. More than 1,600 flights nationwide were cancelled and almost 3,600 were delayed on Sunday, according to FlightAware; airlines on Saturday had cancelled more than 6,400 flights and delayed more than 8,000. The Secretary said flights will come back to normal on Sunday but probably fully normal on Monday, and emphasised the Administration’s focus on keeping passengers safe. On Sunday 27 percent of JetBlue flights and 13 percent of American Airlines flights were cancelled, with Southwest, United and Delta reporting cancellations of 3 to 5 percent of their flights. The Administration issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday that halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours.

Subjective
The Points Guy — nearly 1,700 cancelled by 1350 Sunday, more than 17,000 scrubbed since Friday, and 33 of Monday’s down

Sunday was shaping up to be another rough day at airports across the country, with travellers facing a third straight day of widespread cancellations after Friday’s nationwide ground stop. As of 1:50 p.m. Eastern on Sunday, nearly 1,700 flights had been cancelled and another 5,280 had been delayed, according to FlightAware; all told, more than 17,000 flights have been scrubbed since Friday. Cancellations appeared to slow entering Sunday compared with the past two days, but operations had not returned to normal, especially on some carriers. The Administrator had said disruptions were expected to begin easing by Sunday evening, and that the airline partners believe they will be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday. As of Sunday afternoon, 33 flights for Monday had been cancelled, a total that had not increased much since the morning, suggesting operations may be stabilising. The account records the ground stop’s cause as a communications outage affecting air traffic control discovered late Friday afternoon.

Subjective
SourceFirst News — the El Dorado, Arkansas router, 1,606 cancelled by 1100, and a full return that could slip into Monday

Friday’s nationwide ground stop began when a newly installed router at a remote Administration site in El Dorado, Arkansas, started flooding the air traffic control network, the Transportation Secretary said on Sunday; officials still do not know whether the fault lay with the equipment or with the contractor that installed it. Both routers are now with L3Harris, the contractor that owns and operates the network, while Administration staff are on site and the Federal Bureau of Investigation is offering support. As investigators examine the Arkansas router, FlightAware counted 1,606 United States flight cancellations by 11 a.m. Eastern on Sunday, against 6,696 for all of Saturday, and 3,343 delayed. The Administration’s airport status feed showed no ground stop anywhere at 11 a.m. The Administrator had promised on Saturday that schedules would be back to normal by the close of business Sunday; on Sunday the Secretary moved that toward Monday, saying planes and crews were still out of position.

Subjective
Crisis Zone — Bahrain says it destroyed Iranian aerial attacks as Tehran claims a radar strike

Bahrain’s Interior Ministry issued its first threat alerts since September, naming no threat, while explosions were heard in Manama; the Defence Force then said its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks. The Guards said six drones targeted an American air-defence radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base; no damage or casualties had been reported, and neither American nor Bahraini authorities had confirmed any hit. The Guards’ statement was carried by the state broadcaster’s channel, by Fars and by Press TV. Friday’s claim was denied by Central Command, which said two drones were shot down with no injuries or damage. The account records the President’s Saturday condition, that he might hold off on attacking Iran if there were no new provocations from Tehran or the Houthis, and that he would maintain the naval blockade.

Subjective
Wrivid — Bahrain says it intercepted Iranian attacks, and a Central Command spokesman says there were no impacts to American forces

Bahrain said Sunday its air defenses intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets. The Guard separately claimed it struck a United States radar at Riffa Air Base, near Al-Riffa; Bahrain’s statement did not identify the site or assess damage there. The Guard said six drones targeted the radar and described the operation as successful, according to a statement carried by Tasnim; the account gave no damage assessment or casualty count. Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry said the aerial attacks were intercepted, condemned what it called continued Iranian aggression, rejected Tehran’s stated justifications, held Iran responsible, invoked Article 51 and asked the Security Council to condemn the attacks. A Central Command spokesman, Tim Hawkins, told a newspaper that there were no impacts to American forces; the statement did not say whether radar equipment or other property was damaged, and Bahrain had not answered the newspaper’s question about damage at the site. Sunday’s episode followed a separate reported attack on Friday, when Bahrain said two drones were intercepted and Central Command denied the Guard’s claim that it struck an early-warning radar.

Subjective
Fana News — Bahrain strongly condemns Iran’s continued attacks, citing Resolution 2817 and Article 51

Bahrain has condemned, in the strongest terms, Iran’s continued attacks on its territory after air defence systems intercepted and destroyed drones launched on Sunday, two days after intercepting two others in a similar attack. The Foreign Ministry described the attacks as a resumption of Iran’s aggression against Bahrain and regional countries, in blatant disregard for international law and the Charter; a flagrant violation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which condemned Iranian attacks on Bahrain and neighbouring countries and demanded their immediate cessation; and a foreclosing of de-escalation efforts imperilling regional security and stability. The ministry affirmed Bahrain’s inherent individual and collective right to self-defence under Article 51 and to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty and the security of its citizens and residents. As a member of the Security Council, Bahrain called on the Council to condemn the repeated attacks, shoulder its responsibilities, and take decisive measures to ensure Iran’s full compliance with Resolution 2817.

Subjective
Salaamedia — Arab states condemn Iran’s drone attack on Bahrain, and Tehran rejects a compensation demand

Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemned Iran’s drone attack on Bahrain on Sunday and expressed solidarity with the kingdom. It was the second attack in three days, after two drones were intercepted at dawn on Friday. Bahrain’s defence forces said their air defence systems intercepted the drones before Iran could achieve its goals. The Guards said they launched six drones at a radar at a United States defence site at the al-Riffa helicopter base, in retaliation for hostile United States actions. In Riyadh, the Foreign Ministry condemned the attacks in the strongest terms, saying they violated international law and the principles of good neighbourliness. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said the continued attacks were a flagrant violation of Bahrain’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a breach of international law and the Charter. Jordan’s Foreign Ministry said the attacks violated Bahrain’s sovereignty and threatened its security, stability and territorial integrity. In Cairo, the Foreign Ministry said the attacks were a dangerous escalation that violated Bahrain’s sovereignty and threatened its security. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Mr. Baghaei, rejected a demand by the Gulf Cooperation Council that Iran pay compensation for its attacks.

Subjective
KhabarWire — Iran strikes a Bahrain air base for a second time in days, and the Gulf closes ranks

The Guards said they launched six drones at an American air-defence radar at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain before dawn on Sunday, the second attack on the kingdom in three days; Bahrain’s Defence Force said its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets, and the Interior Ministry issued two public alerts telling residents to seek shelter. The attack came shortly after 4 a.m. local time, with residents reporting a second series of blasts around 6:30. Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry expressed the kingdom’s strongest condemnation, described the attack as a violation of Resolution 2817, said no pretext could justify aggression against a state’s sovereignty, rejected the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores, held Iran responsible, and invoked Article 51 and the Cooperation Council’s joint defence agreement. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemned the attack. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman defended the attack as justified under Article 51 because those states had aided American operations against Iran. No independent assessment of what was targeted or damaged has been published, and the American military had not commented on Sunday’s attack when the account was written.

Subjective
State of Alaska, Division of Elections — the unofficial summary report of November 14 at 1515

The state’s unofficial summary for the 2026 general election, timed 3:15 p.m. on November 14, reports all 401 precincts reported and 283,618 ballots cast of 605,433 registered, 46.85 percent. In the United States Senator race, on 281,587 votes: Mr. Heikes 6,002, 2.13 percent; Ms. Peltola 140,637, 49.94 percent; Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. 4,652, 1.65 percent; Senator Dan S. Sullivan 129,424, 45.96 percent; and write-ins 872, 0.31 percent. The report is headed unofficial results throughout.

Subjective
DINA News — Ms. Peltola widens her lead to 11,213, with the race uncalled and tabulation on November 18

The Alaska Senate count has taken another consequential turn: Ms. Peltola now leads Senator Sullivan by 11,213 first-choice votes, on 140,637 to 129,424, sharpening the question whether the remaining ballots or ranked-choice transfers can erase a margin that has repeatedly moved in her direction. The Press and most major national decision desks had not declared a winner when the report was published; the result is not certified, and the count must finish, any required ranked-choice tabulation must occur, and the state must certify the result. The latest reported batch added approximately 2,397 votes for Ms. Peltola and 1,596 for Senator Sullivan. The state’s public dashboard may round Ms. Peltola to 50.1 percent because unresolved write-ins are excluded from that display calculation. November 18 is the deadline for qualifying overseas ballots, the final regional count, and the anticipated ranked-choice tabulation for contests that require it; November 25 is the target certification date.

Subjective
Beezloop — Ms. Peltola tops 50 percent in the dashboard count, and her campaign says there is no mathematical path

Ms. Peltola is now over 50 percent in Alaska’s Senate race: after about 4,000 more ballots were counted Saturday, she had 50.1 percent of first-choice votes to Senator Sullivan’s 46.1 percent, a newspaper reported. If she stays above 50 percent when counting ends, she wins outright and Alaska never has to run its ranked-choice tabulation. Counting has to wrap up by Wednesday, November 18, which is also the day ranked-choice tabulation would start if nobody has a majority; the state’s target date to certify the result is November 25. The account carries the earlier full-total arithmetic, a lead of 10,412 on Friday night’s count with fewer than 12,000 ballots left to count.

Subjective
LaPresse — European negotiators have not yet contacted Russia, the Kremlin spokesman tells TASS

The negotiators appointed by the European Union have not yet attempted to contact Russia, Kremlin spokesman Peskov stated in response to a question from the TASS agency: “No, not yet.” At the informal European summit in Dublin, the heads of state and government opted for a format that includes the European institutions and the E5 countries—Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland—alongside the European Commission and the Council to represent Europe in the negotiations on Ukraine.

Subjective
LaPresse — without an agreement with Europe, Russia will have to use force, the spokesman tells Vesti

In the absence of a negotiated solution with Europe, Russia will have to achieve its objectives by force, Kremlin spokesman Peskov said in an interview with a Vesti correspondent, according to reports from Russian news agencies. Peskov said that, for Moscow, the resolution of the conflict in Ukraine is inextricably linked to the new European security architecture. Earlier, the spokesperson had told TASS that the negotiators chosen by Europe had not yet attempted to establish contact with Russia.

Subjective
Silent Dossier — the Kremlin confirms the Shenzhen meeting, Washington keeps Ukraine off its agenda, and the host confirms nothing

The Kremlin confirmed on Saturday, November 14, that Presidents Putin, Xi and Trump will meet in Shenzhen on November 19: spokesman Peskov said an agreement has been reached to hold a trilateral meeting on the 19th on the sidelines of the APEC summit, and gave no agenda. A senior American official said Ukraine is not on the agenda and that it does not seem appropriate to discuss Ukraine there; a Kremlin aide said on November 12 that the settlement would be discussed with President Trump in Shenzhen. American officials said President Trump will raise nuclear arms and Iran, and that they expect no nuclear agreement. The APEC leaders’ meeting runs November 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, with President Xi in the chair. No Chinese official has confirmed the three-way meeting on the record.

Subjective
CNN — the President to meet Presidents Xi and Putin at a trilateral sit-down on nuclear non-proliferation

President Trump will meet with China’s President Xi and Russia’s President Putin at a historic trilateral sit-down on nuclear non-proliferation, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 19. The White House confirmed the meeting on Friday. The account carries the American agenda—nuclear arms at the top, Iran to be raised, and no agreement expected—and the itinerary of the President’s Asia trip, departing Monday for Manila and the ASEAN meetings and continuing to Shenzhen.

Subjective
Implicator — the petition at 154,678, its affiliations self-reported, and fake entries named in the same file

The petition to reinstate Mr. Huang read 154,678 names at 1001 Pacific on Sunday, up from 117,112 at 1403 Pacific on Saturday. The account breaks the total down as 7,459 self-described current employees, 1,406 former employees, 81,896 shareholders and 63,917 other supporters, and records in the same file that the affiliations are self-reported and not verified and that fake entries appeared among the names. The petition asks for reinstatement while an independent investigation establishes the facts, for the investigation’s scope, independence and timetable to be made public, for a substantive opportunity to respond, and, if the board insists he leave, for a specific, evidence-backed explanation.

Subjective
WCCFTech — Mr. Huang considers returning, allies assemble a war room, and the petition crosses 156,000

Mr. Huang has discussed a return with confidants, and allies are assembling a lobbying effort—a war room—on his behalf to press the board for his reinstatement. The petition’s counter stood at 156,850 in this account, with more than 7,500 current employees among the names. The account carries the petition’s growth across the weekend and the board’s standing position that no public answer had been given to the petition or to the shareholders’ letter.

Subjective
KuCoin, from the Journal and the Financial Times — a war room on one side, and the Treasury Secretary urging an external replacement with answers in 10 days

Several days after Mr. Huang’s resignation, the battle for Nvidia’s chief executive position has turned into an open contest. On November 15, according to the Financial Times, Mr. Huang has discussed with close allies the possibility of returning, as supporters establish a war room in Silicon Valley to lobby the board to reinstate him and plan to seek support from the White House. The Treasury Secretary, Mr. Bessent, stated on a Fox News programme on Sunday that Nvidia needs drastic leadership changes and that the board should seek an external successor; he questioned whether the company knowingly violated export controls on high-end chips, pointed to sales billed through Singapore and to the company’s having stopped disclosing Singapore revenue separately, and said answers are needed from the board and external counsel within 10 days. A House committee chairman said on Sunday that Mr. Huang has agreed to appear for closed-door testimony before three House committees. On succession, the board has contacted Arm’s chief as a potential successor; the board stated that no formal process has yet been initiated. Ms. Kress leads the company as interim chief.

Subjective
TechSpot — nearly 150,000 sign the petition requesting Mr. Huang’s return, and the petition’s four asks

Nearly 150,000 people have signed a petition requesting that Nvidia’s board reinstate Mr. Huang. The petition asks the board to reinstate him while an independent investigation establishes the facts, to make the investigation’s scope, independence and timetable public, to give him a substantive opportunity to respond, and, if the board insists he leave, to give a specific, evidence-backed explanation. The account carries the signatures’ growth across the weekend and the affiliations the signers report for themselves.

Subjective
Cedar Global Markets — futures open the week higher, S&P up 0.2 percent and Nasdaq up 0.6 percent at 1810, with Bitcoin near $65,200

United States stock futures opened the week higher on Sunday evening. As of 6:10 p.m. Eastern, S&P 500 futures were up 0.2 percent from Friday’s settlement at about 7,600, and Nasdaq 100 futures were up 0.6 percent; Dow futures were little changed. Oil opened slightly lower: United States crude futures were down 0.3 percent, near $88.30 a barrel, and Brent crude was down 0.6 percent. Bitcoin was near $65,200, down about 5 percent since Friday’s stock market close, after briefly touching about $62,000 on Saturday, its lowest since July. This week: the Federal Reserve chairman speaks Monday at noon Eastern, Nvidia reports Tuesday after the close, the Fed releases its October meeting minutes Wednesday at 2 p.m., and Thursday brings a retailer’s earnings, Anthropic’s expected Nasdaq debut and the President’s meeting with China’s President.

Subjective
Summa Money — futures edge lower by 2036, Dow down 0.11 percent, S&P down 0.22 and Nasdaq down 0.58

United States stock futures traded lower overnight late Sunday as markets prepared for Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings later this week, for a public listing, and for the minutes of the Federal Reserve’s October meeting. As of 8:36 p.m. Eastern, Dow futures declined 0.11 percent, S&P 500 futures were down 0.22 percent and Nasdaq-100 futures fell 0.58 percent. On Friday the three benchmark indexes posted a mixed close: the Dow up 0.10 percent at 52,347.55 and the S&P 500 down 0.40 percent at 7,561.67. Brent crude futures were trading at $95.33 a barrel, down about 0.53 percent, and West Texas crude at $88.26, down 0.34 percent. Nvidia said last week that it remains on track to post its third-quarter results under interim chief Kress on November 17.

Subjective
CoinLab — Bitcoin at $65,570 at 0845 after a low of $62,006, the lowest since July

As of 8:45 a.m. Eastern on Sunday, Bitcoin traded near $65,500, down 1.6 percent on the day: overnight selling drove it to $62,006, the lowest since July, before buyers lifted it $3,500 off the low through the Asian and European sessions. The brief records leverage flushed over the week, a Fear and Greed reading in single figures in its file, and the week’s calendar: futures reopening Sunday evening, the central bank chairman’s remarks Monday, retail sales and Nvidia on Tuesday, and the meeting minutes on Wednesday.

Subjective
Le Monde — November 14 demonstrations in Paris and Lyon, diverse but determined crowds, at 106,000 in the Ministry’s count

Across France on Saturday, November 14, demonstrations brought together a range of demands, from protecting children and increasing wages to providing more resources for education, continuing high school blockades and protesting police violence. According to the Interior Ministry, 106,000 people marched, including 24,000 in Paris, a sharp drop from previous weeks, across 137 events; the youth coalition claimed 200,000 demonstrators nationwide, with nearly 100,000 in the capital. The focus for many protesters was the bill called a licence to kill by its critics, scheduled to be examined by the Senate on November 19; the bill aims to introduce a presumption of self-defence after a police officer or gendarme fires a weapon.

Subjective
Particle — France protests continue as the police firearms bill heads to the Senate on November 19

The nationwide demonstrations ran for a fifth Saturday in a row on November 14, and the Interior Ministry put turnout at about 106,000 people, including roughly 24,000 in Paris, while organisers gave higher estimates. The bill approved by the lower house would give officers a presumption of legitimate self-defence when they fire their weapons, a legal change critics call a licence to kill. Senate consideration of the measure is set to follow union plans for a nationwide strike on Tuesday, November 17, called after the unions rejected a 0.6 percent minimum-wage offer.

Subjective
Demócrata — the Sondaxe tracking puts the Popular Party at 130 seats and Vox at 65 against the Socialists’ 106

The first instalment of a new tracking of the general election puts the Popular Party at 30.8 percent and 130 seats, the Socialists at 26.4 percent and 106 seats, and Vox at 18.2 percent and 65 seats, a combined 195 seats for the first and third parties against 176 needed for a majority. The account carries the campaign’s opening positions and the calendar to the vote on November 29.

entry.title: Sunday Closes With More Than 1,600 Flights Cancelled and the Full Return Moved to Monday, the Gulf Closes Ranks Behind Bahrain While Washington Files No Word on the Radar, and the Petition to Bring Back Mr. Huang Passes 154,000 With No Answer From the Board
entry.summary: Sunday closes with more than 1,600 flights cancelled and full return moved to Monday, as the Gulf closes ranks behind Bahrain.
entry.content:
The Evening File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Sunday Closes With More Than 1,600 Flights Cancelled and the Full Return Moved to Monday, the Gulf Closes Ranks Behind Bahrain While Washington Files No Word on the Radar, and the Petition to Bring Back Mr. Huang Passes 154,000 With No Answer From the Board

The evening file: a recovery day that ended smaller than Saturday and larger than promised, with its cause named to a town in Arkansas; a morning of drones in the Gulf answered in writing by five capitals and not answered by a sixth; a count that spent Sunday where Saturday left it; a spokesman’s two sentences repeated to the evening wires; a petition that grew by tens of thousands while its board said nothing; and a week ahead written entirely in dates.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Sunday, November 15, 2026. This edition continues the file from Edition No. 50, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 today, from Edition No. 49, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, from Edition No. 48, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, and from Edition No. 47, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Saturday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the evening figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Evening in Brief: The Day Whole, and the First Considered Responses From Every Side

Sunday’s developments, whole, are a recovery that did not finish, a claim that gained responses without gaining confirmation, and a set of counts that moved everywhere except in Alaska. More than 1,600 flights were cancelled and nearly 3,600 delayed on Sunday in the wire account filed below, nearly 1,700 had been cancelled by 1350 in the tracker account filed below, and more than 17,000 flights have been scrubbed since Friday in the same account; the Secretary’s Sunday version of the promise, back to normal today and probably fully normal tomorrow, is the version the day bore out, and the cause file gained its place in the El Dorado account filed below. In the Gulf, the considered responses arrived: Manama’s statement stands in the ministry account filed below, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemned the attacks in the condemnations account filed below, Tehran’s spokesman defended the strikes as self-defence in the accounts filed below, and no American word on Sunday’s radar claim stands in any account the desk read by 1800. In Alaska no new count came on Sunday; the state’s Saturday report stands at 140,637 to 129,424, and the race stands uncalled. In Nvidia’s file the petition’s counter passed 154,000 and kept rising, and the board filed no public answer. The evening’s other files, Moscow’s two sentences, Shenzhen’s two confirmations and one silence, France’s two counts and Spain’s new tracking, stand below in their places.

The Airlines at Evening: More Than 1,600 Cancelled, a Router at El Dorado, and the Promise Settled on Tomorrow

The recovery’s final shape for Sunday is a system working and a schedule still short. More than 5,200 flights were affected on Sunday in the wire account above, which counts more than 1,600 cancelled and almost 3,600 delayed, against more than 6,400 cancelled and more than 8,000 delayed on Saturday; the tracker account above counts nearly 1,700 cancelled and 5,280 delayed by 1350, and a third account counts more than 5,000 delayed and a further 2,000 cancelled in the day. The desk prints the three counts apart in the Cocked Hat; they were taken at different hours by different counters, and they agree on the order of the day, a third day of disruption far below Saturday and far above a normal Sunday. The shares stand where midday left them: JetBlue cancelled 27 percent of its Sunday operation and American 13 percent, with Southwest, United and Delta at 3 to 5 percent, in the wire account. Monday’s cancellations stood at 33 by Sunday afternoon in the tracker account, against fewer than 30 in the morning; the smallness of that figure is the recovery’s best evidence.

The cause file gained a town, a pair of routers, and an open question. Secretary Duffy said on Sunday that a newly installed router at a remote Administration site in El Dorado, Arkansas, started flooding the network during work by the contractor L3Harris on a copper-to-fiber upgrade, in the El Dorado account above; both routers are now with the contractor, Administration staff are on site, the Federal Bureau of Investigation is offering support, and officials still do not know whether the fault lay with the equipment or with the contractor that installed it, in the same account. The Secretary’s earlier sentence stands beside it: the system did not meet the moment, the contractor did not meet the moment, or the equipment did not. Administrator Bedford’s Saturday promise, full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday, was not met in the form stated; the Secretary’s Sunday form, fully normal tomorrow, is now the standing promise, and Monday will be read against it. No sign of a cyberattack stands in any account in the file.

Bahrain at Evening: Five Capitals Answer in Writing, Tehran Answers Back, and Washington Does Not Answer

The first considered responses to Sunday’s morning are regional, written, and aligned. Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry said the attacks constitute a violation of international law and the principles of good neighbourliness and stressed an immediate halt, in the condemnations account above; Qatar’s Foreign Ministry called the continuation of the attacks a dangerous escalation that will complicate efforts to contain the tension and undermine political and diplomatic endeavours, in the same account; Jordan and Egypt condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with Bahrain, in the same account and in the second-attack account filed below. Manama’s own statement, in the ministry account above, holds Iran fully responsible, rejects the transformation of Bahraini territory into an arena for settling scores, cites Security Council Resolution 2817 and Bahrain’s right of self-defence under Article 51, in coordination with the Gulf Cooperation Council under its joint defence agreement, and calls on the Security Council, where Bahrain sits, to condemn the attacks and take decisive measures. The Defence Force’s account stands: its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets, in the Bahrain account filed below.

Tehran’s answer and Washington’s silence complete the evening file. The Guards say six drones of their Aerospace Force targeted the American air-defence radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base, in a second phase of retaliation, in the Bahrain account above and in the drone account filed below; no damage and no casualties have been reported, and neither Washington nor Manama has confirmed a hit. Tehran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Mr. Baghaei, defended the strikes at a news conference as justified in self-defence and said Iran would keep responding to military aggression by the United States or other states, in the second-attack account above; Article 51 is therefore claimed in the same file by Manama for its defence and by Tehran for its strikes, for opposite acts, and the desk prints both claims as claims. Central Command, which denied Friday’s claim in claim-and-fact form, had filed no word on Sunday’s claim in any account the desk read by 1800, and the desk records the silence as a fact of the file, not as an answer. The President’s Saturday condition, that he might hold off on attacking Iran if there were no new provocations, stands unapplied to Sunday’s claim in any statement in the file.

Where the evening’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Sunday’s cost: more than 1,600 cancelled and nearly 3,600 delayed in the wire count, nearly 1,700 cancelled and 5,280 delayed by 1350 in the tracker account, more than 5,000 delayed and a further 2,000 cancelled in a third account, and 1,606 cancelled at 1100 in the El Dorado account—readings taken at different hours, agreeing on the day’s order and on nothing finer. On the promise: full schedule integrity by the close of business Sunday in the Administrator’s Saturday words, fully normal tomorrow in the Secretary’s Sunday words, and a day that met neither in full and the second in prospect. On the failed thing: a router at El Dorado flooding the network in the Secretary’s Sunday account, with equipment failure and installer error both open. On Bahrain: intercepts and destruction in the Defence Force’s account, six drones on target in the Guards’, condemnations from four neighbouring capitals, Article 51 claimed by both sides, and no confirmation of a hit and no American word from any capital. On Alaska’s share: 49.94 percent on the state’s full denominator, 50.1 on the dashboard that excludes unresolved write-ins, a winner listed on one tracker, no call from the Press, a victory declared by one candidate and a winner declared by the President for the other. The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 27 items.

Subjective
Reuters via Virginia Business — more than 1,600 cancelled and almost 3,600 delayed on Sunday, and a return to normalcy predicted by Monday

United States air travel disruptions continued for a third day on Sunday with more than 5,200 flights already affected, but the Transportation Secretary predicted a return to normalcy by Monday as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule after a systemwide ground stop. More than 1,600 flights nationwide were cancelled and almost 3,600 were delayed on Sunday, according to FlightAware; airlines on Saturday had cancelled more than 6,400 flights and delayed more than 8,000. The Secretary said flights will come back to normal on Sunday but probably fully normal on Monday, and emphasised the Administration’s focus on keeping passengers safe. On Sunday 27 percent of JetBlue flights and 13 percent of American Airlines flights were cancelled, with Southwest, United and Delta reporting cancellations of 3 to 5 percent of their flights. The Administration issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday that halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours.

Subjective
The Points Guy — nearly 1,700 cancelled by 1350 Sunday, more than 17,000 scrubbed since Friday, and 33 of Monday’s down

Sunday was shaping up to be another rough day at airports across the country, with travellers facing a third straight day of widespread cancellations after Friday’s nationwide ground stop. As of 1:50 p.m. Eastern on Sunday, nearly 1,700 flights had been cancelled and another 5,280 had been delayed, according to FlightAware; all told, more than 17,000 flights have been scrubbed since Friday. Cancellations appeared to slow entering Sunday compared with the past two days, but operations had not returned to normal, especially on some carriers. The Administrator had said disruptions were expected to begin easing by Sunday evening, and that the airline partners believe they will be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday. As of Sunday afternoon, 33 flights for Monday had been cancelled, a total that had not increased much since the morning, suggesting operations may be stabilising. The account records the ground stop’s cause as a communications outage affecting air traffic control discovered late Friday afternoon.

Subjective
USA Today — more than 1,600 cancelled and almost 4,200 delayed in the updated count, and the system stable

United States air travel remained disrupted as of midday on November 15 after more than 15,000 flights were cancelled in the last two days following the nationwide ground stop. More than 1,600 flights within, into or out of the United States were cancelled and almost 4,200 were delayed on Sunday, according to FlightAware. The Secretary said on November 14 that the preliminary investigation points to work by the contractor L3Harris during a routine upgrade from copper wiring to fiber.

Washington Post account — airlines scramble to resume flights, with the two promises printed side by side

Airlines scrambled on Sunday to return flight schedules to normal by the evening, two days after a nationwide ground stop triggered widespread cancellations and delays across the United States. While thousands of flights were disrupted over the weekend, with over a thousand more cancellations reported on Sunday, airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crews, after officials expressed confidence that the worst of the disruption is over. Crisis Zone — Bahrain says it destroyed Iranian aerial attacks as Tehran claims a radar strike

Bahrain’s Interior Ministry issued its first threat alerts since September, naming no threat, while explosions were heard in Manama; the Defence Force then said its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks. The Guards said six drones targeted an American air-defence radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base; no damage or casualties had been reported, and neither American nor Bahraini authorities had confirmed any hit. Subjective
Fana News — Bahrain strongly condemns Iran’s continued attacks, citing Resolution 2817 and Article 51

Bahrain has condemned, in the strongest terms, Iran’s continued attacks on its territory after air defence systems intercepted and destroyed drones launched on Sunday, two days after intercepting two others in a similar attack. The Foreign Ministry described the attacks as a resumption of Iran’s aggression against Bahrain and regional countries, in blatant disregard for international law and the Charter; a flagrant violation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which condemned Iranian attacks on Bahrain and neighbouring countries and demanded their immediate cessation; and a foreclosing of de-escalation efforts imperilling regional security and stability. The ministry affirmed Bahrain’s inherent individual and collective right to self-defence under Article 51 and to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty and the security of its citizens and residents. As a member of the Security Council, Bahrain called on the Council to condemn the repeated attacks, shoulder its responsibilities, and take decisive measures to ensure Iran’s full compliance with Resolution 2817.

Subjective
The Guardian live account via The Bull Post — Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemn the attack, with Manama’s full statement

Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt have all strongly condemned the Iranian attack on Bahrain and expressed solidarity with the kingdom, in statements carried by Bahrain’s news agency. Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry affirmed that the attacks constitute a violation of international law and the principles of good neighbourliness, and stressed the importance of an immediate halt and of serious steps towards security and stability for the region and its peoples. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said the continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that will complicate efforts to contain the tension and undermine political and diplomatic endeavours aimed at achieving security and stability. The account reproduces Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry statement in full: the strongest condemnation of continued aggression, drones intercepted and destroyed on Sunday and two on Friday, a flagrant violation of Resolution 2817, rejection of the Guards’ pretexts, rejection of the transformation of Bahraini territory into an arena for settling scores, Iran held fully responsible, Article 51 self-defence in coordination with the Gulf Cooperation Council under its joint defence agreement, and a call for the Security Council to act.

Subjective
KhabarWire — Iran strikes a Bahrain air base for a second time in days, and the Gulf closes ranks

The Guards said they launched six drones at an American air-defence radar at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain before dawn on Sunday, the second attack on the kingdom in three days; Bahrain’s Defence Force said its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets, and the Interior Ministry issued two public alerts telling residents to seek shelter. The attack came shortly after 4 a.m. local time, with residents reporting a second series of blasts around 6:30. Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry expressed the kingdom’s strongest condemnation, described the attack as a violation of Resolution 2817, said no pretext could justify aggression against a state’s sovereignty, rejected the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores, held Iran responsible, and invoked Article 51 and the Cooperation Council’s joint defence agreement. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemned the attack; Saudi Arabia called it a violation of international law and good neighbourliness, and Qatar called the continuation a dangerous escalation. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman defended the attack as justified under Article 51 because those states had aided American operations against Iran. No independent assessment of what was targeted or damaged has been published, and the American military had not commented on Sunday’s attack when the account was written.

CNN — the President to meet with China’s and Russia’s leaders at a trilateral sit-down on nuclear non-proliferation

The President will meet jointly next week with China’s leader and Russia’s President, the White House said on Friday, a first-ever trilateral sit-down between the leaders of the three countries. TechSpot — nearly 150,000 people sign a petition requesting Mr. Huang back as chief executive

Three days after Mr. Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive, a campaign to bring him back is gathering momentum: more than 150,000 people have signed an open letter urging the board to reinstate its co-founder while an independent investigation runs its course. The organisers argue he was forced out without a fair opportunity to defend himself, and ask the board to do three things: reinstate him while the investigation continues, ensure he receives a fair hearing, and publicly explain the reasoning behind his departure. For now the board has announced no change to its succession plans; the next major event is Tuesday’s quarterly earnings report, whose results cover the period when Mr. Huang was fully in charge.

Subjective
WCCFTech — Mr. Huang considers returning, allies assemble a lobbying effort, and the petition crosses 156,000

Mr. Huang has discussed with close confidants the possibility of his comeback, according to a report the account cites, and allies in Silicon Valley are setting up a lobbying effort urging the board to reinstate the former chief executive. Shareholders were pressuring the board to keep the door open for Mr. Huang, with two fund managers spearheading the effort.
