A petition on the campaign website, signed by named technology figures, had collected 156,850 names at the time of publication, including over 7,500 current employees. Mr. Huang is still facing an internal investigation into a reported relationship, in the account’s telling. The account states that it is far from certain whether he can or will return, and in what capacity.

Subjective
KuCoin News — the resignation sparks a petition count of 151,083, with 80,205 shareholders

As of November 15, the petition website calling for the board to reinstate Mr. Huang as chief executive continues to gain momentum: 151,083 individuals have signed, including 7,380 current employees, 1,381 former employees, and 80,205 shareholders, according to a financial news report the account cites. Notable public figures are listed among the signers. The company announced on November 12 that Mr. Huang had resigned as chief executive, effective immediately, ending his 33-year leadership of the company he co-founded. Organisers and signatories express concern that he may have been forced to step down without due process or sufficient opportunity to defend himself, and urge the board to provide clarification; the core demands are reinstatement pending an independent investigation to establish the facts, and, if removal is sustained, an evidence-based justification. The letter states that 33 years of leadership does not exempt a person from accountability, but that accountability requires evidence and due process. The website states the campaign is independent and has not been endorsed by the company or by Mr. Huang personally.

Subjective
CoinLab — bitcoin at $65,570 at 0845 after a low of $62,006, with futures reopening at 1800

As of 8:45 a.m. Eastern on Sunday, bitcoin traded near $65,500, down 1.6 percent on the day: overnight selling drove it to $62,006, the lowest since July, before buyers lifted it $3,500 off the low through the Asian and European sessions. United States stock markets are closed today, but crypto trades around the clock. The morning brief’s base case for the next 24 hours is a range of $63,800 to $66,800 into tonight’s futures open, with a pullback case and a breakout case assigned smaller probabilities; leverage is already flushed, with $1.68 billion of long liquidations and open interest down 14 percent on the week, and a sentiment reading in oversold territory. United States stock futures reopen at 6 p.m. Eastern tonight and Asian markets open around 7 p.m.; Monday brings officials’ remarks, and Tuesday brings October retail sales at 8:30 a.m. and Nvidia earnings after the close.

Subjective
Coindaro — bitcoin at $64,502 on Sunday evening, 6.3 percent below Friday’s close, and the week ahead

Bitcoin traded at $64,502 on one exchange at 17:38 UTC on Sunday, November 15, 6.3 percent below the $68,839 it fetched when Wall Street closed on Friday; in between, the weekend took it down 10 percent to $61,946 at 01:45 UTC on Sunday. A sentiment index printed 10 for Sunday, against 20 on Friday. Open interest in one perpetual contract stood at about 94,117 bitcoin at 17:33 UTC on Sunday, about $6.1 billion at a mark near $64,700, about 7 percent under Friday’s level in coin terms, yet about three accounts in four are still long, and on another venue puts cost far more than calls. The week ahead carries Nvidia’s results call on Tuesday, the minutes of the Federal Reserve’s October meeting on Wednesday, a Senate hearing for two nominees on Thursday, and an options expiry on Friday. The account notes that a regulated bitcoin futures contract has traded around the clock since May 2026, so the contract priced the weekend’s moves as they happened.

Subjective
Le Monde — the November 14 demonstrations in Paris and Lyon, diverse but determined crowds

Across France on Saturday, November 14, demonstrations brought together a range of demands, from protecting children and increasing wages to providing more resources for education, continuing high school blockades and protesting police violence. According to the Interior Ministry, 106,000 people marched, including 24,000 in Paris, a sharp drop from previous weeks. A youth coalition of student unions claimed 200,000 demonstrators nationwide, with nearly 100,000 in the capital. Yellow Vest activists staged their fifth act against the high cost of living. The focus for many protesters was the bill called a licence to kill by its critics, scheduled to be examined by the Senate on November 19; the bill aims to introduce a presumption of self-defence after a police officer or gendarme fires a weapon.

Subjective
Particle News — France’s protests continue as the police firearms bill heads to the Senate

The nationwide demonstrations ran for a fifth Saturday in a row on November 14, and the Interior Ministry put turnout at about 106,000 people, including roughly 24,000 in Paris, while organisers gave higher estimates. The bill approved by the lower house would give officers a presumption of legitimate self-defence when they fire their weapons, a legal change critics call by a name the account quotes. The movement now unites high-school students, trade unions, Yellow Vest activists and child-protection campaigners demanding better school conditions, higher pay and relief from the rising cost of living. Senate consideration of the measure is set to follow union plans for a nationwide strike on Tuesday, November 17, and the account records that unions rejected a 0.6 percent minimum-wage offer.

Subjective
Demócrata — a new tracking puts the Popular Party at 130 seats and Vox at 65 against the Socialists’ 106

A general election poll for a Galician newspaper places the Popular Party as the leading party for November 29, with 30.8 percent of the vote and 130 seats; the Socialists obtain 26.4 percent and 106 deputies. The first instalment of the tracking, published this Sunday, November 15, leaves a gap of 4.4 points and 24 representatives between the two parties. Vox reaches 18.2 percent of the vote and 65 seats; its sum with the Popular Party amounts to 195 deputies, 19 more than the 176 needed for an absolute majority, and the combined percentage of both formations stands at 49 percent. The account states that the projection does not imply a closed pact exists; it describes the parliamentary sum yielded by the poll.

Subjective
Demócrata — Mr. Sánchez begins the campaign in Seville, Mr. Feijóo in Badalona, and the sixteen-institute mean

The President of the Government and Socialist candidate, Mr. Sánchez, gave the starting signal for the campaign for the general elections of November 29 in Seville, while the leader of the Popular Party, Mr. Feijóo, did so in Badalona, and the president of Vox, Mr. Abascal, and the candidates of Frente Amplio, Ms. Colau, and of another list, Ms. Montero, opted for Madrid. At midnight the campaign officially began, in which the heads of the lists will travel around the country requesting support at the ballot boxes through rallies and election events across Spain. The account’s table of the mean of the latest study from each institute over thirty days, dated November 15, 2026 and now across sixteen institutes, stands at Popular Party 31.4 percent, Socialists 26.9, Vox 19.1, Frente Amplio 6.3 and ERC 2.5.

entry.title: Sunday’s Recovery Reaches Nearly 1,600 Cancellations by 1000 Against 875 Down at Dawn, Bahrain Answers Its Morning in Writing—Resolution 2817, Article 51 and a Red Line—While Washington Files No Word on the Radar, and Alaska’s Count Stands at 140,637 to 129,424 With the Next Count Due Monday
entry.summary: Sunday's airline recovery nears 1,600 cancellations by 1000 against 875 at dawn, and Bahrain answers its morning in writing: midday, Nov 15, 2026.
entry.content:
The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Sunday’s Recovery Reaches Nearly 1,600 Cancellations by 1000 Against 875 Down at Dawn, Bahrain Answers Its Morning in Writing—Resolution 2817, Article 51 and a Red Line—While Washington Files No Word on the Radar, and Alaska’s Count Stands at 140,637 to 129,424 With the Next Count Due Monday

The midday file: a recovery counted at nearly 1,600 against 875 expected, and a promise that divides between tonight and tomorrow; a kingdom that answered its morning with intercepts, a resolution and a red line, against a radar claim no capital has confirmed; a count that did not move, printed to the vote; a spokesman’s two sentences in Moscow; a petition counted past 135,000 and questioned in the same accounts; and a Sunday with no session, read in the one market that never closes.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Sunday, November 15, 2026. This edition continues the file from Edition No. 49, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, from Edition No. 48, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, from Edition No. 47, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Saturday, and from Edition No. 46, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Saturday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midday figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midday in Brief: A Recovery Counted Higher Than the Dawn Expected, a Statement From Manama, and a Count That Did Not Move

The midday’s corrections run in one direction: Sunday is costing more flights than the dawn file carried, and the morning’s other files gained statements rather than settlements. Nearly 1,600 flights had been cancelled and 2,570 delayed by 1000 on Sunday in the tracker’s figures, in the day-three account filed below, against 875 of Sunday’s flights already cancelled in the overnight accounts and 1,390 cancelled on Sunday morning in the warnings account filed below; more than 17,000 flights have been scrubbed since Friday, in the day-three account. In Bahrain’s file, the kingdom spoke twice on Sunday morning—the Defence Force on intercepts, the Foreign Ministry on law—in the Bahrain account and the ministry account filed below, while the Guards’ claim of a radar hit at Al-Riffa stands without an American or Bahraini confirmation at 1200. In Alaska, no new count came on Sunday morning; the state’s Saturday-afternoon report stands at 140,637 to 129,424, and the race stands uncalled. In Moscow, the Kremlin’s spokesman answered the European question in two words and the European prospect in one sentence, both filed below. The markets have no Sunday session; the reading is Friday’s closes, the weekend’s one open market, and a week of dates.

The Airlines at Midday: Nearly 1,600 Cancelled by 1000, a Router Named in the Cause File, and a Promise in Two Versions

The recovery’s shape at midday is a system declared stable and a schedule still being rationed. The Administration said late Saturday that the system is stable and returning to normal operations, and its dashboard on Sunday morning reported no active en-route events, in the national account filed below, which records that local traffic-management programs remain possible later today in eight named areas, among them Dallas-Fort Worth, Denver, Houston, Seattle and San Francisco, as airport and route contingencies and not another nationwide stop; Kennedy and O’Hare each reported general delays of fifteen minutes or less on Sunday morning, in the same account. The cost stands against that stability in the tracker’s figures: at 0800, JetBlue had cancelled 27 percent of its Sunday operation, the highest share among the large carriers; American had scrapped 368 flights, the most of any carrier; Delta and Southwest had each cancelled more than 170, and United about 100, in the day-three account above. American’s chief customer officer called the disruption among the most significant operational impacts the carrier has experienced, in a Saturday-evening letter in the same account; American said all its planned cancellations for Saturday night and Sunday had been completed, with individual flights still liable to cancel, and Delta advised passengers with flexible plans to move their travel to Monday, in the same account and the warnings account above. Fewer than 30 flights for Monday had been cancelled by Sunday morning, in the day-three account.

The official statements at midday divide on the day’s one promise, and the cause file gained its most specific account. Administrator Bedford’s Saturday words stand in the day-three account: the airline partners believe they will be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday. Secretary Duffy’s Sunday words stand in the scramble account filed below: things come back to normal today, but probably fully normal tomorrow. The desk prints the two versions apart in the Cocked Hat; the evening collection will read the day against both. On cause, the preliminary investigation points to work by the contractor L3Harris during a routine upgrade from copper wiring to fiber: a newly installed or modified router began flooding other routers with data, disrupting communications and radar information at the control centers, and investigators are determining whether the underlying problem was equipment failure or contractor or installer error, in the national account above. The contractor’s Saturday statement stands in the same account: more than 70 percent of the planned conversion from copper to fiber is complete, and the company is supporting the investigation. The Secretary’s Saturday sentence stands beside it, in the day-three account: the system did not meet the moment, the contractor did not meet the moment, or the equipment did not. Saturday’s corrected totals stand where the morning left them—more than 6,400 cancelled and 8,000 delayed in the tracker’s late count, against nearly 6,500 cancelled in the midnight edition’s—and Friday’s at about 9,200 cancelled and 7,500 delayed, in the national account; roughly 15,600 were cancelled on the two days together before Sunday’s are counted.

The Count at Midday: No New Count on Sunday Morning, 157 Short of a Majority by the Desk’s Arithmetic, and a Winner Listed in One Place

Alaska’s Senate count at midday is Saturday afternoon’s report, unchanged, and the desk prints it whole. The state’s unofficial summary, timed 1515 on Saturday, gives Ms. Peltola 140,637 votes, 49.94 percent; Senator Sullivan 129,424, 45.96 percent; Mr. Heikes 6,002; Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. 4,652; and write-ins 872, on 281,587 votes in the race, with 283,618 ballots cast and all 401 precincts reported, in the state’s report filed below. The lead is 11,213. A majority of the reported vote is 140,794; Ms. Peltola stands 157 votes short of it, by the desk’s arithmetic on the state’s figures. The Press’s count at 0049 UTC on Sunday carries the same figures, estimates 97 percent of the vote counted, and lists the race not called, in the count account filed below, which prices the last batch: 4,219 votes added since the Press’s Saturday 0500 UTC count, 2,397 of them for Ms. Peltola and 1,596 for Senator Sullivan. The state’s dashboard rounds Ms. Peltola to 50.1 percent because unresolved write-ins are excluded from that display calculation, in the lead account filed below, and one results tracker prints the same 50.1 and marks her the winner, in the tracker account filed below; the desk prints the listing and the non-call side by side, as it has printed them all week. Ms. Peltola declared victory on Saturday at the earlier lead of 10,412, in the declaration account filed below; Senator Sullivan has not conceded and has not posted publicly since November 4, in the same account. The next count is due Monday; overseas ballots may arrive through Wednesday, November 18, when the ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled if no candidate holds a majority, and certification is targeted for November 25. A Peltola seat makes the caucus 56; a Sullivan seat, 55.

Bahrain at Midday: Two Alerts, an Intercept Claim From the Defence Force, a Foreign Ministry Statement, and No Word From Washington

Manama’s morning gained its official paper at midday, and the paper names names the alerts did not. The Interior Ministry’s two alerts went out at 0432 and 0650 Bahrain time, urging citizens and residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location and follow news through official channels, and naming no threat, source or target, in the Bahrain account at the top of this report; an agency journalist in Manama reported sirens and explosions at about 0400, and residents a second series at about 0630. The Defence Force then said its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets, and that all units remain at the highest level of readiness, in the same account. The Foreign Ministry’s statement, in the ministry account above, condemns the continued attacks in the strongest terms: drones intercepted and destroyed on Sunday, and two more on Friday; a resumption of aggression in blatant disregard of international law and the Charter; a flagrant violation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which condemned Iranian attacks on Bahrain and its neighbours and demanded their immediate cessation; Bahrain’s inherent right, individual and collective, to self-defence under Article 51, exercised in coordination with the Gulf Cooperation Council, whose joint defence agreement treats an attack on one member as an attack on all; a call, from a member of the Council, for the Council to condemn the attacks and take decisive measures to ensure full compliance; the rejection of the Guards’ pretexts; and the sentence that the kingdom’s security is a red line. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt issued condemnations of their own on Sunday, in the accounts filed below.

Against the paper stand the claim and the silence. The Guards say six drones of their Aerospace Force targeted the American air-defence radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base, in a second phase of retaliation, carried by the state broadcaster’s channel, by Fars and by Press TV, in the Bahrain account above and in the alert account filed below. No damage and no casualties have been reported, and neither Washington nor Manama has confirmed a hit, in both accounts. Central Command, which denied Friday’s claim in claim-and-fact form—two drones launched, both shot down, no injuries, no damage—has filed no word on Sunday’s claim in any account the desk read by 1200, and the desk records the silence as a fact of the file, not as an answer. Tehran’s answer to Manama’s Article 51 is its own Article 51: its Foreign Ministry’s spokesman told a news conference that attacks on Iran’s neighbours were justified in self-defence, and accused the Gulf states of helping Washington strike his country, in the intercepts account filed below, which also dates the resolution Manama cites: adopted March 11, 2026, by thirteen votes to none with China and Russia abstaining, on a Bahraini text with 135 co-sponsors. The President’s Saturday condition stands in the Bahrain account: he might hold off on attacking Iran if there were no new provocations from Tehran or the Houthis, and he would maintain the naval blockade. Whether Sunday’s claimed strike is a provocation in that sentence’s meaning has not been said by Washington by 1200. The seven conditions, the letter to Congress and the strait figures stand where the week left them.

Dublin and Shenzhen at Midday: ‘No, Not Yet,’ a Sentence About Force, and a Departure on Monday

Europe’s file at midday is two answers from one spokesman. Asked by the TASS agency whether the negotiators appointed by the Union have attempted to contact Russia, spokesman Peskov answered: “No, not yet,” in the contact account filed below, which records the Dublin form the question was about—the institutions and the five countries, Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland, with the Commission and the Council. In an interview with a Vesti correspondent, the same spokesman said that in the absence of a negotiated solution with Europe, Russia will have to achieve its objectives by force, and that if the Union does not want peace there is no point in discussing a settlement or a European security framework, in the force account and the wire account filed below. The two answers stand against the standing American position in the file: the White House’s deputy press secretary said on November 13 that the American delegation at Abu Dhabi ensured Europe will be included in future talks, in the assessment filed below, which also carries President Zelenskyy’s November 14 statement that the American delegation at Abu Dhabi proposed that Ukraine gain NATO membership in exchange for a Ukrainian withdrawal from the entirety of the Donbas, and the report that the Russian delegation circulated an unofficial paper of demands at those talks. No date for a next round, and no contact, stands in the midday file.

Shenzhen gained no third confirmation and gained an itinerary. The meeting of the three presidents on Thursday, November 19 stands confirmed by the White House on Friday and by the Kremlin on Saturday, and unconfirmed by its host, in the meeting account filed below and the week’s file; China’s Foreign Ministry’s Friday sentence, that it is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state, stands unamended at 1200. The President travels to Manila on Monday for the ASEAN meetings and continues to Shenzhen, where he is due from November 17 through 19, in the week’s accounts. The agenda split stands: nuclear arms and Iran in the American telling, Ukraine off the trilateral agenda in the same telling and on it in the Kremlin aide’s. Nothing in the midday file moves either sentence.

Nvidia and the Markets at Midday: A Counter at 135,468 and Questioned in the Same Accounts, and a Sunday Read in One Open Market

Nvidia’s file at midday is a number and a challenge to the number. The petition’s counter showed 135,468 signatures at 0037 on Sunday, in the petition account filed below, which classifies 6,776 of the signers as current employees, 1,267 as former employees and 73,181 as shareholders, and records that those affiliations have not been independently verified and that neither the company nor Mr. Huang endorses the campaign. A second Sunday account puts the count at more than 120,000, in the resignation account filed below. A third, in the finance account filed below, puts it at nearly 130,000 on Saturday evening and prints the challenge in the same file: the site lacks real-name verification, the signatures are hard to verify, and a company vice president, Mr. Catanzaro, has said publicly that he never signed and that his name was used without his consent. The petition’s asks stand in all three accounts: reinstatement while an independent investigation establishes the facts, the investigation’s scope, independence and timetable made public, a substantive opportunity to respond, and, if the board insists he leave, a specific, evidence-backed explanation. The board’s succession file gained one sentence over the weekend: it is choosing a search firm and has not formally engaged any potential candidates, in the Monday-prep account filed below. No finding has been made by the board, by any committee or by any court on any allegation in this file. Earnings stand on Tuesday, November 17, at about 1620, with the call at 1700 in one account and at 1320 and 1400 Pacific in another—the same hour, printed two ways; consensus revenue stands at $108.9 billion against the company’s outlook of $108.0 billion, in the same account.

The markets’ reading at midday is a reading of a closed week and an open one. Sunday has no cash session. Friday’s closes stand: the S&P 500 at 7,561.67, down 0.40 percent; the Nasdaq Composite at 25,136.27, down 0.91; the Dow at 52,347.60, up 0.10; the ten-year yield at 5.15 percent; the dollar index at 103.41. The one market that trades on Sunday moved all weekend, and the desk prints its readings apart: $64,830, down 2.97 percent on the day and 8.60 on five sessions, at 0544 UTC in the daily brief filed below; a low of $62,006 overnight, the lowest since July, and $65,570 at 0845 and $64,770 at 1000, in the bitcoin account filed below; and $65,714 at 0420, after a three-month low on Saturday, in the Monday-prep account filed below, which also carries the Federal Reserve’s November 13 finding that 87 percent of the market contacts it surveyed named artificial intelligence a major risk to the financial system, up from 50 percent in the spring and 30 percent a year earlier. Futures reopen at 1800 today; Friday’s futures closes stand at minus 0.42 percent for the S&P 500 and minus 1.23 for the Nasdaq 100, in the same account. The week’s calendar is dated in every file: retail sales and Nvidia on Tuesday, the October meeting minutes on Wednesday, the Anthropic listing on Thursday.

France and Spain at Midday: A Fifth Saturday Closed at Two Counts, a Bill Gone to the Senate, and a Mean That Moved One Tenth

France’s fifth Saturday closed, and Sunday’s accounts price its calm and its counts apart. The Interior Ministry’s figures stand: 106,000 demonstrators nationwide, 24,000 of them in Paris, down from 146,000 and 46,000 the Saturday before, and 219 detained, in the midnight edition’s file and in the rally account filed below, which records the authorities’ reading that Saturday stayed largely calm and turnout declined. The organisers’ figures stand beside them: about 200,000 nationwide and almost 100,000 in the capital, in the week’s accounts. The contested police bill—the measure giving officers a presumption of legitimate self-defence when they use firearms, passed by the lower house—now heads to the Senate, in the Senate account filed below. The unions’ Tuesday strike stands, called after the government’s 0.6 percent minimum-wage promise was rejected as crumbs, in both accounts; Tuesday is also the eighth anniversary of the Yellow Vest movement, whose adherents say they will mark it on roundabouts and toll booths all over France, in the rally account, and a sixth Saturday, Acte VI, is called for November 21, in the week’s accounts.

Spain’s campaign spent its first Sunday with its mean nearly still. The mean of the latest study from each institute, dated November 15 and now across sixteen institutes, stands at Popular Party 31.4 percent, Socialists 26.9, Vox 19.1, Frente Amplio 6.3 and ERC 2.5, in the campaign account filed below: against the fifteen-institute mean the midday edition printed on Saturday, the only movement is Frente Amplio down one tenth. The polls still do not meet—the state survey’s Socialist lead and the 40dB survey’s two-point gap stand in the file where the week left them—and polls may publish until November 23. Spain votes on November 29.

The Afternoon Ahead: An Evening Collection at 1800 and a Week Written in Dates

The afternoon’s measures are the recovery’s and the silence’s. Sunday’s cancellation total will be read against the Administrator’s close-of-business promise and the Secretary’s tomorrow, and against the nearly 1,600 counted by 1000. Any American word on the Al-Riffa claim, and any Bahraini report of damage, will enter the file when it stands. The week ahead is dated: the President departs Monday; Alaska’s next count comes Monday and its tabulation Wednesday, the day the APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen and the Federal Reserve publishes its October minutes; Nvidia reports Tuesday after the close; Alaska’s certification target and the expenditures report share November 25; the European Council takes up Ukraine’s financing on November 26 and 27; Spain votes November 29; Mr. Huang’s interview stands dated December 1; the Federal Reserve decides December 8 and 9. This paper’s Sunday Review of Reviews stands filed separately, ahead of the day’s watches. The Evening Watch collects at 1800.

The Cocked Hat

Where the midday’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Sunday’s cost by midday: 875 cancelled at dawn in the overnight file, more than 900 by late Saturday in one account, 1,390 on Sunday morning in the warnings account, 1,421 in one tracker reading, and nearly 1,600 cancelled with 2,570 delayed by 1000 in the day-three account—a rising series taken at different hours, not a disagreement about one hour. On the promise: full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday, in the Administrator’s Saturday words; fully normal tomorrow, in the Secretary’s Sunday words. On the failed thing: a router flooding other routers during a copper-to-fiber upgrade in the preliminary account, with equipment failure and installer error both open; overloaded switches and routers in the Secretary’s earlier account; and a network handling critical radio frequencies in two airline officials’ account from Saturday. On Alaska’s share: 49.94 percent on the state’s full denominator, 50.1 on the dashboard that excludes unresolved write-ins, a winner listed on one tracker, no call from the Press, and a victory declared by the candidate. On Bahrain: intercepts and destruction in the Defence Force’s account, six drones on target in the Guards’, and no confirmation of a hit from any capital; on the law, Article 51 is claimed by Manama and by Tehran in the same morning, for opposite acts. On Europe: not yet contacted, in the spokesman’s answer to TASS; included in future talks, in the White House’s November 13 sentence; and objectives by force absent a negotiated solution, in the spokesman’s interview. On the petition: 135,468 on its own counter at 0037, more than 120,000 in one Sunday account, nearly 130,000 on Saturday evening in a third, and its signatures unverifiable and at least one name used without consent, in the third account’s own file. On bitcoin: $62,006, $64,770, $64,830 and $65,714 in four readings taken at four hours of a Sunday. On France: 106,000 in the Ministry’s count and about 200,000 in the organisers’. On Spain’s Socialists: 26.9 in the sixteen-institute mean and a lead in the state survey. Inside the triangle is where the midday honestly stands.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 29 items.

Subjective
The Points Guy — nearly 1,600 cancelled by 1000 Sunday, more than 17,000 scrubbed since Friday, and fewer than 30 of Monday’s down

Sunday was shaping up to be another rough day at airports across the country, with travellers facing a third straight day of widespread cancellations after Friday’s nationwide ground stop. As of 10 a.m. Eastern on Sunday, nearly 1,600 flights had been cancelled, according to FlightAware, and an additional 2,570 had already encountered delays. All told, more than 17,000 flights have been scrubbed since Friday. As of 8 a.m., JetBlue had cancelled 27 percent of its operation for the day, the highest cancellation rate of any American carrier on Sunday; American had scrapped more departures than any airline, 368 flights; Delta and Southwest had each cancelled more than 170, and United about 100. American’s chief customer officer, in a letter to customers on Saturday evening, called the disruption among the most significant operational impacts the carrier has experienced and said it expected disruption throughout the weekend as it reset the airline. Delta urged passengers with flexible plans to consider postponing travel until Monday. Administrator Bedford had said the disruptions were expected to begin easing by Sunday evening: based on everything heard from the airline partners, they believe they will be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday. As of Sunday morning, fewer than 30 flights for Monday had been cancelled. The stop was ordered late Friday after a communications outage affecting air traffic control, as crews upgraded equipment amid a switch from copper wiring to fiber at one facility. Secretary Duffy said at a Saturday press conference that this was a system that did not meet the moment, that the contractor did not meet the moment, or the equipment did not, and caused the outages. The account records that passengers whose flights are cancelled or significantly delayed are entitled to a refund if they choose not to travel, regardless of the reason, and that because the disruption was due to issues outside the airlines’ control, carriers are unlikely to reimburse hotel, ground transportation and meal costs.

Subjective
USA Today — the system stable, no active en-route events, the router in the preliminary account, and the contractor’s statement

Air travel remained disrupted on the morning of November 15 after more than 15,000 flights were cancelled in the last two days following the nationwide ground stop, but officials say the system is stable and schedules should largely return to normal by the night of November 15. The Administration said on X late on November 14 that the system is stable and it is returning to normal operations. In all, 875 flights scheduled for Sunday were already cancelled, the tracker said, and another 1,904 delayed. As of the morning of November 15, the Administration’s National Airspace System dashboard reported no active en-route events, a strong indication the communications failure is no longer constraining the national system; local traffic management programs are still possible later today, including in the Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin, San Antonio, Denver, Houston, San Diego, Seattle and San Francisco areas, as airport and route-specific contingencies, not another nationwide ground stop. Kennedy and Chicago O’Hare were each reporting general arrival and departure delays of fifteen minutes or less. November 14 was extremely rough: the tracker counted more than 6,400 cancellations and 8,000 delays by late in the day. On November 13 about 9,200 flights were cancelled and 7,500 delayed after essentially all departures were halted for nearly five hours; roughly 15,600 flights were cancelled Friday and Saturday alone, before Sunday’s are included. Secretary Duffy said November 14 that the preliminary investigation points to work by the contractor L3Harris during a routine upgrade from copper wiring to fiber: a newly installed or modified router began flooding other routers with data, disrupting communications and radar information at control centers, and investigators are determining whether the underlying problem was equipment failure or contractor or installer error. L3Harris, which manages the telecommunications infrastructure supporting about 45,000 daily flights and connecting more than 4,400 facilities, said it has completed more than 70 percent of the planned conversion from copper wires to a fiber optic system and is supporting the investigation to understand the conditions that led to the November 13 ground stop. Administrator Bedford has said the outdated copper wires should be completely replaced by September 2027.

Subjective
The Travel — 1,390 cancelled on Sunday morning, American at 368, and warnings standing for 21 airports

Cancellations continued into Sunday, with the total nearing the 1,400 mark on the morning of November 15 after cancellations on Friday and Saturday exceeded 15,000. American had the most cancelled flights among the 1,390 total, with 368 cancelled affecting at least 10 percent of its flights, according to the tracker. Dallas-Fort Worth, Chicago O’Hare and New York Kennedy were the hubs facing the most cancellations, with triple-digit cancellations. American and Delta are among the carriers to issue updates: both confirmed cancellations are expected to continue into Sunday, though they have made improvements in getting passengers back on flights, and major airlines extended flexible rebooking offers as cancellations trickled into Sunday. American said in an update on Saturday evening that its recovery continues to move forward, that all planned cancellations for that night and the next day had been completed, though some individual flights may still be cancelled as it works to fully restore the operation, and that customers travelling that night or the next day should continue to check their flight status before heading to the airport. Delta encouraged passengers to book flights as of Monday as the carrier continues to restore its system.

Subjective
Vidia News — more than 900 of Sunday’s cancelled by late Saturday, 6,400 on Saturday and 9,200 on Friday

More than 900 flights scheduled for Sunday in the United States had been cancelled by late Saturday as airlines continued to recover from the nationwide ground stop. The tracker recorded 910 cancellations for Sunday, with the figure rising. More than 6,400 flights were cancelled on Saturday, following about 9,200 on Friday; the order halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours on Friday. Administrator Bedford said he did think the worst was behind them, but added that a significant amount of recovery work remained, and that based on everything heard from the airline partners, they believed they would be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday. Secretary Duffy said the disruption began during work to replace old copper telecommunications lines with fibre-optic cables at a facility. The Administration said it ordered the ground stop as a safety measure after communications problems affected 17 of its 22 en-route air traffic control centres.

Subjective
The Washington Post, carried by Wallhop — the scramble to normal by the evening, and the Secretary’s Sunday version of the promise

Airlines scrambled Sunday to return flight schedules to normal by the evening, two days after the nationwide ground stop triggered widespread cancellations and delays across the United States. While thousands of flights were disrupted over the weekend, with over a thousand more cancellations reported Sunday, airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crews, after officials expressed confidence that the worst of the disruption is over. “We’re going to see things come back to normal today, but probably fully normal tomorrow,” Secretary Duffy told a Sunday program. Administrator Bedford said airlines expect they will be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday. The tracker reported that more than 6,600 flights within, into or out of the United States were cancelled on Saturday, with at least 1,300 additional cancellations recorded early Sunday. American said all planned cancellations for Saturday night and Sunday had been completed, although some individual flights could still be cancelled as it works to restore operations. Delta said it was continuing to restore its operations but advising customers with flexible travel plans to move their flights to Monday or later because of the potential for further disruption on Sunday. The ground stop on Friday afternoon marked the first time flights across the entire country had been halted since January 2023, when a computer system failure affected the pilot alerting system; in the latest stop, flights were halted for more than four hours before restrictions were lifted around 2015 on Friday. Secretary Duffy said the outage was believed to have been caused by problems during maintenance at a remote site, where a contractor was replacing old copper telecommunications lines with fiber-optic cables.

Subjective
Alaska Division of Elections — the official unofficial summary of November 14, 1515: 140,637 to 129,424 on 281,587

The state’s election summary report for the November 3, 2026 general election, unofficial results timed 3:15:40 p.m. on November 14, records 401 of 401 precincts reported and 283,618 ballots cast of 605,433 registered, 46.85 percent. For United States Senator it gives Mr. Heikes 6,002 votes, 2.13 percent; Ms. Peltola 140,637, 49.94 percent; Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. 4,652, 1.65 percent; Senator Dan S. Sullivan 129,424, 45.96 percent; and write-in votes 872, 0.31 percent, for a total of 281,587 votes in the race.

Subjective
DINA — the lead at 11,213, the dashboard’s 50.1 explained, and the result not certified

Ms. Peltola now leads Senator Sullivan by 11,213 first-choice votes, in an update the account presents exactly as a major update to the unofficial first-choice count: the Press and most major national decision desks had not declared a winner when the report was published, the result is not certified, and the account is not presenting the count as a projection or certification. The latest reported numbers are Ms. Peltola 140,637, 49.94 percent, and Senator Sullivan 129,424, 45.96 percent, with Mr. Heikes at 6,002 and Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. at 4,652. The latest reported batch added approximately 2,397 votes for Ms. Peltola and 1,596 for Senator Sullivan. The state’s public dashboard may round Ms. Peltola to 50.1 percent because unresolved write-ins are excluded from that display calculation. November 18 is the deadline for qualifying overseas ballots, the final regional count of absentee and questioned ballots, and the anticipated ranked-choice tabulation for contests that require it; November 25 is the target certification date. The count must finish, any required tabulation must occur, and the state—not a campaign, a president, a commentator or a newsroom—must certify the result.

Subjective
Ballot Brief — the Press’s count at 0049 UTC: 4,219 new votes, 49.9 percent, and not called

The Press’s count as of November 15, 2026, at 0049 UTC lists the Alaska Senate race as not called and estimates 97 percent of the vote counted. The count stands at 281,587 votes: Ms. Peltola 140,637, 49.9 percent; Senator Sullivan 129,424, 46.0 percent; Mr. Heikes 6,002, 2.1 percent; Mr. Sullivan Jr. 4,652, 1.7 percent; and write-in votes 872, 0.3 percent. Since the Press’s November 14, 0500 UTC count, 4,219 votes have been newly counted: 2,397 for Ms. Peltola, 1,596 for Senator Sullivan, 117 for Mr. Heikes, 92 for Mr. Sullivan Jr. and 17 write-ins. The account’s own arithmetic, offered as arithmetic and not as a result or a prediction, puts Ms. Peltola’s lead at 11,213 in the newest count, against 10,412 in the earlier count. It records what is not known: the Press has not called the race, the account makes no projection, about 3 percent of the vote is estimated not yet counted, and the count may change.

Subjective
US News Pulse — Ms. Peltola declares victory at 10,412, the race not officially called, and Senator Sullivan not conceded

Ms. Peltola declared victory in Alaska’s Senate race early on Saturday, November 14, after a new batch of ballots widened her lead to 10,412 votes, telling supporters there is no path left for her opponent. Her campaign announced it as the latest results showed her ahead 138,240 to 127,828, about 49.8 percent to 46.2, with roughly 95 to 96 percent counted. She stood about 445 votes short of the 50 percent majority that would avoid a ranked-choice tabulation in that count. The race has not been officially called, and Senator Sullivan has not conceded and has not posted publicly since November 4. A prediction market called Ms. Peltola the winner on Saturday, and one report says a network has called the race for her; the Press, however, has not officially called it. The declaration followed a count that had stood days earlier at a lead of just 626 votes, 102,701 to 102,075, with 394 of the state’s 401 precincts reporting. The next milestone is November 18, when the ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled if she finishes below 50 percent, and state certification is targeted for November 25.

Subjective
Politix+ — the live results page lists 50.1 percent and a winner

The live Alaska results page lists the Senate race with Ms. Peltola at 140,637 votes and 50.1 percent, marked as the winner, and Senator Sullivan at 129,424 votes and 46.11 percent, with Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. at 4,652 votes and 1.66 percent. The page also carries polling averages as of November 15, 2026 for the state’s races.

Subjective
Crisis.Zone — the alerts timed, the Defence Force on intercepts, the Guards on six drones, and the President’s condition

The Interior Ministry sent threat alerts to residents on Sunday, the first such warnings since September; an agency journalist in Manama reported alarm sirens and explosions at about 4:00 a.m. local time, and residents reported a second series of blasts around 6:30 a.m. The two alerts went out at 5:32 a.m. and 7:50 a.m. Emirates time, which is 4:32 a.m. and 6:50 a.m. in Bahrain. The ministry’s posts urged citizens and residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels; it named no threat, source or target. Later that morning the Defence Force said its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets, and that Iran continues its systematic hostile approach through attacks targeting Bahraini territory, with all units at the highest level of readiness. The Guards said six of their drones targeted an American air defence radar in Bahrain; no damage or casualties had been reported, and neither American nor Bahraini authorities had confirmed any hit. The Guards’ statement, carried by the state broadcaster’s Telegram channel, by Fars and by Press TV, said the American air defense radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base was targeted by six drones of the Aerospace Force; the Guards called it the second phase of a decisive and crushing response and said the sound of the drones striking their targets was heard in several parts of Bahrain, while one account reported the statement gave no evidence of damage. On Friday the Guards said they had targeted and destroyed an early-warning radar; Central Command denied it, saying both drones were shot down with no injuries or damage. The account sets out four markers: whether Central Command confirms or denies the new claim as it did on Friday, whether Bahrain reports any damage, whether the President’s conditional pause survives a second claimed strike in three days—a wire reported Saturday that the President said he might hold off on attacking Iran if there were no new provocations from Tehran or the Houthis, while maintaining the naval blockade—and the Qatar-mediated talks, on which the President has said the United States does not need a deal.

Subjective
Geopolitiki — the first nationwide alert since September, six drones claimed at Al-Riffa, and no confirmation of damage

Bahrain sounded a nationwide alert for a possible threat in the early hours of Sunday, November 15, its first since September, while the Guards announced that six drones of their Aerospace Force hit an American air-defence radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base. The Guards call the attack the second phase of their retaliation for American military action against Iran. The claim of damage to the radar came without evidence and has not been confirmed by the United States or Bahrain. The Interior Ministry issued two notices, at 5:32 a.m. and 7:50 a.m. local time in the account’s reading, calling on citizens and residents to stay calm, go to the nearest safe place and get information only from official channels, without specifying the nature of the threat. Residents reported explosions around 4 a.m. and a second series at about 6:30 a.m. The Defence Force then announced that its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets. The Guards’ statement, broadcast by state television and the Tasnim agency, says the strikes were heard in various areas of Bahrain and that more drones were used in this phase than in the previous one. The first phase, in the Guards’ terminology, was the attack of Friday, November 13, when they said they destroyed an American early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for the strike at Sirik.

Subjective
Fana News — the Foreign Ministry’s statement: Resolution 2817, Article 51, and a call on the Council

Bahrain has condemned, in the strongest terms, Iran’s continued attacks on its territory after air defence systems intercepted and destroyed drones launched on Sunday, two days after intercepting two others in a similar attack. In a statement issued on Sunday, the Foreign Ministry described the attacks as a resumption of Iran’s aggression against Bahrain and regional countries, in blatant disregard for international law and the Charter. It called them a flagrant violation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which condemned Iranian attacks on Bahrain and neighboring countries and demanded their immediate cessation, while foreclosing de-escalation efforts and imperiling regional security and stability. The ministry affirmed Bahrain’s inherent individual and collective right to self-defense under Article 51 of the Charter and to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty and the security of its citizens and residents. As a member of the Security Council, Bahrain called on the Council to condemn the repeated attacks, shoulder its responsibilities, and take decisive measures to ensure Iran’s full compliance with Resolution 2817, halt its attacks and threats, and end its support for proxy groups in the region.

Subjective
Global 1 News — the intercepts, the resolution dated March 11, and Tehran’s own Article 51

Bahrain’s air defences fired in anger for the first time since September, and this time the kingdom’s own military is announcing the shootdowns while the American military, which denied Tehran’s last claim two days ago, says nothing. Iran says it sent six drones at an American radar at a helicopter base outside Manama; Bahrain says it stopped the attacks. There has been no confirmation from American or Bahraini authorities that the Al-Riffa installation was struck, and one agency noted there were no claims or details of the drones having caused damage. On November 13 the Guards said they had destroyed an American early-warning radar in Bahrain, retaliation for an air attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, in Iran’s southern Hormozgan province near the Strait of Hormuz. The Foreign Ministry denounced a resumption of Iran’s aggression, said the attacks violated international law, declared that no pretext can legitimise violations of state sovereignty, and added that Bahrain rejects the use of its territory to settle accounts and holds Iran fully responsible for the attacks and their consequences. The Security Council adopted Resolution 2817 on March 11, 2026, at its 10,119th meeting, by thirteen votes to none with China and Russia abstaining; Bahrain tabled it for the Gulf Cooperation Council and it drew 135 co-sponsors. The text condemned in the strongest terms Iranian attacks against Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan, and demanded Tehran immediately and unconditionally cease provocations against its neighbours, including through proxies; Bahrain has called for it to be fully implemented, and its ambassador to the United Nations is named in the account. Tehran’s Foreign Ministry did not treat Sunday as a violation of anything: its spokesman told a news conference that attacks on Iran’s neighbours were justified under Article 51 of the Charter, which sets out a state’s right to defend itself, and he accused the Gulf states of helping Washington strike his country.

Subjective
Sababu — Bahrain and Saudi Arabia condemn the continuing attacks, and the self-defence right restated

Bahrain has strongly condemned continuing Iranian drone attacks on its territory, calling them a violation of its sovereignty and a serious threat to the security of the entire region. In a statement issued on Sunday, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the country’s air defence systems intercepted and destroyed drones launched on Sunday, as well as two drones launched last Friday. The Guards have claimed responsibility for the attacks. Bahrain said the attacks were unacceptable and a direct violation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which called on Iran to stop its attacks on Bahrain and neighbouring countries. Recalling its full right to self-defence under Article 51 of the Charter, Bahrain called on the Security Council to condemn the Iranian attacks and take decisive measures. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also strongly condemned the attacks on Bahrain.

Subjective
LaPresse — the Kremlin: the European negotiators have not yet contacted Russia

Milan, November 15. The negotiators appointed by the European Union have not yet attempted to contact Russia, Kremlin spokesman Peskov stated, in response to a question on the matter from the TASS agency: “No, not yet.” At the informal European summit in Dublin, the Union’s heads of state and government opted for a format that includes the European institutions and the five countries—Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland—alongside the European Commission and the Council, to represent Europe in the negotiations on Ukraine.

Subjective
LaPresse — the Kremlin: without an agreement with Europe, Russia will have to use force

Milan, November 15. In the absence of a negotiated solution with Europe, Russia will have to achieve its objectives by force. This is what Kremlin spokesman Peskov said in an interview with a correspondent of Vesti, according to reports from the Russian agencies. Earlier, the spokesman had told TASS that the negotiators chosen by Europe had not yet attempted to establish contact with Russia.

Subjective
Sagire — the spokesman’s interview: no point in discussing a settlement if the Union does not want peace

Kremlin spokesman Peskov said Russia will have to use force to achieve its goals if there is no prospect of reaching agreements with Europe, in an interview with a Vesti correspondent. According to the spokesman, if the European Union does not want peace, there is no point in discussing a settlement to the Ukraine conflict or the European security framework. Earlier, the spokesman had said that the negotiators chosen by Europe had not yet approached Russia.

Subjective
Institute for the Study of War — the November 14 assessment: a membership proposal stated in Kyiv, a demands paper, and Europe’s inclusion argued

President Zelenskyy stated on November 14 that the American delegation at the November 10–11 peace talks in Abu Dhabi proposed that Ukraine gain NATO membership in exchange for a Ukrainian withdrawal from the entirety of the Donbas region. A newspaper reported on November 13 that it obtained a copy of an unofficial non-paper of demands that the Russian delegation circulated during the Abu Dhabi talks, representing Russia’s opening negotiating position, according to two sources involved in the talks; a German outlet similarly reported that Russian intermediaries presented a series of unofficial demands related to Ukraine, Europe and NATO to European representatives in Abu Dhabi. The United States continues to call for the inclusion of European delegations in upcoming multilateral negotiations: the White House’s Principal Deputy Press Secretary stated on November 13 that the American delegation at the recent trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi ensured that Europe will be included in future peace talks. A wire-service report of November 13, citing a senior European official, reported that European officials designated the national security advisers from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland and a representative of the Union to represent Europe in any future technical-level talks, and that Europe has not yet designated any European leaders to represent it. The assessment also records that the three presidents will meet at the November 18–19 APEC leaders’ meeting in China to discuss nuclear weapons proliferation and the situation in Iran, and will likely not discuss the war in Ukraine, according to the White House’s Assistant Press Secretary.

Subjective
CNN — the President to meet China’s and Russia’s leaders at a first trilateral sit-down on nuclear non-proliferation

The President will meet jointly next week with China’s leader and Russia’s President Putin, the White House said Friday, a first-ever trilateral sit-down between the leaders of the three countries. The meeting, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, will focus on nuclear non-proliferation, a topic the President has said he believes could yield a new agreement between the world’s biggest nuclear-armed states. The Kremlin says the meeting will take place on November 19 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, but there has been no confirmation yet from China. The last nuclear arms treaty between the United States and Russia expired in February.

Subjective
Particle News — the board accepts the resignation, an investigation under way, and the petition past 120,000 by Sunday

The board announced Thursday that Mr. Huang resigned as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect and that the executive vice president and chief financial officer, Ms. Colette Kress, will serve as interim chief executive. An online petition called Stand with Jensen surged to more than 120,000 signatures by Sunday; it was organized by current and former employees, partners and shareholders who demand Mr. Huang be reinstated during an independent investigation. The company has confirmed an independent investigation is under way but has not disclosed its scope, independence or timeline, and the company will still release its fiscal 2027 third-quarter results on November 17 at about 1:20 p.m. Pacific with a 2:00 p.m. Pacific earnings call.

Subjective
TradingView, carrying Benzinga — the counter at 135,468 at 0037 on Sunday, its categories unverified, and Mr. Musk signing

A petition urging the company to reinstate Mr. Huang as chief executive passed 135,000 signatures on Sunday, days after his resignation and ahead of the chipmaker’s third-quarter earnings report. The campaign site’s counter showed 135,468 signatures at 12:37 a.m. Eastern on Sunday. The site classified 6,776 signers as current employees, 1,267 as former employees and 73,181 as shareholders, though those affiliations have not been independently verified. The open letter asks the board to reinstate Mr. Huang while an independent investigation establishes the facts; it also seeks a fair hearing and a public explanation. The site says the company and Mr. Huang do not endorse it. On Friday, Tesla’s chief executive wrote on X that a petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and that he is signing it too. Mr. Huang resigned as president, chief executive and director on November 12, the company said in a press release; the chief financial officer, Ms. Colette Kress, is interim chief executive.

Subjective
BigGo Finance — nearly 130,000 by Saturday evening, three procedural demands, and the authenticity questioned

As of the evening of November 14, Eastern time, an online petition called Stand with Jensen had gathered nearly 130,000 signatures demanding that the board restore Mr. Huang as chief executive. The petition went live almost simultaneously with the announcement of the resignation on November 12; its organizers describe themselves as current and former employees and shareholders and state that they have no affiliation with the company. The open letter makes three requests, targeting procedural issues rather than defending Mr. Huang’s personal conduct: that he be reinstated before an independent investigation establishes the facts; that the scope, independence and timetable of the investigation be made public and that he be given a substantive opportunity to respond; and that if the board insists he must leave, it provide a specific, evidence-backed explanation. A Tesla chief executive’s post on X said he had signed the petition. The petition’s authenticity, however, has been called into question: because the website lacks real-name verification, the signatures are hard to verify, and a company vice president, Mr. Bryan Catanzaro, publicly clarified that he never signed, saying his name had been used without his consent. On November 12 the shares fell more than 14 percent intraday, briefly dropping below a $4 trillion market value before closing down 4.34 percent; measured from November 8, when the board announced the independent investigation, the stock fell 10.96 percent over four trading sessions, wiping out more than $480 billion in market value. The account also records the supply commitments in the filings and the data-center revenue shares of the last reported quarters.

Subjective
MarketAlleys — the daily brief of November 15: bitcoin at $64,830, breadth at 14 up and 18 down, and the week’s calendar

Bitcoin fell 2.97 percent over 24 hours to $64,830.00, and the SPY fund fell 0.36 percent from the prior close to $754.37; breadth among 32 tracked names was 14 up and 18 down. Over 24 hours ether fell 4.56 percent to $1,807.37, Solana 5.89 percent to $71.15 and XRP 2.90 percent. The five-session changes reported as of November 15, 0544 UTC, are bitcoin down 8.60 percent, ether down 9.04, Solana down 9.44 and XRP down 10.56. The week ahead carries twelve upcoming events, including four macro items and eight earnings releases: earnings before the open on Monday, November 16; retail sales on Tuesday, November 17; Home Depot earnings and Nvidia’s fiscal third-quarter earnings after the close on Tuesday; housing starts and permits on Wednesday, November 18; weekly jobless claims and a slate of before-the-open earnings on Thursday, November 19; and consumer sentiment on Friday, November 20. Nvidia’s earnings are listed with an estimate of 2.52 per share. Nvidia’s five-session change is given as minus 12.75 percent, Meta’s as plus 5.18 and Tesla’s as plus 8.93. Personal income and outlays and the gross domestic product are scheduled for Wednesday, November 25.

Subjective
CoinLab — bitcoin’s Sunday brief: a low of $62,006, $65,570 at 0845 and $64,770 at 1000

Sunday, November 15, 2026: the morning brief, released at 9:00 a.m. Eastern with the price at release $65,570, records that bitcoin traded near $65,500, down 1.6 percent on the day; overnight selling, while the United States slept, drove it to $62,006, the lowest since July, before buyers lifted it $3,500 off the low through the Asian and European sessions. The brief’s base case for the next 24 hours is a range of $63,800 to $66,800 with 50 percent probability, into tonight’s futures open and the Fed Chair’s remarks on Monday; a pullback and a breakout are priced at 28 and 22 percent. Leverage is recorded as already flushed, with $1.68 billion of long liquidations and open interest down 14 percent on the week. As of 10:00 a.m. Eastern, bitcoin trades at $64,770: down 1.7 percent over 24 hours, 13.5 over seven days and 20.6 over thirty days. The brief records the calendar: on November 16 the New York Fed President speaks at 9:05 a.m. Eastern and the Fed Chair around noon; on November 17 October retail sales come at 8:30 a.m. and the company reports after the close; the minutes come on November 18 at 2 p.m.; an offering prices on November 18 and starts trading on November 19. It records that on Friday the S&P 500 closed at 7,561.67, down 0.4 percent, and the Nasdaq at 25,136.27, down 0.9, both up 2.3 to 2.5 percent on the week, and that bitcoin fell roughly 8 percent more after Wall Street’s close and has only partly recovered.

Subjective
World Money Roadmap — Monday prep: the Reserve’s 87 percent, a three-month low recovered in part, and the search firm not yet engaged

The Federal Reserve said on November 13, 2026 that 87 percent of the market contacts it surveyed named artificial intelligence a major risk to the financial system, up from 50 percent in the spring and 30 percent a year earlier. Futures reopen at 6:00 p.m. Eastern on Sunday from a soft starting point: the Nasdaq 100 futures fell 1.23 percent on Friday and the S&P 500 futures 0.42. Bitcoin touched a three-month low on Saturday before recovering to about $65,700, and stands at $65,714.34 at 4:20 a.m. Eastern on Sunday in the account’s price feed. The account’s Monday-open checklist prices oil at the Friday WTI figure of $88.56 for the Sunday 1800 reopen, and the Asian opens: Tokyo and Seoul at 1900 Eastern, Shanghai and Hong Kong at 2030, with Japan’s third-quarter gross domestic product at 1850. Nvidia’s earnings date is unchanged: about 4:20 p.m. Eastern on Tuesday, with the call at 5:00 p.m.; consensus revenue is $108.9 billion by one compiler against the company outlook of $108.0 billion, and consensus earnings per share at 2.49 in the account’s table, against 2.52 in another calendar in the file. The board said on November 13 that it is choosing a search firm and has not formally engaged any potential candidates. The Guards said on November 15 that they sent drones at a helicopter base in Bahrain, and Bahrain issued its first nationwide alert in months.

Subjective
Lanka Leader, carrying AFP — more than 100,000 rally, a decline from last week, and Tuesday’s anniversary on the roundabouts

More than 100,000 people have taken to the streets in France in another round of cost-of-living rallies organised by the Yellow Vests and various youth movements. Saturday’s protests saw a decline in turnout compared with previous weekends and stayed largely calm, authorities said. The Interior Ministry reported that 106,000 people took part in protests nationwide, including 24,000 in Paris—down from 146,000 nationwide and 46,000 in Paris last week. The country has been gripped by high-school blockades, mass demonstrations and strikes for more than a month, with protesters rallying against falling educational standards, cost-of-living increases, low wages and police violence. Unions have called for a new day of strikes on Tuesday after rejecting a government promise to increase the minimum wage by 0.6 percent as crumbs. If the demonstrations go ahead, they will take place on the eighth anniversary of the Yellow Vest movement, which rocked the beginning of the Macron government in 2018 with two years of protests triggered by rising fuel prices. On Tuesday the Yellow Vests will celebrate their eight years where it all started: on roundabouts and toll booths all over France, a protest tracking site writes.

Subjective
Particle News — the fifth Saturday at 106,000, the police bill to the Senate, and a strike on Tuesday

The nationwide demonstrations ran for a fifth Saturday in a row on November 14 and the Interior Ministry put turnout at about 106,000 people, including roughly 24,000 in Paris, while organisers gave higher estimates. The movement now unites high-school students, trade unions, Yellow Vest activists and child-protection campaigners demanding better school conditions, higher pay and relief from the rising cost of living. At the centre of the protests is a bill passed by the lower house that would give officers a presumption of legitimate self-defence when they use firearms, a measure opponents call a licence to kill in the account’s words, that they say would weaken accountability. With the Senate vote pending and unions rejecting a 0.6 percent minimum-wage offer, the protests threaten to reshape law-and-order debates ahead of the 2027 presidential race, in the account’s reading, and raise the risk of further strikes and clashes next week. Senate consideration of the contested measure is set to follow union plans for a nationwide strike on Tuesday, November 17.

Subjective
Demócrata — the campaign’s opening, and the mean of sixteen institutes at November 15: 31.4, 26.9, 19.1, 6.3, 2.5

The President of the Government and candidate, Mr. Sánchez, gave the starting signal for the campaign for the general elections of November 29 in Seville, while the leader of the Popular Party, Mr. Feijóo, did so in Badalona in Catalonia, and the president of Vox, Mr. Abascal, and the candidates of Frente Amplio, Ms. Colau, and of another list, Ms. Montero, opted for Madrid. At midnight the campaign officially began, in which the heads of the lists will travel around the country requesting support at the ballot boxes through the usual rallies and election events across all Spain. The account’s table of the mean of the latest study from each institute over thirty days, dated November 15, 2026 and now across sixteen institutes, stands at Popular Party 31.4 percent, Socialists 26.9, Vox 19.1, Frente Amplio 6.3 and ERC 2.5.

entry.title: Bystander Intervention: What the Record Shows About Who Steps In, What Stops Them, and Why the Answer Changes by Place
entry.summary: What research shows about bystander intervention: who steps in, what stops them, and why the answer changes from one place to another.
entry.content:
Special Report

The Bystander Effect · The CCTV Record · The Capable Guardian · Collective Efficacy · The Duty to Rescue · Bystander CPR

Objective

Bystander Intervention: What the Record Shows About Who Steps In, What Stops Them, and Why the Answer Changes by Place

For half a century the standard account of bystanders came from a 1964 New York murder and a set of laboratory experiments: witnesses in a group, the account held, are less likely to help than a witness alone. The archival record has since dismantled the founding story—there is no evidence for the 38 witnesses of the original newspaper account—and camera footage of 219 real public conflicts in Lancaster, Amsterdam, and Cape Town shows at least one bystander intervening in 90.9 percent of cases, with each additional bystander raising the odds that a victim received help. What still suppresses action is narrower and more specific: ambiguity about whether an emergency is occurring, a telephone call nobody has been assigned to make, a camera raised in place of a hand, an assault read as a domestic dispute, and a weapon. Beneath the individual decision sit local structures—the capable guardian of routine activity theory, the collective efficacy measured block by block in Chicago, the informal codes that govern where police protection is not trusted—and beneath those, the law, which differs by jurisdiction: most American states impose no general duty to rescue, while France and Germany criminalize the failure to assist a person in danger. The record’s conclusion is geographic. Protection is a property of a place and its people, and a traveler carries none of it with him.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1045 ET, Sunday, November 15, 2026.

The question this report answers is the one a person in trouble is actually asking: if something happens to me here, in this street, in this city, will anyone step in—and what decides it? The research record, assembled over six decades, gives an answer that is more favorable than the famous story and more conditional than the reassurance. The famous story is the bystander effect, taught for fifty years as the finding that the presence of other witnesses makes each witness less likely to help. That finding is real in the laboratory conditions that produced it. But the murder that founded the field did not happen the way the newspapers reported it, and when researchers finally obtained camera footage of real public conflicts—219 of them, in three cities on three continents—they found intervention in nine cases out of ten, more bystanders producing more intervention, and interveners seldom harmed. The suppressors that survive scrutiny are specific: an event nobody can classify, a call nobody has been assigned, a fight read as a private matter, a weapon, and, in the medical case that has been measured most precisely, a rescuer’s fear of a lawsuit that has never once succeeded. Around those individual decisions stands the structure that decides most cases before they begin: whether the place has guardians, whether its residents trust one another enough to act for the common good, which informal code governs its public spaces, and what its law requires of a witness. Every one of those terms is local. That is the finding the rest of this report documents, study by study and statute by statute.

The founding story, and what the record did to it

The story as printed. On March 13, 1964, Catherine “Kitty” Genovese was murdered outside her apartment building in Kew Gardens, Queens. Two weeks later the New York Times reported that 38 respectable, law-abiding citizens had watched the killer stalk and stab her in three separate attacks over more than half an hour, and that none had called the police until after she was dead. The story became the founding parable of a research field and a fixture of textbooks: a crowd of witnesses, each waiting for another to act, a woman dead of their collective indifference.

The story as documented. In 2007, Rachel Manning, Mark Levine, and Alan Collins re-examined the case in the American Psychologist under the title “The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping: The parable of the 38 witnesses.” Their archival review found no evidence for the 38 witnesses, no evidence that witnesses observed the murder as reported, and no evidence that witnesses remained inactive. The two attacks occurred in different locations, the second in an enclosed stairwell visible to almost no one; most of those who heard anything heard noises they could not classify. The Assistant District Attorney who prosecuted the case found only about six eyewitnesses usable at trial. One witness shouted from a window during the first attack and drove the attacker off. The Times itself later acknowledged that its 1964 account had grossly exaggerated the number of witnesses and what they had perceived. The parable, the reviewers concluded, survives as a parable—a teaching story whose evidentiary base does not support it.

The laboratory finding stands, in its limits. The experiments the murder prompted were real and their result has been replicated. In John Darley and Bibb Latané’s 1968 seizure study, participants who believed they were the only witness to a fellow participant’s seizure sought help 85 percent of the time; those who believed one other person was present helped 62 percent of the time; those who believed four others were present helped 31 percent of the time. The mechanism they named—diffusion of responsibility, each witness’s obligation diluted across the group—is a genuine property of the situations they built: ambiguous events, strangers who cannot see one another, and no way to know whether anyone else has acted. A 2011 meta-analysis by Peter Fischer and colleagues, covering 105 effect sizes and more than 7,700 participants in the Psychological Bulletin, put the overall effect at g = −0.35 and found it attenuated precisely where the laboratory’s conditions break down: in dangerous emergencies, when a perpetrator is present, and when the costs of intervening are physical. The clearer and graver the emergency, the weaker the effect.

What the cameras show

The CCTV record. In 2020, Richard Philpot, Lasse Liebst, Mark Levine, Wim Bernasco, and Marie Lindegaard published in the American Psychologist the first cross-national analysis of bystander behavior in real public conflicts, coded from police and municipal camera footage: 219 conflicts—95 in Lancaster, England, 63 in Amsterdam, and 61 in Cape Town. At least one bystander intervened in 90.9 percent of the conflicts. Intervention was usually plural: the average conflict drew 3.76 interveners. Each additional bystander present raised the odds that the victim received help by roughly 10 percent—the reverse of the laboratory prediction at the level of the event, which is the level at which a victim experiences it. Intervention was defined broadly, as the record of a camera allows: stepping between the parties, pulling an aggressor away, a calming gesture or touch, consoling the victim. The footage carried no audio, so purely verbal interventions went uncounted; the 90.9 percent is, on that account, a floor. The three cities differ sharply in their levels of street violence, and the researchers found no significant difference in intervention rates among them.

The risk to the intervener, measured. A companion study by Liebst and colleagues, published in Psychology of Violence in 2021, examined 93 of the recordings and the 417 interveners they contained, and coded what happened to the people who stepped in. Interveners were physically harmed in 3.6 percent of cases—12 of the 337 who intervened purely to de-escalate. Non-interveners were virtually never harmed: 0.2 percent, one of 602. The severity of the conflict at the moment of intervention did not increase the intervener’s risk. The measured picture is neither of the two popular ones: stepping in is not free of risk, and it is not the near-certain injury of the cautionary tale. It is a small, quantifiable risk, run mostly by people who de-escalate rather than fight.

The model the cameras revised. The popular training literature of the same decades organized the public into three kinds of people. The frame is Lt. Col. Dave Grossman’s, set out in the essay “On Sheep, Wolves, and Sheepdogs” in On Combat (2004), with roots in his On Killing (1995): the sheep, ordinary people not capable of hurting one another except by accident or under extreme provocation; the wolves, who prey on them; and the sheepdogs—soldiers, police, and armed citizens who make the moral choice to protect—who stand between. The essay circulated widely through American police and civilian firearms training; businesses in at least nine states trade under the sheepdog name, and the frame reached its largest audience in the 2014 film American Sniper, whose father delivers the three-types speech at the family dinner table. As a description of what cameras record, the typology does not survive the footage: in the 219 conflicts, the interveners were not a distinct protective caste but the ordinary bystanders themselves, several per incident, most of them unarmed and most of them calming rather than fighting. The desk files the frame as what the record shows it to be—the most successful piece of bystander folk theory of its era, and a publishing phenomenon the CCTV data has overtaken.

What still stops people

Ambiguity is the first gate. Before responsibility can diffuse, an event must be classified as an emergency, and classification is where the record shows most failures begin. A scream may be an attack or an argument; a man slumped in a doorway may be dying or sleeping. Darley and Latané’s own model made interpretation the second step of five, ahead of responsibility, and their subjects in group conditions looked to one another’s calm faces for the classification—pluralistic ignorance, each witness privately alarmed and publicly composed, each reading the others’ composure as evidence that nothing is wrong. The remedy the training literature converged on follows directly from the mechanism: a specific appeal to a specific person—the assigned task, “you, call 911”—which destroys the ambiguity and the diffusion in one sentence. The unspecific scream leaves both intact.

Diffusion survives on the telephone. The camera studies count physical intervention, which is visible. The act that remains most subject to diffusion is the one the cameras cannot see: the call for help, which each witness can assume another has made. The Genovese parable, stripped of its false witness count, reduces to this residue—a call delayed because no one person owned it. Modern dispatch records and the intervention literature treat the assigned call as the standard countermeasure for the same reason.
