entry.title: No Such Thing As Monday Is the Book of the Week, Scrooge Splits the Critics in Half, and the Empress Takes Her Leave
entry.summary: The review of reviews for November 15, 2026: Siân Hughes's No Such Thing As Monday leads the fiction tally, and Scrooge splits the critics in half.
entry.content:
Weekend Features — Sunday Review of Reviews

Objective

No Such Thing As Monday Is the Book of the Week, Scrooge Splits the Critics in Half, and the Empress Takes Her Leave

The week's review lists were tallied, and the tally gave the desk a divided week. The book du jour is No Such Thing As Monday by Siân Hughes, published in the United States on November 10: first in the week's fiction tally with five rave reviews, two positive and one mixed, taken by its reviewers to be the life of Steffie Cartwright of working-class Birmingham—a woman who finds her father dead in his chair, removes stains at a dry cleaner's, and goes looking for the sister who ran away from home at 16. On screen the week belonged to division: Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol, Ti West's telling of Dickens with Johnny Depp as Scrooge, opened November 13 with the critics split at 50 to 53 percent and the argument fixed on its leading man, while its ghosts and its design drew agreement from both camps; and The Empress, the German serial on Netflix, closed its third and final season with verdicts running from masterpiece to 3.5 of 10. A lone capsule, labeled Worth Watching, files John Wilson's documentary feature The History of Concrete. The desk states its position plainly at the head of each part: it has not read the book, and it has not watched the serial, the films, or the documentary. What follows is a review of reviews.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0410 ET, Sunday, November 15, 2026. The second Sunday Review of Reviews of this paper, filed under the Weekend Features ruling of November 4, 2026. The desk tallied the week's review lists—the New York Times Book Review and its peers, the Chicago Review of Books, the Washington reviewing tradition carried in Ron Charles's Tuesday Review, the Guardian, and the aggregating tally at Book Marks—and the week's film and television reviews, international by house rule. The clippings the report was drawn from are filed beneath it, each stamped subjective.

The Week in Brief: The Tally

In fiction, one book stood at the head of the list, and the list beneath it was crowded with clean verdicts. Book Marks' tally of the week, published November 13, ranks No Such Thing As Monday first with five rave reviews, two positive and one mixed. Behind it: Xita Rubert's The Key Biscayne Affair, three rave and two positive; Annie Proulx Stories: New & Selected, four rave and no other verdict recorded; Niall Williams's O Now!, three rave and one positive; and Gabriel Bump's Don't Stop Snowing, one rave and four positive. In nonfiction the tally's order and its arithmetic part company, and the desk prints both as filed: The Telephone: A New History by James Gleick stands first with four rave and three positive, while Nick Paumgarten's The Intangibles stands second with five rave and one positive—more raves, one place lower. Lauren Elkin's Vocal Break and Nancy Isenberg's Aristocracy, American Style share third at three rave and two positive each, and Mona Chalabi's Ten Lives closes the list at one rave and three positive.

The week's five selected single reviews point at a different shelf, and the desk files the difference. The quintet chosen this week—Hillary Kelly in The Atlantic on M. John Harrison's The End of Everything, Merve Emre in The New Yorker on Tom Overton's John Berger, Ed Park on Cleo Birdwell's Amazons, Ryan Ruby in Bookforum on Emily Ogden's Darkness Becomes Bright, and Josef Burton on Akbar Shahid Ahmed's Crossing the Red Line—contains no review of the book at the head of the tally. Last week the book du jour stood in both lists at once. This week it stands on the tally alone: eight reviews counted, seven of them favorable, from the papers and journals the tally tracks. The desk takes the tally as the week's verdict and the selected five as the week's reading, and prints the book the tally chose.

Part One — The Book: No Such Thing As Monday, by Siân Hughes

The desk has not read this book. It says so plainly, as the house rule requires: everything in this part is what the reviewers report, agree on, and dispute, and nothing in it is the desk's reading. No Such Thing As Monday is a novel. Siân Hughes is a British writer who began as a poet; her novel Pearl, published in 2023 and longlisted for the Booker Prize, was written in response to the medieval poem of the same name. This book was published in the United States by Henry Holt and Company on November 10, 2026: 224 pages, $26.99, ISBN 9781250459572.

On what the book is, the reviewers agree completely, and their agreement is the week's firmest fact. Stephanie Cartwright—Steffie—is a chain-smoking, prickly woman in middle age who works at a dry cleaner's in contemporary working-class England and tends to her father. The novel opens with Steffie finding that father, Stan, dead in his favorite chair. Stan dominated her childhood near Birmingham in the 1970s and 1980s: a violent bully who ran dogfights at the local pub, whose wife died before him, and whose favorite Steffie always was—a favoritism that left her carrying guilt for her older sister, Caroline, who fled home at 16 and has not been seen since. With Stan dead, Steffie sets out to find Caroline. The reviewers describe the same construction from every side: a life told in episodes across childhood to middle age, in no straight order, each chapter standing nearly on its own—in the Chicago Review of Books' account, each chapter a set of pages in a photo album, the picture widening as the album fills. And every reviewer who addresses the book's machinery names the same source under it: the medieval poem called Cleanness, or Purity, from the same 14th-century manuscript that holds Pearl and Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, which gives the novel its governing figure of the stain—the laundry Steffie cleans by day, and the past she cannot clean at all.

On what the book is taken to be, the reviewers also agree, in their own words, filed below. Leah Greenblatt of the New York Times calls it fractious and darkly funny: an ouroboros of ongoing traumas that somehow manages not to be head-smashingly bleak, because Steffie on the page is a pretty great hang—spiky, sharp-witted, blazingly self-aware—and because Hughes has a canny, lyrical ear for her misfits and underdogs, and a touch tender enough to nudge their fate toward better things. Kirkus, in its starred notice, credits an alchemy like Douglas Stuart's: Hughes transforms the dross of Steffie's life into literary gold. The Chicago Review of Books calls Steffie compelling—not always likeable, and certainly never unlikeable—and the novel a powerful story that unveils itself with every page. The Bookreporter review reaches the same resting place from the record of the plot: a profoundly sad novel, and a surprisingly hopeful one, whose message is that it is never too late to gain perspective, to make amends, or to try to start anew. The publisher's record places the book in the working-class British realist tradition of Douglas Stuart and Andrea Arnold, and the trade notices filed with it name Hughes an exceptional and compassionate chronicler of precarious and chaotic lives.

The split in the file is about the comedy, and how far it reaches into the childhood chapters. The Times of London, in the coolest review the week filed, grants the premise its full force—humour is how Steffie copes with loss, and how the reader copes with an otherwise harrowing tale of penury and hurt—and then records a falling off: as the novel dives into Steffie's violent childhood in the West Midlands, the dark comedy recedes, and Hughes could have gone further and funnier to wring the last drop of absurdity from each scene. Where the author excels, in that review's judgment, is in meandering through the slippages of memory to reveal what is gnawing at her narrator. Its verdict is measured: a decent follow-up to Pearl, even if by design it seems to position itself as the lesser work—a book that, like Steffie, cannot escape the taint of disappointment. The desk files the disagreement as it stands. Seven of the tally's eight counted verdicts are favorable, and the favorable reviews praise the humour as the book's engine; the one cool review praises the memory work and asks for more of the humour. No reviewer in the week's file faults the sentences, and no reviewer disputes Steffie herself.

Where to get it. No Such Thing As Monday by Siân Hughes is available at Amazon. As an Amazon Associate, Objective Daily News earns from qualifying purchases made through that link.

Part Two — Screen: Scrooge, Split in Half, and the Empress Takes Her Leave

The desk has not watched any of the screen works in this part. It has not streamed The Empress, and it has not sat in a cinema for Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol or How to Rob a Bank. Their status here is the same as the book's: the reviews, reviewed.

The television pick of the week is The Empress, and it is German, and it is finished. The third and final season of the serial—Die Kaiserin in its own language, on Netflix—was released on November 12. The story it closes is the story the serial has told since 2022: Elisabeth of Austria, played by Devrim Lingnau Islamoğlu, the Bavarian duke's daughter who married Emperor Franz Joseph, played by Philip Froissant, for love and spent her reign fighting the walls of the Viennese court. The final season opens a few months after the second season's close, with Franz returned from commanding his army at the front, a changed, cold and distant man, and the imperial marriage on shaky ground; it carries the story through to the establishment of the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy. On the measure that is not a review, the serial's standing is a matter of record: its first season in September 2022 became, in the reports filed below, Netflix's second-most-watched series globally on its debut, and it stands in those reports as the service's most successful German original since Barbarians.

The reviewers agree on the season's materials, and on the bargain its ending strikes. Every review in the file records a darker and more politically tangled season; every review credits the same visible strengths—the chemistry of the two leads, the costumes, in the Absolute Geeks account the work of costume designer Gabriela Reumer standing among the best in streaming period drama, and production design that no reviewer faults. And every review that reaches the ending describes the same transaction: the finale blends fiction and fact, chooses the fairytale the serial has always carried over the history book, and leaves the harrowing later record of Elisabeth's life—the loss of her son Rudolf among it—outside the frame, her assassination handled, in one account, as onscreen text before the credits. The ending turns the founding of the dual monarchy into a fresh start for the marriage, grounded in the understanding that this empress needs the freedom to be herself.

The split is about whether that bargain is the season's achievement or its evasion, and the file runs the full width of the scale. At one end, ScreenRant's November 14 account calls the third season a true masterpiece and the serial a show with no bad season, each installment better than the last. Collider calls the ending a satisfying, poignant conclusion for one of Netflix's best hidden gems, and Absolute Geeks, at four of five, calls the season a strong, confident farewell that sticks the landing where it counts—while recording, in the same review, a rushed and underdeveloped Hungarian subplot and a life-changing relationship with Count Andrássy given too little room. At the other end stands the Midgard Times review, at 3.5 of 10: a rushed finale that turns history into bullet points, a season that never allows any moment, scene, feeling or action to linger, speedrunning its material until investment fails—filed by a reviewer who holds that the serial peaked in a first season that was itself not all that good. Between the poles, the audience record filed on IMDb runs warm: breathtaking, heart-wrenching, viewers who waited two years and binged the season in one go. The desk files the whole width: the materials are agreed, the farewell is contested, and the contest is between a romance that has earned its ending and a history that was owed more time.

In cinemas, the week's film is Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol, and its reviewers agree on its ghosts and divide on its Scrooge. The film opened November 13, directed by Ti West and written by Nathaniel Halpern, rated PG-13 and running 116 minutes, with Johnny Depp as Scrooge in his first studio lead in eight years, Ian McKellen as Jacob Marley, Tramell Tillman, Andrea Riseborough and Daisy Ridley as the three ghosts, and Rupert Grint as Bob Cratchit. The agreement in the file is exact: the production design and the photography—Eve Stewart's design and Checco Varese's dark, fogged London, credited by name in reviews that agree on little else—and the ghost work above all, Tillman's Ghost of Christmas Present named the film's diamond in TheWrap's account and the spirits given layers, in Empire's, that outclass the picture around them. The Rotten Tomatoes consensus, as the service prints it, holds the same two facts in one sentence: evocative production design, a Depp filled with the bah-humbug spirit, and a telling that plays too safe among its long line of remakes. The division is the lead. The Daily Telegraph's Robbie Collin gave the film four of five; the Guardian's Peter Bradshaw found Depp in fact rather good; Deadline recorded a man having a blast, and The Hollywood Reporter a creepily effective comeback vehicle. Against them: the Boston Globe's Odie Henderson, at one of four, called Depp easily the worst Scrooge he had ever seen; IndieWire's David Ehrlich found him unengaging in a film named for his character; the Associated Press, at one of four, called the whole a horror-tinged holiday slog. The counts print the division without ornament: 35 fresh and 34 rotten in one count of 69, and an audience mark, when it posted, of 89 percent against the critics' half.

The week's second film is filed in one paragraph, because its split runs between the critics and the audience rather than through either camp. How to Rob a Bank, David Leitch's heist picture, opened November 13: Nicholas Hoult leads a Pittsburgh crew that livestreams its bank robberies, with John C. Reilly as the veteran FBI agent on the digital trail, and Zoë Kravitz, Pete Davidson and Anna Sawai in the cast; it runs 122 minutes and is rated R. The critics' count stands at 31 to 33 percent across the weekend's tallies—the lowest mark of Leitch's career, in more than one account—under a consensus that calls it frenetic entertainment whose ideas never cohere into a satisfying message; the A.V. Club, at C+, found two or three movies smashed together, and Time Out, at three of five, found a fun, throwaway action-thriller. Verified audiences scored it 77 to 80 percent in the same counts, a gap of more than 45 points, with a B-minus CinemaScore between the two. The desk has not seen either film; it files the week's cinema record as two splits of different shapes—one film divided against itself at its centre, one divided between the people who review films and the people who bought tickets.

Worth Watching — The History of Concrete

The desk has not screened this film. The publisher has, and the publisher is the source of this item; it stands here on his tip, treated by the house method. The History of Concrete is John Wilson's documentary feature—his directorial debut in the form, after his HBO series How To with John Wilson—premiered at Sundance on January 22, 2026 and released by Magnolia Pictures on September 18, 2026, at 100 minutes in the reviews' count. It was reviewed by the New York Times, Time, and IndieWire, among others. The record the reviews converge on is this: a deadpan inquiry into concrete—its Roman endurance, its American crumbling, the oldest concrete street in the country at Bellefontaine, Ohio, a Brooklyn-Queens Expressway described to Wilson as a ticking time bomb—turns, in its final movement, into a portrait of Jack Macco, a Long Island rock musician Wilson meets handing out liquor samples, and of Macco's late fiancée Dorothy Chin Brandt, the first female Asian American judge in New York State, who died on January 27, 2025, at 78. On the film around that turn, the file agrees in its parts: IndieWire's David Ehrlich calls it consistently hilarious and sneakily profound, sustained by a tension between order and entropy—concrete as the material men scratch their names into as a bid for immortality, and use to build the burial vaults that hold them after. The New York Times' Alissa Wilkinson, in the praise carried with the film, records being left wondering how a movie about concrete could leave a lump in the throat; the Guardian's Adrian Horton calls it consistently laugh-out-loud funny, compelling and surprising; the New Yorker's Richard Brody finds it rich in an authentic sense of discovery, and pointedly, urgently political. RogerEbert.com's account files the reservation the favorable reviews concede in passing: the film is in substance a long episode of the HBO series, and the history of its title takes up only a small portion of its running time—and a college review filed November 13 files the cooler edge, a narration and a comic persona that reviewer found an acquired taste. The film took the Best Narration prize at the Critics Choice Documentary Awards, in the November 14 account filed below. The peg on this paper is plain: Friday's Special Report, Concrete: What the Record Shows About the Most Consumed Material on Earth (November 13), covers the material; this item covers the film.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, Scrooge's score: Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol stands at 51 percent from 59 reviews in its opening count, 50 percent from 70 in a second, 51 percent from 111 in the Friday weekend guide, and 53 percent from 116 in the count taken November 14, with Metacritic at 46 in one listing and 47 in another—a film whose measure moves because the review file is still arriving, printed here as a moving measure. Ehrlich's IndieWire grade likewise stands at C-minus in one roundup and C-plus in another; the desk prints both and adopts neither. Second, the Empress's war: Collider places Franz at the front lines of the Sardinian War, while the British reports describe his return from a war against Napoleon, and from conflict with Napoleon; the desk prints the attributions as filed. Third, the book's count: The Times calls No Such Thing As Monday Hughes's second novel, and the Chicago Review of Books calls it her third book; Hughes's bibliography carries a poetry collection ahead of the novels, and the desk prints both counts as their papers filed them. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts are single-valued: No Such Thing As Monday was published in the United States on November 10, 2026, by Henry Holt, at 224 pages and $26.99, and stands first in the week's fiction tally; the third and final season of The Empress was released on Netflix on November 12; Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol and How to Rob a Bank both opened on November 13; and The History of Concrete premiered at Sundance on January 22, 2026, and was released by Magnolia Pictures on September 18, 2026. The desk has not read the book and has not watched the screen works. The log proceeds to Sunday's watches.

The Clippings Filed With This Feature

Everything the desk read for the feature above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk's feature is the only item in this file stamped objective. 19 items.

Subjective
Book Marks — the best reviewed books of the week, November 13, 2026

Book Marks tallies the week's reviews and ranks No Such Thing As Monday by Siân Hughes first in fiction with five rave reviews, two positive and one mixed; Xita Rubert's The Key Biscayne Affair follows at three rave and two positive, and Annie Proulx Stories stands third at four rave. In nonfiction, James Gleick's The Telephone stands first at four rave and three positive, ahead of Nick Paumgarten's The Intangibles at five rave and one positive; Lauren Elkin's Vocal Break and Nancy Isenberg's Aristocracy, American Style share third, and Mona Chalabi's Ten Lives closes the list. The tally quotes Leah Greenblatt of the New York Times on Hughes, Alexandra Jacobs of the New York Times on Gleick, and Fiona Sturges of the Guardian on Elkin.

Subjective
Literary Hub — five book reviews you need to read this week, November 12, 2026

The week's selected quintet: Hillary Kelly in The Atlantic on M. John Harrison's The End of Everything, Merve Emre in The New Yorker on Tom Overton's John Berger, Ed Park on Cleo Birdwell's Amazons, Ryan Ruby in Bookforum on Emily Ogden's Darkness Becomes Bright, and Josef Burton on Akbar Shahid Ahmed's Crossing the Red Line. No review of the week's tally-leading novel stands among the five.

Subjective
Chicago Review of Books — No Such Thing As Monday is a photo album of one woman's trauma and triumphs

The Chicago review, published November 11, takes Hughes's book—which it calls her third—as the lifetime of Stephanie, called Steffie: childhood to middle age against the background of England, carrying abandonment, familial guilt, favoritism and poverty. Steffie is hard-headed and hilarious, compelling, not always likeable and never unlikeable; the novel unveils itself slowly and with intention, its chapter titles foreshadowing what comes, each chapter a set of pages in a photo album that feels complete by the end. The review lists the book from Henry Holt and Company, published November 10, 2026.

Subjective
The Times — a gritty modern black comedy inspired by a medieval poem

The Times review of what it calls Hughes's tragicomic second novel: Steffie, a woman working in a dry cleaner's, cannot escape the taint of her past; the novel opens as she finds her father Stan dead in his chair. Humour is how Steffie copes, and how the reader copes with a harrowing tale of penury and hurt; as the book dives into her violent childhood in the 1970s and 1980s in the West Midlands, the dark comedy recedes, and Hughes could have gone further and funnier. Where she excels is in meandering through the slippages of memory. The title derives from Steffie's account of manipulation and her estrangement from her sister Caroline, and the book's extended metaphor of dirty laundry comes from the medieval poem called Purity or Cleanness. The verdict: a decent follow-up to Pearl, positioning itself as the lesser work.

Subjective
Kirkus Reviews — No Such Thing As Monday

Kirkus, in the notice posted September 14, 2026, records the book's facts—Henry Holt, publication November 10, 2026, 224 pages, ISBN 9781250459572—and its verdict in one line: with an alchemy like Douglas Stuart's, Hughes transforms the dross of Steffie's life into literary gold.

Subjective
Shelf Awareness — review of No Such Thing As Monday, August 28, 2026

Shelf Awareness lists the book at $26.99 in hardcover, 224 pages, ISBN 9781250459572, from Holt, November 10, 2026, and reviews it as a poignant, darkly satirical story inspired by a medieval poem called Cleanness: Steffie Cartwright, who expertly removes laundry stains at the dry cleaner's where she works, cannot erase the memories of her blemished past; she grew up near Birmingham under a violent bully of a father who ran dogfights at the local pub, and with Stan dead she reckons with shame and guilt over her sister Caroline, who ran away in her teens.

Subjective
Macmillan — No Such Thing as Monday, the publisher's record

The publisher's page records the book as a novel by Siân Hughes, Henry Holt and Company, on sale November 10, 2026, 224 pages, ISBN 9781250459572, and describes it in its own copy: from a Booker Prize-longlisted author, a woman tries to overcome her abusive past and find her estranged sister, in a deeply moving and darkly humorous quest for redemption, written in the working-class British realist tradition of Douglas Stuart and Andrea Arnold.

Subjective
Collider — The Empress delivers a satisfying ending for one of Netflix's best hidden gems

Collider's review, published November 12, takes the German period drama as one of Netflix's most underrated gems: the third and final season turns darker and more tense, opening months after Franz left to command his army on the front lines of the Sardinian War. Its ending fudges history in the name of love, glossing the harrowing events of Elisabeth's later life and turning the establishment of the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy into a fresh start for Franz and Elisabeth; not truthful, the review holds, and a satisfying, poignant conclusion all the same, with the chemistry of its leads grounding the geopolitics and the Andrássy relationship rushed.

Subjective
Midgard Times — The Empress season 3: a rushed finale that turns history into bullet points

The Midgard Times review, published November 13 and scored 3.5 of 10, holds that the third and final season never allows any moment, scene, feeling or action to linger, speedrunning its material until investment fails; that the serial peaked in a first season that was not all that good; and that its creator's one guiding instinct in the final season was to wrap everything up because no fourth season follows. It records Franz returning from the war a changed, cold and distant man, and Maximilian becoming Mexico's ruler.

Subjective
Absolute Geeks — The Empress season 3: Netflix's hidden gem finally gets its happy ending

Absolute Geeks scores the final season four of five: a darker, politically charged farewell anchored by superb chemistry and gorgeous production design, with Gabriela Reumer's costumes among the best work in streaming period drama, and Devrim Lingnau Islamoğlu radiant as an empress tasting freedom. A rushed Hungarian subplot and loose history hold it back; the finale is more fairytale than biography, sidestepping the tragedy of her son Rudolf and handling her assassination as onscreen text, and as the ending of the story the serial has told, it is bittersweet, earned and genuinely lovely.

Subjective
ScreenRant — The Empress: hands down Netflix's best historical drama

ScreenRant's November 14 account calls the German original a beautiful, intriguing series in the line of The Crown and Bridgerton, with no bad season: the first installment earned an 85 percent audience score and the second a nearly perfect 92 percent, and the third and final season, now streaming, it calls a true masterpiece, its empress grown and weary and doing what she does best—whatever she wants—with something to say about mental health, women's rights and autonomy.

Subjective
Rotten Tomatoes — Ebenezer (2026)

The Rotten Tomatoes page for Ebenezer records the film's facts—director Ti West, screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern, distributor Paramount Pictures, rated PG-13 for frightening material, released in theaters November 13, 2026—and its consensus: decking its halls with evocative production design while Johnny Depp is filled with the bah-humbug spirit, Ebenezer does not scrooge Dickens's classic tale up, and plays things too safe to stand out among its long line of remakes. The page carries a three-of-four review holding that Depp is terrific as Scrooge and that West brings the right amount of creep factor to the holiday classic.

Subjective
CBR — Johnny Depp's new dark fantasy film is already very polarizing

CBR, published November 12, records the film at 50 percent on Rotten Tomatoes on its opening—as many critics praising it as calling it bad. It files Andrea Chase of Killer Movie Reviews, for whom West lets the audience experience the story as if for the first time, evoking the horror Dickens intended, and Louisa Moore of Screen Zealots, for whom West gives the tale a spooky, terrifying makeover without losing its heart; against them, Elliott Collins of Movie Files, for whom the horror never goes far enough, Depp's eccentricity adds little, and the redemption feels unearned, and CBR's own Chris La Vigna at five of ten, for whom it falls flat in the end.

Subjective
Weekend guide, November 13 to 15, 2026 — Ebenezer's reviews are in, and they're split

A weekend viewing guide verified November 13 records Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol at 51 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 111 reviews, its number still moving, with audiences happier in early exit polls at about four and a half stars; the film took $1.5 million in Thursday previews and was expected to open at about $20 million, enough for first place. The same guide records How to Rob a Bank, David Leitch's heist comedy with Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz and Pete Davidson, at 31 percent from 77 reviews, off $900,000 in previews and headed for a single-digit-millions weekend.

Subjective
MovieWeb — How to Rob a Bank scores big with audiences on Rotten Tomatoes

MovieWeb, published November 14, records How to Rob a Bank at 33 percent from the critics—the worst Tomatometer score of David Leitch's career—against an 80 percent Popcornmeter from verified audiences averaging four of five stars, a gap of 47 points; its consensus calls the film frenetic entertainment with a lot on its mind that cannot make its ideas cohere. The film, 122 minutes and rated R, follows Nicholas Hoult's Pittsburgh crew livestreaming its robberies while John C. Reilly's FBI agent and Zoë Kravitz's software engineer work the digital trail; it took $900,000 in previews, carries a B-minus CinemaScore, and is projected toward a modest opening on a reported budget of $40 to $60 million.

Subjective
IndieWire, via Letterboxd — David Ehrlich on The History of Concrete

David Ehrlich's review, published on Letterboxd January 23, 2026 and continuing on IndieWire, records what John Wilson thinks about when he thinks about concrete: DMX, Hallmark movies, Kim Kardashian, a trailblazing Asian American judge, the world's first 3D-printed Starbucks, and a 3,100-mile footrace honoring a dead Brooklyn cult leader. He calls Wilson a sweetly Dantean scavenger who collages a broken existence back together from first-person video snippets and unpredictable detours, and the film consistently hilarious and sneakily profound, sustained by an internal tension between order and entropy across its 100 minutes—its making and its funding folded into the material itself.

Subjective
RogerEbert.com — The History of Concrete: John Wilson stuns with rock-solid comic observations

The RogerEbert.com review, published September 18, 2026, takes Wilson's feature as in substance a long episode of his HBO series, with proportionately more of his personality and private life: the history of concrete of its title takes up only a small portion of the movie, the first twelve minutes recap the director's life after his show ended, and the film leaps from his personal life to those of his interview subjects, friends and acquaintances in the Wikipedia rabbit-hole manner of the series.

Subjective
In Review Online — The History of Concrete, John Wilson

In Review Online, in the review republished September 18, records the film's facts—director John Wilson, distributor Magnolia Pictures, in theaters September 18, running time one hour 41 minutes—and its reading: Wilson, at a creative and psychic standstill after his series ended in 2023, dives down multiple simultaneous rabbit holes, from a Hallmark movie studio to urban gentrification to the rapper DMX, and finds in Jack, a liquor sales rep fronting a struggling rock band, a late tragedy that throws the whole relationship into relief. For Wilson, in this account, concrete is the ultimate binder and a manifestation of entropy and impermanence, and the film is a tremendous ode to hope and kindness in the face of inevitable collapse.

Subjective
Vancouver International Film Festival — The History of Concrete, with the praise filed with the film

The festival page for the film describes Wilson applying the best practices of a Hallmark pitching workshop to his documentary about concrete, and assembling low-resolution vérité vignettes into collages that complement his deadpan philosophising. It carries the praise filed with the film: Richard Brody of the New Yorker, for whom concrete turns out remarkably, pointedly, urgently political, and the film rich in an authentic sense of discovery; Adrian Horton of the Guardian, consistently laugh-out-loud funny, compelling and surprising; and Alissa Wilkinson of the New York Times, left wondering how a movie about concrete could leave a lump in the throat.

entry.title: Sunday Opens With 875 of Its Flights Already Cancelled and a Promise Due by Its Close, Alaska's Count Reaches 140,637 to 129,424 With the Race Still Uncalled, and Manama Issues Its First Nationwide Alert Since September While Europe's Negotiators Have Not Yet Contacted Moscow
entry.summary: Sunday opens with 875 flights already cancelled and a promise due by its close, and Alaska's count reaches 140,637 to 129,424.
entry.content:
The Night File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Sunday Opens With 875 of Its Flights Already Cancelled and a Promise Due by Its Close, Alaska’s Count Reaches 140,637 to 129,424 With the Race Still Uncalled, and Manama Issues Its First Nationwide Alert Since September While Europe’s Negotiators Have Not Yet Contacted Moscow

The night file: a recovery day that closed above 6,400 cancellations and handed Sunday 875 of its own before the day began; a Senate count that gained its raw numbers at last and stayed uncalled; a Gulf capital that spoke, in the form of an alert to its own residents; a European team that has not yet picked up the telephone, in the Kremlin spokesman’s two words; and a petition past 115,000 signatures waiting on a board that has not answered it in the file.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Sunday, November 15, 2026. This edition continues the file from Edition No. 48, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, from Edition No. 47, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Saturday, from Edition No. 46, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Saturday, and from Edition No. 44, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Saturday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the overnight figures differ from the earlier figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Night in Brief: A Promise Due Today, a Count With Its Numbers, and an Alert From Manama

The night’s three movements are a deadline arriving, a count completing its arithmetic, and a silence ending: Sunday opens with 875 of its flights already cancelled at the last count of Saturday night, against the promise of full schedule integrity by Sunday’s close, so the recovery that began on Friday evening is graded today; Alaska’s latest report, timestamped 1515 on Saturday, puts Ms. Peltola at 140,637 votes to Senator Sullivan’s 129,424, a lead of 11,213, at 49.94 percent with write-ins counted and about 97 percent of the expected vote in, with the race still uncalled and the tabulation on November 18; and Bahrain’s Interior Ministry issued a nationwide alert on November 15 urging citizens and residents to proceed to the nearest safe location, the first word from Manama in a file that has carried two other capitals’ accounts of Bahrain for three days. The Sunday flight figure stands in the wire account of the Saturday briefing filed below, timed at 2135 Eastern, beside Saturday’s closing count of more than 6,400 cancelled and more than 8,000 delayed. The Alaska total stands in the Alaska account filed below and in the count account filed below, which prints the same table and the same caution: unofficial, uncalled, uncertified. The alert stands in the alert account filed below, in the ministry’s own words as posted. In the talks file the night added one sentence, and it is a negative: the negotiators appointed by the European Union have not yet attempted to contact Russia, spokesman Peskov told TASS, in the agency account filed below—“No, not yet.” The desk takes the files in their order.

The Airlines at 0400: Saturday Closed Above 6,400 Cancelled, Sunday Begins at 875 Down, and the Promise Falls Due at the Close of Business

Saturday’s final counts closed the recovery day above every count the day itself had produced, and the desk prints the closing figures as the day’s record. Airlines had cancelled more than 6,400 flights in the United States and delayed more than 8,000 on Saturday as of 2135 Eastern, in the wire account at the top of this report, on the tracker’s data; nearly 6,500 flights were cancelled on the day at the 2200 count, in the midnight edition’s tracker account; about 5,600 had been cancelled by 1800, in the London account filed below; and more than 6,150 were cancelled and over 7,300 delayed in the second wire account filed below. Friday’s figures stand beneath them: about 9,200 cancelled and 7,500 delayed on the day of the stop. The administrator’s arithmetic of the stop itself entered the file on Saturday and stands in the London account: about 20,000 flights still had journeys to complete when the stop began, about 8,000 of them were able to continue afterwards, and approximately 12,000 could not recover—roughly 9,000 commercial flights and 3,000 private flights among them. No second stop was ordered on Saturday or overnight. Departures ran, aircraft and crews were repositioned through the night, and transatlantic services had returned to normal by Sunday morning with knock-on disruption continuing into Ireland and England, in the transatlantic account filed below.

What Sunday holds, at 0400, is a number and a promise, and they do not yet agree. The number is 875: flights scheduled for Sunday already cancelled by 2135 on Saturday night, in the wire account above, up from 160 at 1530 on Saturday in the same file’s earlier reading; the tracker’s midnight figure, nearly 900, stands beside it in the midnight edition. One carrier had cancelled roughly a quarter of its planned Sunday operation by late Saturday; the rates on the other carriers were trending far lower; and a major airline said late on Saturday that it had completed its planned cancellations for that night and Sunday, although individual flights could still be cancelled while it restored its operation, in the London account. The promise is the one the file has carried since Saturday: full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday, in the administrator’s words and the airlines’. The administrator’s own caution stands beside the promise in the second wire account: the worst is behind us, but a significant amount of recovery work remains. On cause, the night added no finding. The account stands where Saturday’s press conference left it: a contractor replacing copper wire with fiber at a remote location, a new router flooding the network with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds in the Secretary’s figure, 17 of 22 en route centers affected and none dark, additional testing under way with the contractor, and the Secretary’s question—installer error, user error, or a faulty router—unanswered, all in the wire account of the briefing. Settled: the stop, its mechanism in outline, and Saturday’s cost. Open: whose error, if anyone’s, and whether Sunday closes whole, which today’s counts will answer.

The Count at 0400: 140,637 to 129,424 in the Full Table, 49.94 Percent Against a Dashboard’s 50.1, and No Call

Alaska’s count supplied overnight the raw total the midnight edition lacked, and the new total moves the lead without moving the race’s state. The Division of Elections’ unofficial report timestamped 1515 on Saturday lists 283,618 ballots counted statewide, an increase of 4,284 over Friday’s report, in the Alaska account at the top of this report. In the Senate race Ms. Peltola has 140,637 votes, 49.94 percent of the vote when write-ins are included, to Senator Sullivan’s 129,424, 45.96 percent; Mr. Heikes has 6,002, Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. has 4,652, and write-ins account for 872. Her lead increased to 11,213 votes, up from 10,412 on Friday; in the latest batch she added 2,397 votes and Senator Sullivan added 1,596. About 97 percent of the expected vote is counted, and turnout stands at nearly 47 percent. The percentage the midnight edition carried—50.1 percent, in the latest national report—is explained in both overnight accounts, and the desk prints the explanation plainly: the state’s public dashboard rounds Ms. Peltola to 50.1 percent because unresolved write-ins are excluded from that display calculation, while the complete denominator, write-ins included, places her at 49.94 percent, just below the outright first-round majority. The two figures are one count read two ways, and neither is a call. The wire and most national decision desks had not declared a winner when the count account was published; one service projected Ms. Peltola after the newest batch and one desk moved the contest into a “likely” category, both recorded in the count account as assessments, not calls. Ms. Peltola’s campaign’s position and Senator Sullivan’s campaign’s position stand as they stood: no mathematical path, in hers; waiting for every ballot, in his.

The rest of the Alaska file moved with the count, and its dates did not. The governor’s ticket strengthened its first-choice majority in the same report, at 141,623 votes, 50.90 percent, up from 50.81 percent on Friday, in the Alaska account; the House leader maintained his advantage, at 133,707 to 116,932; and several legislative contests remain separated by margins between 13 and 23 votes. The legal backdrop stands in the count account: the Justice Department’s suit over the two Sullivans on the ballot was dismissed on November 1 for lack of standing, the Department appealed, and supporting briefs in the appeal were filed on November 13; the count account’s arithmetic is that Ms. Peltola’s lead of 11,213 is more than twice the second Mr. Sullivan’s entire total of 4,652. The calendar is unchanged and now three days off: overseas ballots may arrive until November 18, the final regional count of absentee and questioned ballots and the ranked-choice tabulation for races that require it run November 18, and certification is targeted for November 25. The Senate stands at 55 seats called for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans. Settled at 0400: the lead, its size in full, and the reason the two percentages differ. Open: the call, which the tabulation, not a rounded dashboard, will settle.

The Gulf at 0400: Manama Issues an Alert, the Radar Claim and Denial Stand, and Three Tankers Are Claimed on Mines

Manama spoke overnight, and what it said was addressed to its own residents, not to either capital’s account of Friday. Bahrain’s Ministry of Interior issued an alert on November 15 urging citizens and residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels for the protection of public safety, in the alert account at the top of this report, which carries the ministry’s message as posted. The alert is the first nationwide threat alert from Bahrain since September in the summary account filed below, and it arrived one day after the Guards’ claim against the radar. No official confirmation of the alert’s cause stands in the accounts; informal sources reported drones and missiles overflying the kingdom’s airspace, in the alert account, and the desk prints that as a report of a report, nothing more. Against the alert, the two standing accounts of Friday stand exactly where they stood: the Guards’ claim that its aerospace force attacked and destroyed the early-warning radar of the American forces in Bahrain, in retaliation for the strike on the tower at Sirik, carried in the claims account filed below, which adds the Guards’ figure of six drones against a radar at a helicopter base; and Central Command’s denial, restated in the denial account filed below: two one-way attack drones launched toward Bahrain, both shot down, no injuries, no damage. Neither side has produced evidence the other accepts. The alert does not settle the radar question; it settles only that Manama judged its residents should be told to take shelter, and that fact now stands in the file beside the claim and the denial.

The strait gained a claim overnight of the kind this file has learned to carry unverified. Iran’s Navy said three tankers caught fire on Saturday after colliding with naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, in the claims account above, which records that the wire had not been able to verify the report; the summary account puts the figure at two to three oil and liquefied-gas tankers struck and on fire, against American statements that the main shipping lanes have been cleared of mines. The Guards said the strait remained closed, in the same account. No shipping authority’s confirmation of a tanker fire stands in any account the desk read by 0400, and the desk files the claim at that size. The wider Gulf file also carried, in the claims account, a Saudi report that its air defenses intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched toward Riyadh, attributed by its coalition spokesman to the Houthi militia; and the standing figures of the maritime file, in the same account: 25 seafarers dead and many injured or missing across some 134 incidents in the strait and the wider area as of November 11, in the International Maritime Organization’s count as reported. Tehran’s seven conditions stand unanswered, the mediators’ work on an interim agreement stands as the midnight edition filed it, and the blockade stands in force. What changed overnight is the file’s center of gravity: the next dated occasion in the Gulf is still Shenzhen on Thursday, where Washington says the President will raise the war in Iran, but Manama’s alert is now the file’s newest fact, and it is dated today.

Dublin at 0400: ‘No, Not Yet’ From the Kremlin, a Question From Kyiv’s Account, and a Demands Paper Between Them

Europe’s team, named on Friday, has not yet contacted the other side, and the word on that came from Moscow on the day this edition collects. The negotiators appointed by the European Union have not yet attempted to contact Russia, spokesman Peskov stated on November 15 in response to a question from TASS—“No, not yet”—in the agency account at the top of this report. The team itself stands as Dublin settled it: the Union’s institutions and the E5 countries, Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland, alongside the Commission and the Council, in the same account. The overnight debate in Europe’s own papers is about the team’s shape, not its errand: the E5 decision followed a week of disagreement among European leaders over who should represent the bloc, with at least three camps in the reporting, in the team account filed below, which records that the Union’s foreign policy chief is left out of the named team and that a deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council dismissed any role for her on November 13, saying the Union has not even been invited to the talks. Swedish Prime Minister Kristersson endorsed the framework, in the debate account filed below. At the Abu Dhabi round the Europeans sat as national security advisers at the technical level, in the team account’s record of that round—the United Kingdom by Mr. Powell, Germany by Mr. Sautter, France by Mr. Bonne, Italy by Mr. Saggio—and Poland’s seat at the next round is unfilled in the accounts. No date or place for a next round stands in the file, and the prisoner exchange agreed in principle at Abu Dhabi still carries no number in any account. Settled: the team, its membership, and the fact that it has not called. Open: whether Moscow accepts it when it does.

Kyiv’s account of an American question spent the night being carried by the morning papers, and Washington’s answer to it is a sentence that confirms nothing. President Zelenskyy said the American negotiators raised, for the first time, the question—“What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?”—in remarks made on Friday and released by his office on Saturday, in the BBC account filed below. He did not accept the idea and did not reject it outright: if the American side confirms a package of security guarantees, no limits on Ukraine’s armed forces, and money to rebuild, he will ask Ukrainian society what it thinks, in the agency account filed below, which also records his standing sentence that Ukraine is not retreating and is not giving up its land. The United States has not confirmed his comments, and an American official told the BBC that many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed by both parties, in the BBC account. American officials had previously said NATO membership for Ukraine was off the table, in the same account, which is what makes the question, if it was asked as described, a change in the file. The story’s own timetable stands in the accounts: the wire carried it late Friday, a French broadcaster carried it Saturday morning, and the BBC carried it Saturday evening. Against the question stands the other side’s paper, as the midnight edition printed it from the Institute’s November 14 assessment: the unofficial demands paper circulated at Abu Dhabi, calling for the alliance to pull back to its 1997 lines. Between a membership offered for the Donbas in one account and a paper demanding the alliance withdraw in another, the distance the next round has to cross is unchanged by the night. The war under the diplomacy ran at its stated tempo in the Institute’s assessment, and no new round is dated.

Shenzhen at 0400: Two Confirmations, No Third, and a Departure on Monday

The week’s largest appointment did not move overnight, and the desk files its standing whole so the week opens on the record. The meeting of Presidents Trump, Putin and Xi is set for Thursday, November 19, in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ meeting, which runs November 18 and 19 with President Xi in the chair. The White House announced the meeting on Friday, in the announcement account filed below, which describes it as a first-ever trilateral sit-down between the leaders of the three countries, focused on nuclear non-proliferation; the Kremlin confirmed it on Saturday in spokesman Peskov’s words, in the confirmation account the midnight edition filed; and no Chinese official has confirmed the three-way meeting on the record, the host’s word standing at in communication with relevant parties. Washington’s agenda stands: nuclear arms at the top, the war in Iran to be raised, Ukraine not on the agenda, and no agreement expected, in the announcement account and the agenda account filed below. Moscow’s intention to raise Ukraine in Shenzhen stands against it, as the midnight edition printed. The last treaty limiting the two largest arsenals expired in February, in both accounts. The itinerary in the file has the President leaving Washington on Monday and attending the ASEAN summit in the Philippines before Shenzhen, with a working lunch and bilateral talks with President Xi on Thursday ahead of the trilateral; a second itinerary in the overnight accounts has him arriving in Manila on the 17th and traveling to Shenzhen on the afternoon of the 18th, and both stand in the Cocked Hat. Settled: the meeting, its date, its place, and two of its three confirmations. Open: the host’s word, the agenda, and the departure’s exact day.

Nvidia at 0400: A Petition Past 115,000, a Board That Has Not Answered in the File, and Tuesday’s Report

The Nvidia file’s overnight fact is a number, and the desk prints it with its provenance attached, because the number’s provenance is the story. A petition calling on the company to reinstate Mr. Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon, in the petition account filed below. The petition’s own website said the signers include 5,965 current employees, 1,108 former employees and 63,063 shareholders; those affiliations are self-reported, the screening does not verify identities, and neither the company nor Mr. Huang endorses the campaign, in the campaign account filed below. The named supporters in the petition account are Mr. Musk, Mr. Masad of Replit, Mr. Sweeney of Epic Games and Mr. Tan of Y Combinator; Mr. Musk posted on November 13 that a petition was under way and that he was signing it. The petition’s demand is that the board bring Mr. Huang back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, on its stated concern that he was removed without meaningful due process. The counts beneath the headline figure do not meet: an earlier reading of the same campaign put it past 100,000 with 5,248 current employees, and another account put it above 44,000 signatories, all in the counts account filed below, which also records that the campaign is working to remove fake signatures. No answer from the board to the petition stands in any account the desk read by 0400, and no petition is binding on a board in any account.

The standing of the file around the petition is unchanged, and Tuesday is now two days off. Mr. Huang resigned on Thursday; Ms. Kress is interim chief; the company reports its third quarter on Tuesday, November 17, after the bell, on guidance of $108 billion, plus or minus 2 percent, in the first call led without its founder; and Mr. Huang’s Friday 2000 deadline for written confirmation of a December 1 interview passed with no confirmation and no subpoena in any account the desk read, a state unchanged overnight. The Journal’s financing report, filed in the Saturday overnight edition, stands unanswered by the company in the file: commitments and guarantees of about $530 billion as analysed from the filing. No finding has been made by the board, by any committee or by any court on any allegation in this file, and the desk prints the petition as what it is—a count of names on a website, self-reported, asking a board to reverse a resignation the board accepted.

France and Spain at 0400: A Fifth Saturday Closed, a Strike Called for Tuesday, and a Debate Without a Date

France’s fifth Saturday spent the night in its final numbers, which the morning papers carried whole. The Interior Ministry’s closing count stands at 219 arrests across the country and 106,000 demonstrators nationwide, 24,000 of them in Paris, against about 200,000 in the organizers’ count, with 45 of the arrests in the capital in the prosecutors’ figure and tear gas reported in Paris, Nantes, Bordeaux, Lyon and Marseille, in the France 24 account filed below. A second account of the same day, in the protests account filed below, carries the ministry’s 1800 figure of 121 arrests beside the closing 219, the deployment of some 70,000 police and gendarmes under the Interior Minister, and the movement’s cumulative arrest total past 4,000 over the month. Turnout was the lowest in recent weeks in both counts, down from 146,000 in the ministry’s count the Saturday before. The movement’s origin stands as the file has carried it: a school movement over staff, funding and repairs, joined by the cost-of-living protests. The unions have called a further day of strikes for Tuesday, November 17, after rejecting a government promise to raise the minimum wage by 0.6 percent, in both accounts; Tuesday is also the eighth anniversary of the Yellow Vest movement’s beginning, in the France 24 account. Settled: the fifth Saturday, its size, and its direction. Open: whether the weekday strike carries what the Saturdays are losing.

Spain’s campaign opens its third day with its central appointment still undated, and the overnight file adds precision about the undatedness, not a date. The two main debates for the November 29 election—a head-to-head between Mr. Sánchez and Mr. Feijóo and a meeting of the main candidates—are agreed to be organized by the Television Academy, which has offered an institutional signal every interested medium can broadcast, and their dates are still being specified, in the debates account filed below, updated to November 10 in its own calendar: the head-to-head stands as proposed for November 16 by one network and November 17 by the public broadcaster, with no date agreed, and a four-way debate proposed for November 23 carries three acceptances and not the Prime Minister’s. Saturday’s scheduling reports in this paper’s midnight file carried a Thursday, November 19 date for the head-to-head at 2200; the debates account before the desk this morning does not carry that date, and the desk leaves both in the Cocked Hat rather than choosing between them. The polls stand as the week left them: the mean of the institutes at Popular Party 31.4, Socialists 26.9, Vox 19.1 in the midnight file’s reading, against the state survey’s Socialist lead. The campaign runs to November 27, polls may publish until November 23, and Spain votes on November 29.

Sunday Opens: A Grade Due at the Close of Business, a Court List on Monday, and a Week Written in Dates

The day ahead is graded by one promise and opened by one feature. The airlines’ promise of full schedule integrity by Sunday’s close is the day’s test, and its opening figure is the 875 cancellations Saturday night had already entered against it; the Midday Watch, collecting at 1200, will carry the morning’s count. Sunday also carries this paper’s Review of Reviews, filed separately, ahead of the day’s watches. The week’s dates stand in the order the midnight edition printed them: Monday, the Supreme Court’s order list at 0930, the Senate’s return at 1500 and its votes at about 1730, and the President’s departure for Asia on one of the file’s two itineraries; Tuesday, Nvidia’s earnings after the bell and the French strike; Wednesday, Alaska’s tabulation; Thursday, Shenzhen. The Senate’s affordability votes and the war-powers file wait on the same Monday. Nothing in the night’s file moves any of those dates.

The Cocked Hat

Where the night’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Saturday’s flights: more than 6,400 cancelled and more than 8,000 delayed at 2135 in the wire’s account, nearly 6,500 cancelled at the 2200 tracker count, about 5,600 cancelled by 1800 in the London account, and more than 6,150 cancelled and over 7,300 delayed in the second wire account—four measures of one recovery, at four hours. On Sunday’s opening figure: 875 cancelled at 2135 in the wire’s account, nearly 900 at the midnight tracker count, and about 900 in the transatlantic account, against 160 at 1530 in the afternoon reading. On Alaska: 49.94 percent and a lead of 11,213 in the full table with write-ins counted, against 50.1 percent on the state’s dashboard, which excludes unresolved write-ins from its denominator; and on what remains, about 97 percent counted in the Alaska account against 96 percent in the wire’s earlier estimate. On Bahrain: a radar destroyed by six drones, in the Guards’ account, against two drones shot down with no damage, in Central Command’s, with Manama’s alert standing beside both and settling neither. On the tankers: three on fire after striking mines, in the Iranian Navy’s account as carried, two to three in the summary account, and the main lanes cleared of mines in the American account, with no confirmation from any shipping authority in the file. On the Donbas question: asked for the first time, in President Zelenskyy’s account, against many ideas continue to be discussed, in the American official’s answer, with no American confirmation that the question was put. On the petition: more than 115,000 signatures in TechCrunch’s reading, past 100,000 in an earlier reading, and above 44,000 in another, on figures the campaign itself says are self-reported and unverified. On Shenzhen’s journey: departure Monday with a summit in the Philippines before China, in one itinerary, against arrival in Manila on the 17th and travel to Shenzhen on the afternoon of the 18th, in another. On Spain’s debate: November 16 and November 17 proposed and no date agreed in the debates account, against Thursday, November 19 in Saturday’s scheduling reports. Against the triangle, the night’s single-valued facts are these: Sunday begins with 875 of its flights already cancelled and a promise of full schedules by its close; Saturday cancelled more than 6,400 flights on the recovery day; Ms. Peltola leads in Alaska at 140,637 to 129,424, the race is uncalled, and the tabulation is November 18; Bahrain’s Interior Ministry issued a nationwide alert on November 15, its first since September in the accounts; Europe’s negotiators have not yet contacted Russia, in the Kremlin spokesman’s words of November 15; the Shenzhen meeting is confirmed by Washington and Moscow for November 19 and unconfirmed by its host; France arrested 219 on its fifth Saturday and its unions strike on Tuesday; the Court’s orders come Monday at 0930, the Senate votes Monday, the company reports Tuesday, and Spain votes on November 29. The Midday Watch collects at 1200.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 24 items.

Subjective
Reuters, carried in the briefing account — more than 6,400 Saturday cancellations at 2135, 875 of Sunday’s already cancelled, and the briefing’s cause in full

Airlines had cancelled more than 6,400 flights in the United States and delayed more than 8,000 on Saturday as of 9:35 p.m. Eastern, after about 9,200 cancelled and 7,500 delayed on Friday, and 875 flights scheduled for Sunday were already cancelled at that hour. Administrator Bedford said operations should largely return to normal by late Sunday, and Secretary Duffy traced the failure to a router installed by contractor L3Harris at a remote facility during a copper-to-fiber conversion, with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, 17 of 22 en route centers affected, and investigators examining installer error, user error, or a faulty router. Carriers issued waivers allowing rebooking to later dates without a change fee.

Subjective
London Daily News — schedules expected to recover by Sunday, 5,600 cancelled by 1800 Saturday, and 12,000 flights that could not recover

Airline schedules are expected to recover fully by the end of Sunday, the administrator said on Saturday, an expectation for the overall schedule and not a guarantee for every passenger. About 5,600 flights had been cancelled by 6 p.m. Eastern on Saturday. Of about 20,000 flights with journeys still to complete when the stop began, around 8,000 continued afterwards and approximately 12,000 could not recover, roughly 9,000 of them commercial and 3,000 private. A major airline said late on Saturday that it had completed its planned cancellations for that night and Sunday, although individual flights could still be cancelled. The precise fault remains under investigation, with contractor error and a faulty router both unestablished.

Subjective
Views News Now — back to normal by Sunday’s end, more than 6,150 cancelled and 7,300 delayed on Saturday, and the worst behind us

The agency expects air travel to return to normal by the end of Sunday, Administrator Bedford told reporters on Saturday, cautioning that passengers should still expect delays and cancellations while airlines reposition aircraft, crews and passengers, and saying the worst is behind us but a significant amount of recovery work remains. Airlines cancelled more than 6,150 flights and delayed over 7,300 on Saturday, after nearly 9,200 cancelled and about 7,500 delayed on Friday, a combined disruption above 15,000 cancellations and 14,800 delays over the two days. Secretary Duffy said the disruption began during contractor work to replace copper wiring with fiber-optic connections.

Subjective
Travel Extra — transatlantic flights return to normal, another 900 cancellations for Sunday, and restrictions lifted in Europe

Transatlantic flights have resumed and full schedules are not expected until the end of Sunday, November 15, after Friday’s four-hour nationwide ground stop. An initial European directive restricting flights from Europe to the United States has been removed, flights into and out of Ireland and England continue to face knock-on disruption, and the cancellations included four Dublin-bound flights and two returns, with over 900 additional cancellations recorded for Sunday. The trouble began at 15:36 when air traffic control centers experienced instability in radar and communications. Administrator Bedford stated that airline partners expect full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday.

Subjective
Newsy Today — Bahrain issues an alert urging citizens to seek safe locations

The Ministry of Interior of Bahrain issued an alert on November 15, 2026, urging citizens and residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels. The advisory followed ongoing military operations by Iran across the region; there is no official confirmation of the alert’s cause, and informal sources reported Iranian drones and missiles overflying the kingdom’s airspace. The alert arrived one day after the Guards claimed to have attacked and destroyed an American early-warning radar in Bahrain, a claim Central Command answered by saying its forces downed two attack drones heading toward Bahrain without casualties or damage.

Subjective
Particle News — two drones shot down, a radar claimed, tankers claimed on mines, and a first alert since September

Central Command said American forces intercepted and shot down two one-way attack drones launched toward Bahrain with no injuries or damage. The Guards countered that its forces destroyed an American early-warning radar at the Al-Riffa base, a claim American officials and independent sources have not verified. The Guards and the Iranian Navy reported that two to three oil and liquefied-gas tankers struck naval mines and caught fire in and near the strait, while American statements say the main shipping lanes have been cleared of mines. Bahrain issued its first nationwide threat alerts since September and urged residents to move to safe locations.

Subjective
NewsCord — the Guards target a radar in Bahrain, Saudi Arabia reports missile intercepts, and three tankers are said to have struck mines

The Guards announced a drone attack on an American radar system at a base in Bahrain, and the official agency said the air defense radar at a helicopter base was targeted by six drones of the Guards’ aerospace force. Saudi Arabia’s coalition spokesman reported that its air defense intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched toward Riyadh, which he attributed to the Houthi militia. The Guards also claimed the strait remained closed and threatened a stronger response, and Iranian state media quoted the Navy as saying three tankers caught fire on Saturday after colliding with naval mines in the strait, a report the wire said it had not yet been able to verify. Central Command denied the radar was destroyed and said two drones were shot down with no injuries or damage.

Subjective
Diaspora Digital Media — the United States denies the claim of strikes on radar sites in Bahrain

The American military has denied the Guards’ claim that its forces struck an early-warning radar installation in Bahrain, saying it intercepted two attack drones, which were shot down on Friday with no injuries or damage. The Guards’ statement described the attack as retaliation for a strike on a telecommunications tower in the southern port of Sirik, and as a serious warning over aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the strait. Neither the Iranian nor the American account could be independently confirmed. The account also carries the parliament speaker’s statement of Wednesday that the strait would never return to its pre-war condition.

Subjective
LaPresse — the Kremlin: the European negotiators have not yet contacted Russia

Milan, November 15. The negotiators appointed by the European Union have not yet attempted to contact Russia, Kremlin spokesman Peskov stated in response to a question from TASS: “No, not yet.” At the informal European summit in Dublin, the heads of state and government opted for a format that includes the European institutions and the E5 countries—Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland—alongside the European Commission and the Council to represent Europe in the negotiations on Ukraine.

Subjective
Security Signal — the E5 team named, the foreign policy chief left out, and Moscow’s acceptance unconfirmed

European Council President Costa announced on November 13 that France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland, together with the Union’s institutions, will form Europe’s negotiating team for talks on peace in Ukraine, leaving out the Union’s foreign policy chief. The decision followed a week of disagreement among European leaders, with at least three camps reported: one backing Mr. Costa, one led by France and Germany resisting handing their seats to Brussels, and a third backing the foreign policy chief. A deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council dismissed any role for her on November 13, claiming no one wants her involved and that the Union has not even been invited to the talks. Moscow has not confirmed whether it will accept the configuration.

Subjective
Nexus Europa — the debate intensifies over European representation in future Ukraine talks

Discussions surrounding European representation in potential peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine have gained urgency in Brussels. Following an informal summit in Dublin, European leaders selected a negotiating group composed of the E5 nations—France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom—alongside representatives of the Union, to champion continental interests. Swedish Prime Minister Kristersson endorsed the framework, emphasizing the importance of a unified European stance. Questions remain regarding how effectively the coalition will represent the broader bloc during diplomacy with Moscow and Washington.

Subjective
BBC News, carried by Everywhere News — the United States has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for NATO membership, Mr. Zelenskyy says

American negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership, President Zelenskyy has said, in remarks released by his office on Saturday: “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised.” The United States has not confirmed his comments, and an American official told the BBC that many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed by both parties. American envoys travelled to Dublin on Thursday to meet Mr. Zelenskyy, after a round of talks with President Putin in Moscow.

Subjective
Life News Agency — the United States floated ceding Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, and Kyiv would ask its society

Kyiv, November 14. The United States has for the first time raised the idea of Ukraine withdrawing from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for membership of NATO, President Zelenskyy said in comments released by his office on Saturday, made on Friday and kept under embargo until Saturday. He said he did not accept the idea and did not reject it outright: if the American side confirms a comprehensive package—specific guarantees from NATO and the Union, a strong army with weapons and funding, and a reconstruction plan with clear financing—then he will ask Ukrainian society what it thinks, as he has no right to make that decision on his own. He also said, repeatedly, that Ukraine is not retreating and is not giving up its land. American officials had previously said membership was off the table.

Subjective
CNN — the President to meet China’s and Russia’s leaders at a first trilateral sit-down on nuclear non-proliferation

President Trump will meet jointly next week with China’s leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Putin, the White House said Friday, a first-ever trilateral sit-down between the leaders of the three countries. The meeting, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, will focus on nuclear non-proliferation, a topic the President has said he believes could yield a new agreement between the world’s biggest nuclear-armed states. The Kremlin says the meeting will take place on November 19 in Shenzhen, but there has been no confirmation yet from China. The last nuclear arms treaty between the United States and Russia expired in February.

Subjective
Jagran Josh — the first trilateral meeting at the APEC summit: what is on the agenda

The leaders of the United States, China and Russia are planning a first-ever trilateral meeting at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, likely on Thursday, November 19; the White House confirmed the meeting on Friday and the Kremlin confirmed it on Saturday. The President wants to deliberate on nuclear weapons and explore a new agreement spanning the three countries’ arsenals, after the previous treaty expired in February. A senior official stated the meeting could initiate a conversation on nuclear disarmament, but no deal is confirmed. The President plans to discuss the war in Iran with both leaders, while an American official said Ukraine would not be on his agenda for the trilateral. Experts forecast symbolism rather than large agreements.

Subjective
TechCrunch — Mr. Musk and other executives sign a petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate Mr. Huang, past 115,000 signatures

A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate its recently ousted chief executive appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon. The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current employees, 1,108 former employees and 63,063 shareholders, and the named supporters include Mr. Musk, Mr. Masad of Replit, Mr. Sweeney of Epic Games and Mr. Tan of Y Combinator. The petition states its signers are concerned Mr. Huang was removed without meaningful due process and demands the board bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts. Mr. Huang resigned on Thursday, and the chief financial officer, Ms. Kress, was appointed interim chief executive.

Subjective
AI Affairs — the petition draws thousands of staff signatures, and its figures are self-reported

A petition asking the board to reinstate Mr. Huang had attracted more than 115,000 signatures by Saturday, November 14. The campaign’s website lists 5,965 current employees, 1,108 former employees and 63,063 shareholders among its signers, says its affiliations are self-reported and its screening does not verify identities, and says it is independent of the company and of Mr. Huang. The petition asks the board to bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts. The company announced the resignation on November 12, effective November 11 in a regulatory filing as described, and is scheduled to report quarterly results on November 17.

Subjective
Tbreak — the petition passes 100,000 in an earlier reading, and the board has not answered

A petition urging the board to reinstate Mr. Huang passed 100,000 signatures, with 5,248 signers saying they are current employees, in an earlier report of Saturday, November 14; by Saturday afternoon a second report put it at more than 115,000, with 5,965 current employees listed. The names are self-reported and nothing independently confirms the employee count, and the campaign is actively working to remove fake signatures, in a report the account cites. The letter also asks the board to disclose the scope, independence and timeline of its investigation. The board has not answered the petition in any report at the time of writing.

Subjective
France 24, carried by Hermes Vector — ‘No justice, no peace’: the fifth round of protests sweeps across France

Between 106,000 and 200,000 people took to the streets across France on Saturday for the fifth round of protests, the Interior Ministry counting 106,000 nationwide, 24,000 in Paris, and the student unions counting 200,000, including almost 100,000 in the capital. The ministry said 219 people had been detained across the nation, and Paris prosecutors said 45 were arrested in the capital. Turnout was lower than the previous week, when the ministry reported 146,000 nationwide and 46,000 in Paris. Tear gas use was reported in Paris, Nantes, Bordeaux, Lyon and Marseille. Unions have called a new day of strikes on Tuesday, the eighth anniversary of the Yellow Vest movement, after rejecting a government promise to increase the minimum wage by 0.6 percent.

Subjective
Demócrata — the 29N debates: who participates, the schedules proposed, and no date agreed

The campaign for the general elections of November 29 will include several televised debates, although the schedule of the meetings between the candidates for prime minister is still pending finalization. An agreement between the two main parties gives the Television Academy the organization of the two main debates—a head-to-head between Mr. Sánchez and Mr. Feijóo and a meeting of the main candidates—with an institutional signal all interested media can broadcast. The head-to-head stands proposed for November 16 by one network and November 17 by the public broadcaster, both marked proposed, and a four-way debate proposed for November 23 carries the acceptances of Mr. Feijóo, Mr. Abascal and Ms. Colau, without confirmation from Mr. Sánchez. The campaign began November 13 and ends November 27.

entry.title: The Airlines Close Saturday at Nearly 6,500 Cancellations With Nearly 900 of Sunday's Flights Already Cancelled, Ms. Peltola Stands Above 50 Percent in the Latest Alaska Report With the Race Still Uncalled, and the Kremlin Confirms the Shenzhen Meeting While Its Host Confirms Nothing
entry.summary: Airlines close Saturday at nearly 6,500 cancellations with 900 of Sunday's flights already cut, and Peltola stands above 50 percent in Alaska.
entry.content:
The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

The Airlines Close Saturday at Nearly 6,500 Cancellations With Nearly 900 of Sunday’s Flights Already Cancelled, Ms. Peltola Stands Above 50 Percent in the Latest Alaska Report With the Race Still Uncalled, and the Kremlin Confirms the Shenzhen Meeting While Its Host Confirms Nothing

The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: a recovery day that cancelled more flights than the day it recovered from had left expected, and still promised to end on Sunday; a count that crossed its majority line in a report and stayed uncalled in the record; a meeting confirmed by two of its three capitals; and a protest movement that filled its fifth Saturday smaller than its fourth.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Sunday, November 15, 2026.
