The 1948 text covered origin and creed; race, skin colour, and national and ethnic origin were named in 1970; sexuality was added in 2002; gender identity or expression in 2018. The law’s present operation was fixed in the Quran-burning cases. Through 2023, police granted permits for public Quran desecrations under the constitutional instruments, while the government raised the national terror-threat level in August 2023 citing, among other causes, the burnings and the reaction to them. Prosecutors then charged under the 1948 statute. Rasmus Paludan, who had burned Qurans across Sweden, was convicted of agitation in November 2024 and sentenced to four months’ imprisonment. Salwan Momika, an Iraqi asylum seeker whose burnings outside Stockholm’s central mosque began the sequence, was charged in August 2024 and shot dead on January 29, 2025, the day before his verdict was due. His associate Salwan Najem was convicted on February 3, 2025, on four counts, and received a suspended sentence and day fines; the presiding judge stated the court’s rule in one sentence: freedom of expression is protected in Sweden, but it is not “a free pass to do or say anything.” Sweden has never banned Nazi parties. The statute aimed at an antisemite in 1948 now punishes the desecration of Islam’s book, under the same constitution that protected the burnings as demonstrations; the courts have printed both readings, and both are the Swedish settlement.

Canada: the limits clause, and a list amended twice

Section 2(b) of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees “freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of the press and other media of communication,” and section 1 subjects it to “such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.” The Criminal Code’s hate-propaganda offences—section 318, advocating genocide, and section 319, publicly inciting and wilfully promoting hatred—date to 1970 and defined the protected “identifiable group” by colour, race, religion, and ethnic origin. In R. v. Keegstra (1990), the Supreme Court sustained section 319 by a vote of four to three under the section 1 analysis, upholding the conviction of a teacher who had taught antisemitic doctrine to his students. The list has been amended twice since, each time by a named bill that Parliament debated as a free-speech question: Bill C-250, passed in 2004, added sexual orientation, over objections, recorded in the debates, that sermons would be prosecuted; Bill C-16, which received royal assent on June 19, 2017, added gender identity and gender expression. A parallel provision, section 13 of the Canadian Human Rights Act, was repealed by Parliament in 2013; the government’s Online Harms Act, Bill C-63, tabled in February 2024, died unpassed when Parliament was prorogued in January 2025. The Canadian record thus contains, at the same time, the Western world’s most fully litigated judicial defence of hate-propaganda law and a legislature that has once repealed a hate-speech provision and once declined to enact a larger one.

Australia: no right to quote, and a statute about offence

Australia is the only country in this survey whose constitution contains no general guarantee of expression. What exists is an implication: in Lange v. Australian Broadcasting Corporation (1997), the High Court held that the Constitution’s system of representative government implies a freedom of political communication—a limit on legislative power, not a personal right. The operative speech statute is civil. Section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act 1975, inserted by the Racial Hatred Act 1995, makes it unlawful to do a public act “reasonably likely, in all the circumstances, to offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate” a person or group, where the act is done because of race, colour, or national or ethnic origin; section 18D exempts acts done reasonably and in good faith for artistic, academic, reporting, and fair-comment purposes. In Eatock v. Bolt (2011), the Federal Court found that newspaper columnist Andrew Bolt had contravened section 18C in articles questioning the Aboriginal identity of fair-skinned Aboriginal people who, he wrote, had chosen their identity for professional advantage; the court held the section’s words to require “profound and serious effects, not to be likened to mere slights.” The section still reaches the political class itself: in July 2026 the Full Federal Court dismissed Senator Pauline Hanson’s appeal against a finding that her social-media post directed at a fellow senator contravened section 18C. The criminal side of the system has grown by state increments, most recently New South Wales’s Crimes Amendment (Inciting Racial Hatred) Act 2025, creating an offence of intentionally and publicly inciting hatred on racial grounds. Australia’s settlement is the survey’s limiting case: no proclaimed right stands in the statute’s path, and the operative threshold in its best-known speech case is a verb the American doctrine nowhere contains—offend.

New Zealand: one prosecution in fifty years

The New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 states the right in section 14—“Everyone has the right to freedom of expression, including the freedom to seek, receive, and impart information and opinions of any kind in any form”—and subjects all its rights, in section 5, to “such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.” The hate-speech law is two sections of the Human Rights Act 1993. Section 61 creates civil liability for published matter that is threatening, abusive, or insulting and likely to excite hostility against, or bring into contempt, a group on the ground of colour, race, or ethnic or national origins. Section 131 makes intentionally inciting racial disharmony an offence, prosecutable only with the Attorney-General’s consent and punishable by up to three months’ imprisonment or a fine of NZ$7,000. Religion is not a protected ground in either section. The offence, first enacted in the Race Relations Act 1971 and carried into the 1993 Act, has produced one successful prosecution in its history: a neo-Nazi pamphleteer, in 1977. Parliament repealed the offence of blasphemous libel in 2019. After the Christchurch mosque attacks of March 15, 2019, the Royal Commission of Inquiry recommended extending the incitement provisions, and the government in 2021 proposed offences reaching speech intended to “stir up, maintain or normalise hatred,” punishable by up to three years’ imprisonment. The government reduced the proposal in 2022 to adding religious belief to the existing grounds, withdrew it in early 2023, and referred the subject to the Law Commission; in June 2024 the Minister of Justice directed the Commission to withdraw hate-speech issues from its work programme. The file therefore records a law nearly never used, a repeal, an expansion proposed after a massacre, and the expansion’s abandonment by two successive governments of different parties.

Brazil: the court expands the word “racism”

The Constitution of 1988 protects expression in article 5, item IV—“expression of thought is free, anonymity being forbidden”—and, in item XLII, removes one subject from that protection in terms: “the practice of racism is a non-bailable and imprescriptible crime, subject to the penalty of imprisonment, in accordance with the law.” Law 7.716 of 1989 defines the crimes of prejudice of race or colour, and its article 20 punishes practising, inducing, or inciting discrimination or prejudice on grounds of race, colour, ethnicity, religion, or national origin. The reach of the word racism has been fixed not by Congress but by the Supreme Federal Court. Siegfried Ellwanger, a Porto Alegre publisher, was convicted under the statute for publishing antisemitic books, including works denying the Holocaust; his defence was that Jews are not a race and that his conduct, however offensive, was not the constitutional crime. In habeas corpus 82.424, decided in 2003, the Court denied relief: racism, it held, is a social and political concept, not a biological one, and antisemitism falls within it, carrying the constitutional consequences of non-bailability and imprescriptibility. In June 2019, in ADO 26, eight of the Court’s eleven justices held that homophobia and transphobia are likewise to be punished under the racism law until Congress enacts a specific statute, which Congress has not done. The Brazilian file is therefore a record of a single constitutional word doing successive work: written in 1988 with the country’s racial order in view, read by the Court in 2003 to cover the Jews, and read by the Court in 2019 to cover homosexuals and transgender persons—each extension accomplished by interpretation, in the name of a text that names none of the groups the later readings protected.

South Africa: the constitution names the exception, and cuts the statute

Section 16 of the South African Constitution of 1996 grants freedom of expression, including press freedom, artistic creativity, and academic freedom, and then provides, in subsection (2): “The right in subsection (1) does not extend to—(a) propaganda for war; (b) incitement of imminent violence; or (c) advocacy of hatred that is based on race, ethnicity, gender or religion, and that constitutes incitement to cause harm.” Sexual orientation is not in the list. The Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act 2000, section 10, went wider than the constitutional text: it prohibited words based on any of a long list of prohibited grounds that could reasonably be construed to demonstrate a clear intention “to be hurtful,” to be harmful or incite harm, or to promote hatred. The case that tested both texts began with a newspaper column. In 2008 the journalist Jon Qwelane published, under the headline “Call me names, but gay is not okay,” an attack on gay marriage. The Equality Court found the column hate speech. On July 30, 2021, after thirteen years of litigation, the Constitutional Court held the word hurtful in section 10 unconstitutionally vague and overbroad and struck it, reading the statute down to the constitutional standard of harm and incitement—and held, applying that standard, that the column did constitute hate speech, because it dehumanised its targets and incited intolerance against them. Qwelane had died before judgment was delivered. South Africa’s record thus runs against the direction of the other files in this survey in one particular: the country’s broadest hate-speech formulation was narrowed by its own constitutional court, in the name of the constitution’s speech clause, in a case whose defendant the same court held liable under the narrowed rule.

India: the feelings clause, 1927

Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and expression; article 19(2) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of, among other things, the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the state, public order, decency, and morality. The word hatred does not appear among the constitutional grounds. The operative statutes are older than the Constitution and come from the colonial code. Section 153A of the Indian Penal Code punishes promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, or language. Section 295A is narrower and stranger: it punishes whoever, “with deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings of any class of citizens of India,” insults or attempts to insult the religion or religious beliefs of that class. It was enacted in 1927, and its occasion is on the record. In 1924 a Lahore publisher, Mahashay Rajpal, published Rangila Rasul, a scurrilous pamphlet on the marriages of the Prophet Muhammad. Prosecuted under section 153A, Rajpal was acquitted by the Lahore High Court in May 1927: there was no offence of insulting a religion as such. The imperial legislature supplied the missing offence within the year, as section 295A. Rajpal was assassinated in 1929 by Ilm-ud-Din, who was hanged for the murder and is honoured in Pakistan as a martyr. India’s Penal Code was replaced in 2024 by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which carries both offences forward—promoting enmity as section 196, the religious-feelings offence as section 299. The Indian file is the survey’s clearest instance of a law written for one community’s outrage becoming general property: a provision enacted to protect Muslim feelings after a Hindu publisher’s acquittal is now invoked by complainants of every religion, against speakers of every religion, and its test remains the one written in 1927—not incitement, but feelings, outraged deliberately and maliciously.

Japan: guaranteed in full, punished almost not at all

Article 21 of the Japanese Constitution of 1947 is the survey’s most absolute text: “Freedom of assembly and association as well as speech, press and all other forms of expression are guaranteed. No censorship shall be maintained, nor shall the secrecy of any means of communication be violated.” Japan ratified the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination in 1995 with a reservation against the article obliging states to criminalize the dissemination of ideas based on racial superiority or hatred. National law contains no general hate-speech offence. The Act on the Promotion of Efforts to Eliminate Unfair Discriminatory Speech and Behaviour against Persons Originating from Outside Japan—the Hate Speech Elimination Act, in force since June 2016, passed in response to anti-Korean demonstrations in the Kawasaki and Kyoto areas—declares such speech impermissible and assigns government the duty of education and consultation. The Ministry of Justice describes the Act, in its own guidance, as a law of principles, with no provisions prohibiting discrimination and no penalties. The single penal instrument in the country is municipal: the City of Kawasaki’s ordinance of December 2019, the first in Japan to attach criminal consequences to hate speech, under which a person who repeats prohibited discriminatory speech in a public place after a mayoral recommendation and a mayoral order may be fined up to 500,000 yen and have the facts, including his name, published. Japan’s file completes the survey’s range: the strongest constitutional language of the fourteen, and, beneath it, a national hate-speech law that its own administering ministry describes as carrying no prohibition at all.

The moving target, dated

The commission for this report put five propositions to the desk as questions. The record answers them as follows. A century ago, was anti-Jewish speech hate speech in law? No. In 1926 no country in this survey had a hate-speech offence of any kind; antisemitic newspapers, including Streicher’s Der Stürmer, published legally in the Weimar Republic. The legal category arrived after 1945, and its founding document is a judgment: at Nuremberg in 1946 the International Military Tribunal convicted Streicher of crimes against humanity, holding that his “incitement to murder and extermination at the time when Jews in the East were being killed under the most horrible conditions clearly constitutes persecution on political and racial grounds.” He was hanged on October 16, 1946, the only defendant executed for a career of publication. The statutes followed the judgment: Sweden 1948, Britain 1965, Canada 1970. Fifty years ago, was anti-gay speech hate speech? No. In 1976 no surveyed statute named sexual orientation; Canada’s hate-propaganda sections listed colour, race, religion, and ethnic origin, and homosexual acts themselves had been decriminalized in Canada only in 1969. The era’s speech law ran in the opposite direction, against homosexual expression, under obscenity and indecency provisions. Sexual orientation entered the lists at the turn of this century: Sweden 2002, Canada 2004, England and Wales 2010, Brazil 2019. Five years ago, was anti-trans speech hate speech? In some of the surveyed countries it already was, and in others it still is not. Canada added gender identity and expression in 2017, Sweden in 2018. England and Wales have no such offence as of this filing. Scotland created one with effect from April 1, 2024; its first public test, the Rowling posts, produced a police finding of no crime within a day. Four years ago, was anti-Palestinian speech hate speech—and what changed? No statute in the survey has ever listed Palestinians or any national cause as a protected class, and that remains true. What changed after October 7, 2023, was the subject of enforcement under adjacent laws: Germany treated the movement’s central slogan as a banned organization’s symbol; France’s interior minister ordered pro-Palestinian demonstrations banned before the Council of State required case-by-case assessment; Britain’s Home Secretary wrote to chief constables in October 2023 about the policing of pro-Palestinian marches and flag-waving. In July 2024 Meta revised its hate-speech policy to remove content targeting “Zionists” with dehumanizing comparisons, calls for harm, or denials of existence, on the stated ground that the word “in those instances often appears to be a proxy for Jewish or Israeli people.” And in Germany, is anti-Israel speech now outside the hate-speech net? The record runs the other way, on the German file printed above: slogan prosecutions, assembly bans in the capital, a declaration on the protection of Jewish life written into citizenship law, Israel’s right to exist placed in the naturalization test and, in Saxony-Anhalt, required of applicants in writing. Criticism of Israel remains lawful in Germany and is printed daily in German newspapers; the boundary of the lawful is being litigated, slogan by slogan. But a citizenship applicant in 2026 affirms more about a foreign state than an applicant in 2022 did, and a demonstrator in Berlin says less with legal safety. The movement, on the German record, is toward restriction of anti-Israel and pro-Palestinian expression, not away from it.

“Hate speech is violence”: the career of a claim

One proposition recurs across the surveyed countries’ debates, in forms ranging from a tribunal’s sentence to a platform’s policy document: that hate speech is itself violence, and therefore cannot be free speech. The desk prints its documented career, attributed and dated. Its first legal form is the Streicher judgment of 1946, in which words alone, published over twenty-two years, were held to constitute persecution—a crime against humanity—in the specific circumstance that the extermination the writer demanded was proceeding as he wrote. Its academic form is Words That Wound: Critical Race Theory, Assaultive Speech, and the First Amendment (1993), by Mari Matsuda, Charles Lawrence III, Richard Delgado, and Kimberlé Crenshaw, whose publisher’s summary states the thesis in a sentence: “Words, like sticks and stones, can assault; they can injure; they can exclude.” Its scientific form appeared on July 14, 2017, in a New York Times essay by the psychologist Lisa Feldman Barrett: “If words can cause stress, and if prolonged stress can cause physical harm, then it seems that speech—at least certain types of speech—can be a form of violence”; of abusive speech she concluded, “From the perspective of our brain cells, the latter is literally a form of violence.” The answer appeared four days later in The Atlantic, by Greg Lukianoff and Jonathan Haidt: “Of all the ideas percolating on college campuses these days, the most dangerous one might be that speech is sometimes violence.” In Germany the claim circulates as a slogan of exclusion from the category of opinion itself—Hass ist keine Meinung, “hate is not an opinion”—popularized by Renate Künast’s book of that title in 2017 and carried since on banners at demonstrations and in official campaigns. Its institutional form is the United Nations Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech of 2019, which adopts a working definition—“any kind of communication in speech, writing or behaviour, that attacks or uses pejorative or discriminatory language with reference to a person or a group on the basis of who they are”—and records, in the same document set, that no international legal definition of hate speech exists; Secretary-General António Guterres states the strategy’s premise as a sequence: “Hate speech is an alarm bell—the louder it rings, the greater the threat of genocide. It precedes and promotes violence.” Its commercial form is Meta’s 2024 policy, applying the proxy reasoning above to a political noun. Against the claim, in the record, stand two kinds of document. The first is doctrinal: no statute in this survey defines hate speech as violence; the offences punish incitement, insult, defamation, advocacy, or the stirring of hatred, and the courts that narrowed them—South Africa’s in 2021, America’s in 2017—did so by distinguishing injury of feeling from harm in law. The second is the circumstance of the claim’s founding case: the one tribunal that punished publication as a capital crime did so while a genocide the publisher had demanded was in progress, a limiting fact every later use of the precedent carries with it.

The timeline

1789 — France’s Declaration, article 11, proclaims the free communication of thoughts. 1924 — Rangila Rasul is published in Lahore. 1927 — Rajpal is acquitted; India enacts section 295A. 1934 — The Netherlands enacts group insult, article 137c. 1946 — Streicher is hanged at Nuremberg for crimes against humanity committed by publication. 1948 — Sweden enacts agitation against a population group; Åberg is its first convict. 1965 — Britain creates the first stirring-up offence, for racial hatred. 1970 — Canada enacts its hate-propaganda sections. 1971 — The Netherlands adds incitement, article 137d; New Zealand enacts inciting racial disharmony. 1972 — France’s Pleven Law. 1989 — Ireland’s Incitement to Hatred Act; Brazil’s Law 7.716 defines the crimes of prejudice. 1990 — France’s Gayssot Act criminalizes contesting the Nuremberg crimes; Canada’s Supreme Court sustains its hate-propaganda law in Keegstra. 1995 — Australia inserts section 18C. 2002 — Sweden adds sexuality to its agitation law. 2003 — Brazil’s Supreme Court reads antisemitism into the crime of racism. 2004 — Canada adds sexual orientation. 2010 — England and Wales’s sexual-orientation stirring-up offence takes effect. 2016 — Japan’s Hate Speech Elimination Act declares hate speech impermissible, without penalties; Wilders is convicted of group insult in The Hague. 2017 — Canada adds gender identity and expression; Barrett’s “When Is Speech Violence?” and the Lukianoff–Haidt answer appear four days apart. 2018 — Ireland votes to remove blasphemy from its constitution; Sweden adds gender identity or expression. 2019 — Brazil’s Supreme Court extends the racism law to homophobia and transphobia; Kawasaki enacts Japan’s first penal hate-speech ordinance; the UN adopts its hate-speech strategy, recording that no international legal definition exists; New Zealand repeals blasphemous libel. 2021 — South Africa’s Constitutional Court strikes “hurtful” from its hate-speech statute; Scotland passes its Hate Crime Act. 2023 — In October, Germany lists the river-to-the-sea slogan among banned symbols, France’s interior minister orders pro-Palestinian demonstrations banned and is corrected by the Council of State within the week, and New Zealand withdraws its hate-speech bill. 2024 — Scotland’s stirring-up offences take effect; Germany’s citizenship reform puts the protection of Jewish life and Israel’s right to exist into naturalization law; Meta adopts the “Zionist” proxy rule; Paludan is convicted in Sweden. 2025 — Najem is convicted in Stockholm under the 1948 statute; Linehan is arrested at Heathrow and not charged. 2026 — Britain moves to end non-crime hate incident recording; the Metropolitan Police apologizes to Linehan.

The record as it stands on November 14, 2026, is therefore this. Fourteen democracies proclaim expression free; thirteen of them qualify the proclamation in its own text, in an accompanying statute, or by the absence of any enforceable right against the legislature. The offence that does most of the work, hate speech, is nowhere defined in international law and is defined differently in every capital in this survey, and its protected classes were admitted one at a time, in the order the decades supplied them: the believer’s feelings first, in the colonial code of 1927; race, in the shadow of the tribunal of 1946; sexual orientation, at the turn of this century; gender identity, within the last nine years. In the same period, Germany—whose Basic Law contains the words “there shall be no censorship”—began prosecuting a slogan, banning assemblies, and asking its prospective citizens to affirm the existence of another state. Each of these facts is stated by the country that produced it, in its own texts and figures. The desk has placed them side by side. The comparison is the reader’s.

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—the desk is filing it, not endorsing it—and each is described in plain terms: what it is and what it says. 15 items.

Subjective
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum—Holocaust Encyclopedia, “Assessing Guilt” (encyclopedia.ushmm.org)

The museum’s account of the International Military Tribunal’s propaganda cases: Hans Fritzsche acquitted, and Julius Streicher convicted of crimes against humanity on the strength of twenty-three articles in Der Stürmer, with the tribunal’s sentence quoted: his incitement to murder and extermination, at the time Jews in the East were being killed, constituted persecution and a crime against humanity. Streicher was hanged on October 16, 1946. The article.

Subjective
Center for Law, Brain & Behavior—Lisa Feldman Barrett, “When Is Speech Violence?”, as published in The New York Times, July 14, 2017 (clbb.mgh.harvard.edu)

The essay in full: words can cause stress, prolonged stress can cause physical harm, therefore certain speech can be a form of violence; offensiveness is not bad for the nervous system, but abusive speech is, and from the perspective of brain cells the latter is literally a form of violence. The essay.

Subjective
United Nations—“From Words to Violence: Lives Behind the Fields of Death,” exhibit on the UN Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech (un.org)

The Secretary-General’s strategy as the organization presents it: hate speech defined as communication that attacks or uses pejorative or discriminatory language against a person or group on the basis of who they are, and Secretary-General Guterres’s formulation that hate speech is an alarm bell that precedes and promotes violence. The exhibit.

Subjective
Parliament of Canada—Bill C-250, An Act to amend the Criminal Code (hate propaganda), third reading text, 2004 (parl.ca)

The bill as passed by the House of Commons: the definition of “identifiable group” in sections 318 and 319 of the Criminal Code expanded to any section of the public distinguished by colour, race, religion, ethnic origin, or sexual orientation. The bill.

Subjective
United Kingdom Legislation—Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021, as in force (legislation.gov.uk)

The Act’s own text: the stirring-up offences of Part 3, the characteristics listed—age, disability, religion, sexual orientation, transgender identity, variations in sex characteristics—and, in the same statute, the abolition of the common-law offence of blasphemy; in force from April 1, 2024. The Act.

Subjective
Law Commission of England and Wales—History of Hate Crime Legislation, appendix (webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk)

The official chronology on which the British section rests: section 6 of the Race Relations Act 1965 as the first stirring-up offence; the religious-hatred provisions of 2006; the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008 provisions on hatred on the ground of sexual orientation, in force March 23, 2010; and the recorded absence of equivalent provisions for disability and transgender identity. The appendix.

Subjective
Columbia Journal of European Law—Tom Herrenberg, “Group Defamation and Incitement in the Netherlands: The Conviction of Geert Wilders” (cjel.law.columbia.edu)

The scholarly account of articles 137c and 137d from their origins—the group-defamation ban of 1934 and the incitement ban of 1971—through the December 9, 2016 judgment convicting Wilders of group defamation and incitement to discrimination for the “fewer Moroccans” rally. The article.

Subjective
Reuters—“French court states that pro-Palestinian protests should be banned case by case,” October 18, 2023

The wire report of the Council of State’s ruling: the interior minister’s October 12 instruction that pro-Palestinian protests must be banned upheld as an instruction, but prefects held unable to ban a protest based solely on the note or on the fact that the protest supports Palestinians. The report.

Subjective
InfoMigrants—“Germany: Interior minister says citizenship holders should align with German values” (infomigrants.net)

The report of the interior ministry’s position under the citizenship law as reformed in June 2024: naturalized citizens declared their commitment to the free democratic basic order and to Germany’s special historical responsibility for the protection of Jewish life and the State of Israel, with the declaration’s consequences for those later found not to share those values under active ministerial discussion. The report.

Subjective
European Legal Support Center—“‘Hostile’ Symbols & Slogans: The Attack on Palestinian Presence in Europe” (elsc.support)

The legal-support organization’s documentation of the river-to-the-sea slogan’s treatment in Germany: prosecuted under sections 86a and 140 of the Criminal Code since the November 2023 bans on Hamas and Samidoun, with the Berlin and Bremen higher administrative courts reaching opposite conclusions in 2023 and 2024 and trial outcomes divided. The report.

Subjective
Bulletin of the Transilvania University of Brașov—“Towards Harmonized Hate Crime Laws” (2025)

The comparative study whose Swedish case study the desk used: the Stockholm District Court’s judgment of February 3, 2025 convicting Salwan Najem of agitation against an ethnic group on four occasions for the Quran-burning demonstrations, the court holding that the acts expressed contempt toward Muslims beyond the bounds of legitimate debate. The study.

Subjective
Revista de Direito Público / SciELO—“Ellwanger and the Transformations of the Supreme Federal Court” (scielo.br)

The account of habeas corpus 82.424, decided in 2003: publisher Siegfried Ellwanger’s conviction for racism for publishing antisemitic, Holocaust-denying books sustained on the ground that racism is a social and political concept, the decision that repositioned Brazil’s Supreme Court as a protector of vulnerable groups and that the Court extended to homophobia and transphobia in 2019. The article.

Subjective
Brill—“The Prophet, Law, and Constitution in Pakistani Society,” in The Presence of the Prophet in Early Modern and Contemporary Islam (brill.com)

The scholarly history of section 295A: the colonial Penal Code’s religious offences, the Rangila Rasul pamphlet of 1927 and the insufficiency of section 153A to prosecute its publisher, the enactment of section 295A against acts done “with deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings of any class,” and Rajpal’s assassination in 1929. The chapter.

Subjective
Freedom of Religion South Africa—“ConCourt Decision in Qwelane: Facts, and Findings of the Court” (forsa.org.za)

The findings of the Constitutional Court’s judgment of July 30, 2021: section 10 of the Equality Act declared unconstitutional to the extent of the word “hurtful,” the provision read down to the constitutional test of harm and incitement, and Qwelane’s 2008 column held to be hate speech under the read-down provision. The summary.

Subjective
New Zealand Law Commission—Ia Tangata: terms of reference, as updated June 25, 2024 (lawcom.govt.nz)

The Commission’s own record of the removal of hate speech from its work: sections 61 and 131 of the Human Rights Act 1993, concerning the incitement of racial disharmony, excluded from the review at the Minister of Justice’s request that the Commission withdraw issues relating to hate speech from its programme. The terms of reference.

entry.title: Saturday’s Recovery Cancels More Than 3,700 Flights by Midday Against 700 Expected Overnight, Alaska’s Count Gains Its Raw Numbers at 138,240 to 127,828 With the Governorship Called and the Senate Still Open, and Europe’s Team Meets a Foreign Ministry in Moscow That Says the Subject Was Never Discussed
entry.summary: Saturday's recovery from the FAA ground stop cancels more than 3,700 flights by midday against 700 expected, and Alaska's count moves.
entry.content:
The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 21 items.

Subjective
Reuters — more than 3,700 Saturday cancellations, two airline ground stops of their own, and funds sought for an emergency

Major airlines on Saturday cancelled more than 3,700 flights in the United States and delayed 2,000 more as the country recovered from the longest nationwide shutdown of flights since the September 11, 2001 attacks. The Administration issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday that halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours and forced airlines to cancel nearly 10,000 flights and delay more than 7,000 others. Tens of thousands of people were still stranded at airports on Saturday. United announced a ground stop for its own flights at Chicago O’Hare and Delta at New York LaGuardia, to handle congestion and gate issues, and many major airports said they could not handle more diversions. American said it was prioritizing international flights and smaller cities to position aircraft and crews. The stop followed an outage that appeared to affect a network handling critical radio frequencies used by controllers to communicate with pilots, according to two airline officials; the contractor overseeing the network, L3Harris, did not respond to a request for comment. Secretary Duffy said the trouble began at 3:36 p.m. Eastern, that switches and routers were overloaded with data and gave inconsistencies, that personnel never completely lost radar or communications, and that he seeks $50 billion to upgrade the system, up from $30 billion sought earlier: “This is an emergency.” Secretary Mullin said there was zero evidence so far of a cyberattack or a rogue artificial-intelligence system, neither ruled out, and that the National Security Agency was working with the Department of Homeland Security on the investigation. Because the Administration was responsible for the delays, airlines are not required to provide compensation to stranded passengers. The only other nationwide ground stop since September 11 came in January 2023, for about 90 minutes. Shares of American, United and Delta fell between 1 and 2 percent in after-hours trading on Friday, and JetBlue about 3 percent.

Subjective
USA Today — more than 5,100 flights delayed or cancelled on November 14, and the Secretary’s Saturday statement

Airlines scrambled to resume and reschedule flights after the four-hour nationwide ground stop, and many travellers still faced cancellations and delays on November 14. The instability in radar and communications systems at traffic control centers was identified at 3:36 p.m. Eastern on Friday, Secretary Duffy said; the stop was lifted at 8:15 p.m., and officials and experts warned disruptions could last days. More than 5,100 flights into or out of the United States were delayed or cancelled on November 14, according to FlightAware, though it is not clear how many of those problems resulted from the stop; Atlanta, Chicago O’Hare, New York Kennedy and Dallas-Fort Worth were among the hardest hit. Secretary Duffy said on November 14 that operations are slowly returning to normal, that travellers will continue to see delays and cancellations as carriers reposition aircraft and crews, and that the Department of Transportation would provide further updates at 10:30 a.m. Eastern. More than 3,500 airplanes were flying when the stop was issued. Secretary Mullin said the aging telecommunications system failed as newer technology was being patched in, and that Americans did not have to fear for their safety.

Subjective
Men’s Journal — 3,400 cancelled by Saturday morning, the count by airline, and the refund rule

More than 3,400 flights within, into or out of the United States had been cancelled by Saturday morning, November 14, as airlines worked to recover from the nationwide ground stop, according to FlightAware, which also counted 9,138 cancellations and 7,068 delays on Friday. As of 6:45 a.m. Eastern on Saturday, Delta had cancelled 629 flights, 20 percent of its schedule; United 510; American 471; JetBlue 335, 40 percent of its schedule, the highest share among the major carriers; and Southwest 304. Atlanta led the airports with 114 cancellations, New York Kennedy and Boston Logan had 105 each, and Chicago O’Hare 99. FlightAware listed 1,111 delays as of 6:45 a.m., with most of the day’s schedule still ahead. JetBlue waived change and cancel fees and fare differences for flights from November 13 through 14, with rebooking through November 18; Delta allowed rebooking without fees for travel on or before November 21; American’s waiver covered 21 airports for travel on November 13 or 14, with changes made by November 14; Southwest allowed rebooking or standby within five days; Frontier waived change fees for travel through November 15, with fare differences applying. Under Department of Transportation rules, a passenger is entitled to a refund if an airline cancels the flight and the passenger chooses not to travel, regardless of the reason, and the same applies to a domestic delay of three hours or more; meals and hotels are a different matter, because the carriers’ commitments cover problems within their control. Secretary Duffy said it would take some time to get back to capacity, blamed old technology that became overloaded, asked Congress for $50 billion for a complete overhaul, and warned that more such outages would come. The company behind the agency’s new SMART tool has said its system was not the cause.

Subjective
Fox Weather — more than 9,100 cancelled and 24,500 delayed on Friday, and the second-longest stop in the record

Thousands of flights were cancelled early Saturday in the wake of Friday’s nationwide ground stop, which lasted more than four hours—the longest shutdown of American airspace since September 11 and the second-longest nationwide ground stop in the country’s history, surpassed only by the roughly two-day shutdown after the 2001 attacks. More than 3,000 flights were cancelled early Saturday, according to FlightAware; all told, more than 9,100 flights were cancelled and more than 24,500 delayed on Friday. The Administration said it issued the stop, just before 4 p.m. with 3,500 flights in the air, out of an abundance of caution because of intermittent telecommunications outages. Secretary Duffy posted on Saturday that operations are slowly returning to normal, that planes are pushing back, taxiing and taking off, and that it is safe to fly, and announced a press briefing at 10:30 a.m. Eastern at the Department’s headquarters. Secretary Mullin said there was no indication of a nefarious attack: “This isn’t another 9/11.” Travellers at New York’s LaGuardia told correspondents they had slept on the terminal floor on Friday night, and Amtrak reported higher-than-normal call volumes as stranded passengers turned to the trains. The last nationwide ground stop before Friday was ordered on January 11, 2023, over the system that alerts pilots to flight hazards, and lasted about an hour and a half.

Subjective
The Hindu BusinessLine — the ask boosted to $50 billion, and the $30.1 billion letter priced in parts

The Administration boosted its request for air traffic control funding to $50 billion late on Friday after a communications issue forced a nationwide ground stop that halted thousands of flights for hours. Secretary Duffy and the White House had earlier on Friday asked for $30.1 billion to upgrade the country’s aging airports and air traffic control system. The request in the letter from the budget director and the Secretary seeks $10.1 billion for air traffic control modernization, including $7.2 billion for a common automation platform and controller workstations and $2 billion for cloud computing, and $2 billion to replace and improve control towers. Congress already approved $12.5 billion over five years in July 2025 to upgrade air traffic control and increase controller hiring, and approved $1.9 billion to replace outdated en route centers; the Republican-led Senate Commerce Committee said the incident highlights the need to prioritize modernizing those centers over other projects. The Administration has called for the Republican-led Congress to approve the funding in the final weeks of the year; Democrats are set to take control of Congress in January.

Subjective
Fish 4 News — the lead at 10,412 in the November 13 update, 96 percent counted, and the race uncalled

Mary Peltola leads Senator Dan Sullivan by 10,412 votes in Alaska, the last uncalled Senate race of the 2026 midterms, in totals checked on Saturday, November 14 that reflect the state’s November 13 update and are not a certified result. The latest published first-choice count gives Ms. Peltola 138,240 votes, 49.8 percent, against 127,828, 46.1 percent, for the incumbent; Mr. Heikes holds 5,885, Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. 4,560, and write-ins 855. The Associated Press estimates about 96 percent of expected ballots have been counted and has not called the election; the state’s public media described Friday’s release as adding roughly 22,500 votes and widening the lead. A rounded 50.0 percent on some trackers should not be treated as an outright majority, because the smaller candidates and write-ins count in the total. November 18 is the deadline for overseas ballots and the scheduled ranked-choice tabulation; November 25 is the target for certification. A Peltola victory would give the Democratic caucus 56 seats; a Sullivan retention, 55. Two legal disputes stand in the file: the Justice Department’s suit over possible confusion between the two Sullivans, dismissed by a federal judge and appealed; and the Peltola campaign’s request for records identifying rejected absentee ballots, rejected by Judge Matthews on November 11 as a matter of access to records, not a finding on the ballots.

Subjective
DINA — 445 votes short of a majority, favored and uncalled, with the full table printed

The latest unofficial Division of Elections data show Ms. Peltola with 138,240 votes to Senator Sullivan’s 127,828, a raw advantage of 10,412 among 277,368 reported votes, at shares of 49.84 and 46.09 percent—a margin of about 3.75 points. Mr. Heikes holds 5,885, Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. 4,560, and write-ins 855. Ms. Peltola remains 445 votes short of an outright majority of the reported vote, and the ranked-choice process can still transfer ballots from eliminated candidates to the next continuing preference each voter marked. Senator Sullivan’s remaining path depends heavily on transfers from Mr. Heikes and on the composition of the last accepted ballots; independent reviews of preliminary cast-vote data have placed Ms. Peltola ahead in simulated final rounds, and simulations are not official tabulations. The account’s assessment is that Ms. Peltola is favored and the race remains uncalled. Overseas ballots may arrive through November 18, the tabulation is planned for November 18, and certification is targeted for November 25. Democrats have secured 55 seats, Republicans 44, and Alaska is the one outstanding contest.

Subjective
WHRO — the governorship called for Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins, to take office December 7

Mr. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from the island community of Sitka, won the race for governor of Alaska, according to a race call by the Associated Press published on November 14. At 37, he will be the youngest governor in the state’s history. He will replace Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican who has been governor since 2018 and was term-limited. The call came after more than a week of counting votes, including ballots arriving by mail and from remote parts of the state; in the ranked-choice system he faced three Republican candidates, including one backed by the President. Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins, known by his initials JKT, made a high-energy, bipartisan, problem-solving approach a centerpiece of his campaign. He is set to take office at noon on December 7.

Subjective
NationWire — the team’s likely occupants are advisers, and only Ukraine decides its territory

After an informal summit in Dublin on Friday, President Costa announced that Europe will be represented by the Union’s institutions—the Commission and the Council—together with the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy and Poland. Officials said the representatives were likely to be national security advisers from the five countries, plus delegates from the Commission and the Council, working with all 27 member states and coordinating Europe’s contribution alongside Ukraine, the United States and NATO. President Costa defined the mandate’s limit: the team is not there to negotiate Ukraine’s territory on Kyiv’s behalf, and only Ukraine has the legitimacy to decide on its territory and sovereignty. A ceasefire remains the Europeans’ stated priority, and forty European countries meeting in Dublin on Thursday signed a declaration that any matter affecting European security should be decided with Europeans involved. Ms. Kallas laid claim to the envoy role, saying she is the one who represents Europe in foreign and security policy and that it is not up to Russia to say who should represent the Union. The envoys Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner met President Putin in Moscow on Thursday, then briefed President Zelenskyy in Dublin, and said President Putin had agreed Europe would join the next round; the Kremlin has not confirmed that account, its spokesman said Moscow must first understand the Europeans’ intentions, and the Foreign Ministry said it was unaware of any such agreement. No date or venue has been announced; the European Council returns to Ukraine’s financing on November 26 and 27.

Subjective
Zot News — the Foreign Ministry says the issue was not discussed in Moscow, against the envoy’s account

The Union has named its representatives for potential peace talks, and Moscow questioned the bloc’s role: the Kremlin says it needs to understand Europe’s real intentions before deciding whether to expand the format, and the Foreign Ministry contradicted the envoy’s claim that President Putin was willing to have European representatives join. President Costa said after the Dublin meeting that the Union will take part alongside France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom, and that Europe must speak with one clear and united voice. Mr. Kushner said on Thursday that President Putin was willing to give it a try on European representation; spokeswoman Zakharova told a German news agency that, as far as the Foreign Ministry was aware, the issue had not been discussed during the Moscow talks, and state media reported no Foreign Ministry representatives were present. Ms. Kallas said Russia does not want anybody strong at the table because it wants to push through its maximum demands, and asked whether Europe has a say in who represents Russia. Chancellor Merz asked the President to make no surprises on Ukraine and said Europe does not need to discuss a European security architecture with Russia, because it already exists. The account notes that Russia and the United States have called for one single representative, several nations want a team, and the Union has not settled on a single figure.

Subjective
Magna Bureau — the Dublin decision in full, and a next round expected fairly quickly with no date

European leaders agreed in Dublin that the Union’s institutions and five countries will speak for Europe at the next round of the Ukraine talks, if Moscow lets them in. President Costa announced on Friday, November 13, after an informal summit in Dublin, that the team will be the institutions plus the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy and Poland—the E5 of the Coalition of the Willing, the group of more than 30 countries backing Ukraine and preparing security guarantees for a future ceasefire. The envoys Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner met President Putin in Moscow on Thursday, November 12, and then President Zelenskyy in Dublin, and said President Putin had agreed Europe would join the next round. The Kremlin has not confirmed that agreement: spokesman Peskov said on Friday that Moscow must first understand the Europeans’ intentions and readiness to contribute to peace before deciding on talks in an expanded format, and said he expected a next round fairly quickly, without naming a date. Ms. Kallas laid claim to the envoy role, saying she represents Europe in foreign and security policy and that it is not up to Russia to say who represents the Union.

Subjective
MetroPunch — the first target in a Gulf state in more than two months, and the two accounts of it

Iran targeted an American military installation in Bahrain for the first time in more than two months, amid tensions over the stalled negotiations. The Guards said they launched the attack early Friday in retaliation for an American strike on Iranian territory, and that their aerospace forces targeted and destroyed the early-warning radar of the American military in Bahrain, in response to the enemy’s aerial aggression against a communication tower in Sirik. Central Command said its forces intercepted two drones heading toward Bahrain, and that the incident caused no injuries or damage; it dismissed the claim of a successful attack on a radar system as false. The account also carries the President’s declaration that Washington no longer needed an agreement with Iran: “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed! We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” The President directed Mr. Vance, who had been leading negotiations with Tehran, to shift his attention to corruption and crime in Democratic-controlled states and cities. Central Command claimed at least 4,000 ships had crossed the strait with American military assistance, carrying more than 1.7 billion barrels of crude.

Subjective
Zot News — the negotiator redirected, seven conditions through Qatari mediators, and the ball in the American court

The Guards said on Friday they had destroyed an American early-warning radar in Bahrain, hours after the President declared no deal with Tehran was needed and ordered Mr. Vance to shift his focus from the Iran negotiations to corruption in Democratic-run states and cities. The Guards called the attack a serious warning to Washington to end its aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the strait, and said their forces were on full alert and ready to respond without geographical limits. The President wrote that he had asked Mr. Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the massive corruption and crime in Democrat-run cities and states, and added: “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” Mr. Vance, who led the negotiations for a short-lived truce, has blamed the war and its economic reverberations for the Republicans’ midterm losses, writing that if losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, others should argue so. The President’s messages stand in two directions in the same account: not looking to escalate, and a strike possible right now if things went the wrong way. Diplomatic efforts mediated by Qatar and Pakistan are continuing: Speaker Ghalibaf told his interviewers that Tehran has sent a clear proposal for a ceasefire and the reopening of the strait via Qatari mediators, laying out seven conditions including an end to the naval blockade, the lifting of sanctions, the release of frozen funds and an explicit announcement of an end to the war, and that the ball is now in the American court; the United States has previously refused those demands without an agreement on the nuclear programme first. Speaker Ghalibaf also said the strait would never return to its pre-war status. At least 12 tankers have been hit in the past 12 days, according to Iran; Central Command says about 4,000 ships have crossed with American assistance.

Subjective
New Kerala — the denial restated in the command’s claim-and-fact form

Central Command rejected the Guards’ claim to have destroyed an American early-warning radar installation in Bahrain. In a post, the command stated its form: claim—today the Guards said they attacked a radar; fact—the Guards launched two one-way attack drones toward Bahrain and both were shot down by American forces, and there were no injuries or damage. The Guards had described the strike as retaliation for an American aerial attack on a telecommunications tower in the Sirik region; according to a Fars report, the Guards said their forces targeted the radar approximately an hour after the alleged attack on the tower, and described the claimed destruction as a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the strait. The President had earlier issued a warning to Tehran against threatening American allies and maritime interests, and claimed Washington was making progress in its operations and extracting more oil than before the conflict began.

Subjective
ReadUS247 — the core without trade services at 0.5 percent, energy down on the month, and two officials opposed

Producer prices rose 0.3 percent in October, the last such reading before the Federal Reserve decides in December; energy fell 0.1 percent on the month while the measure excluding food, energy and trade services rose 0.5 percent. The Bureau published the figures on November 13: final demand up 0.3 percent on the month and 6.5 on the year, the largest twelve-month rise since November 2022; without food and energy, up 0.3 and 5.0; without food, energy and trade services, up 0.5 for a second consecutive month against a median forecast of 0.3, and 4.9 on the year; goods up 0.5; services up 0.2, for a fifth straight month; energy down 0.1 on the month, with diesel down 7.9 and crude petroleum down 10.3, and up 37.0 on the year; transportation and warehousing services up 2.0, with truck freight up 3.9, the largest single contributor to the services rise. Secretary Bessent and President Goolsbee disagreed publicly the same morning: the Secretary’s reading is an energy supply shock tied to the conflict, already easing, in very noisy numbers the Federal Reserve should look forward past; the Chicago president’s reading is pressure spread well beyond energy into services and medical care, with old-fashioned demand overheating from the data-centre buildout, and a central bank that has work to do to reestablish its credibility. Mr. Goolsbee is not a voting member this year. The funds range stands at 3.75 to 4.00 percent, set September 17 in the first increase since 2023 and held October 28 by 10 to 2, both dissents preferring a rise. The FedWatch probability of a rise to 4.00–4.25 percent in December stood at 89.4 percent on November 13; Governor Waller said he would support a quarter-point increase unless core consumer inflation came in at 0.3 or more, and would consider a half point depending on the data. The November producer report is published after the December meeting.

Subjective
Startup Fortune — the annual rate at its highest since November 2022, and the hike odds after the print

Producer prices rose 0.3 percent in October, below the 0.4 expected, while the twelve-month rate climbed to 6.5 percent, the biggest annual jump since the 7.4 percent of November 2022. Goods did most of the work: final demand goods rose 0.5 percent and services 0.2, and more than 60 percent of the October advance came from goods other than food and energy; steel mill products rose 2.7 percent and industrial chemicals 3.1. After the release, the FedWatch odds of a 25-point hike in December rose from 85.4 percent on Thursday to 89.7, and the chance of a 50-point move fell from 14.5 to 10.3; a week earlier the December odds stood at 77 percent after a strong jobs report. The next producer release, covering November, is published December 15.

Subjective
Iboro Finance — Saturday’s table of Friday’s closes, and the digital market still falling

Global markets closed a turbulent week with declines in the technology sector and a sharp correction in digital assets. The S&P 500 closed at 7,561.67, down 0.40 percent; the Nasdaq Composite at 25,136.27, down 0.91; the Dow Jones at 52,347.60, up 0.10; London’s FTSE 100 at 10,902.56, up 0.36; the ten-year Treasury yield at 5.15 percent; gold at $3,887.60, up 0.06; crude oil at $88.56, down 0.20; the dollar index at 103.41, up 0.23, with the euro at 1.1028 and the pound at 1.3209. Bitcoin fell 6.15 percent to $66,954.34, ether 6.04 to $1,895.03, Solana 7.73 to $75.35, XRP 4.47 to $0.993 and BNB 6.15 to $615.69, in a sell-off the account attributes in part to speculation that investors are cashing out to fund participation in an anticipated Anthropic offering. Nvidia endured a sixth consecutive week of declines, a streak not seen in 14 years, and its market value shrank by $573 billion in the week. A Federal Reserve survey identified artificial-intelligence risks as the biggest threat to the financial system, in the account’s reading. Nigerian companies cut 2.26 trillion naira of debt in the first nine months of 2026, and pension funds in South Africa and Nigeria have reportedly sought a combined $1 billion stake in the Dangote refinery offering.

Subjective
Ungated — the board removed its chief in this account, 13 downgrades, and testimony before Thanksgiving

Nvidia’s board removed Mr. Jensen Huang as chief executive and named the finance chief, Ms. Colette Kress, interim chief executive, while the stock closed at $162.85 on Friday, down 2 percent on the day and 13 percent for the week. The decline erased more than $570 billion of market value, extending a six-week losing streak that has shaved roughly 30 percent off the share price and cost about $1.7 trillion in valuation. At least 13 analysts have downgraded the stock this month, most during the current week. The board convened after a newspaper reported a second affair involving a senior vice president, in the account’s telling. Mr. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress before the Thanksgiving holiday, and the company will report earnings on November 17. The weekly fall of 13 percent is the biggest since April 2025, and the losing streak is the longest for the company since 2012.

Subjective
ApeX — where the money rotating out of Nvidia went, measured close to close, and the succession reports in conflict

United States markets are shut for the weekend, so every equity figure is measured to the Friday, November 13 cash close. From the November 6 close through Thursday the 12th, the rotation ran one way: the leveraged chip fund rose 41.24 percent, AMD 30.02, Cerebras 25.25 and Broadcom 23.11, while Nvidia fell 10.98. On Friday the whole trade came off: the fund fell 13.23 percent, SanDisk 7.55, AMD 7.24, Marvell 6.67 and Broadcom 5.26, and Nvidia fell 3.11 on the day in this account’s contract measure. From the November 6 close through Thursday, Nvidia lost about $493 billion of market value while AMD and Broadcom together gained about $561 billion. Nvidia ended the week at $162.85, down 12.75 percent, about 30 percent over a six-week streak the account calls its longest since 2012, with its market value closing below $4 trillion. On the succession, the reporting conflicts: a Financial Times report on Friday said the board had approached Arm’s chief executive, Mr. Rene Haas, as a potential successor, and Arm shares fell 4.63 percent on the day; the board told its interviewers on November 13 that it had not yet officially contacted any potential candidates. The company reports on November 17, after the close, with an interim chief executive and no permanent successor named.

Subjective
Demócrata — two numbers in Palma, 75 and 176, and the mean at 26.9 on November 14

The President of the Government and candidate for re-election, Mr. Pedro Sánchez, launched a new call for mobilization on Saturday ahead of the November 29 elections, setting out two figures as the keys to a new progressive majority: 75 percent turnout and the 176 seats of an absolute majority in the Congress. “We must write down two figures: 75 and 176,” he wrote, closing with: “Vote, to win, and to govern for four more years!” The message followed his rally in Palma de Mallorca at the Son Fusteret venue, beside Ms. Francina Armengol, where he said Mr. Feijóo and Mr. Abascal offer no alternative except cuts and the chainsaw, defended his government’s management, and linked the two opposition leaders with Presidents Trump and Milei, Prime Minister Meloni and Prime Minister Orbán. The account’s table of the fifteen-institute mean, dated November 14, stands at Popular Party 31.4 percent, Socialists 26.9, Vox 19.1, Frente Amplio 6.4 and ERC 2.5. The campaign’s first Saturday placed Mr. Feijóo in Galicia, Mr. Abascal with events in Almería and Murcia, and Ms. Colau in Seville. A 75 percent turnout does not alone guarantee the progressive bloc 176 seats, the account notes, because the 350 seats are distributed by provincial constituencies.

Subjective
Particle News — the two-week campaign opens, and turnout and tight provinces will decide it

The official campaign opened on Friday, November 13, with Mr. Sánchez, Mr. Feijóo and Mr. Abascal launching nationwide tour events in key provinces. Mr. Sánchez set a 75 percent participation target for the November 29 vote, and his party is elevating Ms. Gómez, planning an event with Brazil’s President Lula da Silva, and promising further surprises to mobilize the progressive bloc. The Popular Party is pushing a vote-conversion message, with the Galician leader Mr. Rueda urging voters to channel discontent with the government into support for Mr. Feijóo and to prevent Vox from becoming decisive. Public opinion is unstable: one institute’s survey gives the Popular Party a clear advantage while the state survey projects a Socialist lead, so turnout levels and tight regional contests such as La Rioja could decide which bloc reaches the 176 seats of a majority.

entry.title: Presidential Reversal: What the Record Shows About Each Administration Undoing the Last
entry.summary: Every party change in the White House since 1981 opened by undoing the last: revocation orders, regulatory freezes, and the Congressional Review Act.
entry.content:
Special Report

Executive Orders · The Regulatory Freeze · The Congressional Review Act · The Elections of 1980, 2022, and 2024

Objective

Presidential Reversal: What the Record Shows About Each Administration Undoing the Last

Every president who has taken the White House from the other party since 1981 has opened by stopping, withdrawing, or revoking the work of the man before him, using four instruments the record defines: the revocation order, the regulatory freeze memorandum, the Congressional Review Act disapproval, and the withdrawal of pending rules. The counts have climbed across four decades. In their first hundred days, presidents revoked five prior executive orders in 2001, nine in 2009, thirteen in 2017, and sixty-seven in 2021; on January 20, 2025, a single order revoked seventy-eight. The Congressional Review Act, used once in its first twenty years, has now been used twenty-three times in the present Congress. Each administration's documents give its reasons in its own words.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Saturday, November 14, 2026.

Reversal is the standing first act of American government, and it is conducted in paperwork. Since 1981, every president who has taken office from the opposing party has begun his administration by undoing pieces of his predecessor's work, and the undoing runs through four instruments whose texts survive: the executive order that revokes earlier executive orders by number; the regulatory freeze memorandum that stops the pipeline of unfinished rules on the first day; the Congressional Review Act resolution by which Congress and the new president together void a finished rule and bar its return in substantially the same form; and the withdrawal or postponement of rules still pending when the government changes hands. The American Presidency Project's count of the first hundred days shows the volume rising across the modern transitions: five prior executive orders revoked in 2001, nine in 2009, thirteen in 2017, and sixty-seven in 2021, when half of the new president's executive orders carried a revocation inside them. In January 2025 the bulk rescission became a document of its own: Executive Order 14148, signed on the first day, revoked seventy-eight orders and memoranda of the previous administration in a single list, and a second order eight weeks later revoked eighteen more. Congress's instrument has followed the same curve: the Congressional Research Service counts twenty successful disapprovals in the Act's first twenty-eight years—one in 2001, sixteen in 2017–2018, three in 2021—and the trackers of the present Congress count twenty-three more since January 2025. Each era's documents state the era's reasons in the era's vocabulary, and this report prints them from the documents. The elections held in the years of high inflation stand in the same file, and the desk prints those numbers beside the reversal counts, drawing no line between them. The record closes with the forward state of the instruments: reversal is now announced before inaugurations, the current administration continued rescinding through the autumn of 2025, and the statute's own carryover provision has already loaded the next Congress's window with the present administration's late rules.

The four instruments

The first instrument is the revocation clause. An executive order governs until a later president revokes it, and the revocation is ordinarily one sentence inside a successor order: a list of numbers, followed by the words “are hereby revoked.” Because a president's orders bind only the executive branch and rest on his own authority, a successor of either party may strike them at any hour of his tenure, and the Federal Register preserves each strike beside the order it struck. The second instrument works earlier in the pipeline. The freeze memorandum, issued on or within days of inauguration, directs agencies to send no new rule to the Office of the Federal Register until a department head appointed by the new president has reviewed it, to withdraw rules sent and awaiting publication, and to postpone, commonly by sixty days, the effective dates of rules published under the old administration and still pending. The third instrument belongs to Congress. The Congressional Review Act, enacted in 1996 and codified at 5 U.S.C. §§801–808, requires agencies to report each rule to both houses and gives Congress a window, sixty days of continuous session from receipt, to pass a joint resolution of disapproval in a text the statute itself dictates: “That Congress disapproves the rule submitted by the [agency] relating to [name of the rule], and such rule shall have no force or effect.” A rule disapproved is “treated as though such rule had never taken effect,” and the statute adds the provision with no parallel elsewhere in the reversal machinery: the rule “may not be reissued in substantially the same form” unless a later law authorizes it. Senate consideration runs on fast-track procedures without a filibuster. The fourth instrument is the quietest: the withdrawal of pending rules from the Unified Agenda of Regulatory and Deregulatory Actions, the government's semiannual inventory of work in progress, and the formal withdrawal notices agencies publish in the Federal Register when they abandon a proposed rule outright. Between the freeze and the withdrawal, an incoming administration can stop nearly everything its predecessor left unfinished, and the record shows each administration doing so.

The revocation counts

The American Presidency Project's comparison of the four party-changing transitions of this century counts executive orders only, through the first hundred days of each term, and the desk prints its figures with that scope attached. George W. Bush published eleven executive orders in the window and revoked five prior orders. Barack Obama published nineteen and revoked nine. Donald Trump published thirty-three in the first hundred days of 2017 and revoked thirteen. Joseph Biden published forty-two and revoked sixty-seven, with twenty-one of his orders carrying revocations inside them; across every category of presidential document in his first hundred days, the Project counts seventy-six prior orders explicitly rejected—revoked, amended, suspended, or reversed—in twenty-five of one hundred six documents. The unit of reversal then changed. Earlier presidents revoked predecessor orders inside orders of their own, a few at a time; the dedicated rescission order, a document whose whole content is a list of the dead, appears in the recent transitions. On January 20, 2021, Executive Order 13992 revoked six named regulatory orders of the Trump administration, including the two-for-one regulatory budget order of 2017, and a companion order the same day, Executive Order 13990, revoked nine further executive orders, three memoranda, and a pipeline permit on the American Presidency Project's reading of its text. Two further orders in February and May 2021, titled “Revocation of Certain Presidential Actions,” lengthened the list. On January 20, 2025, the instrument reached its present scale: Executive Order 14148 revoked seventy-eight presidential orders and memoranda of the Biden administration in Section 2, items (a) through the end of the alphabet twice over, and directed the president's domestic, economic, and national security advisers to compile lists of further candidates. The follow-up order of March 14, 2025, states the running total in its own first section—“I rescinded 78 Presidential orders and memoranda issued by then-President Biden”—and revoked eighteen additional actions, executive orders, national security memoranda, presidential memoranda, and determinations among them. Ninety-six bulk rescissions stand in the two orders within the administration's first eight weeks, ahead of the individual revocations carried in subject-matter orders across the same period.

The Congressional Review Act ledger

Congress's instrument slept for its first twenty years and then became routine. The Congressional Research Service's tally, which the George Washington University Regulatory Studies Center's cumulative count matches, records 461 resolutions of disapproval introduced between 1996 and 2024 and twenty enacted. The first success came on March 20, 2001, when the disapproval of the Labor Department's ergonomics rule, issued in the final months of the Clinton administration, became Public Law 107-5 under President Bush's signature. The second success waited sixteen years. In the 115th Congress of 2017–2018, sixteen disapprovals were enacted under President Trump's signature: the Regulatory Studies Center counts fifteen signed in 2017, fourteen of them against rules of the outgoing Obama administration, and Ballotpedia counts fourteen signed in the first four months alone. The sixteenth, signed May 21, 2018, disapproved a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau auto-lending guidance document, on the strength of a Government Accountability Office opinion holding that the guidance was a rule within the Act's meaning—the precedent that widened the instrument from rules to guidance. In the 117th Congress, three disapprovals were enacted under President Biden's signature, all on June 30, 2021: an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission conciliation rule, an Office of the Comptroller of the Currency “true lender” rule, and an Environmental Protection Agency rule that had itself rescinded the previous administration's methane standards, so that the disapproval restored the standards of two administrations back. The present Congress has exceeded the earlier record in a single session of work. The Regulatory Review's empirical analysis of the 2025 signings counts twenty-two disapproval resolutions signed into law during 2025, thirteen of them reaching rules submitted in the ordinary way during the statutory lookback window and nine reaching actions outside it: three California emissions waivers granted under the Clean Air Act, four Bureau of Land Management resource management plans, and further agency actions drawn in through Government Accountability Office opinions. The American Action Forum's tracker for the 119th Congress, in its update of October 26, 2026, counts twenty-three disapprovals enacted in the Congress and 148 resolutions introduced, addressing rules carrying an estimated $175.5 billion in compliance costs; the Senate majority leader's office, citing the same tracker as of November 2, 2026, records twenty-five resolutions passed and twenty-three become law. The desk prints the counts with their counters named, because the trackers differ at the edges over which agency actions count as rules, and the underlying statute's ledger—twenty enactments in twenty-eight years, then twenty-three in under two—is consistent on every count the desk reviewed.

Rules stopped in the pipeline

The freeze memorandum is the oldest of the four instruments in continuous use, and its documentary lineage is unbroken. President Reagan's memorandum postponing pending federal regulations issued on January 29, 1981, nine days into his term. The Clinton transition produced an Office of Management and Budget regulatory review memorandum published at 58 Federal Register 6074 on January 22, 1993. Thereafter the memorandum arrives on inauguration day itself, signed by the incoming chief of staff: Andrew Card's “Regulatory Review Plan” for President George W. Bush, published at 66 Federal Register 7702, dated January 20, 2001; Rahm Emanuel's “Regulatory Review” for President Obama, at 74 Federal Register 4435, dated January 20, 2009; Reince Priebus's “Regulatory Freeze Pending Review” for President Trump, dated January 20, 2017; and Ronald Klain's memorandum of the same title for President Biden, dated January 20, 2021. In 2025 the document rose a grade: the “Regulatory Freeze Pending Review” of January 20, 2025 issued as a presidential memorandum over President Trump's own signature. The one transition in the series without a freeze is 1989, when President George H. W. Bush succeeded a president of his own party and had, as the Davis Polk memorandum on the Priebus freeze records, little reason to block the publication of regulations developed under his predecessor's appointees. The language of the recent memoranda is near-identical across parties. The Priebus memorandum of 2017 and the Klain memorandum of 2021 open with the same sentence, word for word: “The President has asked me to communicate to each of you his plan for managing the Federal regulatory process at the outset of his Administration.” Each continues with the same purpose, in order to ensure that the President's appointees or designees have the opportunity to review any new or pending regulations; each directs that unpublished rules be withdrawn from the Office of the Federal Register; each postpones or asks agencies to postpone the effective dates of published rules by sixty days. What the freeze stops, the withdrawal finishes. On September 11, 2025, the Department of Justice published a single Federal Register notice withdrawing sixteen notices of proposed rulemaking, advance notices, and supplemental notices, together with thirty-eight further regulatory actions carried in the Unified Agenda, fifty-four items in one document, “as part of the Federal Government's deregulatory initiative.” Eleven days into the same administration, Executive Order 14192 of January 31, 2025 had set the arithmetic the withdrawals serve, directing that for each new regulation an agency issue, it identify ten existing regulations for repeal—the successor, at five times the rate, of the two-for-one order of 2017 that Executive Order 13992 had revoked in 2021.

Every era's reason

The justifications are filed inside the instruments, and they change vocabulary on the same schedule as the instruments change hands. The freeze memoranda justify themselves identically in every era, as a pause for review: the new president's appointees must have the opportunity to examine what the old president's appointees left in the pipeline, and the memoranda claim no larger warrant than the calendar. The revocation orders speak in the moral vocabulary of their administrations.
