After over four hours, the nationwide ground stoppage at all airports, including Milwaukee Mitchell International, on Friday, November 13, has been lifted. Secretary Duffy held a briefing Friday night in which he blamed old software and a legacy network problem in the air traffic control system for the telecommunication issues, and said normal operations will take time. Secretary Mullin said there was no evidence of a cyber or artificial intelligence attack. The live file records 3,500 airplanes in the air at the time of the stoppage, Delta and United resuming operations, JetBlue resuming its flights on Saturday morning, and Air Canada cancelling all flights to and from the United States. The account calls the stop the third nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks.

Subjective
The Traveler — the ground stop lifts, and weary travellers regroup into Saturday

A rare nationwide ground stop across the United States ended Friday evening after a communications failure hit air traffic control facilities, but passengers at major hubs woke on Saturday to lingering disruptions, crowded terminals and improvised plans. The agency ordered the halt on Friday, November 13, citing extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns tied to a telecommunications outage affecting regional air route traffic control centers, and cancelled the stop shortly after 8:15 p.m. Eastern once controllers had restored enough communications capacity. The incident is described as the first full nationwide ground stop since the January 2023 failure in the Notice to Air Missions system. By early Saturday, November 14, flight tracking data showed departures slowly recovering but volumes still well below typical levels for a November weekend, with airlines re-sequencing aircraft and crews overnight.

Subjective
BlogMickey — flights resume after the four-hour stop, with about 90 Saturday cancellations expected at Orlando

The Federal Aviation Administration lifted its nationwide ground stop on Friday evening, November 13, after more than four hours with no departures from American airports, including Orlando International, and officials warned delays and cancellations will continue while airports and airlines return to full capacity. Secretary Duffy blamed aging air traffic control technology and overloaded routers, said the return to normal will be slow and depends on crew availability, and said airlines will move more aircraft starting Saturday morning. About 15,000 flights were delayed or cancelled across the country on Friday, according to FlightAware data cited by CNN; more than 700 flights within, into or out of the United States are already cancelled for Saturday, and Orlando International told WFTV it expects about 90 cancellations on Saturday.

Subjective
Live and Let’s Fly — the ground stop lifted, the recovery not finished

The Federal Aviation Administration lifted its nationwide ground stop, allowing departures to resume after a communications outage disrupted air travel across the country, but reopening the system does not mean airline schedules are back to normal. Secretary Duffy announced Friday evening that the system had reopened at 8:15 p.m. Eastern and warned that restoring operations would take time, with recovery efforts continuing Saturday. Secretary Mullin said, “We have seen zero evidence this is a cyber attack,” and officials were also examining how older equipment interacts with newer technology. By 8 p.m. Eastern, FlightAware showed more than 10,000 delays and 5,000 cancellations involving American flights. The agency ordered the stop effective 3:54 p.m. Eastern, according to the Air Traffic Control System Command Center as reported by Gizmodo.

Subjective
CNN — Russia evasive after the United States says Europe will join the next talks

Russia remained evasive on Friday after American negotiators said European delegates would join the next round of peace talks with Ukraine. Mr. Kushner posted that both sides had agreed to a European presence, and Mr. Witkoff called the move a very big deal, but the Kremlin responded coolly, neither endorsing a European delegation nor flatly rejecting it: “Putin has never refused to engage with the Europeans,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov told journalists on Friday, adding that Moscow would decide on a dialogue in an expanded format once it understood the Europeans’ actual intentions. On Friday, European Council President António Costa said the European team would be represented by the European Union’s institutions and the E5 nations of France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom, and Chancellor Merz told the Americans, “Please, no surprises.” The account also reports the ground war: at least 10 people killed and 48 injured in Ukraine from Thursday into Friday by regional officials’ figures, nearly 1,198 Ukrainian drones intercepted overnight into Friday in the Russian defense ministry’s account, at least eight people killed in Russia in a CNN tally of governors’ figures, Ukrainian strikes on drone production and repair sites at Rostov-on-Don on Friday, and continuing Starshield speed limits on the front line.

Subjective
Europe Says — the envoys to meet Mr. Putin and President Zelenskyy after the Abu Dhabi talks

American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner plan to meet Russian leader Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday to continue a push for a peace deal after a second day of talks in Abu Dhabi ended in less than two hours. The envoys want to make more progress on the issues discussed, Mr. Kushner told reporters Wednesday, because they see openings and opportunities; territorial issues remain the hardest part, though the sides agreed on a substantial exchange of prisoners. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Mr. Putin will meet the envoys on Thursday morning, according to Interfax. One aim of the Moscow meeting will be to see if Europeans can be added to the format, Mr. Kushner said. The exchange will exceed 1,000 people on each side and may take place within two to three weeks, Russian General Staff official Alexander Zorin said, according to Interfax; the sides also considered an exchange of up to 1,500 prisoners each. Representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Union met the Ukrainian delegation in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday to align positions.

Subjective
HeadlinesXtra — Europe seeks a role in the talks as Washington pursues the largest prisoner exchange

Envoy Jared Kushner said on Thursday that Washington is working toward what he described as the largest prisoner exchange of Russia’s war against Ukraine, potentially reuniting thousands of people with their families; he provided no timetable, list or terms, and no completed exchange has been announced. Mr. Kushner also said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to include European countries in the next round of American-brokered talks. The distinction is drawn plainly: until Moscow and Kyiv confirm the lists, categories of detainees, verification process and transfer arrangements, the exchange remains a negotiating goal rather than a completed humanitarian operation. The Kremlin did not explicitly confirm that Russia had accepted direct European participation. Names in the debate over Europe’s seat include European Council President António Costa, foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and leaders of the Union’s 27 member states gathered in Dublin on Friday, November 13, after the European Political Community summit.

Subjective
SSBCrack News — Ms. Peltola widens her lead in the uncalled Alaska Senate race

Mary Peltola widened her lead over Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan in the latest count of Alaska’s Senate race, though the contest remained uncalled as ballots continued to be tallied. Incomplete results released Friday night showed Ms. Peltola with 49.8 percent of the vote, nearly four percentage points ahead of Senator Sullivan. A New York Times analysis found she was on track to win, but the outcome will depend on the final count and, if neither candidate secures more than half of the first-choice votes, on Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation, expected next week. “We’re still waiting for every ballot to be counted,” Nate Adams, a spokesman for Senator Sullivan, said Friday night. The two other candidates, Republican Gerald L. Heikes and Dan J. Sullivan, an unaffiliated candidate whose name resembles the senator’s, have together received about 4 percent of the vote so far. Democrats have won 55 Senate seats in the analysis’s results; a Peltola victory would bring the total to 56.

Subjective
NewsCord — Ms. Peltola extends her lead after the Alaska ballot count

Alaska’s Division of Elections tallied an additional 5,000 ballots on Thursday, bringing the total counted to over 256,000 and extending Democrat Mary Peltola’s lead over Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan. Ms. Peltola had 49.1 percent of first-choice votes after Thursday’s count, while Senator Sullivan had 46.8 percent, and her lead grew to 5,800 votes, about 1,825 votes more than her lead on Wednesday. The race remained uncalled as officials expected to have counted all eligible ballots by November 18, and the state would use ranked-choice tabulation if no candidate gets more than 50 percent of first-choice votes. Certification is expected November 25.

Subjective
USA Today — the Alaska Senate race remains uncalled: live results

Democrat Mary Peltola is holding a narrow lead over Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, putting Democrats within striking distance of another Senate pickup nearly two weeks after Election Day. The paper’s latest tally as of November 13 shows Ms. Peltola with 49.2 percent of the vote to Senator Sullivan’s 47 percent, with about 91.3 percent of ballots counted and more than 256,000 ballots counted as of Friday, according to Alaska’s Division of Elections. With neither candidate above the 50 percent threshold, the race remains uncalled and could advance to ranked-choice tabulation beginning November 18. A Peltola victory would give Democrats 56 Senate seats.

Subjective
The Business Standard — Iran targets an American radar installation in Bahrain

Iran said its forces hit an American early-warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday, while the United States said it had intercepted the attacks. The Revolutionary Guards initially said in a statement that their air force targeted and destroyed the radar on the island of Bahrain, claiming the attack was retaliation for an American attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, on the shores of the Strait of Hormuz. Several hours later, the American military’s Central Command denied the Guards’ claim that the radar was destroyed and said it stopped two one-way attack drones targeting Bahrain, reporting no casualties or damage. The account’s summary of the war, which began with American and Israeli strikes on February 28, describes the present state as de-escalation with the main issues unresolved.

Subjective
Indian Economic Observer — Central Command denies the radar claim and says two drones were shot down

The United States Central Command on Friday rejected Iran’s claim that its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps destroyed an American early-warning radar installation in Bahrain, stating that two Iranian one-way attack drones targeting the country were intercepted by American forces without causing any injuries or damage. In a post on X, Central Command wrote: “CLAIM: Today, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it attacked a ‘U.S. early-warning radar’ in Bahrain. FACT: The IRGC launched two one-way attack drones toward Bahrain and both were shot down by U.S. forces. There were no injuries or damage.” According to Iran’s Fars News Agency, the Guards said their forces targeted the radar approximately an hour after the alleged attack on the telecommunications infrastructure at Sirik.

Subjective
Times of Maldives — Iran claims the radar strike as President Trump rejects the prospects of a peace deal

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed it destroyed an American early-warning radar system in Bahrain in retaliation for an American strike on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran. Central Command disputed the claim, saying American forces intercepted two Iranian drones and denying that the radar system had been destroyed. President Trump has also dismissed the prospect of a negotiated settlement, declaring that Washington no longer needs a deal with Tehran.

Subjective
Forbes — Iran brings a new peace proposal after the White House claims the war is terminated

President Trump told Congress in a Friday letter that the war in Iran was terminated, issuing the letter just before a deadline that would have required congressional approval to continue military operations; the White House said approval is not necessary because the war has been terminated. Defense Secretary Hegseth also said Thursday that the ceasefire implemented on April 7 means the 60-day clock pauses or stops. Meanwhile, Iran sent a new peace proposal to Pakistani mediators on Thursday, Iranian state media reported Friday. The Senate rejected the Iran War Powers Resolution for a sixth time on Thursday, and the account notes that President Trump, telling reporters Iran is dying to make a deal, did not intend to seek congressional approval.

Subjective
The Apex Wire — Nvidia funded startups to buy its own chips, a Journal report says

Nvidia used its own balance sheet to finance artificial-intelligence startups and data-centre operators so they would keep buying its chips instead of letting prices fall, according to a Wall Street Journal report, as the chipmaker closed its worst week since April 2025, down 13 percent and $573 billion in market value. The report says the financing answered a surplus of silicon and memory ordered from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company: instead of cutting prices, the company funded the customers that would absorb it. Ms. Kress, now interim chief executive, pushed back in a tense August meeting, cutting a proposed OpenAI guarantee from about $250 billion to $125 billion. Nvidia’s filing shows commitments and guarantees of about $530 billion, up from $184 billion a quarter earlier, including $279 billion of supply and capacity obligations and $108.5 billion of maximum gross guarantee exposure. The board is searching for a permanent chief executive and has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as one of several candidates, the account says. Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, November 17, with Ms. Kress presenting.

Subjective
Medium — the man who was Nvidia: what happens now that Mr. Huang is gone

At 7:17 p.m. Indian time on Thursday, November 12, Nvidia posted a press release only a few lines long: Mr. Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately, carrying no words from Mr. Huang. Five weeks earlier, on October 6, Nvidia closed at a record $239.24 a share, worth about $5.78 trillion; on Friday it traded near $160. The November 14 update records that the House Foreign Affairs Committee moved Mr. Huang’s appearance from November 18 to December 1 and warned it would subpoena him if he stopped cooperating; that Representative Mast said Mr. Huang had signalled he would appear; that Wired reported an internal petition asking the board to bring Mr. Huang back had passed 1,600 comments; and that the board is searching for a permanent chief executive, weighing candidates from inside and outside the company. Earnings land on November 17, with guidance of $108 billion in revenue, assuming no data-centre chip sales to China, and Ms. Kress will host the call.

Subjective
Stockbiz — Mr. Huang faces a subpoena from Congress

Nvidia’s board of directors confirmed on November 12 that Mr. Huang had stepped down as chief executive following pressure over allegations involving his private life, and appointed finance chief Colette Kress to lead the group temporarily. On the same day, leaders of three House committees sent a letter asking Mr. Huang to attend a closed-door interview on December 1; the former chief executive had until 8 p.m. on November 13 to agree, or could face a compulsory subpoena, Reuters reported. In the Senate, Banking Committee chairman Tim Scott also asked Mr. Huang and Commerce Secretary Lutnick to testify voluntarily on December 3, while warning subpoenas could be issued if the two did not cooperate. The item runs under the paper’s international headlines for November 14.

Subjective
Reuters, via WIXX — producer prices rise moderately in October, but inflation broadens out

American producer prices rose moderately in October, but inflation at the factory gate posted its largest annual gain in four years, supporting the view that the Federal Reserve could continue raising interest rates after next month’s widely expected increase. The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3 percent last month after an upwardly revised 1.4 percent surge in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said, and shot up 6.5 percent year over year in October, the largest annual gain since November 2022, after advancing 6.3 percent in September. With the producer and consumer data in hand, economists estimated core personal consumption expenditures inflation rose 0.3 percent in October, and forecast it advancing 3.2 percent over the year. Financial markets anticipated another increase in borrowing costs in January, the CME FedWatch tool showed, wavering between a quarter-point hike in December and room for a half-point increase. Governor Waller’s comments and the hot consumer readings stand behind the pricing; the target range stands at 3.75 to 4.00 percent.

Subjective
CoinGabbar — the October producer data puts the December Federal Reserve hike in focus

The October producer price data landed on November 13, 2026, and sent a mixed message: monthly producer inflation slowed to 0.3 percent, below the 0.4 percent economists expected, yet the annual rate climbed to 6.5 percent, the highest since November 2022, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The Federal Reserve meets December 8 and 9. According to market-based reports, the odds of a 25-basis-point hike rose from 76 percent to 89 percent after the consumer release. Chicago Fed President Goolsbee is quoted saying inflation is going the wrong way. The account’s caution stands in its own text: no data release can confirm a hike; only the Federal Reserve can announce its decision, after its December meeting.

Subjective
Particle News — Spain’s two-week campaign kicks off as parties race to mobilize voters

The official campaign opened on Friday, November 13, with Prime Minister Sánchez, Mr. Feijóo and Mr. Abascal launching nationwide tour events in key provinces. Mr. Sánchez set a 75 percent participation target for the November 29 vote, and his party is elevating Ms. Begoña Gómez, planning an event with Brazil’s President Lula da Silva and promising further surprises to mobilize the progressive bloc. The Popular Party is pushing a vote-conversion message, with regional leader Alfonso Rueda urging voters to channel discontent with the government into support for Mr. Feijóo and to prevent Vox from becoming decisive. A GAD3 survey for ABC gives the Popular Party a clear advantage while the state survey projects a Socialist lead, so turnout and tight regional contests such as La Rioja could decide which bloc reaches the 176 seats needed for a progressive majority. Recent events shaping the campaign include the Urda train accident and ministerial fallout and judicial probes touching Socialist circles.

Subjective
RussPain — the Wild interviews lay bare divisions over housing and migration in Spain

Broadcaster Jordi Wild’s campaign interviews put competing positions on housing and migration in focus, alongside a dispute over Ceuta. On housing, Mr. Sánchez wants to change the land law to enable more construction, Ms. Colau opposes speculation, and Mr. Feijóo backed building more homes, linking a million new properties to 500,000 jobs, in a campaign unfolding amid an acute housing-affordability crisis; the housing measures followed a general strike and large demonstrations over housing costs, the Associated Press reported. On the economy, Mr. Sánchez said Spain was experiencing one of the strongest periods in its democratic history and pointed to increases in the minimum wage and pensions; Mr. Feijóo disputed the positive assessment, saying he did not believe the data. On migration, Mr. Feijóo claimed half a million immigrants were receiving payments despite not having worked a single hour in the previous year. Ms. Colau called for tax reform so people with greater wealth pay more, and described Mr. Feijóo as a sincere man of the right.

Subjective
Demócrata — Mr. Sánchez reproaches Mr. Feijóo for not having learned English

The president of the Government and candidate for re-election, Pedro Sánchez, criticized the leader of the Popular Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, for not speaking English or having made an effort to learn it, and highlighted what he called the lack of knowledge Mr. Abascal showed about the pension system, at the official start of the campaign in Arnedo, La Rioja. Mr. Sánchez called for mobilization to reach 75 percent turnout on November 29 and to secure an absolute majority. The paper’s mean of polls, at November 13 across 15 institutes, stands at Popular Party 31.4 percent, Socialists 26.8, Vox 19.1, Frente Amplio 6.3 and ERC 2.4.

entry.title: The Nation's Departures Stop for More Than Four Hours and Resume at 2015, Mr. Huang's 2000 Deadline Passes With No Confirmation in the File, and Friday Closes With the Radar Denied, the War Terminated by Letter and Alaska Still Uncalled
entry.summary: The nation's departures stop for more than four hours and resume at 2015, and the Nvidia deadline passes unconfirmed: the midnight file.
entry.content:
The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

The Nation’s Departures Stop for More Than Four Hours and Resume at 2015, Mr. Huang’s 2000 Deadline Passes With No Confirmation in the File, and Friday Closes With the Radar Denied, the War Terminated by Letter and Alaska Still Uncalled

The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: an afternoon when no departing aircraft could leave an American airport, and an evening when they could again; a congressional deadline that passed in silence; a radar claimed and denied; a war terminated in a letter and continued in a speech; and two counts that spent Friday on paperwork and produced no new total by midnight.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Saturday, November 14, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 42, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Friday, in Edition No. 41, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Friday, in Edition No. 40, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Friday, and in Edition No. 39, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 on Friday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Friday Settled, What It Left Open

Friday settled its newest file in four hours and left its oldest files exactly where the evening edition put them: the nationwide ground stop that began in the afternoon ended at 2015 with departures resumed and no cause established beyond overloaded equipment in an old system; Mr. Huang’s 2000 deadline passed with no written confirmation and no subpoena reported in any account the desk read; the Bahrain radar stands denied by Central Command and claimed by the Guards, with Manama silent; the war stands terminated in the President’s letter to Congress and continued in his Florida speech the same evening; and Alaska and Mississippi produced no new statewide total on their paperwork day. The stop stands in the resumption account filed below: instability at 1536, the order just before 1600, the lift at 2015. Secretary Duffy’s explanation stands in the same account and in the aviation account filed below: switches and routers overloaded with data, in an incredibly old system. Secretary Mullin’s caution stands beside it: no indication of a cyberattack, and nothing ruled out. The Huang deadline stands in the deadline account filed below, at 2000 for a December 1 interview, and midnight records its passing, not its answer. The letter stands in the Forbes account filed below, and the speech in the Florida account filed below. Alaska stands at 125,157 to 119,357 in the official summary filed below, uncalled. Saturday holds the recovery of the airlines’ schedules, and nothing else in this file has a Saturday date.

The Ground Stop: No Departures in the Afternoon, Departures Again at 2015, and No Cause Established

The day’s largest settled fact did not exist when the midday edition collected and was still running when the evening edition collected. At 1536 Eastern the air traffic system experienced instability in radar and communications in its centers and terminal facilities across the country, Secretary Duffy said at a White House briefing after the lift, in the resumption account above and the aviation account above. Just before 1600 the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for all airports, in its words due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety, citing a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers, in the lifting account filed below and in the agency account filed below. Aircraft already in the air were allowed to land; aircraft on the ground could not take off; inbound international flights were managed case by case, in the lifting account. Some international departures on both coasts were approved during the afternoon, in the same account. The advisory as printed carried an end of 2330, in the grounding account filed below and in the corporate account filed below, which timed the order at 1554.

The lift came at 2015, more than four hours after the order, and the accounts of the lift do not agree on the hour to the quarter. The resumption account and the lifting account both give 2015; the agency account gives shortly before 2030 for the cancellation of the stop. Departures resumed; normal operations did not, in every account: planes and crews are out of position, recovery depends on crew availability, some aircraft will move Saturday morning instead, and it will take some time to unwind the afternoon, in the aviation account above. Delta issued a waiver for Friday and Saturday and United a waiver for rescheduling, in the resumption account. On cause, the file holds two official sentences and no finding: the switches and routers got overloaded with data and gave inconsistent data, and fixes reduced the overloading, in Secretary Duffy’s account; and newer technology overwhelming the older system, in Secretary Mullin’s preliminary account, which the aviation account notes did not establish whether an upgrade contributed. On attack, Secretary Mullin said there is no indication of a cyberattack, that it appears mechanically driven, and that officials are still looking and do not rule anything out, in the resumption account and the lifting account. The National Weather Service reported nationwide internet and communications issues the same day, with no immediate indication of a connection, in the lifting account. Settled: the stop, its hours, and its lift. Open: its cause, and Saturday’s schedules.

The counts of what the stop cost stand apart by thousands, and the desk prints them as counts of different things at different hours. Reuters, in the lifting account, reports more than 1,000 flights canceled and nearly 10,000 delayed. FlightAware, in the resumption account, shows nearly 5,000 flights canceled on Friday and nearly 800 cancellations already listed for Saturday. The agency account, at 2042, reports more than 750 delayed and more than 573 canceled. Cirium, in a briefing at 1905 supplied to the aviation account, counts 4,103 flights as canceled or no-fly out of 26,284 scheduled departures—a combined measure its own briefing cautions may include earlier cancellations—and 827 diverted-flight records for the day, of which 670 returned to their origin. About 11,000 flights and more than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to depart after 1600, in the same briefing; how many were ultimately disrupted is not established in any account. Two historical sentences also stand apart and stand in the Cocked Hat: the second nationwide ground stop since September 11, 2001, in the agency, grounding and resumption accounts, against not the first since September 11, because of January 11, 2023, in the aviation account.

Bahrain at Midnight: The Denial Stands, the Warning Stands, and Manama Has Not Spoken

Nothing entered the Bahrain file between the evening edition and midnight, and the desk records the standstill at its full size, because the file is the day’s war file in miniature. The Guards’ claim stands: their Aerospace Force targeted and destroyed an American early-warning radar on the island of Bahrain, at Jabal ad Dukhan in one account, in retaliation for an air attack on a telecommunications tower at Sirik, in the CNN account filed below and in the drones account filed below. Central Command’s denial stands: two one-way attack drones launched toward Bahrain, both shot down, no injuries, no damage, and the radar claim false, in the agency account filed below. The Guards’ warning stands: the Aerospace Force on full alert to respond without limits in the strait, and Commander-in-Chief Vahidi’s warning that the slightest aggression would draw devastating and painful strikes, in the warning account filed below. No imagery, no coordinates accepted by the other side, no intercept footage and no Bahraini statement stands in any account the desk read by midnight; the drones account notes Manama had not confirmed any attack on a radar installation as of Friday evening. The tanker claim of the morning stands unverified, and the strait’s traffic stands at roughly 65 percent below pre-conflict levels in the British agency’s weekly report through November 10, in the warning account. Settled, on both governments’ accounts: two drones were launched toward Bahrain. Open: everything they hit or did not hit, and who struck Sirik.

The War at Midnight: Terminated by Letter at the Deadline, Continued by Speech in the Evening

The President’s two Friday sentences stand side by side in the midnight file, and the desk does not reconcile them. In the letter to Speaker Johnson on the 60-day War Powers deadline day, the hostilities that began on February 28 have terminated, there has been no exchange of fire since the ceasefire of April 7, and approval from Congress was never needed, in the Forbes account at the top of this report. In Florida hours later, at The Villages, the President claimed victory, repeated that virtually all of Iran’s military assets have been eliminated, and said the United States will not leave early and have the problem arise in three more years, because Iran is not coming through with the kind of peace deal the United States has to have, in the Florida account at the top of this report. The same account carries his Friday position on the statute itself: he did not intend to seek congressional approval, and the War Powers Act was, in his word, totally unconstitutional. The blockade, which neither the letter nor the speech ends, continues to prohibit ships from reaching or leaving Iranian ports, in the resolution account filed below.

Congress’s Friday stands as the evening edition printed it, and midnight adds nothing to it. The chamber left Washington without acting; the Senate’s sixth rejection of a war powers resolution, 47 to 50 on Thursday, stands as its last word; Senator Murkowski’s authorization, described by its author as restraint, stands in preparation, with a further measure promised when the Senate reconvenes if the deadline passed without a credible plan, in the deadline account filed below. Against the letter, the same account states the other reading in one sentence: without action from Congress, the administration now has 30 days to wind down military actions absent authorization. The letter’s own side carries its own split on the ceasefire date: April 7 in the President’s letter and Secretary Hegseth’s testimony as the Forbes account carries it, April 8 in the Secretary’s testimony as the resolution account carries it. Settled: the letter was sent on deadline day, the speech was given the same evening, and Congress did not vote. Open: which reading of the clock governs the next 30 days, and what terminated means for a blockade still in place.

Nvidia at Midnight: The 2000 Deadline Passed, the After-Hours Price Fell, and November 17 Is the Next Date

At midnight the Nvidia file’s clock has run out, and the desk files the deadline as passed, not as answered. Three House chairs—Mr. Mast, Mr. Moolenaar and Mr. Crawford—required Mr. Huang’s written confirmation by 2000 Eastern on Friday of a closed-door, transcribed interview on December 1, or a subpoena from the Foreign Affairs Committee, in the deadline account at the top of this report and in the wire account filed below. No written confirmation, and no issued subpoena, stands in any account the desk read by midnight. The agreement in principle stands where Thursday left it: Mr. Huang has agreed to answer lawmakers’ questions, Chairman Mast said, in the testimony account filed below, which adds that Mr. Huang and the company have not commented on the December 1 date. The rest of the calendar stands: Mr. Teter for December 2 on the same terms, Under Secretary Kessler at a December 3 hearing at 1000, Senator Scott’s track asking Mr. Huang on December 3 and Secretary Lutnick—who has agreed to appear—on December 10, in the summons account filed below. Inside the company nothing moved in the evening hours: Mr. Huang resigned, Ms. Kress is interim chief executive, the Justice Department has reached no conclusion on Ms. Alice Huang, and Beijing’s denial stands. No finding has been made by the board, by any committee or by any court on any allegation in this file.

The stock’s evening was a continuation of its day, at a lower price. Nvidia closed at $162.85, down $3.34 or 2.0 percent, on volume of 360.7 million shares, in the market data page filed below and in the downgrade account filed below, which carries HSBC’s move of the day: a downgrade to hold and a price target cut from $375 to $170, on the uncertainty until a permanent succession plan is laid out. The after-hours price at 2000 Eastern stood at $161.041, down 1.11 percent from the close, in the market data page—against $161.9299 at 1655 in the evening edition’s print of the same page, two prints of one evening, both filed. For the week the shares stand down about 12 percent, and below $4 trillion in one closing account and at $4.19 trillion in the market data page, in the corporate account at the top of this report and the market data page; the difference stands in the Cocked Hat. The company’s November 17 report, its first under Ms. Kress, is the next dated fact in the file.

Prices, Markets and Oil at Midnight: The Prints Stand as the Evening Printed Them

Midnight adds no new figure to Friday’s economic file, and files its three facts once, as they stand. Producer prices rose 0.3 percent in October against 0.4 percent expected, September revised to 1.4 percent, and the year at 6.5 percent, the largest 12-month rise since November 2022, in the Bureau’s release filed below. The closes stand: the Dow Jones Industrial Average up 0.10 percent at 52,347.55, the S&P 500 down 0.40 percent at 7,561.67, the Nasdaq Composite down 0.91 percent at 25,136.27, in the closing account filed below. The selling was in the chips: the Philadelphia semiconductor index down 6 percent in the wire’s intraday account, in the wire account filed below, and Advanced Micro Devices down 8.75 percent at $534.06 at the close, in the closing account. Oil stands with the agency’s surplus above it: the International Energy Agency’s November report puts supply above demand for the first time since the war began, inventories up 52 million barrels in October, in the report filed below; Brent stood at $95.77 and West Texas Intermediate at $88.57 in the late print timed 1746 GMT, both down about 2 percent for the week, in the wire account filed below. Settled: the print, the closes and the surplus, on their sources. Open: the Federal Reserve’s December path, which Friday’s annual figure argued over and did not settle.

Dublin at Midnight: No Name, No Number, No Date, for a Second Night

Friday produced no new sentence in the talks file in any account the desk read, and the desk files the silence as the day’s entry in that file. The shape stands as Thursday made it: the envoys’ claim that Europe will join the next round and that the prisoner exchange is agreed and will be the largest of the war, in the envoys account filed below; Moscow’s readout confirming no European seat, in the talks account filed below; and the wire’s summary that the exact figure is still to be announced and that Europe is to appoint a single person, in the Australian agency account filed below. President Zelenskyy’s figure of the day before—1,000 to 1,200 a side—stands as the only number in the file, unattributed to any agreement. Ms. Kallas’s treaty reading, Chancellor Merz’s E3 and five, and President Macron’s format-to-be-determined stand as the three answers to who fills the chair. The Coalition of the Willing in Berlin next week is the next occasion named in the file, and the Presidents’ meeting at APEC in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19 is the next dated meeting of any kind. Settled for a second night: the expansion is announced in Washington and Kyiv. Open for a second night: the name, the number, the date, the place, the land and the ceasefire.

The Cocked Hat

Where the midnight’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On the ground stop’s lift: 2015 in the resumption and lifting accounts, against shortly before 2030 in the agency account. On its cost: more than 1,000 canceled and nearly 10,000 delayed in Reuters; nearly 5,000 canceled in FlightAware; more than 573 canceled and 750 delayed at 2042 in the agency account; and 4,103 canceled or no-fly at 1905 in Cirium’s combined measure, which cautions it may include earlier cancellations. On its history: the second nationwide stop since September 11, 2001, in three accounts, against not the first since September 11, because January 2023 paused departures too, in the aviation account—and first since January 2023 in the agency account, which is the same fact in the other direction. On Bahrain: a radar destroyed, in the Guards’ statement, against two drones intercepted with no injuries and no damage, in Central Command’s, with no evidence produced that the other side accepts and no word from Manama. On the war: terminated with the April 7 ceasefire, in the President’s letter, against will not leave early, in his Florida speech the same evening, and a 30-day wind-down now running in the deadline account’s reading of the statute; and the ceasefire dated April 7 by the President and April 8 in one account of the Secretary’s testimony. On Mr. Huang’s deadline: passed at 2000, with an agreement to testify in principle in the testimony account and no comment on the December 1 date in the same account, and neither a confirmation nor a subpoena in any account. On Nvidia’s value: below $4 trillion at the close in the corporate account, against $4.19 trillion in the market data page. On Alaska’s counted share: about 88 percent in the wire-derived accounts, against about 91.3 percent in the national account, on the same 125,157 to 119,357 total. On Mississippi: Mr. Colom at 479,197 votes in the results record, against a call-time margin of 4,669 out of 962,237 in the timeline account, on a day given to county certification with no statewide total reported. On Spain: the Socialists at 26.8 percent in the fifteen-institute average, at 33.3 percent in the state survey. Against the triangle, the midnight’s single-valued facts are these: the ground stop was issued just before 1600 on Friday and lifted in the evening, departures resumed, and no cause was established beyond the officials’ preliminary accounts; Mr. Huang’s 2000 deadline passed with nothing reported; Central Command denied the radar claim and reported two drones intercepted without damage, and the Guards warned of an unlimited response; the President’s letter was sent, his Florida speech was given, and Congress did not act; producer prices rose 0.3 percent in October and 6.5 percent on the year; the Dow closed up 0.10 percent, the S&P 500 down 0.40 percent and the Nasdaq down 0.91 percent, with Nvidia at $162.85 and $161.041 after hours; Brent stood at $95.77 in the late print; Alaska stands at 125,157 to 119,357, uncalled, with its Friday batch unreported at midnight; Mississippi’s counties spent Friday certifying, with December 3 the state’s date; Spain’s campaign completed its first full day; and Europe’s chair, the prisoner number and the next talks date remain open for a second night. The log turns. Saturday holds the airlines’ recovery, and the Overnight Watch collects at 0400.

Subjective
WVLT, from wire reports — the nationwide ground stop is lifted, the agency says

The Federal Aviation Administration said airplane departures could resume after it lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems. The agency had grounded flights nationwide on Friday afternoon, causing hundreds of flights to be diverted; the stop was issued due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety, in an alert at around 4 p.m., and was canceled shortly before 8:30 p.m. Officials said the extraordinary circumstances were caused by communications problems at regional air traffic control centers, and that a telecommunications outage prompted the stop, which halted thousands of flights. More than 750 flights had been delayed and more than 573 canceled as of 8:42 p.m., and Delta Air Lines issued a travel waiver for its passengers. The account calls the stop the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023 and the second since the aftermath of September 11, 2001.

The results record carried 479,197 votes for Mr. Colom in the tally the evening edition printed, in a race the Associated Press called for Mr. Colom on November 11. Senator Hyde-Smith conceded on Wednesday. The state’s counties were to submit certified results on Friday, November 13, and statewide certification is scheduled for December 3; Mississippi has no automatic recount in a statewide race.

Subjective
People — the President offers praise to the Mississippi Democrat

Mr. Colom campaigned on the line outside the President’s own October rally, telling everybody in the line what a good job he did, and the President gives him a lot of credit for it. “I don’t know the gentleman, but I give him credit,” the President said, in the account’s words. The praise came after the Associated Press called Mississippi’s Senate race for Mr. Colom and Senator Hyde-Smith conceded.

Subjective
Mississippi Independent — a look back at how Mississippi went Democratic for the first time in more than 40 years

A dated timeline of the Mississippi race: on November 11 Hinds County finalized its count, accepting 817 of 2,426 affidavit ballots and pushing Mr. Colom’s lead past 4,400 votes, and just before 5 p.m. Central the Associated Press called the race after a Jackson County update, with Mr. Colom leading by 4,669 votes out of 962,237 counted. Counties certify results November 13, the secretary of state declares final results December 3, candidates have 20 days to file a contest, and Mississippi has no recount law. Mr. Colom takes office January 3, 2027, when Democrats assume the majority in the account’s telling.

Subjective
Demócrata — Mr. Sánchez takes aim at Mr. Feijóo in La Rioja

Prime Minister Sánchez used his first campaign rally in Arnedo, La Rioja, on Friday, starting at 17:00 at the frontón, to attack Mr. Feijóo for his explanations of photographs with Marcial Dorado and for acknowledging he does not know English in an interview. The page carries the average of the polls as of November 13, the mean of the latest study from each of 15 institutes: the Popular Party 31.4 percent, the Socialists 26.8, Vox 19.1, Frente Amplio 6.3 and ERC 2.4.

Subjective
El Constitucional — Mr. Sánchez opens the campaign in La Rioja and asks for 176 seats

Prime Minister Sánchez set two figures for his campaign launch this Friday in Arnedo, La Rioja: 75 percent participation and 176 seats for the Socialists. In his first rally after the official start of the campaign, he called for mobilization to achieve an absolute majority and prevent a Popular Party government with Vox; if Mr. Feijóo reaches La Moncloa with Mr. Abascal, he warned, the Vox leader could end in the Vice Presidency, and his own bet for that office is Mr. Carlos Cuerpo. After Arnedo, the next stop on Friday is the Labrit frontón in Pamplona, with the Navarrese president and the Socialist candidates.

Subjective
Brussels Signal — Spain’s campaign opens with polls pointing to a right-wing majority

The general election campaign has officially begun, with the main parties holding opening rallies across the country ahead of the November 29 vote; the campaign started at midnight on November 13 and runs until November 27. Prime Minister Sánchez opened his campaign on Thursday evening at the Fibes congress centre in Seville before about 4,000 supporters, according to EFE. Mr. Feijóo launched his bid at a sports centre in Badalona, near Barcelona, under the slogan El cambio necesario. All 15 private polls published up to November 12 gave the Popular Party and Vox a combined absolute majority, averaging 50.6 percent of the vote. The state survey put the Socialists first on 33.3 percent.

entry.title: NIMBYism: What the Record Shows About the Veto Over Housing, Energy, and Data Centers
entry.summary: Why support for housing, energy, and data centers collapses at specific addresses: the research on NIMBY opposition, hearings, and vetoes.
entry.content:
Special Report

Concrete · Cement · Rome · The Concrete Club · Carbon · John Wilson

Objective

NIMBYism: What the Record Shows About the Veto Over Housing, Energy, and Data Centers

Support for housing, clean energy, data centers, and homeless services runs high in the abstract and collapses at specific addresses, in every ideology and tenure, for reasons the research literature has now measured: losses weigh roughly twice gains, a home is an undiversifiable asset, developer profit alone raises opposition by twenty points, and the hearings that decide hear almost only from opponents.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1945 ET, Friday, November 13, 2026.

The opposition has a consistent structure across fifty years of American land-use fights, and the research literature now describes it with unusual precision. Residents support housing, clean energy, data centers, and homeless services in the abstract at high rates. They oppose the same facilities at specific addresses near their homes at high rates. The gap between the two positions is not explained by ideology: renters in expensive cities register it at nearly the same level as homeowners, and liberal homeowners register it alongside conservatives. Three mechanisms account for most of the measured effect. Losses register roughly twice as heavily as equivalent gains. A home is most owners' largest asset and cannot be diversified, so its protection dominates local voting. And opposition rises measurably when a developer's profit is made salient, by twenty percentage points in the best-known experiment, an effect its authors attribute to resentment of the developer's gain rather than fear of the resident's loss. The venues that decide these questions hear almost exclusively from opponents: in the largest study of hearing participation, about two-thirds of commenters opposed the housing before them and about fifteen percent supported it. The outcomes are legible in the record: a 495-home project on a San Francisco parking lot reversed on environmental grounds in 2021 and still unbuilt in 2026; a 25,000-job Amazon campus withdrawn from Queens in 2019 while polls showed most New Yorkers approved of it; data-center projects worth $130 billion blocked or delayed in the first quarter of 2026 alone.

The gap, measured

Michael Hankinson's study of San Francisco's 2015 election and a national survey, published in the American Political Science Review in 2018, found that renters in high-rent cities express opposition to market-rate housing near them at a level similar to homeowners, while simultaneously supporting large increases in their city's overall housing supply. Hankinson calls the preferences scale-dependent: support at the scale of the city, opposition at the scale of the street. William Marble and Clayton Nall, in the Journal of Politics, found the same split running through ideology. Liberal homeowners, in their title's phrase, are where "self-interest trumps ideology": they endorse egalitarian and redistributive housing policies in principle and oppose dense housing development in their own communities, with homeownership predicting local opposition more reliably than party or professed belief. New York City's 2023 Housing and Vacancy Survey supplies the context in which these preferences operate: a net rental vacancy rate of 1.41 percent, the lowest since the survey began in 1968, with roughly 33,000 units available for rent in a city of 8.3 million.

The mechanisms in the literature

Prospect theory, the framework Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky published in 1979 and extended in 1992, estimates that losses weigh roughly twice as heavily as equivalent gains; their 1992 estimate of the loss-aversion coefficient was 2.25, and later meta-analyses center somewhat lower without disturbing the asymmetry. Applied to a development proposal, the accounting is structural: the costs, construction, traffic, shadow, change itself, are immediate, visible, and assigned to identifiable households, while the benefits, marginally lower regional rents, a larger tax base, grid capacity, are delayed and divided among millions. William Fischel's homevoter hypothesis, set out in his 2001 book of that name, adds the balance sheet. For most owners the home is by far their largest financial asset; unlike stockholders they cannot diversify it across communities, and Fischel argues that fear of a capital loss turns owners into systematic voters for whatever protects the asset, including restrictions on nearby density. The third mechanism is the least comfortable. Paavo Monkkonen and Michael Manville of UCLA ran a survey experiment with more than 1,300 Los Angeles County respondents and found that telling respondents a developer would earn a large profit raised opposition to a housing project by twenty percentage points, double the increase produced by a traffic warning and comparable to the neighborhood-character warning. Their published conclusion: "some opposition to housing is motivated not by residents' fears of their own losses, but resentment of others' gains." Opposition, in the experiment, could be purchased by framing alone, without changing anything about the project.

The venue

Katherine Levine Einstein, David Glick, and Maxwell Palmer coded thousands of comments from planning and zoning hearings across 97 Massachusetts communities for their 2019 book Neighborhood Defenders. The people who speak are not a cross-section of the public. They are disproportionately older, whiter, more male, and longer-tenured than their communities, and they are far more likely to own their homes; about 41 percent lived on the same block as the proposed project. Roughly two-thirds of commenters opposed the housing under consideration; about fifteen percent spoke in favor. The people who would occupy unbuilt housing have no standing in this venue: they do not yet live in the jurisdiction, and many do not know the hearing exists. In California, the environmental-review statute supplies a second venue. A September 2026 Holland & Knight study of 498 appellate decisions under the California Environmental Quality Act found that housing was the largest single category of appealed project, at 25.5 percent of decisions; about 90 percent of the challenged housing projects were infill; project approvals ultimately prevailed in 75 percent of the decisions, after the delay the litigation imposed; and earlier analyses by the same firm found that suits filed in 2020 alone challenged roughly 48,000 approved housing units, and that only 13 percent of CEQA lawsuits were brought by anyone with a prior record of environmental advocacy. In 2025 the California legislature exempted most urban infill housing from CEQA review, a statutory concession that the channel had become a general-purpose instrument of delay.

Case file: a parking lot in San Francisco

At 469 Stevenson Street in San Francisco, a developer proposed a 27-story building with 495 rental homes, 73 of them affordable, on a 28,790-square-foot surface parking lot holding 176 cars. The Planning Commission certified the project's environmental impact report on July 29, 2021. On appeal by a neighborhood consortium, the Board of Supervisors voted 8 to 3 on October 26, 2021 to reverse the certification and require further study, citing, among other things, gentrification and geotechnical questions, on a site that was a parking lot. The state housing department warned the rejection risked violating the Housing Accountability Act. A partially recirculated report followed; the project was re-approved in 2023, into a high-interest-rate construction market. As of 2026, nine years after the project was first proposed, the site remains a surface parking lot and no homes have been built.

Case file: Amazon in Queens

On November 13, 2018, Amazon announced it would split its second headquarters between Arlington, Virginia, and Long Island City, Queens: 25,000 jobs and $2.5 billion of investment at each site. New York's package comprised $1.525 billion in performance-based state incentives, including up to $1.2 billion in job-linked tax credits and a $505 million capital grant; with city tax benefits the total was universally reported as roughly $3 billion, most of it contingent tax relief on activity that had not yet occurred rather than cash in hand. Opposition organized immediately, led by state and city officials and by Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, whose district borders Long Island City, on grounds that included the subsidies, the secrecy of the negotiation, and Amazon's labor practices. Polling cut against the opposition's premise and for its strongest argument simultaneously: Quinnipiac found New York City voters approved of the deal 57 to 26 percent, while splitting 46 to 44 on the incentive package itself; Siena found 56 percent of state voters approved even with the incentives stated. On February 14, 2019, Amazon withdrew, citing the opposition of state and local politicians, and quoted a 70 percent support figure that matches neither published poll. Ocasio-Cortez, celebrating the withdrawal the same day, said: "if we were willing to give away $3 billion for this deal, we could invest those $3 billion in our district ourselves if we wanted to," naming teachers and subway repairs. The statement treated contingent tax relief as a spendable fund, which, as critics across the spectrum noted at the time, it was not. The aftermath is on the record: the centerpiece city-owned site, a Department of Education warehouse at 44-36 Vernon Boulevard, remained in that use for roughly six years; in February 2025 the city issued a request for expressions of interest to redevelop it. Amazon, for its part, expanded in Manhattan instead, leasing office space at Hudson Yards and hiring thousands of employees in New York without a headquarters campus or the Queens incentives.

The complication: data centers

The data-center fights of the last three years follow the same geometry, concentrated costs against diffuse benefits, but the local benefit side of the ledger is genuinely thinner, and the record supports part of the opposition's case. Virginia's Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, in its December 2024 study of the world's largest data-center market, reported industry figures of approximately 50 full-time permanent workers, about half of them contractors, at a typical 250,000-square-foot facility, against roughly 1,500 workers on site at peak construction. The fiscal side runs the other way: in the five Virginia localities with mature markets, data-center revenue supplied from under 1 percent to 31 percent of total local revenue in fiscal 2023, the 31 percent in Loudoun County. The resource side is the opposition's strongest ground: data centers consumed 26 percent of Virginia's electricity sales in 2023, and the commission's independent forecast found that unconstrained demand would double the state's total power demand within about a decade. Nationally, Data Center Watch, the tracking project whose figures Bloomberg and the banks cite, counted projects worth $130 billion blocked or delayed amid local opposition in the first quarter of 2026 alone, with at least $156 billion across 2025; the project's period figures overlap and are not additive. Opposition groups numbered more than 800 across 49 states by early 2026.

The complication: shelters and supportive housing

The facilities most often opposed on predicted-harm grounds have the most direct evidence available, and it runs against the predictions. The NYU Furman Center's study of New York City supportive housing found that property values within 500 feet of the developments dipped modestly during construction and then rose steadily after opening, performing no worse than comparable properties elsewhere. A 2026 working paper by Brown, Amoah, and co-authors found the temporal structure of the opposition itself: voters living 100 to 300 meters from newly opened homeless facilities became more supportive of homelessness spending after the facilities opened. The opposition, in their phrase, is "more prospective than retrospective": it is strongest before the facility exists and weakens on contact with it.

The responses on the record

Three bodies of evidence describe what happens when the veto is overridden or removed. Evan Mast's moving-chain research, published in the Journal of Urban Economics in 2023, traced some 52,000 residents of new market-rate buildings through six rounds of moves: building 100 new market-rate units leads 45 to 70 people to move out of below-median-income neighborhoods within about five years, as each vacated unit opens for the next household. Asquith, Mast, and Reed, in the Review of Economics and Statistics, found that large new apartment buildings in low-income areas lower rents within a few hundred meters by 5 to 7 percent relative to comparable areas farther away. At the scale of a whole city, Auckland's 2016 Unitary Plan upzoned roughly three-quarters of the city's residential land; a synthetic-control study by Greenaway-McGrevy and So found that eight years after the reform, Auckland rents were about 23 percent lower than the no-reform counterfactual, alongside a documented construction boom. New York's City of Yes, adopted December 5, 2024, is the American test now running: the Department of City Planning projects it will enable 82,000 homes over fifteen years, a projection of permitted capacity rather than of completed buildings.

What the record does not show

No study in this literature measures hypocrisy, and none needs to. The findings are consistent with sincere holders of every position involved: the loss-aversion asymmetry is a property of human cognition, the homevoter's incentive is rational given the asset, the hearing skew is a property of who can attend a weeknight meeting, and the spite component, though measured, accounts for a share of opposition rather than its whole. What the record shows is a system in which each of those individually comprehensible forces points the same way, toward refusal, and in which the beneficiaries of building, future residents, future employees, future taxpayers, are structurally absent from every room where the decision is made. The outcomes are therefore not a mystery requiring a theory of bad faith. They are the arithmetic of the rooms.

entry.title: Central Command Denies the Bahrain Radar Was Hit and Says Two Drones Were Shot Down, the President Tells Congress the War Is Terminated on the War Powers Deadline Day, and Wall Street Closes Mixed With Nvidia Down 2.0 Percent
entry.summary: Central Command denies the Bahrain radar was hit and reports two drones downed, and the president tells Congress the war is terminated.
entry.content:
The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 33 items.

Subjective
Military.com, from the Associated Press — the military downs two Iranian attack drones as Iran claims a strike on a radar in Bahrain

The United States military said it intercepted two Iranian attack drones headed toward Bahrain, as the Revolutionary Guard claimed it struck an American early warning radar system in the kingdom. Central Command said there were no injuries or damage. Iran’s official IRNA news agency quoted a Guard statement saying the attack on the radar system followed an American strike on a telecommunications pole in the southern Iranian port of Sirik. Neither Iran’s claim of striking the radar nor its account of the tanker incident could be independently verified.

Subjective
CNN — Iran targets an American military site in the Gulf for the first time in two months as hopes for a deal fade

Iran said it targeted an American military installation in Bahrain early Friday in retaliation for what it described as an American attack on Iranian territory, marking its first attempt to strike a military facility in a Gulf state in more than two months. Central Command said later Friday that American forces shot down two Iranian drones launched toward Bahrain, reporting no injuries or damage, and said the claim that Iran attacked a radar system was false. The Guards, carried by Tasnim, called the action a serious warning to Washington.

Subjective
House of Saud — the Guards warn of an unlimited response over the Strait of Hormuz

The Guards’ Aerospace Force declared on Friday that it stands on full alert to respond without limits to any repeated aggression in the Strait of Hormuz, hours after the Guards claimed a destroyed American radar in Bahrain; Central Command denied the claim, saying it intercepted two Iranian one-way attack drones with no injuries or damage. Commander-in-Chief Ahmad Vahidi separately warned through Tasnim that the slightest aggression would draw devastating and painful strikes. The account puts commercial transits in the strait at roughly 65 percent below pre-conflict baselines in the British agency’s weekly report through November 10, and notes the Guards did not name the United States specifically over Sirik and Central Command has not publicly acknowledged the Sirik strike.

Subjective
Magna Bureau — Iran says it destroyed a radar in Bahrain; Washington says it shot the drones down

The Guards said on Friday, November 13, 2026, that they targeted and destroyed an American early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for an air attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, and framed the strike as a warning over aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz. Several hours later Central Command denied any radar was destroyed and said two one-way attack drones were launched toward Bahrain and both intercepted, with no casualties and no damage. Neither side has produced evidence the other accepts, and neither claim has been independently confirmed.

Subjective
Forbes, mirrored — the President tells Congress the Iran war is terminated

President Trump said the war in Iran has been terminated, in a letter to Congress on Friday as the administration argues it does not need congressional approval to continue the military operation. The letter, to Speaker Mike Johnson, was issued on the 60-day deadline established by the War Powers Act, which requires congressional approval to continue military operations. The President noted there has been no exchange of fire between the United States and Iran since a ceasefire began on April 7. Secretary Hegseth said Thursday the April 7 ceasefire means the 60-day clock pauses or stops, a position that drew pushback from some Republicans. The Senate rejected the Iran War Powers Resolution for a sixth time on Thursday.

Subjective
Gold Coast Vets News — Congress ignores the key deadline as Republicans ready restraint on the war

Congress left Washington without acting against the President’s Iran war, despite growing concern among Republicans about what comes next. The 60-day deadline in the War Powers Resolution, requiring Congress to authorize or halt the war, came and went Friday while lawmakers were back home. Senator Murkowski has been working on an Authorization for Use of Military Force that she describes as more than an authorization, as restraint; a senator quoted in the account intends to introduce a measure once the Senate reconvenes if the 60-day mark passes without a credible plan. The President wrote to congressional leaders Friday that he never needed their say-so and that hostilities, despite scant skirmishes and an ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, had terminated: there has been no exchange of fire since April 7, and the hostilities that began on February 28 have terminated. Without action from Congress, the account states, the administration now has 30 days to wind down military actions absent authorization.

Subjective
Outside the Beltway — the War Powers Resolution and the Friday deadline

Under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, the President must notify Congress within 48 hours of military action and withdraw troops 60 days later unless lawmakers declare war or authorize force; the expectation on Capitol Hill was that the deadline expires on Friday. In testimony Thursday, Secretary Hegseth said the ceasefire with Iran, which he dated to April 8, stopped the countdown. While airstrikes have halted, the American military continues to enforce a blockade prohibiting ships from reaching or leaving Iranian ports. A Senate measure to halt the conflict failed for the sixth time on Thursday, by 47 to 50, with Senator Collins the only new vote in support.

Subjective
Bureau of Labor Statistics — Producer Price Indexes, October 2026

The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3 percent in October, seasonally adjusted. Final demand prices advanced 1.4 percent in September and 0.4 percent in August. On an unadjusted basis, the index for final demand increased 6.5 percent for the 12 months ended in October, the largest 12-month rise since moving up 7.4 percent in November 2022. For the 12 months ended in October, the index for final demand goods increased 10.2 percent, the largest 12-month rise since advancing 10.5 percent in October 2022. The November release is scheduled for December 15.

Subjective
Reuters, via SRN News — Wall Street slides as the Nvidia overhang weighs on technology shares

The major American stock indexes fell on Friday as fresh concerns about Nvidia reignited a selloff in technology shares, while softer October producer prices offered little relief. Nvidia’s shares plunged 4.3 percent intraday and were on track for their longest streak of weekly losses since October 2012 after Mr. Huang’s resignation on Thursday, following scrutiny of his relationship with a businesswoman suspected by the United States of spying for Beijing. The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell 6 percent, with Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom dropping 10 and 7 percent respectively. At 11:23 a.m. Eastern, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 122.12 points, or 0.23 percent, to 52,174.97, the S&P 500 lost 76.88 points, or 1.01 percent, to 7,515.49, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 441.78 points, or 1.74 percent, to 24,923.79. The technology index was the biggest loser on the S&P 500, dropping 3 percent. The producer index shot up 6.5 percent year over year, its largest annual gain since November 2022.

Subjective
TradingKey — the Nasdaq extends its drop as technology leads the declines at the close

On Friday, November 13, American stocks diverged as Nvidia extended its decline, dragging down the Nasdaq and the S&P 500, while the Dow closed slightly higher. At the close, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.10 percent to 52,347.55, the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.91 percent to 25,136.27, and the S&P 500 fell 0.40 percent to 7,561.67. Advanced Micro Devices fell 8.75 percent to $534.06. The October producer index rose less than expected on the month, which had lifted stocks in early trading; the year-over-year increase climbed to its highest since November 2022, keeping inflation pressure and the Federal Reserve outlook in focus.

Subjective
SMW Markets — the biggest movers of November 13, at the close

Wall Street finished mixed on Friday, November 13, as the selling in artificial intelligence stocks picked up again. The S&P 500 slipped 0.40 percent to 7,561.67 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.91 percent to 25,136.27, while the Dow edged up 0.10 percent. Nvidia closed down 2.0 percent at $162.85 in the closing table, sourced to Yahoo Finance at the 4:00 p.m. Eastern close, a second day of losses after Mr. Huang’s resignation, with the finance chief, Ms. Kress, stepping in as interim chief executive.

Subjective
Stock Market Watch — market digest, Friday, November 13, 2026

The closing digest gives the Dow Jones at 52,347.55, up 0.10 percent; the S&P 500 at 7,561.67, down 0.40 percent; the Nasdaq at 25,136.27, down 0.91 percent; the Russell 2000 at 2,790.49, down 0.31 percent; the VIX at 19.29, up 3.16 percent; gold at $3,878.70, down 0.17 percent; and West Texas Intermediate crude at $89.01, up 0.30 percent. The digest describes a fractured close, with a shock resignation in the technology sector and sticky inflation data, and notes semiconductor peers AMD down 10.4 percent and Broadcom down 5.3 percent in its account of the selloff.

Subjective
Finnhub — Nvidia market data, November 13

The market closed at 4:00 p.m. Eastern on November 13 with the latest price at $162.85, a reported change of minus $3.34, or minus 2.0097 percent, from the previous close of $166.19; the session is given open $169.905, high $170, low $158.39. The after-hours price at 4:55 p.m. is given at $161.9299, down 0.56 percent from the regular close. The November 12 session closed at $166.19 and November 11 at $173.73. Market value is given at $4.19 trillion, the five-session return at minus 10.32 percent, and third-quarter results are estimated for November 17, with expected earnings per share of 2.523 on revenue of $111.203 billion.

Subjective
AI Stock Wire — AMD and Broadcom erase the post-resignation rally as the chips slide

Chip stocks fell sharply on November 13, and the two rivals that rallied the day Mr. Huang resigned gave the rally back: AMD was down 10.5 percent at $524.09 at 12:25 p.m. Eastern, and Broadcom was down 5.3 percent at $344.90, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down 4.5 percent at that hour. Nvidia was down 3.1 percent at $161.07 at the same hour and on track for its longest streak of weekly losses since October 2012; it had closed lower in each of the previous five weeks and stood well below its November 6 close of $186.64. The Nasdaq Composite was down 1.3 percent and the S&P 500 down 0.8 percent at 12:25 p.m.

Subjective
Reuters, via Euronext Live — oil set for a second straight weekly decline on growing signs of surplus

Oil prices sagged on Friday, set for a second straight weekly decline, as signs of a growing global supply surplus weighed on the market and Washington’s focus on blockading Iran while ramping up other economic pressures allayed fears of renewed hostilities in the nine-month war. Brent futures were down 5 cents, or 0.05 percent, to $95.77 a barrel at 11:46 a.m. Central time (1746 GMT); West Texas Intermediate futures fell 17 cents, or 0.19 percent, to $88.57. For the week, both benchmarks were on track for a drop of around 2 percent, after falls of 16 and 13 percent the previous week. American crude and fuel inventories rose last week, the Energy Information Administration said Thursday.

Subjective
Invezz — Brent holds near $96 as the agency sees the first surplus since the war

Oil prices fell slightly, with Brent just below $96 a barrel on Friday, close to Thursday’s settlement of $95.82; the January contract traded at $95.77 at 0950 GMT and ranged between $95.07 and $96.75 on the day. West Texas Intermediate for December was at $88.45, down 0.3 percent from $88.74. Brent climbed 3.3 percent on Thursday but remains 2.4 percent below last Friday’s close of $98.32, on course for a second weekly decline after a 16 percent fall the week before. The agency said global oil supply rose by 2.3 million barrels a day to 105.4 million in October, after a 3 million-a-day jump in September; it raised its fourth-quarter supply estimate by 3.3 million a day and kept a forecast 2027 demand rebound of about 2 million a day, with demand returning to growth around March.

Subjective
International Energy Agency — Oil Market Report, November 2026

The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran. Observed oil inventories rose by 52 million barrels, or 1.7 million barrels a day, in October as Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand. North Sea Dated prices plunged by more than 30 percent from a high of $136 a barrel on October 8 to around $93 at the time of writing, but remained $22 above pre-war levels. Global supplies surged by 2.3 million barrels a day to 105.4 million a day in October, lifting output by 5.3 million a day since August. Fourth-quarter supply estimates were raised by 3.3 million a day; the balances suggest a return to surplus in the fourth quarter, with a more substantial build in 2027, while the severe tightness in product supply, especially diesel, remains the overriding concern.

Subjective
Sovereign Magazine — Mr. Huang and Secretary Lutnick agree to testify

Mr. Huang has agreed to answer lawmakers’ questions, Chairman Mast said on Thursday, the day Mr. Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive. In a letter dated the same day, Mr. Mast and the chairs of the House intelligence and China committees asked Mr. Huang to sit for a closed-door, transcribed interview on December 1, and gave him until 8 p.m. Eastern on Friday to confirm in writing or face a subpoena. Secretary Lutnick, who oversees approval of Nvidia’s exports to China, has also agreed to testify; his spokeswoman said he has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Senate Banking Committee, whose chairman, Senator Scott, has asked the Secretary to a public hearing on December 10 and Mr. Huang to appear on December 3. Their questions concern Ms. Alice Huang, a former executive of the Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom a classified American memo describes as a recruit of China’s Ministry of State Security, according to the New York Times and the Financial Times.

Subjective
Decrypt — Congress summons the former Nvidia chief and Secretary Lutnick over chip exports to China

Senator Scott has asked the former Nvidia chief executive and Secretary Lutnick to testify in December, warning of subpoenas. The chairs of three House committees separately want Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel, Mr. Teter, to sit for closed-door interviews on December 1 and 2. The inquiries focus on export controls and Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer whose former executive American officials suspect of spying for China. In a letter dated November 12, Senator Scott asked Mr. Huang to appear voluntarily at a public hearing on December 3; he asked Secretary Lutnick to testify on December 10, noting the Commerce Department’s role. On Thursday, the Republican chairs of the House Foreign Affairs, China and Intelligence committees wrote to Mr. Huang, Mr. Teter and Under Secretary Kessler. Mr. Huang was asked to sit for the December 1 interview and Mr. Teter for December 2, each given until 8 p.m. on Friday to agree or face a subpoena; Mr. Kessler was invited to a hearing on December 3. A first letter, dated November 4, had asked Mr. Huang to brief the committees on November 18.

Subjective
Agenccy — the House chairs give Mr. Huang a Friday deadline or a subpoena

Three Republican committee chairs told the former Nvidia chief to confirm a closed-door interview by 8 p.m. Eastern on November 13 or face a subpoena, and called the Commerce export chief to a December 3 hearing on Megaspeed. The letters, to Mr. Huang, Nvidia’s general counsel and Under Secretary Kessler, were released at 0038 UTC on November 13 and call the request a second request. The letter to Mr. Huang, dated November 12 and addressed to him as founder through his lawyers at Paul, Weiss, asks him to appear for a closed-door, transcribed interview on December 1, 2026, and states that failure to cooperate will result in the House Foreign Affairs Committee issuing a subpoena; written confirmation is required by 8 p.m. Eastern on November 13, 01:00 UTC on November 14. Mr. Mast separately asked Mr. Kessler, who runs the Bureau of Industry and Security, to appear at 10 a.m. on December 3 for a hearing on chip smuggling, adversary military use of advanced chips, reported interference by private companies into export control policy and enforcement investigations, and Megaspeed. The chairs tie the affair to legislation: the AI OVERWATCH Act, the Chip Security Act, the MATCH Act and the Remote Access Security Act, to be passed in the defense authorization.

Subjective
Australian Associated Press — Europe to have a voice in the peace talks

Europe now looks set to play a role when peace negotiations resume between Russia, Ukraine and the United States, after a round of shuttle diplomacy by Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner, who held talks with President Zelenskyy in Ireland directly after meeting President Putin in the Kremlin. Mr. Kushner indicated on Thursday night that President Putin is willing to accept the bloc’s involvement. The American-brokered session in Abu Dhabi this week brought the first direct discussions between Ukrainian and Russian representatives in nine months; it produced no major breakthrough aside from agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, the exact figure still to be announced. Mr. Kushner said one goal of the Kremlin meeting was to get the Russian leader’s blessing for European representatives to take part, and that the talks are looking at the continent’s broader security arrangements. The United States and President Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.
