The sons petitioned President Obama, with 60,000 signatures, and he left office in January 2017, in Robert Meeropol's words, without ever acknowledging the request. The Gardner memorandum relaunched the campaign for President Biden; the Office of the Pardon Attorney requested the campaign's materials from Representative McGovern's office, which is to say the request was considered, and Biden left office in January 2025 without acting and without explaining. Representative McGovern apologized to the family on the House floor on February 10, 2025, in a member's speech, which is the only official federal acknowledgment in the file. New York City's Council had stated in a proclamation of September 28, 2015, Ethel's hundredth birthday, that the government wrongfully executed Ethel Rosenberg; the count of its signers is given as thirteen by the Rosenberg Fund for Children and eleven in other summaries, and the desk prints the proclamation, not the count. The Fund marked the seventy-third anniversary of the executions on June 19, 2026, with the campaign still open. No exoneration, pardon, or official revision of the verdict against Ethel Rosenberg has issued from any administration. Julius's espionage is established by two hostile archives that agree with each other. Ethel's execution rests on testimony her own brother withdrew. Both statements are in the record, and the record, seventy-three years after Sing Sing, is where the argument still lives.

Where the Sources Disagree

The desk prints its cocked hat. On the value of the Greenglass material, the file holds corroboration of real worth (Kramer, from the Soviet atomic project's own volumes), the first news of implosion (Rhodes), limited corroboration at best (Kurchatov, as read from the same Soviet documents), and a secret of nothing (the 1966 scientists, as reported by Michael Meeropol); it holds unanimity only on the ranking below Fuchs and Hall. On Ethel's participation, it holds the Venona and Gardner record, no covername, does not work, did not engage in the work herself, against the Vassiliev record as read by Klehr, Haynes, and Kramer, an active participant in the network, rightly convicted of the conspiracy and wrongly executed. On the character of the execution, it holds peacetime, in the institutional summaries, against wartime, in the sentencing judge's own opinion, which adds that he had no power to impose death for the peacetime offense. On the judge's conduct, it holds the Federal Judicial Center's finding that Kaufman solicited privately what he denied soliciting publicly, and Cohn's denial of illegal ex parte discussion beside his boast that the sentence was his recommendation, and a reported bar association exoneration of both men, and the unresolved question of whether the Justice Department was prepared to recommend death at all. On Ruth Greenglass's bargain, it holds no formal deal, in the Judicial Center's history, against on the condition, in the historians' court filing, with agreement only on what the bargain bought. On small facts the file disagrees with itself in the open: Harry Gold's release, 1965 against 1966; the Venona corpus, about 2,900 against approximately 3,000; one word of Kaufman's sentencing peroration; the number of shocks that killed Ethel Rosenberg, five on the strongest count, after the agreed fact that her heart was beating when the normal course ended; the Gardner memorandum's release, received in August 2024 on one account, publicly announced on September 10 on another; the signers of the 2015 proclamation, thirteen against eleven. None of these disagreements is resolved here, because the record does not resolve them, and a newspaper that rounds a disputed fact into print has stopped reporting it.

Sources and Method

This report was compiled from the primary and institutional record: the National Security Agency's Venona releases and its official Venona history; the Venona cable of November 27, 1944, read in the agency's own document; the Federal Judicial Center's history of the trial and its sentencing materials; the opinions in United States v. Rosenberg, 109 F. Supp. 108, and Rosenberg v. United States, 346 U.S. 273; President Eisenhower's statement of February 11, 1953, in the Public Papers; the National Archives' releases of the grand jury transcripts in 2008, 2015, and 2017; the Wilson Center's publication of the Vassiliev notebooks; the CIA's Studies in Intelligence; the Seton Hall Law School review of 2016; the Meredith Gardner memorandum as transcribed in the Rosenberg Fund for Children's press materials and reported by the Associated Press on September 10, 2024; the New York Times reporting of September 12, 2008, and July 15, 2015; Sam Roberts's The Brother and the Associated Press dispatch of December 5, 2001, on David Greenglass's recantation; and the November 2026 coverage by TMZ, Fox News, Inc., and Mediaite. Material supplied to the desk as search-engine summary was used as leads only and was verified against the sources above before any of it was printed; two items carried in that summary did not survive verification and are not printed: a claim that November 2026 coverage of a federal capital trial in Buffalo cited the Rosenbergs, for which no reporting was found, and the premise under it, since the last federal execution carried out in New York was not the Rosenbergs' but Gerhard Puff's, at Sing Sing on August 12, 1954. The Rosenbergs are the last federal executions for espionage. That narrower statement is the one the record supports, and it is the one this report prints.

The File, Clipped

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective, a source with a position, printed because it is useful, and described by what it says. The desk's report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Eight items.

Subjective
National Security Agency—the Venona releases, including cable No. 1657 of November 27, 1944, and Robert L. Benson, The Venona Story (nsa.gov)

The decrypted Soviet cables at the center of sections one and four: the September 2, 1944 cable changing ANTENNA to LIBERAL for reasons of encoding economy, the November 27, 1944 profile of LIBERAL's wife stating that she knows about her husband's work and in view of delicate health does not work, and the agency's history of the program that identified Julius Rosenberg while assigning his wife no covername.

Subjective
Central Intelligence Agency, Studies in Intelligence—Steven T. Usdin, “Tracking Julius Rosenberg's Lesser Known Associates” (2005), and the review of Sam Roberts, The Brother (2002) (cia.gov)

The ring's ledger as the intelligence literature keeps it: more than 20,000 pages of weapons documents, the P-80 manual entire, the Barr and Sarant studio, the proximity fuze delivered as a Christmas present, the Soviet radar production that followed, and the service records of Gold, Greenglass, and Sobell used in the table in section three.

Subjective
Federal Judicial Center—The Rosenberg Trial (2013), its teacher materials, and the sentencing statement of Judge Irving R. Kaufman as reproduced in the Center's history (fjc.gov)

The court's own historian on the court's own case: the statement that no documentary evidence tied the Rosenbergs to espionage, the finding that Judge Kaufman privately solicited the prosecution's sentencing views while stating in court that he had not, the full text of the sentencing speech with its Korea passage, and the record of the execution hour moved for the Sabbath.

Subjective
Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, Cold War International History Project—The Vassiliev Notebooks (2009), and Haynes, Klehr, and Vassiliev, Spies: The Rise and Fall of the KGB in America (Yale, 2009) (wilsoncenter.org)

The KGB archive side of the file: 1,115 pages of notebooks on Soviet intelligence in America, published in original and translation, deepening the record of Julius Rosenberg's recruiting, adding Russell McNutt at Oak Ridge, and carrying the reading of Ethel Rosenberg as an active participant in her husband's network that Klehr, Haynes, and Kramer maintain against the Venona reading.

Subjective
National Archives and Records Administration—press releases of September 9, 2008, and July 14, 2015, on the Rosenberg grand jury transcripts; National Security Archive briefing of July 15, 2015 (archives.gov; nsarchive.gwu.edu)

The mechanics and the contents of the grand jury releases: the 2008 opening under Judge Hellerstein's order, Ruth Greenglass's testimony with its longhand transcription and no typing, and the 2015 release of David Greenglass's testimony, with its statement that he never spoke to his sister about the work at all, printed with the New York Times' caution that absence is not contradiction.

Subjective
Associated Press—“Declassified memo from US codebreaker sheds light on Ethel Rosenberg's Cold War spy case,” September 10, 2024; Rosenberg Fund for Children, Exonerate Ethel press kit, revised October 11, 2024 (ap.org; rfc.org)

The Gardner memorandum file: the handwritten August 22, 1950 memorandum of the codebreaker Meredith Gardner, its sentence that Ethel Rosenberg knew about her husband's work but did not engage in the work herself, the Meeropols' 2022 Freedom of Information request that produced its release, and the historians on both sides of its meaning, Klehr's active-participant answer among them.

Subjective
New York Times—Sam Roberts, September 12, 2008, on Morton Sobell's admission, and July 15, 2015, on the Greenglass transcript; Associated Press dispatch of December 5, 2001, on David Greenglass's recantation (nytimes.com)

The two admissions that frame the modern case: Sobell at 91 confirming his own spying, calling the atomic material junk, and asking what Ethel was guilty of beyond being Julius's wife; and Greenglass in 2001 withdrawing the typing testimony, stating he had no memory of it, and giving his reason, that his wife was more important to him than his sister.

Subjective
TMZ—November 4, 2026, on Scott Galloway's Pivot remarks; Fox News, November 2026, on the Prof G Pod restatement; Mediaite, November 12, 2026, on Bill O'Reilly and Jensen Huang (tmz.com; foxnews.com; mediaite.com)

The November 2026 occasion of this report, at the size the desk verified it: Galloway's two statements calling Elon Musk a traitor to the West against the Rosenbergs' execution, with the coverage's own correction that the Rosenbergs died in the electric chair and not against a wall, and Mediaite's report, printed as a report, that O'Reilly drew the Rosenberg parallel in calling for a prosecution.

entry.title: Producer Prices Rise 0.3 Percent Against 0.4 Expected While the Bahrain Radar Stands Unconfirmed at Midday, Alaska Posts 125,157 to 119,357, and the Agency Finds a Surplus in Oil
entry.summary: Producer prices rise 0.3 percent against 0.4 expected, the Bahrain radar claim stands unconfirmed, and Alaska's count moves at midday, Nov 13, 2026.
entry.content:
The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Producer Prices Rise 0.3 Percent Against 0.4 Expected While the Bahrain Radar Stands Unconfirmed at Midday, Alaska Posts 125,157 to 119,357, and the Agency Finds a Surplus in Oil

The news at midday: a producer figure a tenth soft on the month and a tenth soft on the year with September revised hotter behind it; a radar claimed in Bahrain and confirmed by no one named in it; a tanker claimed in the strait and reported by no British agency; an oil surplus found by the agency while the price printed four figures before noon; a new official total in Alaska and no new batch yet; an answer due by evening in Washington; and a campaign in its first full day in Spain.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Friday, November 13, 2026. This edition continues the file from Edition No. 40, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, from Edition No. 39, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, and from Edition No. 38, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Thursday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midday figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midday in Brief: A Tenth Soft on Both Columns, a Claim Still Standing Alone, and a New Total in Alaska

Midday corrected the morning in the one place the morning had promised a correction and left the day’s largest claim exactly where the night had left it: the October producer prices printed at 0.3 percent on the month against 0.4 percent expected, with September revised up behind them, and Iran’s radar in Bahrain stood at 1200 confirmed by no government named in it. The Bureau of Labor Statistics release, in the release filed below, puts final demand at 0.3 percent for October, 1.4 percent for September as revised from the 1.3 percent the earlier editions carried, and 6.5 percent for the year against 6.6 percent expected—the largest 12-month rise since November 2022. Goods rose 0.5 percent and services 0.2 percent, in the wire account filed below. Wall Street read the print as cool and then read Nvidia as heavier: futures rose, the opening gains faded, and at 1053 the shares stood at $160.04, down 3.7 percent, in the market data page filed below. On Bahrain, the midday file adds words around the claim and no confirmation inside it: the Associated Press could not independently verify the radar claim or a new tanker claim in the strait, and Central Command and Bahrain’s Information Ministry did not immediately respond, in the agency account filed below. President Trump’s account of why large strikes have not resumed—five Gulf governments asked him to hold off—stands in the interview account filed below, unconfirmed and undenied by any of the five. The energy agency found a surplus where the war had kept a deficit. Alaska posted a new official total and no new count. Mr. Huang’s answer is due by evening.

Producer Prices at Noon: 0.3 on the Month, 6.5 on the Year, and September Revised to 1.4

The correction the overnight edition promised at 0830 is a revision, and the desk prints it first, in the open: September was hotter than the file carried it. The Bureau’s release above revises September’s final-demand rise to 1.4 percent from the 1.3 percent printed in this paper’s earlier editions and in the consensus the desk carried at 0400; those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands, and the corrected figure stands here. October itself came in a tenth under the forecast on both columns the desk carried: 0.3 percent on the month against 0.4 percent expected, and 6.5 percent on the year against 6.6 percent expected, in the wire account above and in the annual account filed below. The composition is goods-led: goods up 0.5 percent, mostly food and basic organic chemicals, and services up 0.2 percent for a fifth straight month, in the wire account above. Final-demand goods stand 10.2 percent higher than a year ago, the largest 12-month rise since October 2022, in the release above. The two core readings in the file do not use the same basket and are printed as found, in the Cocked Hat: 0.5 percent for the measure excluding foods, energy and trade services, the same as September, in the monthly account filed below, against 0.3 percent for the measure excluding food and energy, with that measure at 5.0 percent on the year, in the December account filed below.

The figure lands, as the overnight edition said it would, in a market already pricing a December increase, and it did not move that pricing far. The wire’s reading is that the largest annual gain in four years supports expectations the Federal Reserve could continue raising rates after next month’s widely expected hike, in the wire account above. The post-print pricing in the file puts a quarter-point December increase at 88 percent, in the futures account filed below; the half-point question stands where the week put it, with members openly discussing whether 50 basis points at the December 8–9 meeting would be more fitting, in the December account above. Five officials speak on Friday in the day’s calendar accounts, and the November producer release follows on December 15, after the meeting. Settled: the print, its revision, and its year. Open: 25 or 50.

The Markets’ Reading at Noon: Futures Up on the Print, the Opening Gone by Mid-Morning, and Yields Above Five

Wall Street’s midday is two sessions in one morning, and the desk files them in order. Before the bell, futures yo-yoed on the Nvidia departure and on oil, then the cool print lifted sentiment and pushed futures into the green, in the futures account above. At the open, all three indexes opened higher and then gave it back: at 0938 the S&P 500 stood down 0.09 percent at 7,585.65, the Nasdaq Composite down 0.38 percent at 25,269.40, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average up 0.27 percent at 52,436.17, in the opening account filed below. A later print, timed in Beijing hours, puts the S&P 500 down 0.3 percent at 7,568.31, the Nasdaq down 0.7 percent at 25,187.14, and the Dow slightly higher at 52,316.45, in the give-back account filed below. Thursday’s closes stand beneath both prints: the S&P 500 down 0.35 percent at 7,592.40, the Nasdaq down 0.39 percent at 25,366.09, and the Dow down 0.36 percent at 52,297.09.

Nvidia supplied the weight in both halves of the morning. The shares opened up about 0.6 percent at $167.22 and fell to $163.81, down 1.4 percent, by 0938, in the opening account above, on course for a sixth straight weekly loss. By 1053 the market data page above puts the price at $160.04, down $6.15, or 3.7 percent, from Thursday’s $166.19 close, with the session’s low at $159.04, the high at $170, and market value at $4.19 trillion. The five-session return on the same page is minus 11.87 percent. Europe’s midday ran the other way from its records of the two days before: shares largely fell as Nvidia uncertainty lingered, in the European briefing filed below. The bond market barely moved on the print and stayed where Thursday’s selloff left it: the two-year stabilized near 4.855 percent, the ten-year rose above 5.120 percent, and the thirty-year rose toward 5.500 percent, in the futures account above; the December account’s prints, 5.137 percent on the ten-year, 5.467 percent on the thirty-year and 4.852 percent on the two-year, stand beside them in the Cocked Hat. Bahrain at Noon: No Confirmation, No Denial, a Second Claim in the Strait, and the President’s Reason for Holding Off

At midday the Bahrain file contains the claim, two requests for comment that went unanswered, and nothing else from the two capitals named in it. The Guards said its Aerospace Force targeted and destroyed an American early-warning radar on the island of Bahrain; no independent confirmation that the radar was hit or destroyed had emerged, and Washington and Manama had not immediately commented, in the unconfirmed account filed below. The agency account above adds the desk’s two sentences in their exact form: the Associated Press could not independently verify the claim, and Central Command and Bahrain’s Information Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The imagery bearing from the night stands as the overnight edition printed it—satellite imagery released by Al Jazeera said to show damage to radar domes at the naval base in Manama—and no second picture, no casualty figure and no account of the weapon stands beside it at noon. On the Sirik end, the midday accounts divide on attribution and the desk prints the division: two Israeli outlets now describe the Sirik strike as an American attack on the port city, where earlier reporting carried the Guards’ description of an enemy air attack on a telecommunications tower with no attacker named, in the Israeli account filed below. The attribution is not independently verified in that account.

The strait gained a fifth hull in Tehran’s telling and no hull in the British record. The Guards said a liquefied petroleum gas tanker struck a sea mine and exploded while transiting the strait, in the agency account above; the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre had no immediate report of the incident, in the same account. The four tankers of Thursday’s Iranian account stand as the overnight edition printed them, against the one vessel independently reported struck near Ras Al Khaimah on Wednesday. The Guards warned, through Tasnim, that further attacks and violations in the strait could prompt an unrestricted military response, and its Aerospace Force said it remained ready to engage if aerial provocations and oil smuggling continued, in the strait account filed below.

The one new official statement in the file is the President’s, and it is about restraint, given as his reason. In an interview released Thursday, President Trump said Saudi Arabia had asked him to let it be the way it is now for a while, and named Qatar, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain as preferring the waiting period; he said he is holding off at the request of the nations he is looking to protect, that he is not sure he agrees with it, and, asked whether he would have hit Iran again without the request, that yes, he would, in the interview account at the top of this report. He said the United States could destroy Iran’s energy, bridges and manufacturing in three days, in the same account. None of the five governments has confirmed the account or denied it, in the same account. The midnight edition’s two unreconciled sentences on the war’s clock—a Friday deadline under the War Powers Resolution, and an administration position that hostilities ceased with the April ceasefire—stand unreconciled at noon; no vote, extension or statement on the deadline stands in the midday file. Both blockades stand.

Oil at Noon: A Surplus Found by the Agency, Exports at 74 Percent, and Four Prices Before Dinner in London

The day’s oil fact is not a price; it is a balance, and it reverses the war’s. The International Energy Agency’s November report, in the report filed below, says global supplies surpassed demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war: observed inventories rose by 52 million barrels in October as Gulf exports recovered much faster than demand, supplies surged by 2.3 million barrels a day to 105.4 million a day in October, and fourth-quarter supply estimates were raised by 3.3 million a day. The wire’s account of the report, in the surplus account filed below, puts fourth-quarter supply at an average of 105 million barrels a day, 1.7 million a day above forecast demand, against a deficit forecast a month ago; Gulf exports have rebounded to 74 percent of pre-war levels; 71 million barrels from the emergency-reserve release pledged in March will be made available by the end of February, including 15 million barrels of diesel; demand falls by 2.7 million barrels a day this year to 102.3 million, and the 2027 surplus is put at about 3.8 million a day. The report’s own caution stands in both accounts: the severe tightness in product supply, especially diesel, remains the overriding concern, and attacks on shipping undermine the recovery the balances assume.

The price spent the European morning ignoring the balance in both directions, and the desk prints its prints with their hours. Brent rose 0.6 percent to $96.43 in early European trading, in the European briefing above; Brent fell 37 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $95.45 at 1015 GMT, in the weekly account filed below; and Brent reversed its earlier gains after the agency report at 0900 GMT to stand down 0.1 percent at $95.71, in the surplus account above. West Texas Intermediate prints at $88.89, $88.06 and $88.59 across the same accounts. On the week, both crudes are headed for a second weekly decline of nearly 3 percent, in the weekly account above, after the previous week’s falls of 16 and 13 percent. The market’s reading, in the wire’s sentence, is that the continued blockade eased fears of renewed direct conflict while shipping attacks remained a supply risk. Settled: the surplus, on the agency’s balances. Open: whether the strait lets it stand.

Spain at Noon: The First Full Day, Fifteen Private Polls One Way and the State’s Survey the Other

Spain’s campaign ran its first full day on Friday, and its first-day record is rallies held and interviews published, over the same divided polls the night carried. Prime Minister Sánchez opened at the Fibes congress centre in Seville before about 4,000 supporters, according to EFE, in the campaign account filed below; Mr. Feijóo skipped the midnight poster-hanging ahead of a rally in Madrid’s Plaza de Colón on November 13, in the same account, and the two men debate on Monday, November 16. The campaign runs to November 27 and Spain votes on November 29. The polls’ division is now countable in a new way: all 15 private polls published up to November 12 gave the Popular Party and Vox a combined absolute majority, averaging 50.6 percent of the vote, and a Sigma Dos survey for El Mundo on November 9 put the Popular Party on 131 seats, the Socialists on 105 and Vox on 68—199 seats between the two right parties, above the 176 needed, in the same account. Against that stands the state survey’s 33.3 percent for the Socialists, printed in the overnight edition, and the private readings of 26 to 29 percent for the Socialists that the wire reports. The issue under both remains housing, Wednesday’s strike behind the campaign’s first day, and the standing body’s split of Thursday—the broad decree validated 35 to 34, the renewal decree rejected—inside the campaign’s first sentences. On Monday the Brazilian president visits Spain to support the Socialist campaign.

House leaders are negotiating with Mr. Huang and Nvidia for a closed-door briefing, potentially as early as next week, and he is expected to testify before Thanksgiving. Chairman Mast told reporters Mr. Huang had tentatively agreed to appear on Wednesday night, shortly before his resignation; Mr. Mast, with Chairmen Moolenaar and Crawford, had formally requested the testimony on November 4. The chairmen were prepared to issue a subpoena if Mr. Huang withdrew his agreement.

Subjective
Alaska Division of Elections — Election Summary Report, November 12, 6:36 p.m.

The unofficial summary, timed November 12, 2026 at 6:36:41 p.m., carries all 401 precincts reported, with 256,823 voters cast of 605,433. In the Senate race, on 255,010 total votes: Mr. Heikes 5,490, or 2.15 percent; Ms. Peltola 125,157, or 49.08 percent; Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. 4,199, or 1.65 percent; Senator Dan S. Sullivan 119,357, or 46.80 percent; and write-ins 807, or 0.32 percent.

Subjective
Action Network — Alaska Senate race: live results and market prices, November 13

As of November 13 at 9:09 a.m. Eastern, the Associated Press count shows Ms. Peltola with 125,157 votes, or 49.2 percent, and Senator Sullivan with 119,357, or 47.0 percent, with an estimated 88 percent of votes counted; the full Associated Press line adds Mr. Heikes at 5,490 and Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. at 4,199. The race has no call from the Associated Press. About 5,000 more ballots were counted Thursday, in the Anchorage Daily News account carried here. Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18, with certification targeted for November 25; Friday’s count is the next test, and prediction-market prices are carried with Kalshi at 99.6 cents for the Democrat.

Subjective
Associated Press — election results, Senate, Alaska

The Associated Press results page carries the race as too early to call, with precincts reporting at 88.09 percent, 355 of 403 precincts, and an estimated vote percentage of 88.17. The candidates listed carry Ms. Peltola at 125,157 votes, Senator Dan Sullivan at 119,357, and Mr. Daniel Sullivan at 4,199, with no call marker for any candidate.

Subjective
Brussels Signal — Spain’s campaign opens with polls pointing to a right-wing majority

The general election campaign has officially begun, with the main parties holding opening rallies across the country ahead of the November 29 vote; the campaign started at midnight on November 13 and runs until November 27, following a general strike over housing and wages on November 11. Prime Minister Sánchez called the snap vote on October 5 after Congress rejected two housing decrees, and went into the campaign after the standing committee rejected his rental decree on November 12. Mr. Sánchez opened his campaign at the Fibes congress centre in Seville before about 4,000 supporters, according to EFE. All 15 private polls published up to November 12 gave the Popular Party and Vox a combined absolute majority, averaging 50.6 percent of the vote; a Sigma Dos survey for El Mundo on November 9 put the Popular Party on 131 seats, the Socialists on 105 and Vox on 68, giving the two parties 199 seats, above the 176 needed.

Subjective
Conservative Front — Mississippi certifies today, Alaska counts on November 18

Counties in Mississippi must submit certified results today, Friday, November 13. In the last full Associated Press tally carried here, dated November 5, Mr. Colom led Senator Hyde-Smith by 1,138 votes—464,926 to 463,788—with later tallies widening Mr. Colom’s lead. Voters who cast affidavit ballots without photo identification had until November 10 to present identification, and roughly 3,600 mail ballots postmarked by Election Day were eligible to arrive within five business days. Mississippi has no automatic recount: if the certified margin stays close and either campaign wants one, it will take a court order. Alaska’s tabulation is scheduled for Tuesday, November 18.

entry.title: Iran Claims a Radar Destroyed in Bahrain While Washington and Manama Say Nothing, Europe’s Chair Is Agreed in Two Capitals and Opposed in a Third, and Mr. Huang’s Answer to the House Is Due by Evening
entry.summary: Iran claims a radar destroyed in Bahrain while Washington and Manama say nothing, and Europe's chair at the talks is agreed in two capitals.
entry.content:
The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 22 items.

Subjective
Market Flux — Iran’s Guards claim a strike on an American early-warning radar in Bahrain

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps announced early Friday that it targeted and destroyed an American early-warning radar installation in Bahrain, saying the strike was direct retaliation for an American airstrike on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, in Iran’s southern Hormozgan province near the Strait of Hormuz. The Guards said their aerospace force is fully prepared for an unlimited confrontation and warned that further American aggression would trigger retaliation without geographical restrictions. Neither the United States nor Bahrain had offered an immediate public comment. The account also reports claims of damage to radar systems across the Gulf, more than ten missiles launched toward the strait and American naval assets, and supertankers catching fire or hitting mines, none of it independently verified as of early Friday.

Subjective
UmmahAtlas — Iran claims a strike on an American radar in Bahrain as four tankers are reported hit in the strait

The Guards said on Friday that their aerospace forces targeted and destroyed an American early-warning radar in Bahrain, in retaliation for an air attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, where Iran’s state agency had reported enemy fire on Thursday without naming the attacker; the United States has not commented on Sirik either, and no independent evidence of damage, casualties or the weapon used in Bahrain was available. Iran’s military said four oil tankers had been hit by explosions in the strait: the Guards’ navy said two supertankers were disabled Wednesday night after using a route Tehran calls unauthorised, with state media saying they hit naval mines and carried more than four million barrels between them, and the army said two more tankers east of the strait caught fire after hitting a mine. The vessels’ names and nationalities were not given. The British maritime agency UKMTO said a vessel was hit by an unidentified projectile about 14 nautical miles northwest of Ras Al Khaimah on Wednesday while leaving the strait, with a fire in its engine room—the only independent confirmation of a ship struck in the area this week.

Subjective
The Ground Narrative — the Bahrain radar claim, with satellite imagery of the Manama base

Iran’s claim of hitting an American early-warning radar in Bahrain is presented as a new escalation in the war, the first Iranian claim of a direct hit on an American asset in the Gulf since early September. Satellite imagery released by Al Jazeera is said to show damage to several radar domes at the Naval Support Activity base in Manama, the headquarters of the United States Fifth Fleet. No official comment from Washington or Manama was immediate. The retaliation narrative begins with the reported attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, in Hormozgan province, which Tehran described as an air assault by the United States; residents are reported to have described shattered windows and disrupted communications, and casualties have not been independently verified.

Subjective
OppHub America — the Guards claim the Bahrain radar, based on Al Jazeera English reporting

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed responsibility for targeting an American early-warning radar site in Bahrain on Friday, November 13, 2026, the first such claim against American regional assets since early September, following reported enemy fire in Iran’s Hormozgan province. The Guards framed the action as retaliation for an alleged air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran and as a warning against aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz, and warned companies working with the United States over oil shipments through the strait. American Central Command is reported to have confirmed ongoing enforcement of the naval blockades on Iranian ports, and Iran’s security chief is reported to have warned that military bases from West Asia to Europe could become targets if hostilities expand.

Subjective
Reuters, via 102.7 WBOW — Mr. Kushner says Washington is working toward the largest prisoner exchange of the war

President Trump’s envoy Jared Kushner said on Thursday that Russia and Ukraine agreed to expand the next round of talks to include European nations, as Washington works toward what would be the largest prisoner exchange of the war, potentially reuniting thousands of people with their families; he gave no details of the deal. Expanding the next round with European partners would allow the talks to take up broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia, he said, adding that Washington was encouraged by the progress while significant differences remained. President Zelenskyy, speaking after talks with Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner, said it was important the process had resumed after the Abu Dhabi round, the first in nine months. Mr. Witkoff said President Putin agreed to let European representatives join the next round, and also that the Russian president urged Washington to work with its European allies to understand whether they wanted peace or war in Ukraine. Kyiv and Moscow both said major differences remained, particularly on territory.

Subjective
Newsy Today — how Europe’s role in the peace talks is changing, from the Czech reports

European representatives will take part in the negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, as reported by Seznam Zprávy following the Thursday meeting in Dublin, where President Zelenskyy and Mr. Kushner confirmed the development after the envoys arrived from Moscow. The Abu Dhabi discussions produced an agreement on a large-scale prisoner exchange and no ceasefire or broader settlement, iROZHLAS noted. Novinky reported that the American negotiators, joined by General Grynkewich, the American European Command chief, asked the Russian side to draft a new proposal addressing its security concerns alongside symmetric steps for de-escalation. The head of the Russian delegation, Mr. Medinsky, is quoted in the same reporting saying he does not understand what there is to talk about with the European leaders, whom he accused of deceiving the Ukrainian people and contributing to the dying of civilians. In Moscow, President Putin opened the Kremlin discussion by proposing a humanitarian mission regarding the Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka, TASS reported, and Mr. Ushakov said the meeting would discuss issues aimed at resolving the crisis around Ukraine.

Subjective
EA WorldView — Ukraine war, day 1,723: no advance, but Europe to join the talks with Russia

President Putin is maintaining his maximum demands against Ukraine, but Europe will join the next round of talks. After the Abu Dhabi talks on Tuesday and Wednesday, the envoys visited President Putin in Moscow on Thursday and then President Zelenskyy at a military airport outside Dublin, conferring with national security advisers from Ukraine, Germany, Italy, France, Ireland, Poland and the European Union. Mr. Kushner’s language of meaningful progress is read here as implying no advance on a ceasefire, territory or security guarantees. President Zelenskyy’s own statement of the week’s outcomes lists the prisoner release and the largest exchange of the war first, European representatives at the negotiating table on equal terms second, and the preparation of the next multilateral meetings third.

Subjective
Demócrata — President Zelenskyy reopens the dialogue and seals a historic exchange

President Zelenskyy has announced that the trilateral dialogue format with Russia and the United States has been reactivated following his meeting with the White House envoys, and highlighted the understanding reached to carry out the largest exchange of prisoners of war since the start of the invasion, as well as the direct incorporation of European partners into the discussion table at the next round, and not in a separate channel. Mr. Kushner highlighted the agreement for the repatriation of prisoners, and Mr. Witkoff confirmed that the agreed exchange will involve the largest release of hostages and prisoners of the war. The joint appearance followed the diplomatic round in Abu Dhabi and the envoys’ trip to Moscow to meet President Putin. Washington is also reported to be working with President Zelenskyy’s team and General Grynkewich on an economic program for the reconstruction of Ukraine and on the design of postwar security guarantees.

Subjective
Stockbiz — Congress gets involved in the case of Mr. Huang

Three House committees—Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and the Select Committee on China—sent a joint letter asking Mr. Huang to take part in closed-door questioning on December 1, warning they would issue a subpoena if he did not cooperate voluntarily; he was asked to respond by the evening of November 13. In the Senate, the Banking Committee chairman, Senator Scott, sent a letter asking Mr. Huang and Commerce Secretary Lutnick to testify voluntarily on December 3, warning the committee was prepared to use all necessary measures, including subpoenas. Senators of both parties are pressing Mr. Lutnick on national security and chip sales to China. A person familiar with the matter told CNN that President Trump contacted Mr. Huang several times this week to check on him and encourage him to resist pressure to resign, and that the President is concerned the departure could affect the company and the stock market; whether Mr. Huang will join the President’s APEC trip to Shenzhen is unclear. The Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman, Ms. Mao Ning, said on November 12 that the United States should stop fabricating stories about espionage as a pretext for technology blockades on China. Nvidia’s shares fell 4.34 percent in the session reported, and stand 30.5 percent below their October 6 record.

Subjective
Stocktwits — Nvidia employees reportedly rally behind Mr. Huang as Congress seeks answers

Several Nvidia employees have reportedly petitioned the company to bring back Mr. Huang, who resigned as chief executive on Thursday. An internal suggestion-box post submitted before the resignation by a longtime engineer, urging the board to consider employee sentiment before acting, attracted more than 1,600 comments, many asking the board to find a way to bring Mr. Huang back, Wired reported. Nvidia shares were down 1.3 percent in overnight trading ahead of Friday and have slid 11 percent this week as of Thursday, while retail sentiment on the platform held in the extremely bullish zone. Three House committees have directed Mr. Huang to appear for closed-door testimony on December 1 or risk subpoenas; CNBC reported earlier in the day that Mr. Huang had agreed to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving. A spokeswoman for Secretary Lutnick told NBC News that the Secretary has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee. Lawmakers are scrutinizing why the Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed was stalled last year. Nvidia named its finance chief, Ms. Kress, interim chief executive on Thursday.

Subjective
Reuters, Morning Bid, via WNFL — the scandal topples the AI star: a look at the day ahead in European and global markets

A new era dawns for Nvidia with its longtime figurehead abruptly out, plunging the chipmaker into crisis and sending shockwaves across the artificial intelligence industry. Washington is turning up the heat: House Speaker Johnson signalled a hardening consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China, the Senate Banking chairman sent letters on Thursday to Secretary Lutnick and Mr. Huang asking them to testify, and senior White House officials are separately discussing whether Mr. Lutnick should be pushed out. Asian shares managed to find their footing on Friday. The repricing of rate expectations sent the two-year Treasury yield to a one-month high in Asia on Friday. The day’s listed key developments begin with Nvidia developments.

Subjective
Reuters, via MIX-FM — stocks struggle on Nvidia whiplash, the dollar climbs with American yields

Global stocks gave up early gains to trade lower on Friday after the turbulent week of the Huang revelations and resignation. Treasury yields climbed, the two-year hitting a one-month high and peaking at 4.8920 percent in the early Asian session, and the ten-year rose to a three-week high of 5.1433 percent; investors now see a 13 percent chance of a 50-basis-point Federal Reserve hike in December, up from zero a week ago, and the dollar was on track for a weekly gain of 0.9 percent, its biggest in more than a month, with the yen close to 160 per dollar. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan reversed early gains to trade 0.42 percent lower; South Korea’s Kospi slid 0.85 percent while Japan’s Nikkei added 0.55 percent. Nasdaq futures fell 0.3 percent and S&P 500 futures 0.1 percent; European futures eased. Shares of Nvidia’s customers fell, South Korea’s Naver by more than 5 percent, and Chinese and Hong Kong AI model stocks fell sharply on worries of reduced access to advanced chips. Brent crude futures were up 0.25 percent at $96.06 a barrel and American crude eased 0.26 percent to $88.52, both set to lose more than 2 percent for the week. Spot gold gained 0.5 percent to $3,896.33 an ounce.

Subjective
investingLive — Asia-Pacific market news: rate-hike bets ripple through Asia

In afternoon trade the Nikkei 225 was up about 0.8 percent near 61,300, down from a gain of about 1.4 percent at midday, and the Topix rose about 0.3 percent. The Kospi reversed an early 2 percent advance to trade about 0.7 percent lower near 5,300, with SK Hynix down more than 2 percent and Samsung Electronics off about 0.6 percent, while the Kosdaq held a gain of about 1.5 percent. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell about 1 percent to near 23,770 and the Shanghai Composite edged up about 0.2 percent. Brent traded near $95.70 and West Texas Intermediate near $88.40, both slightly lower, and the Guards’ Bahrain claim is noted with Brent holding near $96 despite it. Bitcoin fell more than 6 percent to below $69,000 amid continued exchange-traded fund outflows. Dollar-yen traded near 159.90, Japan’s ten-year yield jumped to around 2.87 percent, and airlines face higher fuel bills as pre-war hedges expire with jet fuel near $148 a barrel.

Subjective
FeedsMonitor, carrying ForexLive — Asian stocks steady as the Nikkei gains 1.4 percent and the Hang Seng slips

Asian stock markets found steadier footing at lunchtime on Friday. The Nikkei 225 opened higher and kept climbing, trading around 61,650 at about 0330 GMT, up roughly 1.4 percent, with the Topix up close to 0.8 percent. The Kospi opened about 2 percent higher but faded to little changed, while the Kosdaq rose close to 2 percent. The Hang Seng fell close to 0.9 percent to around 23,800 and the Shanghai Composite edged up about 0.2 percent. Nvidia shares fell about 3 percent after hours following Mr. Huang’s resignation, and South Korea’s Naver dropped close to 3 percent. Citi sees investors looking at AMD, Arista and Broadcom as alternatives to Nvidia. Bitcoin fell about 6 percent to below $70,000, gold rose close to 1 percent, and Brent eased to near $95. Oil’s small dip despite the latest Iranian claim is read here as traders waiting for confirmation before adding a risk premium.

Subjective
Reuters, via WNCY — as the election nears, Mr. Sánchez struggles to rally a disillusioned left

When Prime Minister Sánchez called the snap election last month, he was betting that anger over housing and fear of the far right would rally all shades of the left behind his Socialists. Interviews and polls suggest many potential supporters are too furious about the status quo and the failings of his own government to oblige: backing for his party still hovers around the 26 to 29 percent recorded before he called the election, and without a shift in the next two weeks an alliance of the Popular Party and Vox is seen as the most likely next government. The eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in September, and her subsequent death, triggered protests that culminated in a general strike which unions said brought more than three million people onto the streets on Wednesday. On the trail, Mr. Sánchez has deployed the phrase all on red, appealing for tactical votes in provinces with few seats; more than a million voters are still undecided. Podemos refused to join the new Broad Front or consider an alliance with the incumbents.

Subjective
The Times — the state pollster gives Mr. Sánchez the lead as the campaign kicks off

Spain’s state pollster has given Prime Minister Sánchez a commanding lead on the eve of the campaign, in a survey that contradicts almost every other poll in the country. The Centre for Sociological Research predicted the Socialists would win 33.3 percent of the vote, ahead of the Popular Party on 25.5 percent and Vox on 18.4 percent, in the largest survey it has ever carried out for a general election: 45,074 telephone interviews between October 7 and 30. The campaign opens at midnight on Thursday, and polls may be published until November 23, six days before Spaniards vote on November 29. Parliament passed the new housing measure on Thursday by 35 votes to 34 in the Permanent Deputation: a two-year extension for rental contracts expiring before the end of 2028, a suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants without alternative accommodation until December 2030, and restrictions on speculative purchases by investment funds. A second proposal, for automatic extensions of rental contracts, was defeated after the Basque PNV refused to support it. The Popular Party has promised to repeal the approved measures if it wins power.

Subjective
EuropeSays — Mr. Sánchez faces a political test as a deadly train crash casts a shadow over the campaign

Prime Minister Sánchez hoped to leverage discontent over unaffordable housing when he called the snap elections in October. With the campaign officially underway, he is working to keep the train tragedy from derailing his message to voters, arguing that a right-wing government would be worse for Spaniards who need government help for housing, healthcare and infrastructure. The campaign of two and a half weeks will be dominated by domestic concerns—housing, immigration and corruption. Several opinion polls conducted before and after the October 28 train crash showed the Socialists behind the combined support of the Popular Party and Vox. On Wednesday a nationwide protest over rents and home costs drew over 100,000 people to Spain’s major cities, part of a general strike, the first in 14 years and the first whose main driver was housing. His government passed one of the two emergency housing decrees through the smaller interim parliament on Thursday. On Monday the Brazilian president will visit Spain and lend his support to the Socialist campaign.

Subjective
SSBCrack News — Alaska’s Senate race tightens as Ms. Peltola’s lead over Senator Sullivan narrows

Alaska’s Senate race narrowed slightly in the latest results released Wednesday, with Ms. Peltola holding 48.7 percent to Senator Sullivan’s 47.1 percent. Her lead fell to 3,975 votes, down from 4,250 the previous day, and the margin is now smaller than the 4,100 votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., the Petersburg candidate whose name resembles the incumbent’s. The results added 5,612 early, absentee and Election Day ballots, about 5,000 of them absentee ballots from House districts in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough. The Associated Press estimates 14 percent of the vote remains uncounted. Both campaigns said the outstanding ballots would decide the race and that counting is not complete. The next scheduled results update is Friday, the deadline for most mailed ballots to arrive; overseas ballots may arrive through November 18, which is also the final day for counting and the date of the ranked-choice tabulation in races where no candidate has more than 50 percent of first choices.

Subjective
Poliwave — the live Alaska results

The live tally, updated at 0426 GMT on Friday, shows Ms. Peltola with 125,157 votes and 49.2 percent, Senator Sullivan with 119,357 votes and 47.0 percent, Mr. Heikes with 5,490 and Mr. Daniel Sullivan with 4,199—a lead of 5,800 votes, or 2.3 points. The figures are marked as official state results with counts via civicAPI, and the page states that no new numbers have come from civicAPI since 11:07 p.m. Eastern. No winner has been called; a race shows a winner only when its source declares one, and the page’s estimate is a projection, never a call.

Subjective
Alaska Division of Elections — the official summary report, general election of November 3, 2026

The Division’s summary report, timed 5:47 p.m. on November 11, records 401 of 401 precincts reported and 251,094 ballots cast. In the Senate race it records Ms. Peltola with 121,487 votes and 48.73 percent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan with 117,512 and 47.13 percent, Mr. Heikes with 5,426 and 2.18 percent, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. with 4,100 and 1.64 percent, and 800 write-ins—a lead of 3,975 votes on 249,325 Senate votes counted.

Subjective
Finance Calendar — the producer price index release of November 13, 2026

The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release the producer price index for October 2026 on Friday, November 13, at 8:30 a.m. Eastern, following a surprise rise of 1.3 percent month on month in September and 6.3 percent year on year, with core producer prices up 0.7 percent on the month and 5.0 percent on the year. Consensus sees October slowing to 0.4 percent on the month and rising 6.6 percent on the year, with core at 0.3 percent on the month and steady at 5.0 percent on the year. A monthly figure above 0.6 percent, or a yearly rise above 7 percent, would surprise to the upside; below 0.2 percent on the month, or below 6 percent on the year, would surprise to the downside. The release is the first major inflation reading of the November calendar, arriving three days after the consumer price report of November 10, and together the two frame expectations for the Federal Reserve’s December meeting.

Subjective
OX8 — October producer prices: what to watch after the consumer report

Consumer prices rose 0.4 percent in October from September, after rising 0.6 percent in September, in the Bureau of Labor Statistics release of November 10. Friday’s producer report provides a second view of inflation, measuring the prices domestic producers receive. The preview directs readers to compare final-demand goods and services and to check final demand excluding food, energy and trade services: a pickup across goods and services alongside a firmer reading on that narrower measure would point to broader price pressure, while a headline rise concentrated in energy would provide weaker evidence of persistent pressure.

entry.title: Europe Is Said to Have a Chair at the Next Table With No Name to Fill It and No Number on the Prisoners, Mr. Huang Agrees to Testify as Congress Sets Its December Dates, and Tehran Answers the Strike Warning With a Warning of Its Own
entry.summary: Europe is said to have a chair at the next talks with no name to fill it, and Jensen Huang agrees to testify as Congress sets a hearing.
entry.content:
The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Europe Is Said to Have a Chair at the Next Table With No Name to Fill It and No Number on the Prisoners, Mr. Huang Agrees to Testify as Congress Sets Its December Dates, and Tehran Answers the Strike Warning With a Warning of Its Own

The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: an hour at an airfield outside Dublin that gave the talks a European chair with no name on it and a prisoner exchange with no number on it; a resignation in California that became a congressional calendar running into December; a strike briefing in Washington and air defences in Tehran; a campaign opening at midnight in Madrid; and a count in Alaska that produced a judge’s ruling and no new figures.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Friday, November 13, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 38, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Thursday, in Edition No. 37, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Thursday, in Edition No. 36, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Thursday, and in Edition No. 35, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 on Thursday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Thursday Settled, What It Left Open

Thursday settled the shape of its three files and left the substance of each one open: the talks have a European chair that no European has been named to fill and a prisoner exchange that three governments call the largest of the war and none will number; Nvidia has a former chief executive who has agreed to testify and a calendar of congressional dates that now runs into December; and the Iran file has a briefing on new strikes in Washington, a legal deadline on Friday, and air defences heard over Tehran in the night. At Casement Aerodrome in Baldonnel, west of Dublin, President Zelenskyy stood with Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner on Thursday night and said the envoys had told him the exchange will be the biggest yet and that Europe will be in the negotiating team at the next meeting, in the Baldonnel account filed below; Mr. Kushner said the deal cannot be concluded without the Europeans at the table, and Mr. Ushakov, in Moscow’s evening statement, said the parameters of the exchange are still being agreed and named no agreement on Europe. In Washington, Mr. Huang agreed to testify before Thanksgiving, three House chairmen set transcribed interviews for December 1 and 2 and a hearing for December 3, and the Senate Banking chairman asked Mr. Huang and Secretary Lutnick to testify, in the wire account filed below. Attorney General Blanche said the Justice Department has not reached a conclusion on whether Ms. Alice Huang is a spy, and China denied that she is. Nvidia rose after hours. On Iran, President Trump was briefed on Thursday on plans for further strikes, in the Tehran account filed below, and Tehran answered with its spokesman’s defence of the closed strait and a Guard official’s promise of long and painful strikes. Spain’s campaign opened at midnight. Alaska counts again on Friday.

Dublin at Midnight: An Hour at Baldonnel, a Chair Asserted in Two Capitals, and No Name and No Number

The briefing the evening edition waited for took place, and it produced sentences from all three men and figures from none of them. The envoys spent about two hours with President Putin in Moscow on Thursday afternoon and about an hour with President Zelenskyy and his chief negotiator, Mr. Umerov, at the Irish military airfield, in the Baldonnel account above. President Zelenskyy said: “Our soldiers will come home,” and called the exchange “a real result,” in the same account and in the Dublin account filed below. Later in the night he wrote that the week had produced three things: prisoners will be released in the largest exchange of the war; European representatives are being involved in diplomacy more actively, at the negotiating table on equal terms; and the next multilateral meetings are being prepared, in the Baldonnel account above. Mr. Kushner said the envoys were able to finalize on the prisoner exchange, spoke of returning thousands of people to their families, and later posted that both sides had agreed to expand the next round to include the European partners, in the Dublin account above. Mr. Witkoff said another meeting is on the schedule. No date, no place and no prisoner figure was given by any of the three.

On Europe, the night holds two accounts of the same Kremlin conversation, and the desk prints them at full size, as it found them. Mr. Kushner, standing beside President Zelenskyy, said of President Putin that he is willing to give it a try with Europeans at the table, in the Baldonnel account above. Mr. Ushakov’s statement, published the same evening, called the conversation substantive, constructive, frank and useful, said President Putin backed the initiative for another, apparently the largest, exchange, with its parameters currently being agreed, and said of the Europeans that they must decide whether they want peace or the continuation of the war, their practical actions so far pointing to the latter, in the same account. Mr. Peskov added that Europe must first name a representative, in the same account. In Dublin, more than 40 European leaders ended their summit without naming one: Ms. Kallas said the treaties give the seat to Mr. Costa, who chairs the European Council, and to herself; Chancellor Merz named the E3 of Germany, France and the United Kingdom, and a group of five adding Italy and Poland; President Macron said the format will be determined later; and Mr. Costa said work would continue in several formats, in the Baldonnel account above. The Coalition of the Willing meets in Berlin next week, the next occasion named in the file for Europe to fill the chair it is said to hold. Mr. Ushakov’s statement carried a second road and a reminder: President Putin reminded the Americans of the draft treaties Russia handed to the United States and NATO in 2021—no expansion of the alliance, no weapons systems near Russia’s borders that threaten it, and a return of the alliance’s forces to their 1997 positions—and the two presidents will continue discussions at the APEC summit in China, in the Baldonnel account above and the Dublin account above. Settled: the briefing happened, the next meeting exists on a schedule, and the exchange is agreed in the word of every delegation. Open: its number, its date, Europe’s name, the land and the ceasefire.

Nvidia at Midnight: Testimony Agreed Before Thanksgiving, Interviews Set for December, and a Third Allegation Printed as an Allegation

The company file stopped being a company file on Thursday afternoon and became a congressional calendar. Mr. Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26; the testimony is expected behind closed doors, and Chairman Mast believes it will be recorded and transcribed, in the timeline account filed below. The three House chairmen—Mr. Mast, Mr. Moolenaar and Mr. Crawford—wrote to Mr. Huang and to the company’s general counsel, Mr. Teter, requiring closed-door transcribed interviews on December 1 and December 2 respectively, or subpoenas to compel them, and asked Under Secretary Kessler to testify at a December 3 hearing, in the wire account at the top of this report. Senator Scott, the Senate Banking chairman, sent letters on Thursday to Mr. Huang and to Secretary Lutnick asking both to testify, said he would consider subpoenaing Mr. Huang, and wrote that recent reports raise serious concerns about national security and the protection of sensitive American technology, in the same account; the account adds that senior White House officials were separately discussing whether Secretary Lutnick should be pushed out, over the administration’s refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a trade blacklist and over oversight of the company’s exports to China.
