Settled: the positions, restated by every authorized voice on both sides. Open: the strait, the material, and the war’s end, whenever either capital dates it.

Spain at Midnight: The Strike Ends, the Count of It Does Not, and the Decrees Go to Thursday

Spain’s first general strike in 14 years ran its 24 hours and ended, and the argument the day leaves behind is about its size. The unions’ figure stands at four million workers; the employers’ confederation put average participation at about 5 percent, and Madrid’s regional government said 9 percent of its public employees joined—three figures measuring three different things, printed as they were given, in the strike account filed below. Barcelona’s march drew 400,000 in the housing activists’ count and 55,000 in the city’s. The Interior Ministry’s running totals at 1700 stood at 919 incidents and 52 arrests, against the 476 incidents and 40 arrests the midday accounts carried; the newspaper figures carried in the Madrid account filed below put more than 280 flight cancellations on the day and at least 42 arrests across several cities. The electricity figures divide by their bases: consumption up to 1100 ran 7.5 percent below the grid operator’s forecast for a day without the strike, on the wire service EFE’s figure, while demand between 1000 and 1100 fell by as much as 15.5 percent on the figures the strike-day account filed below carried. Madrid’s Metro ran 42 percent below the same peak a week earlier; Barcelona’s ran only at the commuting peaks.

The strike’s politics move to parliament on Thursday, on the government’s own scheduling. Prime Minister Sánchez defended the strike and backed its demands; his government brings two housing decrees to a vote on November 12, and a property portal’s reading of the smaller chamber, carried in the Madrid account above, gives the broader package enough support and the lease-renewal decree no majority yet. The official campaign for the November 29 election opens on Friday, November 13. The housing deficit that made the day stands at about 750,000 homes on the central bank’s figures, growing past a million by 2028. Settled: the strike happened, on a national scale no account disputes, and the election is 17 days out. Open: how large it was, and Thursday’s votes.

The Rest of the File: Mildenhall’s Count Clarified, a Name in Kraków, and Two Files That Did Not Move

At RAF Mildenhall the week’s dispersal acquired better figures without acquiring an explanation. The flight-tracking data carried in the dispersal account filed below counts nine KC-135R tankers and three CV-22B Ospreys departing on Monday, the tankers to Ramstein, Morón and Glasgow Prestwick and the Ospreys to RAF Lakenheath; a second account counted ten tankers on Monday, and the running account filed below counts two further tankers departing on Tuesday—at least 15 aircraft over the two days, in the repositioning account’s tally. The evening edition’s 13 stands inside the counters’ range rather than against it. The security posture at Mildenhall and Lakenheath stands at Force Protection Condition Charlie, the second-highest level. What no official has supplied, on any day of the file, is the threat’s nature: the European Command and the Air Forces in Europe declined specifics again on Tuesday, citing operational security and intelligence, and the reported connection to Iran remains attributed to the reporting, not to any official statement.

In Kraków, the city’s mourning ran its last day, and the file gained a name. The British victim of the six killed in the square has been identified in The Telegraph’s reporting as James Thomas Campbell, 32, a DJ from Prestwick in Ayrshire, in the identification account filed below. The same account carries the investigation’s published details—the computer research into serial killers, the locker inscription reported by the Polish outlet Onet, more than 500 rounds and four pistols found in the car, no note and no manifesto, a specialist taskforce appointed—and the standing position that the exact motivations are still to be determined. No forensic opinion on the nine victims has been published; the wider investigation into motive and assistance continues, with the justice minister’s thread of extremism and the prosecutors’ caution unjoined, as the midnight edition of November 11 printed them. In Jerusalem, no new published fact entered the file between the evening and midnight: Mr. Kahana’s speaker vote stands for November 17 at 1600, Mr. Eisenkot’s mandate runs to December 6, and the government is unformed. In Washington, the House held no votes on the holiday, and the eight articles rest in Mr. Jordan’s Judiciary Committee, where the evening edition left them. The desk fills none of the space where those findings will go.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On Mississippi’s margin, 4,669 in the wire’s call and its published totals—473,336 to 468,667—against 4,645 in a Wednesday-night account, 4,585 in the at-call totals one program published (472,188 to 467,603), 4,404 on Wednesday afternoon in a third, and 3,041 in the evening’s afternoon tally: one winner, five margins, the call itself in every account at 1758. On Nvidia’s fall, about 8 percent after hours in the wire and futures accounts, 8.6 percent to $158.76 at 1959 ET in the price account, and more than 9 percent in a fourth. On Asia’s open, the Nikkei up 0.17 percent in one account’s open figures and up 0.5 percent in the wire’s later snapshot, having opened 226.52 points higher and turned lower in between; the Kospi down 0.068 percent at the open, down 0.21 percent at 0915 Seoul time, and up 0.2 percent in the later snapshot; the TAIEX down 0.24 percent at the open and up 0.5 percent later. On Brent, a settlement of $92.76 on Wednesday, $93.64 in Wednesday’s midday print, and about $92.46 in early Asia trade. On the December half-point, 12.7 percent in Thursday’s pricing against 13.2 percent on Wednesday afternoon, 15.3 percent on Tuesday and 11.5 percent on Wednesday morning. On Spain, four million strikers in the unions’ count against about 5 percent average participation in the employers’ and 9 percent of Madrid’s public employees in the regional government’s; 52 arrests and 919 incidents at 1700 against 40 and 476 at midday; a march of 400,000 in the activists’ count and 55,000 in the city’s. On Mildenhall, nine tankers in the flight data against ten in a second account for Monday, 13 in the evening edition’s count, and at least 15 departures across two days in the running tally. On Alaska’s remainder, about 40,000 ballots in one account, about 46,000 in another, and 637 votes of margin in a Wednesday-night account the afternoon tallies had already moved past. Against the triangle, the day’s single-valued facts are these: Mississippi was called for Mr. Colom at 1758 and conceded within the hour, and the caucus stands at 55 with Alaska alone uncalled; Nvidia closed higher and fell after hours on a board reported to be preparing its chief’s removal, and the board announced nothing by midnight; the Abu Dhabi delegations went home with the exchange agreed in principle and its numbers due Thursday, and the capitals exchanged fire in the night; Tehran restated that no enriched material leaves and the strait stays shut; Spain struck and stopped; and no threat was named at Mildenhall, no forensic finding published in Kraków, and no government formed in Jerusalem. Thursday holds Moscow, the numbers, Spain’s decree votes, the bond market’s return and the crude figures. The log turns.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 33 items.

Subjective
Associated Press, via NPR — Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi’s Senate race

The Associated Press called Mississippi’s Senate race for Mr. Colom on Wednesday, narrowly defeating Senator Hyde-Smith after more than a week of counting outstanding, absentee and affidavit ballots, in the closest Senate race in the country. Senator Hyde-Smith conceded in a video posted to social media shortly after the wire’s call on Wednesday. The account was published at 1804 ET and updated at 1931 ET.

Subjective
EURweb — Mr. Colom makes history: Mississippi elects its first Black senator since Reconstruction

After eight days of counting, Mr. Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, defeated Senator Hyde-Smith, becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first Black person elected to the Senate from Mississippi by popular vote. With approximately 99 percent of the vote reported, Mr. Colom led 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent, a margin of roughly 4,700 votes. The account records that the senator he defeated is the senator who blocked his nomination to become a federal judge in 2023, and that his victory gives the Democrats their eighth Senate pickup of the midterms. The results remain unofficial pending certification.

Subjective
The Shade Room — Mr. Colom wins, Senator Hyde-Smith concedes

The Associated Press declared Mr. Colom the winner at 5:58 p.m. EST on Wednesday, November 11, by 4,669 votes, after he had led by 43 votes on the first night. Less than an hour after the call, Senator Hyde-Smith publicly conceded, captioning her video post “Thank you, Mississippi,” and saying she wanted to congratulate Mr. Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing the state.

Subjective
BiographyPoints — Mr. Colom wins Mississippi’s Senate race, defeating Senator Hyde-Smith

The Associated Press called the race at 5:58 p.m. Eastern on Wednesday after eight days of counting; NBC News and CNN’s decision desks separately projected Mr. Colom the winner, and Reuters reported that Senator Hyde-Smith had lost her re-election bid. The unofficial totals carried here stand at 473,336 votes, 49.2 percent, for Mr. Colom, 468,667, 48.7 percent, for Senator Hyde-Smith, and 20,234, 2.1 percent, for the independent candidate, Mr. Pinkins. The account says the decisive update came from Jackson County, and that counties must submit certified results by Friday, November 13.

Subjective
DINA News — Mr. Colom wins: the wire calls Mississippi as Senator Hyde-Smith concedes

The wire called the contest at 5:58 p.m. Eastern on Wednesday, and the later reported margin is 4,669 votes on totals of 473,336 to 468,667. The wire’s published explanation, carried here from the account that printed it, says the decisive update came from Jackson County, which reported another 2,173 votes, and estimated fewer than 12,000 ballots still requiring county review. The account distinguishes the call and the concession from certification, which remains a separate governmental step, due from the counties by November 13.

Subjective
NewsCubby — Mr. Colom wins Mississippi’s Senate seat as Senator Hyde-Smith concedes

Projections by CBS News and NBC News joined the wire’s call on Wednesday. The unofficial totals published by CBS News, citing the wire’s data, show Mr. Colom at 473,336 votes, 49.2 percent, Senator Hyde-Smith at 468,667, 48.7 percent, and Mr. Pinkins at 20,234, 2.1 percent; a second account put Mr. Colom’s Wednesday-night lead at 4,645, printed in the Cocked Hat. Senator Hyde-Smith’s concession is quoted: “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters.” A source close to Mr. Colom’s campaign said she called him to concede before releasing the video.

Subjective
Big Sarge — she asked Mississippi to count every vote; it did

An account of the slow count, built on the wire’s figures: by 1817 ET on Wednesday the wire had Mr. Colom’s lead at 4,669 votes, up from 2,990 that morning, and in Hinds County officials accepted 817 affidavit ballots, of which 703 went to Mr. Colom, while rejecting 1,609. Nothing is certified: counties finish Friday and the state makes it official on December 3. On Alaska, the account puts Ms. Peltola ahead by 4,250 with 84 percent counted and the final count due November 18, and records that a judge dismissed the administration’s suit over certification and the Justice Department appealed.

Subjective
The BRAD BLOG — the Democrats appear on track to win both remaining uncalled Senate seats

Both challengers are reported ahead and widening. In Mississippi, Mr. Colom’s advantage is put at 4,404 as of Wednesday afternoon, as the grace period for late-arriving ballots closed and the provisional ballots were counted. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola’s lead is put at 4,250, at 49 percent of the first choices; if she exceeds 50 percent there is no ranked-choice tally, and if she does not, the tabulation runs on November 18, with an estimated 46,000 ballots left to arrive or be tallied in this account.

Subjective
Al Jazeera — what is delaying the Senate results in Mississippi and Alaska

As of Wednesday night in this account, both races remain undecided, with the Democrats assured of at least 54 seats in the Senate that convenes on January 3. The Mississippi margin is put at 1,138 votes with a few thousand provisional and mail ballots left, and the secretary of state’s Wednesday statement is quoted counting roughly 3,600 mail ballots still to be tallied and an unknown number of affidavit ballots. The Alaska margin is put at 637 votes in this account—figures the afternoon tallies have since moved past, printed here as the account states them.

Subjective
While You Slept, on YouTube — Alaska’s lead hits 4,250, with a Mississippi update pinned

The program’s pinned update, posted Wednesday evening, reports that the wire called Mississippi’s Senate race for Mr. Colom—472,188 to 467,603, about 99 percent in, when the call came in this account’s figures—and that Senator Hyde-Smith conceded, leaving Alaska the last uncalled Senate race and the Democratic caucus at 55 seats. The program’s Alaska file stands as the evening edition carried it: Ms. Peltola ahead by 4,250 on Tuesday’s update, about 40,000 ballots remaining, the next count on Friday, November 13, and the tabulation on November 18.

Subjective
Associated Press — election results: the House, District 27, Florida

The wire’s results page for Florida’s 27th District carries the race-call status Called: Representative Salazar, Republican, 124,519 votes, marked with the call, against Mr. Rodriguez, Democrat, 123,433 votes, with 216 of 219 precincts reporting and an estimated 99 percent of the vote in.

Subjective
The Miami Focal — Representative Salazar wins Florida’s 27th District by 1,086 votes after the recount; the canvassing board certifies Friday

Representative Salazar won re-election by 1,086 votes—124,519, or 50.22 percent, to Mr. Rodriguez’s 123,433, or 49.79 percent—after an automatic machine recount, the margin of 0.44 percentage points having triggered the recount under Florida law. Mr. Rodriguez conceded on Tuesday. The Miami-Dade canvassing board reconvenes Friday to make the result official; a manual recount would have been required at a margin of a quarter of a point or less, and at 0.44 percent the machine recount stands.

Subjective
Reuters — Asian stocks fragile, Nvidia plummets as the board decides its chief’s fate

Global stocks wobbled at the start of Asian trade on Thursday, and Nvidia’s shares slid more than 8 percent after the bell on news that its board may oust its longtime chief executive. The board was meeting late Wednesday to decide whether to oust Mr. Huang, a source familiar with the matter said, and The New York Times has also reported that Mr. Huang had a relationship with a company executive who reported to him. In the regional snapshot carried here, South Korea’s Kospi rose 0.2 percent, Taiwanese shares gained 0.5 percent, Japan’s Nikkei 225 climbed 0.5 percent, and the broad Asia-Pacific index outside Japan was 0.1 percent lower, weighed down by Hong Kong. The dollar index stood steady in Asian trade at 102.87, its highest level since April 9 of last year, and the FedWatch pricing carried here puts a 25-basis-point December increase at 87.3 percent against 12.7 percent for the half-point move.

Subjective
MarketWatch, via Morningstar — Nasdaq futures fall as Nvidia sinks 8 percent after hours on the report the board may oust Mr. Huang

Stock futures traded lower late Wednesday. Nasdaq-100 futures fell nearly 1 percent on Wednesday evening after Nvidia’s shares dropped about 8 percent in after-hours trading, following the report in The Wall Street Journal that the chipmaker’s board was preparing to oust Mr. Huang. The Journal’s report came about an hour after Wednesday’s closing bell and followed the revelations of two relationships, including one with a woman American officials suspect of working with Chinese intelligence. The New York Times reported earlier Wednesday that Mr. Huang also had a relationship with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Filed at 2012 ET.

Subjective
Daily Caller — report: Nvidia moves to oust its chief executive after a second relationship allegation

The Nvidia board is preparing to remove Mr. Huang as chief executive, The Wall Street Journal reported, and directors could gather as soon as Wednesday to decide his future. The board opened an independent investigation on November 8 and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to review the allegations. Nvidia’s shares dropped more than 9 percent in after-hours trading once the report broke, in this account’s figure, and the company carries no public succession plan. Several members of Congress have called on Mr. Huang to resign, and Senator Cramer repeated his demand on Wednesday.

Subjective
MacObserver — Nvidia’s stock sinks 8.6 percent after hours as Mr. Huang faces a reported ouster

Nvidia’s shares fell 8.6 percent in after-hours trading after The Wall Street Journal reported that the board is preparing to remove Mr. Huang. The stock closed the regular session at $173.73 and slid to $158.76 by 1959 ET, a drop of $14.97 a share, on the price data carried here. Nvidia has announced nothing; Mr. Huang is still the chief executive, and the company did not comment on the board meeting when Reuters asked. The Times report is identified here as naming the executive as Ms. Powell, the company’s vice president of health care. Bloomberg is reported to have said the company has been working with an outside firm to identify possible replacements.

Subjective
Gizmodo — Republicans threaten to subpoena Nvidia’s chief executive

Lawmakers are pressing Mr. Huang as details emerge about his relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Senator Cramer of North Dakota told Politico on Tuesday that Mr. Huang’s actions amount to a national security risk, and at least one senator is calling for his resignation. Representative Moolenaar of Michigan, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, told Fox Business on Wednesday that Mr. Huang had until the end of the day to respond to a request for a closed-door briefing or suggest another date, and a subpoena is likely if he does not agree. The account records that Mr. Huang admitted on Sunday that he had had a relationship, that the company on Tuesday announced it had retained a former federal prosecutor, Mr. Kim, and the firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the independent investigation, and that Bloomberg reported on Monday that the company’s general counsel intervened in the Commerce Department’s investigation into Megaspeed, asking whether American authorities were involved in the detention in Singapore of the woman in the case.

Subjective
Trend Brief Today — Nvidia after the probe: the board preparing to oust him, shares sink after hours, and what to watch before the November 17 earnings

A running file on the Nvidia case. The stock fell 9.5 percent in the two sessions to Tuesday’s close of $168.89 after the board opened its investigation, closed Wednesday at $173.73, and fell about 8 to 9 percent after hours when the Journal reported the board preparing to oust Mr. Huang. In this file’s update at 0043 GMT on Thursday, the wire service CBS News, citing two sources, also reported that the board is preparing to oust Mr. Huang soon, directors were expected to meet on Wednesday night, and no decision, interim chief or company statement had been announced. The file also carries the House side: the China committee’s chairman gave Mr. Huang until the end of Wednesday to answer the briefing request, with a subpoena likely, and a second committee is reported to be preparing one.

Subjective
CNBC TV18, via TradingView — the Asian markets open, November 12

Asian markets opened mixed on Thursday, November 12, with little conviction, as investors weighed the turmoil at Nvidia. Japan’s Topix gained 0.51 percent and the Nikkei 225 added 0.17 percent; South Korea’s Kospi slipped 0.068 percent and Taiwan’s TAIEX lost 0.24 percent, while Hang Seng futures dropped 0.7 percent. In the chip supply chain, SK Hynix slid and Samsung Electronics surrendered part of its early gains. Brent crude remained steady at about $92.46 a barrel in early Asia trade. The movement’s trigger, in this account, came in late American trading as Nvidia’s shares tumbled about 9 percent.

Subjective
TradingView, carrying Kabutan, Yonhap and HKET — the Asia market open: the Hang Seng opens down 194 points, the Kospi turns lower after a higher start

Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 opened Thursday at 61,475.11, up 226.52 points, rising for a fourth straight session, and the broader Topix opened at 3,943.52, up 14.13 points; the Nikkei turned lower shortly after the open. Japan’s corporate goods price index rose 7.1 percent year on year in October, above the 6.5 percent median forecast. Seoul’s Kospi opened 0.2 percent higher and turned negative, losing 11.32 points, or 0.21 percent, to 5,364.04 at 0915 local time. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng opened down 194 points at 24,121, Taiwan’s TAIEX opened down 76.69 points, and the mainland indexes opened mixed.

Subjective
Reuters — Russia and Ukraine exchange attacks on the capitals as the American envoys head for Moscow

Russia and Ukraine exchanged attacks on each other’s capitals early on Thursday, a day after the peace talks ended and as the American envoys were set to travel to Moscow to meet President Putin. Explosions were heard in the Ukrainian capital in the early hours of Thursday, a Reuters witness said; it was not immediately clear whether the city had incurred damage. Russia downed five drones that were heading for Moscow, Mayor Sobyanin said on Telegram, without additional details. The envoys are expected in Moscow to raise the question of adding European partners to the talks, and then to fly to Ireland to meet President Zelenskyy, who is due to attend a meeting of European leaders there.

Subjective
Qazinform — the Russia–Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi yield a prisoner exchange deal, key issues unresolved

Speaking at a briefing after the talks, Mr. Kushner said the sides had agreed on the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, with the numbers to be finalized on Thursday, and acknowledged that deep divisions persist, saying there is currently no trust between the two sides, which he described as expected after such a conflict; territorial issues were discussed and would be the most difficult to resolve. Mr. Umerov, who headed the Ukrainian delegation, wrote that the negotiators were returning to their capitals to finalize the details of the exchange: “We have concluded two days of negotiations in the United Arab Emirates. The main result is that we reached an agreement on a large-scale POW exchange. We are now working to finalise the details and further practical realisation.” Published at 0005 GMT on Thursday.

Subjective
The Daily Flare — Russia and Ukraine agree in principle to a prisoner swap expected to exceed 2,000

Ukraine and Russia confirmed an agreement in principle for a large-scale prisoner exchange, with exact numbers still to be finalized. A Russian general said the planned exchange could involve more than 1,000 prisoners from each side and take place within two or three weeks, which would put the total above 2,000. The two-day talks addressed security guarantees, occupied territory and Ukraine’s reconstruction and produced no major breakthrough on ending the war. The Wednesday session lasted just under two hours.

Subjective
Demokratis — Iran rejects the uranium transfer as the talks stall

Iran has ruled out transferring its enriched uranium to another country. On November 11, Mr. Rezaei, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, reaffirmed the position; the broadcaster IRIB reported his declaration, and a Lebanese channel released excerpts from an interview scheduled for broadcast later Wednesday. He said Tehran had communicated its decision to Moscow, and he dismissed reports of a recent meeting between Iranian and American representatives in Qatar as fabricated, saying no negotiations were currently taking place between Tehran and Washington. The account also carries the Revolutionary Guard’s claim on Wednesday that two additional oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire while attempting to leave the strait, and a maritime operations centre’s report from Tuesday evening of a tanker struck by a projectile in the waterway.

Subjective
Kashmir InFocus — Iran sets seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz

Tehran is linking the restoration of normal shipping through the strait to sanctions relief, the removal of the American naval blockade, the release of frozen assets and an end to fighting across the region. Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf, Tehran’s chief negotiator, said in an interview published on November 11 that Iran had sent Washington a detailed response through Qatari mediation and was waiting for an official answer, and he warned that the waterway would never return to its pre-war arrangements. The complete text of the seven conditions has not been publicly released. The account also records the Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman’s confirmation on November 11 that Moscow continues to offer to receive Iranian enriched uranium on Russian territory.

Subjective
CrossGlobalNews — Iran issues its conditions: the strait stays at the centre of the energy crisis

Tehran declared it would not restore unrestricted shipping through the strait until Washington meets its seven conditions, and the complete official text of the conditions has not been made public. On November 11 Reuters reported, citing three sources, that Iranian forces had attacked navigation systems on Oman’s Didamar Island that are used to support maritime traffic. The account carries the November 11 oil prints—Brent up about 2.35 percent at $93.64 a barrel and American crude at $87.73 in the midday print—and the spokeswoman’s statement in Moscow that Russia continues to offer to receive the uranium.

Subjective
Straits — the index of strait incidents and developments

An indexed archive of dispatches on the strait: military strikes, maritime incidents, declared closures and diplomatic developments, each entry linked to its originating outlet. The most recent entry indexed, at 0010 GMT on Thursday, November 12, carries the headline that Iran says the strait will remain closed until the leader of the revolution orders it opened. The day’s earlier entries carry the claim of an attack on navigation systems on Oman’s Didamar Island, Speaker Ghalibaf’s sentence that Iran will not reopen the strait until the United States meets the seven demands, and the Revolutionary Guard’s claim that two more tankers exploded in the strait.

Subjective
CNN — millions of Spaniards stage the first general strike in 14 years as anger rages over housing

Four million workers took part in a general strike on Wednesday, the unions said, in protest against the housing affordability crisis, less than three weeks before a snap general election on November 29. It is the first general strike since 2012. Shops on Madrid’s Gran Via drew their shutters under a heavy police presence; turnout was strongest at the ports and the automobile plants; electricity demand fell by as much as 15.5 percent between 1000 and 1100 on the grid operator’s figures; and police reported 40 arrests by midday from 476 incidents. The country’s housing deficit is put at about 750,000 homes, growing to more than a million by 2028 on the central bank’s figures.

Subjective
EuropeSays — Spain’s nationwide strike over rent: why the prime minister supports the protesters

Spain’s biggest unions called their first nationwide general strike together in 14 years on November 11, demanding affordable housing, higher wages and stronger public services, and Prime Minister Sánchez defended the strike and backed its demands. His government is trying to get two housing decrees through a vote on November 12, before Spaniards elect a new parliament on November 29; the official campaign begins November 13. The account carries the newspaper El País’s figures: tens of thousands on the streets in each of Madrid and Barcelona, more than 280 flight cancellations during the day and at least 42 arrests across several cities, and the wire service EFE’s figure that electricity consumption up to 1100 was 7.5 percent below the grid operator’s forecast for a day without the strike. A property portal reported on November 11 that the broader housing package appeared to have enough support in the smaller parliamentary body and that the lease-renewal decree still lacked a majority.

Subjective
Wrivid — Spain’s strike disrupts transport and factories over housing costs

A 24-hour general strike disrupted Spanish transport and factories on Wednesday. The two largest unions said four million workers took part; the employers’ confederation put average participation at about 5 percent, and Madrid’s regional government said 9 percent of its public employees joined—figures that measure different groups. Barcelona’s march drew competing estimates: housing activists counted 400,000 people, while the city put the crowd at 55,000. At 1700 the Interior Ministry reported 919 incidents and 52 arrests. Madrid Metro said peak-hour use was 42 percent below the same period a week earlier, and Barcelona’s Metro ran only during commuting peaks.

Subjective
ADS Advance — the Air Force disperses aircraft from RAF Mildenhall amid a fresh Iran threat

The Air Force moved a number of aircraft away from RAF Mildenhall following a reported new threat from Iran, with heightened security at other American-operated bases in Britain. Flight-tracking data showed nine KC-135R Stratotanker aircraft of the 100th Air Refueling Wing, along with three CV-22B Osprey tiltrotors of the special operations wing, departing Mildenhall during the late afternoon and evening of November 9. Most of the tankers transferred to Ramstein in Germany or Morón in southern Spain, one diverted to Glasgow Prestwick, and the three Ospreys went to nearby RAF Lakenheath. The security posture at both bases was raised to Force Protection Condition Charlie, the second-highest level, and neither the Air Force nor the British Ministry of Defence has publicly confirmed the specific intelligence behind the measures.

Subjective
The War Zone — Air Force aircraft continue to reposition away from RAF Mildenhall amid reports of Iranian threats

The departure of the tankers from Mildenhall continued on Tuesday: two further tankers of the 100th Air Refueling Wing departed in the afternoon, after the ten tankers and three Ospreys that left on Monday in this account’s running count—at least 15 aircraft over the two days. The White House referred questions on Tuesday morning to the European Command, which declined to offer specifics about the movements or the increased security measures, in a statement nearly identical to Monday’s; the Air Forces in Europe also declined to provide details, citing operational security, and said it would be inappropriate to comment on matters of intelligence.

Subjective
The Telegraph, carried in a collected account — a Scottish DJ identified as a Kraków shooting victim

The British victim of the shooting in Poland has been identified by The Telegraph as James Thomas Campbell, a DJ from Scotland: Mr. Campbell, 32, from Prestwick in Ayrshire, was one of six people shot dead in Kraków. The account carries the investigation’s published details: searches of the gunman’s computer showed research into serial killers including Breivik, Manson and Kaczynski in the weeks before the attack; officers found an inscription on his work locker that appears to glorify Elliot Rodger, on sources cited by the Polish outlet Onet; police found more than 500 rounds of ammunition and four pistols in his car; and no suicide note or manifesto was found at his home, with the exact motivations still to be determined. A specialist taskforce has been set up in Kraków to investigate.

entry.title: Abu Dhabi Closes With Prisoners and No Ceasefire, Wall Street Buys Back the Chips, and the President Claims a Won War at Arlington
entry.summary: Abu Dhabi closes with a prisoner exchange and no ceasefire, chip stocks rebound, and the president claims a won war at Arlington on Veterans Day.
entry.content:
The Evening File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Abu Dhabi Closes With Prisoners and No Ceasefire, Wall Street Buys Back the Chips, and the President Claims a Won War at Arlington

The evening file: the day’s developments whole, and the first considered responses from every side. Abu Dhabi produced prisoners and no peace; the market took back Tuesday whole on one earnings report; the president used the holiday to claim a war already won; and both uncalled Senate races moved, without ending.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Wednesday, November 11, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 33, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 today, and from Edition No. 32, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today. Where the evening figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open, and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

The Evening in Brief

The day closed its talks, its market and its holiday, and it left its two counts, its one committee file and both of its wars exactly where the evening finds them: decided in form, open in substance, with the next step named and dated. The two days in Abu Dhabi ended with a large prisoner exchange agreed in principle and nothing else signed—no ceasefire, no joint statement, no date for a next round—and the process now travels: Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff meet President Putin in Moscow on Thursday and President Zelenskyy in Dublin after it, with the exchange numbers to be finalized the same day, in the wire account filed below. Wall Street reversed Tuesday whole: the S&P 500 closed up 1.31 percent at 7,619.38, the Nasdaq Composite up 1.60 percent at 25,466.19 and the Dow up 0.49 percent at 52,486.49, on one earnings report, with the bond market shut for the holiday and no cash rate to read the move against, in the closing account filed below. At Arlington the president laid the wreath at 1100 and then defended the Iran war from the amphitheater: America did not start it, Iran has waged war on America since 1979, the United States won, and what remains is the timing of a total victory, in the Arlington account filed below. The eight articles against Secretary Hegseth rest in a Judiciary Committee chaired by the man the House Republicans elected their leader for the next Congress on the same day as the referral. Neither Senate race was called: the afternoon tallies moved both Democratic challengers further ahead, to 3,041 in Mississippi and 4,250 in Alaska. In Spain, four million workers struck over housing in the first general strike in 14 years.

This edition continues the log from Edition No. 33, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 today, and from Edition No. 32, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today. Where the evening figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open, and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

Abu Dhabi, Whole: Under Two Hours, an Exchange in Principle, and the File Packed for Moscow

The talks are over, and their whole announced product is a prisoner exchange. Wednesday’s session ran just under two hours, against four hours on Tuesday, and closed with the agreement Mr. Kushner stated in one sentence: “One of the positives is we agreed that we’re going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we’re going to finalize the numbers tomorrow.” Mr. Medinsky, for Russia, and Mr. Umerov, for Kyiv, both confirmed the planned exchange, Mr. Medinsky with the qualification that the agreement is in principle, in the wire account above. On the size, the file still holds ranges and not a figure: more than 1,000 a side in the Russian general’s account, 1,000 to 1,500 in the plans President Zelenskyy announced, and an exchange in two to three weeks in General Zorin’s account, all carried at midday and unamended at 1800. No ceasefire was agreed. No joint statement was published. No date for a next round was announced. Foreign Minister Lavrov rejected the European demands for a ceasefire framework on the margins, and Mr. Kushner said no agreement could be reached until the territorial dispute was settled.

The first considered responses arrived in the afternoon, and they divide on what the two days were. The assessment filed below calls the exchange a success and good news for Ukraine, and in the same pages calls the ending predictable: no breakthrough, and no apparent progress on the ceasefire that remains Kyiv’s priority while, in one analyst’s words, Ukrainians endure another dark and cold winter. Washington is reported to have floated security guarantees modeled on the alliance’s Article 5, with the warning beside it that President Putin would likely seek additional territorial cessions in exchange. A negotiator found a little bit of flexibility in private conversations and gave no specifics. The conclusion printed is plain: none of this suggests that a clear step toward peace was made. The principals’ own registers stand apart from the assessment and from each other. Mr. Medinsky said the meeting helped the two capitals edge closer to peace; the Kremlin’s adviser, Mr. Ushakov, called the talks substantive and quite useful; President Zelenskyy wrote that Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy; and Mr. Kushner wrote that the exchange will reunite families, build trust and create momentum toward peace, all in the wire account above.

Europe’s seat is the file’s standing disagreement, and Wednesday sharpened it rather than settling it. The European governments, the European Union and the alliance were in the capital and did not attend the three-way sessions, after Moscow objected; Kyiv’s delegation was to meet them separately on Wednesday. Kremlin spokesman Peskov said European representatives could eventually join but that their current statements show no desire to contribute to movement toward peace, and that Moscow complains Europe finances and supplies Ukraine’s weapons. Mr. Kushner said one goal of the Moscow meeting is to get the Europeans added to the talks, and Mr. Arakhamia, for Kyiv, said the next talks should be multilateral rather than trilateral, in the comparison account filed below. The itinerary is the next fact in the file: Moscow on Thursday, November 12, then Dublin and President Zelenskyy. Settled: the talks ended, the exchange is agreed in principle, the numbers are Thursday’s work. Open: the land, the ceasefire, and Europe’s chair.

The War, Whole: The Talks Closed Over a Day of Strikes in Both Directions

The fighting ran through the closing session for a second day, and the evening file carries one new count the midday file did not hold. A daytime attack on a market in the southern Odesa region killed three people and injured 11, and residential buildings were damaged, on the regional administration’s figures in the wire account above. The overnight counts stand as the midday edition printed them, unreconciled: Russia struck the Zaporizhzhia region and Kharkiv overnight, wounding seven civilians; Russia’s Defense Ministry counted 627 Ukrainian drones downed overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, against the governor’s earlier count of 92 over the Leningrad region, with a fire at the port of Ust-Luga injuring three workers. The industry figure stands unamended: Ukrainian attacks since late October have disrupted about 30 percent of Russia’s refining capacity. One smaller file entered the record in the afternoon: a 49-year-old Indonesian man is in Ukrainian custody after, on his account carried in the wire report, he signed what he believed was a construction contract in Moscow and was taken to the fighting in the Zaporizhzhia region without training; his embassy is seeking access, and neither government commented. The talks and the strikes proceeded on the same hours for two days; neither file mentions the other.

The Close, Whole: Tuesday Reversed on One Earnings Report, With No Bonds to Read It Against

Wall Street’s verdict on the day was given at the close, and it was a reversal, not a repair. The S&P 500 closed up 1.31 percent at 7,619.38, the Nasdaq Composite up 1.60 percent at 25,466.19 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average up 0.49 percent at 52,486.49, in the closing account above and the closing table filed below, which agree to the figure. A second closing table filed below runs the same session higher—the Nasdaq up 2.06 percent at 25,583.42 and the S&P 500 up 1.4 percent at 7,626.55, with the Dow lower than the first table at 52,337.86—and both tables stand in the Cocked Hat; the desk does not average them. The instrument behind the move was the same earnings report that lifted the morning: CoreWeave closed up 24.71 percent at $60.77, on quarterly revenue of $3.66 billion against a $3.56 billion consensus and a raised outlook, having said it would become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028, and Nvidia closed up 2.92 percent at $173.73 after two days of losses that took about $430 billion from its value. The technology index stood up nearly 4 percent in the afternoon, on track for its largest daily gain since August 4, and the volatility index fell for a fourth straight session, to 17.63 in the afternoon from 18.48 at midday.

The rally was not a rate story, and the file says so in its own figures. Traders fully price an increase of at least a quarter point in December, with the half-point move at 13.2 percent in the afternoon pricing—against 11.5 percent in the morning figures, 10 percent in the overnight print and 15.3 percent in a Tuesday instrument, all printed in the Cocked Hat. Governor Waller’s stated test stands met by Tuesday’s core print of 0.3 percent, and the committee’s decision stands untaken. The session ran, as the holiday required, without its second witness: the cash bond market stood closed for Veterans Day and reopens Thursday, and the official crude inventory figures, due Wednesday, come Thursday for the same reason. Oil closed the day’s other sentence upward. Brent settled up 1.39 percent at $92.76 and American crude up 0.57 percent at $86.53, in the closing account above, after a midday print at $93.64 on the sentence from Tehran that no enriched nuclear material will leave the country, in the wire account filed below; the morning’s prints ran from $92.01 to $92.81. Gold futures fell 0.93 percent, and the spot price stood below $4,000 in an afternoon reading. Friday’s producer price report is the next inflation fact in the file. Settled: the close, the earnings, and that December brings an increase on every pricing in the file. Open: 25 or 50, and whether the chip rally holds a second day.

Arlington, Whole: A Wreath at 1100, and a Won War Claimed From the Amphitheater

The capital’s holiday ran on its printed schedule, and the evening file now holds the text the midday file could only schedule. The president and the first lady took part in the wreath-laying at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at 1100, and the remarks followed in the Memorial Amphitheater at the 73rd annual National Veterans Day Observance, with the vice president, the secretary of veterans affairs and Secretary Hegseth among those attending. The president’s address was a tribute built around named veterans—a survivor of the 1983 Beirut barracks bombing, in which 241 service members were killed; a 103-year-old veteran of the Bulge whose battalion was among the first into Dachau; a medevac pilot credited with 1,874 combat missions; a Green Beret who returned to combat after 27 surgeries—and a defense of the Iran war ran through the whole of it, in the Arlington account above.

The war sentences, as the accounts filed below quote them, are these. “America did not start a war with Iran. Iran has been waging war on America since 1979.” “We won. It’s just a question of when we want to end it.” “We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93 percent victory. It’s going to be total.” The president put the American dead in the conflict at 18, said the campaign began seven months ago with only a few weeks of intense fighting, said Iran would need 25 years to rebuild what was destroyed, and gave no date for an end. He praised Secretary Hegseth from the platform the day after the referral vote—“He’s done a fantastic job, and he loves you, and he protects you”—and he renewed the arch: “Soon, we’re going to dedicate a magnificent, triumphal arch to our veterans,” who have, in his words, been waiting for it for 200 years, in the second Arlington account filed below. One warning stood in the speech without a name attached: the country will not be allowed to be hurt by what he called a horrible ideology, and everyone knows what he means. On veterans’ services the president’s figures and his own proclamation’s figures do not match, and both stand in the Cocked Hat: a backlog cut by 71 percent and nearly 100,000 homeless veterans housed, in the speech as the Arlington account carries it, against a cut of more than 70 percent and nearly 52,000 housed in the proclamation filed at midday.

One exchange in the afternoon file belongs to the election as much as to the holiday. The president said the vice president was largely correct in blaming the Iran war for the party’s defeat, and the vice president’s post is quoted beside it: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night”—with the president’s eldest son backing the assessment, in the account filed below. The desk prints the agreement as the day’s political fact: the war’s authors and its critics in the president’s own house now give the same cause for the midterm result, and differ on what follows from it. Tehran’s standing sentences stand unamended beside the speech: no negotiations with the Americans are under way, no enriched material leaves the country, and the two blockades—Iran’s of the strait, America’s of Iran’s ports—both stand. No agreement on reopening the strait exists. The desk’s own record of the day stands in the Special Report filed this morning outside the watches.

Washington, Whole: The Articles Rest With the Leader’s Committee, and the Senate Picks Its Own

The impeachment file produced no new vote on Wednesday, and its state at 1800 is the state the midnight edition settled, with one alignment the day made visible. The eight articles against Secretary Hegseth rest in the Judiciary Committee after Tuesday’s referral vote of 211 to 204. The committee’s chairman, Representative Jordan of Ohio, is the man the House Republicans elected, the same day, as their minority leader for the 120th Congress, by 106 to 73 over Mr. Scalise, in the leadership account filed below. Mr. Jordan’s sentence for the next two years is on the record: when the Democrats provide more government, the Republicans will provide more freedom; and his stated purpose, in the accounts filed below, is to regain the majority. The expected chairman of the same committee in the next Congress, Representative Raskin, has said his party is sober about impeachment, and Leader Jeffries has indicated the Democrats will reassess when they take the majority on January 3, when this Congress’s articles expire and new ones would be required, in the fallout account filed below. Eleven Democrats were absent from Tuesday’s vote; Mr. Massie was the only Republican against the referral. The House scheduled no votes on the holiday. Across the Capitol, the Senate Republicans re-elected Senator Thune as their leader on Tuesday and chose Senator Moreno to lead the committee for the 2028 cycle, and one senator’s arithmetic entered the file: Senator Justice of West Virginia said his party can forget about winning back the Senate in 2028 after losing at least seven seats, in the 2028 account filed below. Settled: the referral, both leaderships, and the chairman’s double office. Open: January.

The Count at Evening: Both Challengers Wider Ahead, Neither Race Called

For a tenth day neither Senate race was called, and Wednesday’s part in both files is at last arithmetic and not only administration. In Mississippi, Mr. Colom led Senator Hyde-Smith by 3,041 votes—49.11 percent to 48.79 percent, with the independent candidate at 2.1 percent and about 98 percent counted—in the tally account filed below, up from about 2,607 in the last tally this paper printed. A second account puts the lead at 3,176 as of Tuesday night, as the grace period for late ballots closed and the provisional ballots were counted, in the count account filed below; a third account, printed in the Cocked Hat, still carries 1,138. The machinery stands as filed: about 14,200 provisional ballots processed with about 80 percent accepted, counties certifying by Friday, November 13, the state certifying December 3, and no automatic recount provision in Mississippi law, in the uncalled-races account filed below.

In Alaska, the afternoon tally moved the margin the midday file could only imply. Ms. Peltola led Senator Sullivan by 4,250 first-choice votes—118,926, or 49 percent, to 114,676, or 47.2 percent—up from 2,517 on Monday’s count, in the tally account and the count account above. An estimated 46,000 ballots remain to arrive or be tallied in one account. The rule that decides the calendar is unchanged: if Ms. Peltola passes 50 percent of the first choices there is no ranked-choice tabulation; if she does not, the tabulation runs on November 18, with the next count on November 13 and a target certification date of November 25. More than a dozen House races also remain too early to call, and the size of both majorities is therefore still undetermined a week after the vote. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide; the evening question is whether the majority stands at 54, 55 or 56. Settled: both margins widened, and both deadlines. Open: both seats.

The Rest of the File: A Strike in Spain, and Three Files That Did Not Move

The day’s largest event outside the American files was a strike. Four million workers took part in a general strike across Spain on Wednesday, the unions said, in protest against the housing crisis, less than three weeks before a snap general election on November 29; it is the country’s first general strike since 2012, in the Madrid account filed below. Shops on the Gran Via drew their shutters under a heavy police presence, turnout ran strongest at the ports and the automobile plants, electricity demand fell by as much as 15.5 percent in the late morning on the grid operator’s figures, and police reported 40 arrests by midday from 476 incidents. The housing deficit stands at about 750,000 homes on the central bank’s figures, growing past a million by 2028. Two storms threatened the afternoon marches, and the demonstration in Cadiz was suspended. The prime minister’s stated purpose in calling the election—to turn the argument to housing and away from the corruption cases and the train crash in the file—is now the strike’s argument as well, and the vote is 18 days out.

Three files the desk carries produced no new published fact between midday and evening, and the evening records the absence as the fact. At RAF Mildenhall, the 13 American aircraft relocated on Monday on a threat no official has named stand relocated; the counts beneath the 13—ten tankers and three Ospreys in the flight-data accounts, 12 in total in another—stand unreconciled, the reported connection to Iran stands unattributed to any official statement, and no official has named the threat. In Jerusalem, the machinery named at midday stands: Mr. Kahana for speaker on November 17 at 1600, Mr. Folkman to chair the Arrangements Committee, the committee composition to the plenary on November 18, Mr. Eisenkot’s mandate running to December 6, and the government unformed. In Kraków, the city’s mourning ran its last day with no forensic finding published: the detailed opinions on the nine victims may take weeks, the proceedings against the dead suspect will be discontinued, and the wider investigation into motive and assistance continues, with the justice minister’s sentence on a strong thread of extremism standing beside the prosecutors’ position that motive remains unresolved, unjoined by them. The desk fills none of the space where those findings will go.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On the close, two tables that agree to the figure—the S&P 500 up 1.31 percent at 7,619.38, the Nasdaq up 1.60 percent at 25,466.19, the Dow up 0.49 percent at 52,486.49—against a second table’s Nasdaq up 2.06 percent at 25,583.42, S&P 500 up 1.4 percent at 7,626.55 and Dow at 52,337.86: one direction, two landfalls, the Dow’s two readings 149 points apart. On Brent, a settlement of $92.76 in the closing account against $92.81 in a morning account, $93.64 at 1204 in the wire print, and $92.01 to $92.53 across the early prints. On the December half-point, 13.2 percent in the afternoon pricing against 11.5 percent in the morning, 10 percent overnight and 15.3 percent on Tuesday. On the exchange, more than 1,000 a side in the Russian general’s account—his name spelled Zorin in the wire account and Sorin in one earlier account—1,000 to 1,500 in the president’s announced plans, the biggest release in the envoy’s, agreed in principle in a fourth. On the drones, 92 counted down over the Leningrad region in the governor’s first account, 150 over the St. Petersburg region and 627 in the whole country in the ministry’s count. On the veterans’ figures, a backlog cut of 71 percent and nearly 100,000 homeless veterans housed in the speech as one account carries it, against more than 70 percent and nearly 52,000 in the proclamation. On Mississippi, 3,041 ahead in the afternoon tally, 3,176 in a Tuesday-night account and 1,138 in a third account that the day has moved past. On Alaska, 4,250 ahead in the afternoon tally against the 637 one account still carries. On Mildenhall, 13 aircraft in the trackers’ count, ten tankers and three Ospreys in the flight-data accounts, 12 in total in another. Against the triangle, the evening’s single-valued facts are these: the Abu Dhabi talks ended with a prisoner exchange agreed in principle and no ceasefire, no joint statement and no next date, and the envoys travel Thursday; Wall Street closed higher on all three indexes on every table in the file, led by the chips, with the bond market shut; a wreath was laid at 1100 and the president claimed a won war and a total victory to come; the articles rest with Mr. Jordan’s committee and Mr. Jordan leads his party in the next Congress; both Senate challengers widened their leads and neither race was called; four million Spaniards struck; and no finding was published in Kraków, no government formed in Jerusalem, and no threat named at Mildenhall. The log proceeds to the midnight watch.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 24 items.

Subjective
Associated Press, via NPR — Russia and Ukraine agree to a prisoner exchange as talks end with no big breakthrough

Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war as two days of talks in Abu Dhabi concluded with no major breakthrough on ending the war. Wednesday’s session lasted just under two hours after a four-hour session on Tuesday. Mr. Kushner’s sentence is quoted whole, Mr. Medinsky’s confirmation is qualified as in principle, and General Zorin’s account puts the exchange in the next two or three weeks. The account also carries the day’s fighting: three people killed and 11 injured in a daytime attack on a market in the Odesa region, seven civilians wounded overnight in Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv, and the Russian Defense Ministry’s count of 627 Ukrainian drones downed overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, with a fire at the port of Ust-Luga injuring three workers.

Subjective
Atlantic Council — where the Russia-Ukraine peace talks stand after Abu Dhabi

Four analysts assess the close of the talks. The prisoner agreement is called a success and good news for Ukraine; the talks are also said to have ended predictably without a breakthrough, with no apparent progress on a ceasefire. Washington is reported to have floated security guarantees modeled on the alliance’s Article 5, with the warning that President Putin would likely seek additional territorial cessions in exchange. A negotiator is reported to have found a little bit of flexibility in private conversations, and the conclusion printed is that none of it suggests a clear step toward peace was made. Broadening the agenda to Europe’s security architecture is called a mistake by one analyst and damage control by another.

Subjective
political.org — Russia and Ukraine agree in principle to a large prisoner exchange as the Abu Dhabi talks end without breakthrough

The two sides agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war as the talks concluded on Wednesday, the main tangible result of the first meeting between the delegations in nine months, with no announced breakthrough on a ceasefire or on territory. Mr. Medinsky and Mr. Umerov both confirmed the planned exchange, Mr. Medinsky describing it as in principle, and Mr. Kushner said the final numbers would be settled on Thursday. The account notes that neither the exact number nor the timing has been disclosed, and that the exchange is not yet complete.

Subjective
NewsCord — Russia and Ukraine agree a large-scale prisoner exchange in the Abu Dhabi talks, no ceasefire

Twenty-seven outlets compared on the closing of the talks. The second day is described as focused on humanitarian issues while the negotiations continued on postwar security arrangements; Mr. Umerov is quoted on good momentum. Kremlin spokesman Peskov is reported to have said the Russian delegation did not engage with European representatives and that there were no plans for such contacts; Mr. Arakhamia is reported to have said the next talks should be multilateral, with Europe represented. The exchange is expected in two to three weeks if finalized.

Subjective
The Retest — CoreWeave jumps 25 percent, and tech has its best day in months

The closing table in this account: the S&P 500 up 1.31 percent at 7,619.38, the Nasdaq Composite up 1.60 percent at 25,466.19 and the Dow up 0.49 percent at 52,486.49. CoreWeave closed up 24.71 percent at $60.77 after reporting quarterly revenue of $3.66 billion against a $3.56 billion consensus and raising its outlook; Nvidia closed up 2.92 percent at $173.73 after two days of losses. The technology index stood up nearly 4 percent in the afternoon, traders fully priced a December increase with a 13.2 percent chance of the half-point move, the volatility index fell for a fourth session to 17.63 in the afternoon, Brent settled up 1.39 percent at $92.76, gold futures fell 0.93 percent, and the bond market stood closed for Veterans Day.

Subjective
World Money Roadmap — CoreWeave jumps 24.71 percent, Nasdaq gains 1.60 percent on a chip rally

The close in this account agrees with the closing table filed above: the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.60 percent to 25,466.19, the S&P 500 gained 1.31 percent to 7,619.38 and the Dow added 254.60 points, or 0.49 percent, to 52,486.49. Index closes are attributed to the financial cable figures carried here.

Subjective
TradingView, carrying a market commentary — the Nasdaq jumps over 4 percent this week as chip names drive a sharp midweek rally

A second closing table, printed in the Cocked Hat against the first: the Nasdaq Composite up 2.06 percent on the session to 25,583.42, the S&P 500 up 1.4 percent to 7,626.55, the Dow at 52,337.86, and the Russell 2000 up 0.81 percent to 2,844.20. The commentary describes a broad midweek advance led by the chip shares.

Subjective
Reuters — CoreWeave sparks an AI cloud stock rally and lifts Nvidia as results ease bubble fears

CoreWeave jumped on Wednesday, igniting a rally in the AI cloud shares, as its spending yielded strong revenue growth and the company signaled a pullback from the borrowing that had set off alarms. The earnings lifted Nvidia, its backer, after a two-day slide. The chief executive told the wire that greater scrutiny could slow data center construction across the industry but was not expected to alter the company’s expansion plans significantly. The company raised its annual revenue forecast and said it would not tap the unsecured debt markets after a recent spike in borrowing costs.

Subjective
Reuters, via SRN News — CoreWeave sparks an AI cloud stock rally as results ease bubble fears

CoreWeave jumped more than 20 percent on Wednesday, igniting a rally in the battered AI cloud shares. The account carries the same revenue and borrowing facts as the wire account filed above, with the peer shares—Nebius, Iren, Oracle and Applied Digital—climbing between 6 and 14 percent in this account’s figures, and records that all the cloud shares but Nebius had lost 32 to 48 percent on the year as of Tuesday.

Subjective
Reuters, via Kitco — oil up 2 percent as an Iran official says the country will keep its enriched nuclear material

Oil prices rose about 2 percent on Wednesday after Iran’s security chief said Tehran would not allow any enriched nuclear material to leave the country. Brent futures stood up $2.15, or 2.35 percent, at $93.64 a barrel at 1204 ET, and West Texas Intermediate up $1.69, or 1.96 percent, at $87.73, in this midday print—printed in the Cocked Hat against the settlement figures in the closing account filed above. The account carries the Washington Institute figures: 37 ships attacked in October, the highest monthly total since the war began.

Subjective
OilMonster — oil rebounds 1.4 percent as Hormuz attacks persist

Brent rebounded 1.4 percent from a two-month low to $92.81 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate gained about 1.3 percent to $87.12, as continuing attacks on shipping around the strait offset hopes of de-escalation. The account carries the same vessel counts: 37 attacked in October and 10 recorded so far in November, and the maritime agency’s report of a tanker struck on Tuesday about 19 nautical miles northeast of Lima, Oman.

Subjective
Newsmax — the president honors veterans and vows total victory over Iran

The president pledged to pursue total victory against Iran at the wreath-laying ceremony and the speeches in the Memorial Amphitheater. He said 18 American service members had died in the Iran conflict, that Iran would need 25 years to rebuild what American forces had destroyed, and that America did not start the war: Iran has been waging war on America since 1979. He praised Secretary Hegseth in the audience, said the claims backlog had been cut by 71 percent and nearly 100,000 homeless veterans housed, and said a triumphal arch would soon be dedicated to veterans and the military. The account names the veterans honored from the platform, among them a survivor of the 1983 Beirut barracks bombing and a 103-year-old veteran of the Battle of the Bulge.

Subjective
New York Post — the president claims we won the Iran war during the Veterans Day speech

The speech is reported as a tribute that also carried a warning: the president did not name the incoming majority, and warned against those who would damage the country with what he called a horrible ideology. The arch sentence is quoted—they have been waiting for it for 200 years—and the Iran sentences are quoted whole: we won, and the question is when to end it, with a total victory and not a 93 percent victory. The account records that the president said on Monday the war is effectively over militarily while the isolation of Tehran continues.

Subjective
The Washington Sun — the president touts veterans—and his arch

Much of the speech praised veterans and thanked them for serving, and the defense of the Iran war ran through it: the Beirut bombing of 1983, for which Iran was found responsible by an American court, and a veteran severely injured in the attack, introduced from the platform. The arch is placed in this account between the cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial, and the president’s dedication sentence is quoted. Secretary Hegseth’s presence a day after the impeachment effort was referred is noted.

Subjective
The Sun — the moment the president says America did not start a war with Iran

The president’s two sentences are quoted: America did not start a war with Iran, and Iran has been waging war on America since 1979. The account adds the exchange the other accounts do not carry: the president said the vice president was largely correct in blaming the conflict for the party’s defeat, and records the vice president’s post—the reason we lost is the war; the president himself said so last night—with the president’s eldest son backing the assessment.

Subjective
NPR, via WEKU — the House effectively ends the Hegseth impeachment, and three men accused of plotting attacks in Britain

The House voted 211 to 204 to send the articles back to the Judiciary Committee, circumventing any floor vote and virtually ensuring the matter will not be addressed before this Congress ends. The morning-after account carries the attendance reading of the vote, Mr. Jordan’s election as the House Republicans’ leader, and the federal indictment of three men accused of being backed by Iran in connection with plots in Britain, which is also carried in the midday file.

Subjective
ASEAN NOW — the 106-to-73 vote puts Mr. Jordan in charge of House Republicans

Mr. Jordan was elected to lead the House Republicans after the midterm defeat, beating the outgoing majority leader, Mr. Scalise, by 106 votes to 73 in the closed-door contest. The account places the leadership decisions on the same day as Secretary Hegseth’s dismissal of the impeachment effort as a farce and a stunt at his first Pentagon press conference in about six months, and carries the expected Judiciary chairman’s sentence for the next Congress: the party is sober about impeachment.

Subjective
Michael R. Cronin — House Republicans block the Hegseth impeachment push as Mr. Jordan takes the helm

The procedural vote of 211 to 204 referred the eight articles to the Judiciary Committee. The articles are described as accusing the secretary of high crimes and misdemeanors related to the conduct of the Iran conflict, including violations of the War Powers Resolution and unauthorized operations. The president is reported to have celebrated the result and praised the secretary’s performance; Leader Jeffries is reported to have indicated the issue is not closed and will be reassessed when the majority changes. Mr. Jordan’s leadership sentence is quoted: more freedom against expansions of government.

Subjective
Newsmax — Senator Justice: the Republicans’ 2028 Senate dreams are dead

Senator Justice of West Virginia said his party can forget about winning back the Senate majority in 2028 after the midterms cost the Republicans at least seven seats. The account lists the seven flipped seats—Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas—and records that the Democrats were leading in both still-uncalled races on Wednesday. Senate Republicans are reported to have re-elected Senator Thune as their leader on Tuesday and to have picked Senator Moreno to lead the committee for the 2028 cycle.

Subjective
political.org — Mr. Colom’s lead over Senator Hyde-Smith tops 3,000 votes in the uncalled Mississippi race

Mr. Colom led Senator Hyde-Smith by 3,041 votes in the latest tally carried here, with about 98 percent of ballots counted, and the race remains uncalled. Mr. Colom held 49.11 percent to the senator’s 48.79 percent, with the independent candidate at 2.1 percent. Counties must certify by Friday, November 13, and the state certifies on December 3. The account carries the Alaska figures on the same page: Ms. Peltola at 118,926 first-choice votes, or 49 percent, to Senator Sullivan’s 114,676, or 47.2 percent.

Subjective
The BRAD BLOG — the Democrats appear on track to win both remaining uncalled Senate seats

Both challengers are reported ahead and widening. In Mississippi, Mr. Colom’s advantage is put at 3,176 as of Tuesday night, as the grace period for late-arriving ballots closed and the provisional ballots were counted. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola’s lead is put at 4,250, at 49 percent of the first choices; if she exceeds 50 percent there is no ranked-choice tally, and if she does not, the tabulation begins on November 18, with an estimated 46,000 ballots left to arrive or be tallied in this account.

Subjective
Spectrum News — more than a dozen key races remain too early to call

The size of the majorities in both chambers remained undetermined a week after Election Day, with more than a dozen races still too early to call. The account carries the Mississippi deadlines—mail ballots received by Tuesday, certified county results due Friday, state certification December 3—and the secretary of state’s Monday figures of about 14,200 provisional ballots processed, about 80 percent accepted, and about 2,700 mail ballots not yet returned. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola led by about 2,500 votes on Tuesday afternoon in this account, with the ranked-choice tabulation set for November 18 if no candidate passes 50 percent and a target certification date of November 25.

Subjective
Al Jazeera — what is delaying the Senate results in Mississippi and Alaska

As of Wednesday night in this account, both races remain undecided, with the Democrats assured of at least 54 seats in the Senate that convenes on January 3. The Mississippi margin is put at 1,138 votes with a few thousand provisional and mail ballots left, and the secretary of state’s Wednesday statement is quoted counting roughly 3,600 mail ballots still to be tallied and an unknown number of affidavit ballots. The Alaska margin is put at 637 votes in this account—figures the afternoon tallies filed above have since moved past, printed here as the account states them.

Subjective
CNN — millions of Spaniards stage the first general strike in 14 years as anger rages over housing

Four million workers took part in a general strike on Wednesday, the unions said, in protest against the housing affordability crisis, less than three weeks before a snap general election on November 29. It is the first general strike since 2012. Shops on Madrid’s Gran Via drew their shutters under a heavy police presence; turnout was strongest at the ports and the automobile plants; electricity demand fell by as much as 15.5 percent between 1000 and 1100 on the grid operator’s figures; and police reported 40 arrests by midday from 476 incidents. The country’s housing deficit is put at about 750,000 homes, growing to more than a million by 2028 on the central bank’s figures. Afternoon marches were threatened by two storms, and a demonstration in Cadiz was suspended.

entry.title: Abu Dhabi Ends With a Prisoner Exchange Agreed and the Land Untouched, the Chips Are Bought Back at Midday, and a Wreath Is Laid at Arlington
entry.summary: Abu Dhabi ends with a prisoner exchange agreed and territory untouched, chip stocks recover, and a wreath is laid at Arlington on November 11, 2026.
entry.content:
The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

Abu Dhabi Ends With a Prisoner Exchange Agreed and the Land Untouched, the Chips Are Bought Back at Midday, and a Wreath Is Laid at Arlington

The news at midday: the week’s one negotiation produced its one agreement, on prisoners, and adjourned without a date; the market that sold the chips on Tuesday bought them back on Wednesday morning, in a session with no bond market to answer it; the capital kept a holiday—a wreath at 1100, remarks at 1130, no votes in the House—and the two Senate counts moved by paperwork and by pile, not by margin.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Wednesday, November 11, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 32, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, and from Edition No. 31, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today. Where the midday figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open, and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

The Midday in Brief

Midday closed the Abu Dhabi file with an agreement on prisoners and nothing else signed, read a market buying back what it sold on Tuesday, and kept the capital’s holiday while the counts and the investigations ran on underneath it. The second day of the three-way talks ended after less than two hours with a large prisoner exchange agreed—the biggest humanitarian release, in Mr. Kushner’s words, with the numbers to be finalized on Thursday—in the Associated Press account and the closing account filed below; no ceasefire was agreed, no joint statement was published, and no date for a next round was announced. The envoys travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet President Putin and then to Dublin to meet President Zelenskyy. In New York, at 0949 the S&P 500 stood up 0.76 percent and the Nasdaq Composite up 1.16 percent on CoreWeave’s earnings and a chip rebound, while the Dow stood down 0.13 percent and the bond market stood closed for Veterans Day, in the Reuters morning account filed below. At Arlington National Cemetery the president and the first lady took part in the national wreath-laying at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at 1100, and the president’s remarks followed at 1130, on the White House schedule filed below. The eight articles against Secretary Hegseth rest in the Judiciary Committee, whose chairman was elected the House Republicans’ leader for the next Congress on the same day as the referral. Thirteen American aircraft stand relocated out of RAF Mildenhall on a threat no official has publicly named. Neither Senate race was called.

Abu Dhabi at Noon: Under Two Hours, an Exchange Agreed, the Numbers Left for Thursday

The talks the overnight edition filed as entering their second day are, at noon, over, and their whole announced product is a prisoner exchange. Wednesday’s session wrapped up after less than two hours, against nearly four hours on Tuesday, in the TASS and Interfax reports carried in the day-two account filed below. Mr. Kushner’s sentence is the agreement’s text as published: “One of the positives is we agreed that we’re going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we’re going to finalize the numbers tomorrow.” The Russian delegation head, Mr. Medinsky, and Kyiv’s delegation head, Mr. Umerov, both confirmed the planned exchange. On the size, the accounts give ranges and not a figure: more than 1,000 prisoners on each side, in the Russian general’s account carried in the talks account filed below; between 1,000 and 1,500 in the plans President Zelenskyy announced; and an exchange in two to three weeks, in the TASS report carried in the wire account filed below. The exchange is to run under the facilitation of the International Committee of the Red Cross, in the closing assessment filed below. A date for the exchange itself has not been published by either side.

Everything else the two days were convened for stands where Tuesday left it, and the principals said so in their own registers. No ceasefire was agreed; Foreign Minister Lavrov, on the margins, rejected the European demands for a ceasefire framework, in the closing assessment above. Mr. Kushner said progress had been made on postwar security guarantees and that no agreement could be reached until the territorial dispute was settled, in the talks account above. Mr. Medinsky said the discussions centred on security guarantees for Ukraine and for Russia alike, and that his side had no contact with the European representatives present in the capital. Mr. Arakhamia, for Kyiv, said the Russian side had arrived with rigid positions and spoke of really big progress on other issues he could not detail, and of hope for a breakthrough by the end of the year. Europe’s seat remains the file’s standing disagreement: the European governments, the European Union and NATO were in Abu Dhabi consulting the Ukrainian delegation, and Mr. Umerov’s delegation was to meet them on Wednesday; Moscow opposed their presence at the table itself. The process now moves by airplane: Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff meet President Putin in Moscow on Thursday, November 12, and then fly to Dublin to meet President Zelenskyy, in the Associated Press account above; a European Political Community summit convenes in Dublin on November 12 in one account, and an informal summit of European Union heads of government is scheduled in Dublin on Friday, November 13, in another. No joint statement had been published at noon, and no date for a next round of talks has been announced.

The War at Noon: Seven Wounded in Two Cities, and a Drone Count That Will Not Sit Still

The fighting ran through the closing session, and the midday file carries the overnight exchange of strikes in the two capitals’ own counts, which do not agree. Russia struck the southern Zaporizhzhia region and the eastern city of Kharkiv overnight, wounding seven civilians and damaging property, in the Associated Press account above. On the other direction, Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, according to Governor Drozdenko, and that the drones started a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, injuring three workers, in the same account. The overnight edition carried the governor’s own earlier count of 92 drones shot down over the Leningrad region in the attack on the terminal and the refineries; the midday figures—627 in the ministry’s national count, 150 in the regional one—are printed beside it in the Cocked Hat, unreconciled. The industry figure the overnight edition carried stands unamended in the morning file: Ukrainian attacks since late October have disrupted about 30 percent of Russia’s refining capacity. The talks and the strikes proceeded on the same hours for a second day; neither file mentions the other.
